articles.title: Bell mistakenly texts Ontario residents about permanent DST
articles.text:
For some Canadians, the clocks are changing this weekend. But for many others, there will be no fall back on Nov. 1, as several provinces have decided to stick with Daylight Saving Time (DST).
The mishmash of time changes (and lack thereof) is shaping up to be rather confusing. And Bell isn’t exactly helping, after the carrier accidentally sent a text blast about the DST change to people living in Ontario and other regions where the time will change as usual.
MobileSyrup saw a few social media posts from people who received the text, which says:
“Bell: As of Nov 1, your area is keeping Daylight Saving Time year-round. To ensure your device doesn’t fall back and stays on the correct time, please restart your device (turn off and on) by Nov 1.”
A Bell support account on Reddit responded to a post about the text going out to people in the wrong provinces, acknowledging the text was sent to more people than intended.
“Earlier today, a text message intended for a limited group of customers who may be affected by the change was sent more broadly than planned,” the support account clarified. It also said it would send a follow-up text to impacted customers.
Hey, @Bell, I don’t think so! 😅🤣 Still #EST for the #GTA @iPhoneinCanada @MobileSyrup https://t.co/IsBOXj0jMt
— 𝑯𝒐𝒘𝒂𝒓𝒅 𝑪𝒉𝒖 🇨🇦 𝕏  (@tweet4howi) October 30, 2026
Additionally, the text includes a link to a Bell support document about the DST changes with some additional information. The support doc notes that Bell updated its network in preparation for the time change, but warned that some users “may experience minor technical quirks” because mobile devices “rely on global software databases to display time zone names.”
Most of Bell’s advice amounts to making sure your device is set to update the time zone or date and time automatically, and restarting your phone if you have any issues.
The move to permanent DST will apply to B.C., Alberta, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories, and some parts of northwestern Ontario (Kenora, Dryden, Fort Frances, Atikokan, Rainy River District, Pickle Lake, and New Osnaburgh). Saskatchewan and the Yukon already stay in DST year-round. And while Quebec hasn’t made a change yet, the province plans to abolish seasonal time changes.
Notably, Google has also shared some tips for dealing with the new time change rules. The search giant has warned that some people with Android devices may see an incorrect time on Nov. 1 and offered tips on how to deal with it. Moreover, Google said it would make some changes to the Calendar app to address the time change.

articles.title: MeitY unveils DEPA handbook to enable trusted data sharing for AI training
articles.text:
MeitY unveils DEPA handbook to enable trusted data sharing for AI training
The handbook outlines a techno-legal framework that allows institutions to collaborate on data for AI training while keeping control of their data.
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has launched a handbook on Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI training, an official release said Saturday.
The handbook outlines a techno-legal framework that allows institutions to collaborate on data for AI training while keeping control of their data.
IT Secretary S Krishnan unveiled the handbook, which was developed with support from the iSPIRT Foundation, at a roundtable in Bengaluru.
"The framework combines contractual permissions, controlled computing environments and privacy-enhancing safeguards. It also incorporates data provenance, enabling the origin, permissions and use of data to be traced throughout the training process, supporting accountability and transparency," the release said.
As AI becomes central to economic and social development, access to diverse, high-quality data is critical.
Yet concerns around privacy, confidentiality, intellectual property and institutional control often limit data sharing, the release said adding DEPA training addresses these challenges.
"India's AI ambitions must be matched by the ability to use data responsibly and securely," Krishnan said, adding that MeitY is committed to taking the framework forward.
Principal Scientific Adviser Ajay Kumar Sood explained that under DEPA, the model travels to the data rather than the reverse.
He said this enables multi-party and cross-border collaboration, and described DEPA as India's contribution to global science diplomacy.
The roundtable drew representatives from government, industry, academia, research among other stakeholders.

articles.title: How Much Deep Sleep Do You Need? What Sleep Researchers Say Before You Buy a Sleep Tracker - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Two different sleep trackers can read the same night and print two different deep-sleep percentages, and the internet’s reference numbers argue among themselves the same way, with figures from 10 to 25 percent all claiming to be the norm. How much deep sleep you need comes down to one benchmark: healthy adults spend about 13 to 23 percent of total sleep in deep sleep. The disagreement has a structure, and it takes about five minutes to learn. What follows is the benchmark, why wrist readings of sleep stages wobble, and a five-question check to run before paying for any tracker.
How Much Deep Sleep Do Adults Need? Two Bands Behind the Conflicting Percentages
Two citation bands explain most of the conflict in deep-sleep numbers. Under the AASM staging framework, healthy adults spend about 13 to 23 percent of total sleep in the N3 stage, while 10 to 20 percent is the looser band many sources still quote. A quoted 25 percent usually means retelling inflated the range.
The fix is a two-second reading habit, check the band’s origin before the percentage. AASM staging figures put N3 at 13 to 23 percent of total sleep, commonly cited figures answer with the looser 10 to 20 percent band, and the number 25 percent is what inflated retelling looks like. Results on the high end usually come from sources quoting the wider bands, so the argument never ends until the reader checks which one is in use.
Structure gives the percentages their meaning. Deep sleep percentages conflict because sources quote two bands — AASM’s N3 range at 13 to 23 percent of total sleep versus the looser 10 to 20 percent. Deep sleep loads toward the first half of the night while REM leans late, and the night moves in four to five cycles of roughly 90 to 120 minutes each, so where the deep sleep sits matters as much as how much of it there is.
The concern behind the search is common, and it is measured. The 2025 national healthy-sleep white paper, compiled with the China Sleep Big Data Center and iResearch under technical support from the China Sleep Research Society, from a 31-province sample of 2,500 respondents, put short deep sleep among its three most typical complaints, 49 percent of the 1,554 respondents reporting sleep troubles, with light or easily broken sleep ahead of it at 55 percent, and 66 percent of the full sample calling wake-up refreshment their clearest picture of a good night.
Ranges this wide are population coordinates. Personal baselines differ with age and sleep efficiency, and a single night’s percentage was never meant to grade anyone. The individual read that matters is the trend on your own timeline, which is where the rest of this piece goes.
Can You Trust the Deep-Sleep Number on Your Wrist?
Partly, and the trustworthy part is the trend. Sleep researchers’ archived commentary on consumer devices calls stage estimates rough, with heart rate and movement standing in for the brain signals that define the stages. The night-to-night pattern survives the estimation layer, and it is the part worth reading.
The short answer from the research side is blunt. Sleep researchers advise ignoring absolute deep-sleep readings from wrist trackers — the night-to-night trend beats any single percentage. In archived commentary by sleep researchers who reviewed a reader’s digest of fourteen laboratory studies, consumer wrist and ring devices were called “generally not great” at staging sleep, the advice for N3 readings was to “just entirely ignore” them, and the reasoning was that the devices “base it on averages” and let the arithmetic stand in for the stage.
The mechanism is no secret. As a sleep scientist writing in The Conversation lays it out, a wrist tracker reads movement with an accelerometer and heart rate with an optical sensor, then estimates stages from those signals, while the overnight wiring of a laboratory study adds the brain-wave readings that define the stages in the first place. Estimating a stage from its physiological neighbors is a genuine technical feat, and it remains an estimate, which is why two devices can split one night.
The literature puts numbers on the wobble. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Medical Internet Research, covering 22 studies of Fitbit-class wristbands with 8 feeding the quantitative synthesis, assessed the devices against overnight lab monitoring and found the nonsleep-staging models overestimated total sleep time by roughly 7 to 67 minutes, while concluding that stage estimates are convenient gross estimates of limited specificity. A companion systematic review in Current Sleep Medicine Reports, pooling 7 studies of commercially available trackers, reported objectives and methods that varied widely, a spread its authors flagged as a reason to read the field with care.
Johns Hopkins Medicine’s consumer guidance lands in the same place, framing wrist trackers as collectors of useful patterns with real limits on what any single number can tell you. None of this argues for putting the watch in a drawer. It argues for knowing which layer of the reading is measurement and which is arithmetic, and the five questions below sort that out before money changes hands.
Before You Buy: A Five-Question Accuracy Check for Any Sleep Tracker
Run five questions before buying any tracker, and the spec sheet answers most of them. What the device measures, what the research says about that class, what your own baseline is, what action the numbers feed, and whether the trend line survives a rough night all filter the field fast. A device that clears all five earns its place.
The check works at the category level, brand agnostic, and it takes one sitting.
-  What does it actually measure? A wrist device infers stages from heart rate and movement, while a sensing layer collects readings directly, and the route decides what the number is. An estimate and a reading deserve different levels of trust.
2. What does the research say about this class? Look for systematic reviews of the device category, conditions and limits attached, and treat a product page’s own claims as one voice among many.
3. What is your baseline? Heart-rate variability runs in tens of milliseconds between individuals, with no universal passing grade, so decide what you will compare against before you buy. For the deeper drill on reading metrics against your own baseline, the official walkthrough how to read sleep tracker metrics against your own baseline carries the method.
4. What will the number make you do? A number that feeds a decision, an earlier bedtime, a cooler room, a quieter week, is worth paying for, and a number that feeds no decision is decoration.
5. Where does its accuracy break? Ask whether the device still shows a usable trend after a short or restless night, because the trend is the part that survives the estimation layer.
The check is a filter, and a friendly one. Most devices miss one question and pass four, and the miss tells you how to use the device. The correct usage, trend against baseline, is the next section’s whole business.
What the Numbers Are Still Good For — and the Non-Wearable Route
The numbers stay worth reading once they are read correctly. Log nights under fixed conditions, compare each reading to your own running baseline, and let a real drift trigger one concrete adjustment. Single nights belong to the benchmark, personal meaning belongs to the trend line, and both have a job.
A reader who tracked every sleep variable for ninety straight days distilled the value question into one line, people want measurement that serves a decision, and measurement that serves nothing else wears out its welcome. The archived record and the indicator-value argument built on it arrive at the same test. An indicator matters when it is wired into something adjustable, and a trend line is where the wiring shows.
In practice the method runs three steps. Record under consistent conditions, a set bedtime, a set room, the same device. Read relative changes against your own running baseline. Let a sustained offset trigger one change at a time, in schedule, load, or bedroom. Percentages borrowed from population tables step out of the way, and the trend does the talking.
The measurement route also has more than one lane. Wrist devices estimate stages from the outside, the way a meter reader might infer which rooms are in use from the power draw, while sensors built into the mattress read heart rate, breathing readings, and sleep stages through the night with nothing to charge, wear, or remember. The two lanes serve the same habit, a readable record of the night, waiting in the app.
On the tiers from DeRUCCI’s T11+ up, that record carries visible quality gates. A daily report generates once a night holds at least three hours in bed with two of actual sleep, the overseas recording window runs 20:00 to 10:00 local time, and per the brand’s official documentation the T11+ sensing layer detects heart rate with 97% accuracy. The gates matter as much as the readings, they define which data earns a place in the trend line. For the wider arc from sleep problems to mattress decisions, the sleep problems to mattress guide collects the official walkthrough.
Your Deep-Sleep Numbers: FAQ
How much deep sleep do adults need?
About 13 to 23 percent of total sleep for the N3 stage in healthy adults under the AASM framework, with 10 to 20 percent still commonly cited as a looser band. The figures here match DeRUCCI’s published sleep-guide article on the question, and both bands are population coordinates, and neither grades a person.
What should I check before buying a sleep tracker?
Five things, what the device physically measures, what systematic reviews say about its class, what your own baseline is, what action the numbers will feed, and whether the trend line survives a rough night. The full list sits in the section above, and it applies to wrist and non-wearable devices alike.
Why do different sources give different deep-sleep numbers?
Mostly because the bands get mixed, the AASM staging range of 13 to 23 percent of total sleep versus the looser 10 to 20 percent band many sources quote. A quoted 25 percent usually reflects inflated retelling, and it is rarely a new finding. Check which band a source is using before comparing it with another.
How accurate is the deep-sleep percentage on a wrist tracker?
Sleep researchers call it the weakest estimate in the chain, since the stage is inferred from heart rate and movement, with the stage itself going unmeasured. Their archived advice treats absolute single-night percentages as rough and the night-to-night trend as the trustworthy part, and a 2019 meta-analysis found even total sleep time can be overestimated by minutes at a stretch.
What are deep-sleep numbers still good for?
Direction and drift. Read against your own baseline, a sustained change tells you whether an adjustment worked, and that is the decision the measurement exists to feed. The population benchmark says what normal looks like, and your trend says what changed.
Can you track trends without wearing anything?
Yes, mattress-integrated sensing is the established non-wearable lane, reading heart rate, breathing, and stages from the sleep surface. Such systems carry their own quality gates, on T11+ and above a night needs three hours in bed and two of sleep before a daily report generates, so the trend line holds data that cleared the bar.

articles.title: ChatGPT Pro : face à la polémique, OpenAI renonce à amputer l'abonnement
articles.text:
OpenAI prévoyait de réduire de moitié, à partir du 30 octobre, l’allocation d’usage incluse dans son abonnement Pro 200, facturé plus de 200 euros par mois, sans toucher au prix. La décision avait déclenché une vague de protestations chez les abonnés. Jeudi, à quelques heures de l’échéance, l’entreprise a annoncé exactement l’inverse. Les limites doublent, avec effet immédiat.
Deux fois plus au lieu de deux fois moins
« Nous doublons toutes les limites d’usage pour tous les paliers Pro 100, 200 et 500 ainsi que Business Premium, avec effet immédiat », a écrit sur X Thibault Sottiaux, l’un des responsables de ChatGPT et de Codex. « Nous avons entendu vos aimables retours et ne réduirons pas les limites d’usage du Pro 200 ».
 Day 25/
We are doubling all usage limits for all Pro 100/200/500 tiers and Business Premium, effective today.
We heard your kind feedback and won’t be reducing usage limits for Pro 200, so your Work and Codex usage will stay the same. We’re also going to continue offering extended limits for dots for now, and usage of your dot will still continue to be separate from your default usage.
And we’ll of course also keep shipping better models and other efficiency improvements that increase your effective usage over time.
— Tibo (@thsottiaux) October 29, 2026
Dans le détail, le doublement porte sur l’enveloppe partagée entre ChatGPT Work, dédié aux tâches longues, et Codex, l’agent de programmation de la société. Les abonnés Pro 100 et Pro 500 la voient doubler, tandis que les comptes Pro 200 logés au niveau le plus bas rejoignent le palier supérieur. Les abonnés existants en profitent automatiquement, les nouveaux dès l’inscription. Les trois paliers fonctionnent par ailleurs sans fenêtre de cinq heures, ce qui ne signifie pas un usage illimité pour autant, et les agents permanents Dots conservent des limites étendues, décomptées séparément. Ces formules visent les plus gros consommateurs du service, ceux qui laissent tourner des agents Codex sur des tâches au long cours. OpenAI ne publie en revanche aucun chiffre précis par palier, et les abonnés Plus restent à quai.
Le troisième épisode d’un feuilleton commencé en septembre
Ce rétropédalage prolonge une série entamée le 10 septembre, quand OpenAI suspendait les inscriptions au Pro 200, débordée par une demande qu’elle ne parvenait plus à servir. Depuis le 5 octobre, Thibault Sottiaux s’est engagé à livrer chaque jour une amélioration pour Codex et ChatGPT Work, des gains de vitesse aux quotas en passant par la mise en cache. Son annonce de jeudi porte d’ailleurs la mention « jour 25 ». OpenAI venait par ailleurs de distribuer des crédits d’API gratuits à ses abonnés Pro et Business.
Une chaîne de caractères repérée dans le code de la page de paiement de ChatGPT évoque toutefois, pour décembre, une limite d’usage partagée entre l’ensemble de ChatGPT et Codex. Rien n’est déployé ni confirmé à ce stade. Si cette fusion des compteurs se concrétisait, elle pourrait rogner une partie du doublement du jour, en faisant puiser conversations et sessions de code dans la même réserve.
Pour les abonnés, le bilan immédiat est tout bénef’ : deux fois plus d’usage au même tarif, sans monter en gamme. La preuve, s’il en fallait, que même à 200 euros par mois, râler reste gratuit.

articles.title: Hemos encontrado un pequeño pueblo en Cerdeña donde las mujeres tienen una vida excepcionalmente longeva
articles.text:
Durante décadas, los investigadores han estado buscando descifrar el secreto que hay en las llamadas "zonas azules", que no son más que regiones del planeta donde vivir muchos años (incluso más de 100) parece ser la norma y no la excepción. Uno de estos casos tan peculiares lo tenemos en la isla de Cerdeña (Italia) donde existe un área montañosa que fue identificada ya a principios de los 2000 por su inusual proporción de hombres centenarios.
Un nuevo caso. Ahora, un nuevo estudio apunta a un pequeño municipio sardo, Bolotana, como una nueva y sorprendente "zona azul candidata", esta vez protagonizada casi en exclusiva por mujeres.
Esta investigación ha sido publicada este mismo año y ha analizado la supervivencia en la vejez de este pueblo italiano, viendo que las mujeres de Bolotana alcanzan cifras de récord con una probabilidad del 13,83% de llegar a los 100 años tras haber cumplido los 70.
Poniéndolo en perspectiva, el comunicado de la Universidad de Illinois Chicago destaca que esta probabilidad ronda un modesto 3,5% en Italia y un 3,6% en Estados Unidos. Pero lo más destacado es el género, puesto que si la zona azul original en un área montañosa destaca por tener hombres muy mayores, Bolotana tiene una ventaja demográfica marcadamente femenina.
En concreto, de los 19 vecinos que alcanzaron el siglo de vida entre 2021 y 2025, 14 eran mujeres. Y la pregunta es: ¿por qué?
Muchas razones. Al igual que ocurre en otras zonas azules como las que hay en Japón, los motivos para vivir allí parecen un conjunto de factores muy variados. Entre estos podemos encontrar el estilo de vida que se sigue, que puede ser mucho más relajado que el de las grandes ciudades, el tipo de dieta, la actividad física que se haga y también la genética de las personas de esta zona.
Este conjunto de factores, y otros muchos más, hace que sea difícil aislar el 'tratamiento para vivir 100 años'. Pero si que nos va dando una idea de que la longevidad puede que no esté en una pastilla que cree una farmacéutica, sino en una filosofía de vida muy concreta.
Tiene problemas. Más allá de estos datos, el estudio en el que se basa no es del todo perfecto, puesto que entre los autores hay conflicto de intereses al ser trabajadores de proyectos privados encaminados a entender las zonas azules. A esto se suma una importante contradicción sobre la financiación, puesto que, mientras que el estudio oficial declara no haber recibido apoyo económico, la nota de prensa de la UIC afirma que el proyecto contó con el respaldo de National Geographic.
Todo esto, junto al hecho de que no han aislado alguna de las causas que pueden estar detrás, hace que Bolotana sea un lugar interesante, pero que todavía no se puede calificar como la ubicación con una grandísima longevidad. Para ello todavía queda un gran recorrido en el campo de la investigación para sacar conclusiones claras.

articles.title: WinRAR en LEGO : ce projet cache une excellente blague sur sa période d’essai
articles.text:
Les célèbres livres d'archive de WinRAR ont inspiré un projet déposé sur LEGO Ideas. Derrière la sangle de l’archiveur, trois petites scènes racontent le fonctionnement du logiciel, avec un clin d’œil à cette licence dont tant d’utilisateurs ont repoussé l’achat.
Trois livres violet, bleu et vert, une sangle marron et une boucle métallique : même sans le nom du logiciel, les habitués de Windows devraient reconnaître l’icône. Sur LEGO Ideas, le créateur carlos_silva94 propose de la transformer en objet à exposer sur un bureau ou dans une bibliothèque. Mais l’intérêt de cette construction se trouve aussi à l’intérieur.
Une compression très physique et un responsable des licences endormi
Chacun des trois volumes dissimule une scène miniature. Dans celui consacré à la compression, un ouvrier emploie une méthode assez éloignée des algorithmes : il s’assoit sur les fichiers pour les faire tenir dans moins de place. Le deuxième compartiment accueille un archiviste, occupé à trier et ranger des informations dans des boîtes.
Le troisième réserve la meilleure plaisanterie. Dans le bureau chargé de valider les licences, l’employé s’est endormi à son poste. Une manière d’expliquer pourquoi la période d’essai de WinRAR ne semble jamais vraiment prendre fin : le responsable a tout simplement cessé de s’en occuper.
La plaisanterie est connue de longue date, mais WinRAR n’est pas gratuit pour autant : la période d’essai dure officiellement 40 jours, après lesquels une licence est nécessaire. Le créateur évoque par erreur 30 jours dans sa présentation.
Un projet de fan qui doit encore convaincre
Publié il y a quelques mois, ce projet WinRAR affichait 477 soutiens lors de notre consultation, avec 282 jours pour atteindre le palier des 1 000. Les étapes suivantes sont fixées à 5 000 puis 10 000 soutiens, avec des prolongations du délai à chaque palier franchi. Faute de réunir les votes nécessaires à temps, la proposition expire.
- Nombreux formats pris en charge
- Chiffrement AES 256 bits
- Réparation et découpage d’archives
Les 10 000 soutiens déclencheraient son examen par LEGO, sans garantir sa commercialisation. Il resterait aussi à obtenir les autorisations nécessaires pour adapter WinRAR, le logiciel édité par win.rar GmbH. LEGO précise que les négociations avec les titulaires des droits peuvent retarder un projet ; aucun accord n’est mentionné dans la présentation du créateur.
En attendant, le projet donne une forme bien concrète à une vieille habitude informatique : comprimer beaucoup de choses dans trois petits livres, y compris quelques années de rappels pour acheter une licence.

articles.title: Role-based access control decides if AI agents can be trusted - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
The race to deploy AI agents finds a familiar hurdle in data access
Enterprises racing to put AI agents into production are discovering that role-based access control, not model choice, decides whether those agents can be trusted. Rising inference costs, privacy worries and sovereignty demands are also pulling more AI workloads back inside corporate data centers.
That shift favors companies that have spent years governing sensitive data at scale. Cloudera Inc. is betting on Cloudera Anywhere Cloud, a hybrid data and AI platform that spans public clouds and on-premises environments. The company has long been strong on governance, security and scalability but weaker on usability, a gap the new platform was built to close, according to Leo Brunnick (pictured), chief product officer of Cloudera.
“It turns out that the model is ultimately not going to be what separates your success from your competitor’s success,” Brunnick said. “The things that are going to separate you are, number one, your unique data. Your unique data and your unique processes, your alpha — what makes you a business.”
Brunnick spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why AI agents must follow users’ data permissions, the forces pushing AI workloads back into corporate data centers and how packaged blueprints and partnerships can simplify private AI adoption. (* Disclosure below.)
Why role-based access control now extends to AI agents
Customers rarely want a new platform for its own sake, so Cloudera is selling solutions to specific problems instead. Its packaged blueprints and expanded partnerships with Mistral AI SAS, Nvidia Corp. and Vast Data Inc. target private AI use cases such as fraud detection. Mistral, which specializes in open-weight models for on-prem inferencing, also lends Cloudera something it has lacked in the AI market.
“Cloudera already had the capabilities. What we don’t have is a lot of credibility around AI. People don’t think of us as an AI company,” Brunnick said. “What Mistral is allowing us to do is increase our capabilities slightly and increase our credibility astronomically.”
The harder work lies in governance. Agents need to see data across the entire company to be useful, so each one must know who the user is and what that user is permitted to see, Brunnick explained.
“Since the agent needs to be able to see everything in the company, the agent needs to know who you are and what your permissions are,” Brunnick said. “That’s what they need to get right so they can actually put stuff into production that doesn’t blow up on them.”

articles.title: Chips para notebooks baratos estão esgotados, revela Intel • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Chips para notebooks baratos estão esgotados, revela Intel
Intel afirma que escassez de memória não deve melhorar ao longo de 2027.
A Intel afirma ter esgotado a oferta dos processadores da linha Wildcat Lake, voltados principalmente a notebooks de custo intermediário com fichas técnicas mais avançadas. A demanda pela linha, lançada como Core Série 3, aumentou com a tentativa das fabricantes de compensar a alta nos preços das memórias.
A situação foi comentada por executivos durante a apresentação de resultados financeiros da Intel. O diretor financeiro David Zinsner afirmou que a Intel registrou um crescimento significativo na procura por estes chips para colocar em notebooks que não precisam dos componentes mais avançados.
Alguns modelos com o chip também adotam apenas 8 GB de memória RAM, configuração que reduz custos, mas pode limitar o desempenho, segundo o The Verge.
Wildcat Lake é o codinome dos Intel Core Série 3, apresentados pela fabricante como uma opção para notebooks de custo intermediário. Eles ficam abaixo dos Core Ultra Série 3, voltados a máquinas mais avançadas, e usam o processo de fabricação Intel 18A. Os modelos têm cinco ou seis núcleos de CPU, gráficos integrados e NPU de até 17 TOPS.
Alguns notebooks com esses processadores estão no Brasil, como o Dell XPS 13, com preço sugerido de R$ 8.999, e o IdeaPad Slim 3i, que sai a partir de R$ 4.399,99. Ambos carregam o Intel Core 5 320 por dentro.
O aumento da procura pelos processadores intermediários ocorre em meio à escassez de memórias que afeta a indústria de computadores. Questionado sobre o fornecimento dos componentes, Zinsner afirmou que a Intel não espera uma melhora significativa no próximo ano.
“Teremos que ver em 2028 se as coisas melhoram, mas nossa expectativa é que isso não melhore em 2027”, afirmou. Fornecedoras de chips de memória têm revelado que a capacidade produtiva para os próximos anos já está sendo vendida. A SK Hynix, por exemplo, anunciou nesta semana que esgotou os lotes esperados até 2029. A companhia sul-coreana espera que o desequilíbrio siga até 2030.
Lip-Bu Tan relacionou a escassez à forte demanda por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, que absorve uma parcela crescente da produção de componentes.
Segundo o CEO, a indústria enfrenta “uma das faltas de componentes mais significativas da história”, impulsionada pelos investimentos em infraestrutura para IA.

articles.title: The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.
articles.text:
In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies?
Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.”
At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects.
The advisory committee ultimately voted narrowly to recommend approval, and the FDA followed that advice, greenlighting the drug on October 7, 2021. The drug, marketed as Tavneos, started making its way into clinics. A year after approval, ChemoCentryx was acquired by Amgen, one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies. The cost, even today, isn’t minor: $220,000 per year, according to Drugs.com. In fiscal year 2025, sales of Tavneos reached nearly half a billion dollars.
This financial windfall has unfolded despite a long-roiling investor lawsuit—one that incidentally uncovered what the FDA today believes is evidence that ChemoCentryx employees manipulated the data in the pivotal trial submitted to the agency. In April of this year, the FDA issued a letter proposing that Tavneos be withdrawn from the US market, citing reports of serious, sometimes fatal, liver injury, and arguing that the drug now lacks “substantial evidence” that it works.
These revelations have triggered a dramatic cascade of events. This summer, the New England Journal of Medicine retracted a paper describing the clinical trial and Tavneos was taken off the market in the European Union. The United Kingdom has announced that it, too, will remove the product from the market. And on October 29, a court hearing is expected to proceed over Zoom to consider a proposed $69 million settlement for the lawsuit.
But the fate of Tavneos, at least in the United States, is far from sealed. Amgen has pushed back against its critics, insisting that—whatever the details of ChemoCentryx’s data handling—its drug works as advertised and should stay on the market. In July, the company submitted a 104-page document to the FDA stating that “the totality of the evidence supports the continued availability of TAVNEOS.”
Some patients and academic experts also believe the drug is an important treatment option. “This appears to be an efficacious medication,” said Eric Roberts, an epidemiologist at the University of California, San Francisco, who co-authored an independent registry study of Tavneos.
The dispute is emblematic of the FDA’s longstanding struggle to regulate drugs of uncertain efficacy, said Reshma Ramachandran, a physician and co-director of the Yale Collaboration for Regulatory Rigor, Integrity, and Transparency. Absent more rigorous studies, either before or after a drug goes on the market, Ramachandran worries, “we’re just going to be living in uncertainty in terms of whether or not these drugs actually work.”
For American consumers, the saga of Tavneos also raises potent questions around the safeguards in place to ensure the integrity of drug approvals, particularly when a relatively small company conducts the pivotal trial and has so much riding on the success of a single drug.
Chloe Cusano was a 20-year-old college student when she was struck, this past December, with unbearable pain in her legs, as well as bouts of breathlessness from routine tasks like walking upstairs or bending down to retrieve her dog’s water dish. After going to the emergency room, she was hospitalized for more than two weeks, during which she was diagnosed with ANCA-associated vasculitis, or AAV, an umbrella term for a group of rare diseases in which the immune system mistakenly attacks its own blood vessels. When it was first identified, the condition was usually fatal.
Over the past four decades, scientists have developed drugs that allow many AAV patients to live a relatively normal lifespan. Because the disease can rapidly lead to organ failure, particularly of the kidneys and lungs, patients are immediately started on a high dose of steroids to rapidly tamp down inflammation. They also typically receive slower-acting medications that target the underlying disease process.
Steroids, however, have severe side effects. Within a month and a half of going on the steroids, Cusano recalled, she gained 40 pounds. Her emotions were “just like crazy,” swinging from intense sadness to anger. She had trouble falling asleep, and when she did fall asleep, she was haunted by another side effect: nightmares. “I did not like it at all,” she recalls.
AAV patients may need to take steroids for months to years, and Tavneos was supposed to replace or reduce their use.
David Pisetsky, a rheumatologist and researcher at the Duke University School of Medicine, was on the FDA advisory committee that considered the ChemoCentryx trial data. He voted against recommending approval, in part because many patients in the control group received just one round of a slower-acting medication — rituximab — in addition to steroids when, in the real world, they would have received two, according to Pisetsky. The trial’s design, he said, made the results difficult to interpret.
In an editorial in the journal Rheumatology, Mike Putman, medical director of the Vasculitis Program at the Medical College of Wisconsin, and co-authors would later make a similar case: Patients in the comparison group did not receive treatment consistent with the current standard of care. “It is somewhat debate-able about what the ‘standard of care’ would have been” when the study was done, Putman wrote in an email to Undark. “We had not yet established rituximab as maintenance therapy at that point, though most people were already doing that.”
Other members of the advisory committee were persuaded, including Walter Kraft, a clinical pharmacologist and researcher at Thomas Jefferson University. He voted yes to approval. “I felt the evidence, though limited, met the societal and therapeutic goals,” he said during the meeting. Requiring another trial, he added, could delay the drug’s approval by several years.
But that vote, he told Undark in a recent interview, was “based upon an assumption that the sponsor was following the rules of the road.”
These days, a significant number of drugs approved by the FDA start out at a small company with few or no medications on the market, said Sean Nicholson, an economist at Cornell University. Large companies increasingly recognize that their comparative advantage is not in developing breakthrough science, which is more likely to come from “nimble, small startup biotechs,” so rather than trying to compete, Nicholson said, a big company will look to buy or partner with the smaller company.
That’s what happened with ChemoCentryx, which was bought by Amgen for nearly $4 billion one year after the FDA issued its approval of Tavneos.
When bringing a drug to market, small companies face a slightly different set of incentives from large companies, said David Ridley, a health economist at the Duke University Fuqua School of Business. A large company with many products in its pipeline may more readily abandon an experimental drug rather than invest in costly late-stage testing. “Small companies have more to lose,” he wrote in an email to Undark. “The entire company can be at stake. That urgency can drive them to work harder and move faster.”
“In rare cases,” he added, “they might cut corners.”
Back in May 2021, Tavneos’ approval appeared far from certain. Almost immediately after the FDA released its briefing document for the advisory committee meeting, ChemoCentryx’s stock valueplummeted, and its shareholders sued for securities fraud.
Four years later, as part of that lawsuit, a report was filed, alleging that ChemoCentryx had not, in fact, followed the rules of the road. The report indicated that the company’s own trial analysis originally found that the patients receiving Tavneos had not achieved better one-year remission rates than the patients who received the usual treatment.
After company employees unblinded the trial data—meaning they looked to see which study participants had actually received the drug and which had received a placebo—they selected a handful of patients whose remission status would be reassessed. This readjudication, as it is called by the FDA, violated the study’s protocol. What’s more, the agency alleges, the patients were cherry-picked to get the results the company needed for approval.
ChemoCentryx did not disclose the original results, nor the fact that it had reassessed the original data, to the FDA.
In December 2025, Tracy Beth Høeg became acting director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, or CDER.
In an email to Undark, Høeg noted that legally, she can’t speak to the specifics of how this issue came to her attention. But, she noted, “One of my key roles as CDER acting director was letting everyone know my door was open, and I encouraged CDER employees to speak openly with me, especially about matters potentially affecting public safety.”
“When I learned of this case,” she continued, “I distinctly remember thinking this story had so much intrigue that it could easily be made into a movie.”
But the repercussions, Høeg argued with unusual candor, are very real. “Essentially ChemoCentryx swindled billions of dollars by developing a drug that gained FDA approval only because they manipulated the data,” she wrote. Since the drug went onto the market, it has been linked to eight deaths and dozens of hospitalizations. “This can be a deadly drug,” wrote Høeg, “and we don’t know if it works.”
Such was the essence of the FDA’s letter sent in April to Amgen, in which the agency proposed to withdraw approval of Tavneos. The retraction of the Tavneos trial data by the New England Journal of Medicine followed two months later, at the request of the study’s two academic authors.
“This will be a pivotal moment for rheumatology,” wrote Putman, in a lengthy essay on Substack. It’s a story not just about Tavneos, he argued, but evidence that the normal systems of scientific oversight — including peer review and regulatory approval — “failed to detect a shocking case” of alleged data manipulation.
According to Amgen, ChemoCentryx’s actions were less than ideal, but they don’t amount to data manipulation—and they certainly don’t warrant withdrawal of Tavneos.
In the 104-page document submitted to the FDA this summer, Amgen said that ChemoCentryx’s re-adjudication doesn’t “align with the approach Amgen would have taken.” Amgen called it “unfortunate” that ChemoCentryx didn’t disclose its actions to the FDA, noting that it, too, had been in the dark about this.
Still, Amgen pointed out, none of the underlying data were actually changed, and the reassessment of the data, Amgen maintains, was “conducted to correct a small number of errors.” ChemoCentryx was not legally required to disclose the fact that it revisited the data to the FDA, Amgen maintains.
In an emailed response to questions from Undark that Alison Chartan, director of Amgen’s global media relations team, requested be attributed to a company spokesperson, Amgen reiterated many of the points made in the document submitted to the FDA. “As stated in our response to CDER,” the email noted, “the 2019 data readjudication conducted by ChemoCentryx followed a prespecified procedure to correctly and consistently apply prespecified trial rules to adjudicated outcomes. No clinical data were altered.” The email also emphasized the real-world impact a withdrawal would have on those currently taking Tavneos. “Preserving treatment options for these patients,” Amgen wrote, “is central to our mission.” (The company plans to present new data on Tavneos at a conference in November.)
The FDA does have the authority to withdraw its approval of a drug, said Patricia Zettler, a law professor at The Ohio State University who formerly served as an attorney for the Department of Health and Human Services. The law requires a stepwise approach. As an opening gambit, the agency must give notice and offer the drug’s manufacturer an opportunity for a public hearing. If the manufacturer can demonstrate a genuine disagreement about the facts, then the hearing may be held. After that, the FDA can withdraw approval of the drug. If Amgen disagrees with the decision, it could sue the agency.
All of this leaves patients and physicians in a potentially protracted state of uncertainty about whether Tavneos actually works.
Amgen says it does. To make its case, the company has pointed to an independent re-adjudication of its pivotal trial, conducted by researchers at the Duke Clinical Research Institute, part of the Duke University School of Medicine. Although the drug still didn’t meet the FDA’s bar of higher one-year remission rates, the study participants who received the drug fared no worse on this measure. The company also pointed to real-world data, meaning data collected via routine medical care, suggesting that Tavneos can indeed reduce steroid use.
Chloe Cusano is among those who would like to see Tavneos retain its approval. She received it while in the hospital and credits it with helping her taper off steroids more rapidly. Roberts, the UCSF epidemiologist, said his team’s registry study found low rates of drug-induced liver injuries among patients in the U.S., a finding he characterized as “incredibly reassuring,” particularly when care is coupled with careful monitoring. It’s important to keep in mind, he said, that the current alternative to Tavneos is “much higher levels” of steroids.
Others, though, remain skeptical.
Under the law, Tavneos “really shouldn’t remain on the market,” said Joshua Skydel, a clinical fellow in rheumatology at Yale New Haven Hospital and a researcher at the Yale Collaboration for Regulatory Rigor, Integrity, and Transparency. The FDA has standards for drug approval, including substantial evidence of safety and effectiveness. In this case, the pivotal trial has been called into question, and several of the studies that Amgen has pointed to have yet to be published: “I’d at least like to see them go through peer review,” Skydel said, “before hanging my hat on them.”
Høeg, meanwhile, is skeptical that clinical evidence gathered since Tavneos was approved will do much to support its case. “I suspect real world data, much of which were already available when we requested withdrawal in April, will not meet the FDA’s evidentiary bar for approval,” she wrote. “We do know the data were insufficient for ongoing marketing authorization [in] the EU and UK.”
Skydel additionally noted that at the time of Tavneos’ approval, the FDA requested that additional post-marketing studies be conducted. But Amgen has fallen behind on deadlines for those studies. “This episode really, for me, highlighted the way that drugs are allowed to reach the market with open questions,” Skydel said. “Our capacity to answer those questions is really only as strong as FDA and industry’s collaboration,” he continued, as well as FDA’s willingness to use its authority after a drug has gone on the market.
In its April letter, the FDA argued that the stakes of this debate go beyond patients with one rare disease, stating that withdrawing the drug “is critical to protect the public health and the integrity of the drug approval process.” Absent such a consequence, the agency stated, other companies will have an incentive to act deceptively.
Walter Kraft, who voted to recommend approving the drug based on what he knew at the time, also worries about the potential for knock-on effects. The clinical trial system “is built on a level of trust,” he said. “And when that trust is put into question for a narrow parochial gain, it puts the whole system at risk for other subsequent actors in the space.”

articles.title: Pile-ins, payouts, and pacing pressure: the investors behind the VCs open up | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The limited partners who provide the capital to venture firms — the “money behind the money” — are feeling great right now. They’re in uncharted territory in many ways, but also potentially exceedingly lucrative territory.
Normally, LPs typically spread their bets across many firms to diversify their own portfolios. They write checks to emerging managers and established ones, to generalist firms and specialists. The goal is a strong return, but also to minimize risk.
That’s the typical playbook. But typical is out the window. OpenAI and Anthropic’s valuations have shot up so quickly that nearly everyone has piled into the same two companies on the way up, often inside the same venture firm, despite the longstanding venture convention of avoiding investments that conflict with one another. No one is complaining, either. The LPs I speak with seem unbothered by this big gamble, given the potential returns; they’re expecting a bonanza.
But they do see danger ahead, even if they describe this as a “yellow light” situation, and they’re uneasy about how quickly VCs are coming back to raise new funds.
I talked about all of it recently with Beezer Clarkson of LGT Capital Partners, a Zurich-based diversified asset manager, and Amit Bhatti of TrueBridge, a Chapel Hill firm that focuses solely on venture. This conversation has been edited for length.
These are strange days — exciting but also scary. How are you feeling about your roles right now, and your place in this startup ecosystem?
Beezer Clarkson: It’s very busy, but I wouldn’t say it’s scary. There’s a lot of change and a lot of variables at play. I love venture, so I find the chaos fun. I’ve been doing this for a couple of decades, so seeing the cycles makes it less scary. You appreciate that these things happen, and that we should enjoy the upside, because sometimes there’s downside, and the up is a lot more fun than the down.
Amit Bhatti: If anything, it’s exciting. Venture is sometimes looked at as a niche, and now that AI is all-consuming, all the attention is on venture. This feels like our moment more than it is like, “Oh gosh, what’s going to happen?” The pace of investing and the valuations may be different, but really meaningful stuff is happening, and all the attention is focused on this corner of private equity.
Your funds all hold the same brands now, OpenAI and Anthropic, multiplied across however many funds you back, and your job is to keep your institutions diversified. How do you think about that? Obviously it’s great right now, but if things turned, it would be less great.
Amit Bhatti: Venture has always been a power law business, so I actually view the concentration as a good thing. If we were getting to the maturity of one of our funds and there were still lots of tiny positions, something’s gone wrong. Our funds that are 10-plus years old are starting to consolidate into a few names. There’s a lot of Databricks, a lot of SpaceX, a lot of Stripe. In this generation of funds, I would hope there’s a lot of Anthropic and a lot of OpenAI. That’s a feature, not a bug. Not every one of these companies is going to work out, but that consolidation is typical. What’s different is how quickly it’s happened. I don’t view it as an immediate panic signal.
Beezer Clarkson: At the early stage, you still see quite a diversity of opportunity sets, and the dollars are smaller. It aggregates up into the same companies, but early-stage funds obviously aren’t doing the big late-stage stuff, so you have more diversity there, if that’s what you’re looking for.
Funds that invested on four-year cycles have shrunk that to three, then two, then 18 months. Is the pacing okay, or is it concerning?
Beezer Clarkson: We’re seeing funds come back on one-year pacing, which is fast. The norm was probably two to two and a half years. Some funds are deploying much faster because they’re taking concentrated, big-check positions. That could be a worrisome sign. It could work out, we don’t know, but it’s typically harder to do a one-year vintage and get it right.
Amit Bhatti: Similar for us. I would have said 24 to 36 months was roughly normal. Now 12 to 18 is not crazy for some of the funds going really quickly. A lot of funds are bumping up their fund sizes mid-cycle, which is definitely unusual. That’s partly because rounds have gotten so large. If Anthropic is raising a giant quantum of capital and you put 20% of the fund into it, you’re obviously going to be ahead of pace. Seed round sizes have gone up almost 2x, too, so if you want to lead, you’re writing 2x the check. It’s definitely a yellow light. It gives us a little bit of heartburn.
But when we look at what these managers actually bought, the numbers are different. The last time we had accelerated pacing, there was a lot of investing in zero-revenue crypto moonshots. Now we’re seeing a lot of companies go from zero to $100 million in revenue, which was totally unheard of before.
If you’ve got a great manager who comes back every year but the returns are still on paper, can you say “call me next time,” or do you lose your seat at the table?
Beezer Clarkson: It’s very hard to leave a manager and then come back. It happens, but it’s more typical to downsize your check. In 2021, a lot of LPs said, “If I was going to give you $10 million, I’ll do $5 million, because $10 million was for two years.” In our portfolios, the pacing gets pulled through, so we think about our pacing as well as yours.
Amit Bhatti: Same here. We’re building out a calendar of when we expect to make commitments, so if someone goes way off that map, we need to make sure the capital is there. You see people downsize or communicate it up front. It’s hard to say you’re sitting it out altogether, because then you’re not reliable capital. That’s also why you’re seeing upsizes; managers don’t want to come back and say they’re raising a whole new fund, so they bump up the old one.
Beezer Clarkson: People also rotate out of venture sometimes because capital calls keep running with no distributions coming back, and they still have to meet operating commitments, whether it’s the endowment, the hospital, or the foundation. That puts a lot of strain on those situations.
LPs like time diversification, yet a lot of funds were raised in recent years, including that backed startups at high valuations during the pandemic. How are those funds doing, and how would you describe 2026 so far?
Beezer Clarkson: The 2021 vintages are still early, five years in, but they argue against doing one-year funds. Some will catch a piece of an AI company and look excellent, but your odds of getting it right in one year are just tougher, and the valuations were extreme.
Amit Bhatti: If I look at the last 15 years of our portfolio, I wouldn’t bet on the COVID vintage being the best one. But a couple of breakouts will come from it. OpenAI was around in that era, and Cursor started pretty far back, so they’re in some of those funds. And liquidity has started flowing. The past two years were definitely slower, but SpaceX is the headline, Cerebras was a big exit this year, there have been a couple of other IPOs, and a lot of M&A. We’re seeing $10 billion-plus M&A exits, a $60 billion one [with Cursor]. Liquidity is going beyond just IPOs.
How are your venture fund managers thinking about secondaries? If I were a VC, I’d have been tempted to take money off the table in OpenAI or Anthropic.
Beezer Clarkson: Secondaries have become much more sophisticated in venture over the last, call it, five years. It’s localized in the top handful of companies, but it’s much more prevalent than before, which I think is good, because the ecosystem needs liquidity options. Venture is predicated on that, and if you wait 20 years for an IPO, that is not what structurally we all thought it could be. They’re also happening at multiple levels now. LPs sell stakes of their GPs, a strip of their portfolio, and the taboo around it is less.
Amit Bhatti: It’s the third leg of liquidity now: IPOs, M&A, secondaries. Private equity has always had a well-developed secondaries market, and venture didn’t. It was kind of a dirty word. You were only selling if you were distressed. Then people were holding the bag in 2021 and thought, “I should have sold.” Now more managers use it as a tool, and more judiciously. If you still believe it’s the power law company, you’re probably not exiting the whole position. But if you can sell 20% of your position and return your fund, you should probably do it.
There’s a lot of founder selling and employee tenders — often very early into the company’s “journey.” How do you feel about that?
Amit Bhatti: We were talking before about the analogy to crypto, where things got very difficult in part because employees were paid in tokens that were liquid immediately. What’s your motivation to stick around when things get hard? So I think it’s great that there are employee tenders, especially for companies that have been around a long time, like Stripe and Databricks, with a very clear financial picture. For them to offer partial liquidity to employees is totally reasonable. But a lot of the enforcement falls on the lead investors. Investors we back have told companies, “We don’t want you to do an employee tender right now.” Those conversations are happening behind the scenes, and people have learned some lessons from last time. It’s all based on leverage, though. If the founder has incredible leverage . . .
Forget it.
Amit Bhatti: Yeah.
When these companies go public and employees get liquid, will they become partners or competitors to your venture managers? These employees have amazing networks.
Beezer Clarkson: We’ve seen it multiple times: when a company becomes very productive, employees can become LPs or GPs themselves. It’s entirely possible there’ll be a whole new raft of emerging managers backed by people coming out of OpenAI and Anthropic. It happened in the Google days. But being an LP means signing up for many millions of dollars and a multi-decade business.
Amit Bhatti: The real estate part [given the soaring cost of home prices in San Francisco] is going to be tough. But those people stay in the ecosystem, investing in others, building new companies, starting new firms. That’s why no other place is taking SF’s place anytime soon.
Housing costs here in San Francisco have shot up so fast. Do we price out the next generation of founders, and does the next hub end up in New York or somewhere else?
Beezer Clarkson: History would argue that the density effect in the Bay Area is a great pull. Maybe it moves out of San Francisco and back into the suburbs. Back in the day, YC was in Mountain View. New York obviously has its own very deep tech scene, but there’s such a density here that it’s been really hard to push back against.
A handful of venture funds now lock down most of the committed capital from limited partners. Is there a wedge in for emerging managers?
Beezer Clarkson: There are still first-time and emerging managers, funds one through three, being raised this year, last year, the year before. You still need a differentiated point of view, a reason for being. Fundraising has gotten harder, but we see them being funded, and the fund sizes are just smaller. Fifty percent of the money might go to the big funds, but if your average first fund is $25 million to $50 million, there can still be enough of those to add up to $1 billion.
Amit Bhatti: There are people raising $5 million or $10 million right here in SF, maybe formalizing their angel investing. A lot of really well-known funds started with a $5 million fund. It’s much better for an emerging manager to build the track record, prove out the thesis, your access and your judgment with whatever capital you have, and then fund two will be easier to raise. If you try to raise $50 million or $100 million on day one, you’re creating a giant hill to climb.
Beezer Clarkson: If you’ve only angel invested, that’s a different story from spinning out of a platform where you have an installed base of LPs who know you. Those managers typically raise more.
Can you talk about specific kinds of emerging managers you’ve backed, and what made you write the check?
Amit Bhatti: People define “emerging” very differently. We’ve backed founders who are still running their companies and investing on the side. We’ve backed people leaving a bigger firm for something earlier. And we’ve backed extremely young GPs, 22 and 23 years old, who have really close access to the next generation of AI-native founders. They started an accelerator program at MIT, Harvard, and Stanford, and the first couple of batches had Cursor and Mercor in them. They’re young, but they’re around an incredible density of talent. The VC job is sourcing, picking, winning, and they did a pretty decent job of picking when there was no money involved. Success begets success in venture, so we were happy to give them a shot.
Beezer Clarkson: There’s much more flexibility now. I remember a time when an LP wouldn’t fund somebody who had a job and was also investing, and people are open to that now. I’ve been investing in emerging managers, along with established ones, for 14 years, and they run the whole gamut, from an operator-turned-investor raising $10 million, to a spinout raising a few hundred million [dollars]. It’s interesting when they’re still operating, because it gives them insights. The trick is whether they’re doing what they need to do to win the right to be on the best cap tables.
Amit Bhatti: Especially early stage, there’s no one-size-fits-all. You can be part-time, you can be diversified, you can be concentrated. There are more outs in the deck, if you will, for returning something that’s small and experimental.
What’s the smallest check you’ll write to a fund, and how much of a fund will you take?
Beezer Clarkson: Given our program, it’s hard to do less than $5 million. I’ve generally taken the view that if you’re [representing] too much of a fund, there are challenges for the GP going forward, so I’d want to be no more than 20%. There are situations where I’d consider more.
Amit Bhatti: Three to five million for us, and on occasion smaller in very specific scenarios. We don’t really care about concentration if it’s the right scenario. We’ll do half or all of it. But Beezer’s right that it’s not ideal for the GP, and we tell them up front to diversify their LP base. We’ve done a fund where we were half the capital, and the next fund we were closer to 20%, because they did well.

articles.title: Samsung disses iPhone Duo with ads across Canada
articles.text:
Samsung likes to poke fun at Apple, but the company is going in pretty hard this time.
We’ve talked about the new ‘crackgate,’ as iPhone Duos have started cracking in the same place due to an issue with the hinge.
Well, Samsung is having fun with the whole incident by posting pictures, TikToks and now even billboards insulting the Cupertino tech giant — I even got a text message about it.
View this post on Instagram
Samsung now has a mobile billboard in Toronto and Vancouver today, showing the cracked display and saying “switch to Galaxy Z Fold 8.”
The company is also pushing the fact that they’ve released eight generations of Galaxy Z Fold devices, so they have more experience than Apple. This isn’t entirely incorrect, as Samsung has been releasing these foldabes since 2019.
The South Korean tech maker typically releases multiple folding phones per year by releasing both Z Fold and Z Flip series devices. Last year, Samsung even released a TriFold as well.
It’s worth mentioning that I’ve had my iPhone Duo for two weeks now, and the display is still fine. While there are many reports of the iPhone Duo cracking, Apple has said the issue only affects a “small number” of units.
While I’m still working on a full review for the iPhone Duo, I’ve been comparing both the Z Fold 8 and the iPhone Duo a lot, and both have some pros and cons. I’ll have a feature that more closely compares the two in the coming weeks.
Image Credit: Samsung Canada

articles.title: OpenAI CEO says it's 'quite terrible' for your PC to have RAM
articles.text:
OpenAI CEO says it's 'quite terrible' for your PC to have RAM — Sam Altman says data centers offer better utilization
With data centers full of RAM, your PC is apparently the problem.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem. In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."
When discussing local inference on home computers with open-source models, Altman discussed the assumption that people will be able to run local AI on their own computers, the ones they may already own or want to build. Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark):
"From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."
While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model.
OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.
Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down. It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally.
The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.

articles.title: HP’s OmniBook X Flip 14 is a surprisingly high-end 2-in-1 laptop with a mid-range price tag
articles.text:
HP's OmniBook X Flip 14 is a surprisingly high-end 2-in-1 touchscreen laptop with a mid-range price in Best Buy's latest sale
A premium 2-in-1 2K touchscreen laptop with all-day battery life
If you want a laptop that doubles as a tablet for notes, streaming, and sketching without paying premium prices, the OmniBook X Flip delivers a lot for the money. The 2K touchscreen laptop comes equipped with a Core Ultra 5 226V chip that supports up to 40 NPU TOPS for general AI tasks. The 16GB LPDDR5 RAM, and 512GB SSD that makes it ideal for work, study, and downtime.
Now, as part of Best Buy's Halloween Doorbuster sale, the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 is $649.99 (was $999.99). Considering I see sluggish 8GB laptops selling for that price (and I urge you not to buy them), this is an easy recommendation.
• Best for: students and professionals who want a stylish, versatile 2-in-1 for work, note-taking, and entertainment.
• Why we like it: a sturdy all-metal 2-in-1 design, a high-resolution 14-inch touchscreen, efficient Intel Core Ultra 5 performance with Copilot+ AI features, and battery life that comfortably lasts a workday.
A 14-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a 1920 x 1200 IPS touchscreen, an Intel Core Ultra 5 226V processor, 16GB of memory, a 512GB SSD, and Copilot+ PC features, finished in Atmospheric Blue.
Why we recommend it
While we haven't reviewed this specification, our sister site Tom’s Guide tested the exact configuration and found it a premium, durable 2-in-1 with a solid display, strong mid-range performance, and more than eight and a half hours of battery life. He did note that it comes loaded with bloatware you’ll want to remove, that the gapless keyboard takes some getting used to, and that the chassis warms up under heavy loads. Those are small trade-offs for a laptop that looks and feels far pricier than it is.
Price Context & Historical Value
This is $350, or 35%, off the $999.99 list price, but the OmniBook X Flip regularly sells well below that, and Tom’s Guide reviewed it when it was going for $599. That means $649.99 is a good price but not the lowest we’ve seen, and a newer Core Series 3 version is also listed alongside it. Buy now if you need a 2-in-1 today, but it may drop lower over Black Friday next month.
Should You Buy It?
✅ Buy the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 if... you want a laptop that converts into a tablet for notes and streaming, you value a sturdy, premium-looking metal design, or you need battery life that lasts a full workday.
❌ Skip the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 if... you’d rather not spend time removing preinstalled bloatware, you prefer a traditional keyboard layout, or you’re willing to wait in case it drops back to $599 for Black Friday.

articles.title: Enterprise data platforms must get AI pilots into production - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI’s production push puts data platforms on the hook for results
Enterprise data platforms must turn AI pilots into measurable business returns while overcoming the data access, sovereignty and cost barriers that stand between experimentation and production.
The conversation is shifting from what AI can do to how companies make it pay off. One data platform provider has responded by folding its post-sales teams under a single leader, giving customers one voice from onboarding through renewal, according to Patricia Bogoevici (pictured), chief customer officer of Cloudera Inc. The mandate now is to align those teams with customers’ business objectives and help them make better use of the technology they have already paid for.
“When I look at things in terms of customers, for me, technology makes sense only when customers are using it,” Bogoevici said. “I am measured on how customers realize value with Cloudera.”
Bogoevici spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed moving AI into production, improving customer adoption and measuring business value. (* Disclosure below.)
Why enterprise data platforms shape AI’s path to production
The barriers customers face fall into three categories, starting with data access, according to Bogoevici. A study of more than 1,300 information technology specialists found that roughly 80% named data access as the biggest obstacle. Governance and sovereignty come next, because data sits scattered across silos with differing rules on where it can live.
“Not [all] data can be moved to cloud. Not [all] data needs to be in every place,” she said. “It’s about protection, it’s about sovereignty, it’s about on-prem and it’s about air-gap environment.”
The final hurdle is scale. A pilot running on a subset of data rarely shows what a full deployment will cost or return, which leaves total cost of ownership and return on investment unclear, she explained. Cloudera’s answer is Anywhere Cloud, which it plans to release in November, alongside a partnership with Mistral AI SAS that brings open-weight models into the platform.
“It’s one thing to run the pilot in a subset of data,” Bogoevici said. “It’s a completely different thing to run it [at] full scale and understand the results you get from the AI models and understand the value and how you calculate it.”
