articles.title: A primer to key LLM concepts — KV cache, weights, quantization, and more
articles.text:
A primer on key AI LLM concepts — KV cache, weights, quantization, and how inference actually works
Everyone knows about hallucination, but a handful of topics are often unclear. We'll fix that.
As hardware for running local AI models continues to move to the forefront, such as Nvidia's RTX Spark, a new set of acronyms, definitions, and terminology is popping up. Given the pace of releases, we've put together a list of AI's new nomenclature to familiarize you with new concepts and pieces of terminology that you'll likely see in Tom's Hardware Premium articles.
This primer should get you started on the world of AI and be handy the next time news on the topic comes around, and possibly when you're downloading some models to try out and tweak for yourself. For the context of this article, we're going to stick with notions related to text LLMs, or in common parlance, chat, programming, and most agentic bots.
Model
This is probably the easiest one: a model is the LLM itself (a Large Language Model), computed from training sets of mostly text data on the scale of terabytes to petabytes. That training information comes from the internet, books, video and audio transcripts, and other sources.
The model is roughly analogous to a set of highly advanced layers of statistical analysis of relationships between tokens — words or parts of words, computer code, punctuation, and other symbols. The tokens themselves aren't part of the model, but they are packaged along with it. An AI model generates tokens in its outputs.
Weights
Those computing layers within an AI model would be useless without corresponding weights, which represent how strong the connection is between sections of tokens, sort of like how a pathway between neurons is more traveled than others. When the model runs, these values end up establishing how tokens end up relating to each other.
Example: the weights of the connections between "na" and each next part for "naval", "nachos", or "naruto" will all be different, and the higher the weight, the more often that word appears in training data. Importantly, weights cannot change without re-training the model, or parts of it.
When you see LLM specs online, you'll see something like "4B", "8B+", "20B", and so on and so forth. That shows how many parameters, or weights, the model uses, and it's generally measured in billions for consumer-grade models, and trillions for frontier models like GPT, Claude, and Kimi.
Note that a model having more weights than another doesn't automatically mean it's smarter. Just like with CPU clock speeds, it's not just about getting a higher number — bigger is usually better, yes, but you want those weights to be meaningful for the output.
You may also have heard about "open-weight" models versus "closed" models. Those refer to models like Llama, DeepSeek, and Kimi, which are effectively free-to-use, since the entities behind them freely publish the weights online. You can tweak the weights to your heart's content, if you wish, and come up with your own spin on things, as long as you have the hardware to run it. Note that downloading a free model doesn't reveal anything about how it was trained or how the weights were calculated — think downloading a free customizable application, not open-source software.
Data types and quantization
FP16, INT8, FP4, all sound like acronyms in some military handbook, but they're simple to interpret. All programs use numbers of varying width and precision, depending on their purpose: a simple money counter in your favorite game might be fine with a 32-bit integer that can represent 0 to 2^32 (INT32), while a value held in memory for a highly precise scientific measurement may need floating-point 64-bit arithmetic (FP64).
As memory is an exceedingly finite resource, good developers try to use the smallest units they can get away with, a notion that's particularly important in the VRAM-limited world of GPUs. Predictably, these chips became particularly adept at handling lower-precision values as a tradeoff between processing speed and numerical accuracy. A particular datatype isn't better or worse, as that assessment will depend on what it's used for.
When training an AI model, the labs will want to use as high a precision as they can for the weights, but keeping that in the final version would make for a prohibitively large and slow LLM. That's where the concept of quantization comes in, which is a fancy word for "clever rounding." As one of the steps after training, several passes are made to transform highly precise weights. Each AI lab has its own secret sauce about how to do this, as it's a critical step.
Frontier models predominantly use relatively high precision for their weights (BF16), in order to maintain response quality, nuance, and reasoning ability (an analogy would be deciding how accurate you want a GPS location to be — miles or inches). Open-weight models often have several versions with different quantization levels depending on what your hardware can bear — for example, Llama 3.3 70B can be run in full BF16 or quantized INT4 flavors.
The lower the precision, the more likely it can be run on consumer hardware. AI models listed on Hugging Face may have several quantization levels to fit certain levels of hardware, trading response accuracy for size. Consumer-grade models use smaller data types so they can fit on your Mac Studio, RTX Spark, or graphics card.
Context window
"Context window" is another term you've heard a lot and probably seen firsthand, likely in Claude Code's UI as a broad indicator of how long your session can go before the bot starts acting a little dumb. It's measured in tokens, with one million being a common number for frontier models, and it's almost directly analogous to RAM in a computer.
The context window is the LLM's thinking space, and it needs to contain everything associated with your session, not just the current question. Along with all your questions and its replies, it contains system-level prompts, all files you uploaded, the content of links it looked up, plus any associated data.
Crucially, while for you all these things are distinct concepts, for the LLM, they get reduced to tokens in one large pile: the context window. This is also why separating "data" from "code" is technically impossible — the best that modern models do is an approximation of that distinction.
LLMs don't think — when answering a new question, they re-run a statistics program over all the tokens and predict the next handful, so having a larger context window is beneficial (at the cost of VRAM), hence the one-million figure that's currently popular. But even statistical algorithms have their limits.
Even if you increase the window to, say, three million tokens, you may find that your LLM's prediction starts breaking down even though it hasn't run out. This is amusingly called the "lost in the middle" effect, where the bot will pay attention to the start and end of the conversation but will forget things down the middle. Thus, each model is finely tuned to the size of its context window.
KV Cache
If you've looked into using LLMs locally, or by way of running a remote GPU, you may have heard about the "KV cache" time and again, and that you need to reserve VRAM for it, or store it on a fast SSD if you absolutely must. This is a set of data that's created when the model runs, but that's actually reusable between queries in the same session.
The data that's saved and reused can be described as "the relations between tokens for this session." For example, the ever-popular sentence "you're right to push back" can be tokenized as "you-'re-ri-ght-to-pu-sh-back". The dashes between each token represent a vector (or array), called KV for key-value, that is used for determining which token gets picked next.
Since the text generation is linear, the math for calculating each new token needs every KV preceding it. Thus, if you're asking repeated questions in the same session, you'll want the KVs reused to avoid the expense of recalculating them over and over again not just with each round of conversation, but with each additional token.
Remember, an LLM doesn't simply answer the question you just posted — it always analyzes the entire conversation from the top to eventually generate tokens for your response. In a long conversation with 300,000 tokens, not having the cache would mean recalculating the KVs for all of them, a slow operation that gets disproportionately slower still as the interactions grow. This excellent blog post has a more detailed example.
Remember quantization? That's also applied here — modern models reduce the precision of the KV cache's content compared to their initial values, trading a minor accuracy loss for all new tokens in the session, in exchange for keeping VRAM usage down. In fact, with large context windows and conversations, the KV cache may well eat more space than the model and weights themselves.
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)
Previously, AI firms touted how many more parameters their newest model had. Now, the race seems to have shifted to who can include more experts in any given model. That description may conjure a mental image of many tiny scientists living inside a knowledge laboratory, each handling a specific topic, but that's not quite how it works.
Mixture-of-experts, or MoE, is essentially a set of sub-models within the main model. When training starts, all sub-models get the same dataset, but the choice of weights is randomized ever so slightly for each one. Each sub-model will value tokens a bit differently from the rest, and due to how the training process reinforces patterns (called the "rich-get-richer" effect), related tokens will tend to converge together, so you end up with "experts" on sets of tokens.
A common misconception is to think that these experts are related to topics (like programming), but they're only establishing relations between tokens, meaning they'll be more accurate for certain words and text patterns, but devoid of any concept of what they're about. The fact that an expert might offer pretty good responses in regard to landscape painting is a happy accident, not a feature.
You may be thinking that this makes the models larger, and that maybe just the one generalist expert may prove a wiser choice. That's correct, but the trick is that the models only activate certain experts, meaning that only a portion of the model is actually running, thus at higher speed than a generic LLM.
This model selection happens on a per-token basis, too, as a router re-selects experts for each incoming token. For visualizing this, think of brain scan patterns where different areas light up depending on words heard. In practical terms, it means the model can answer more accurately in certain sections, while answering the question faster — albeit at the cost of higher VRAM usage.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
RAG is a concept that's pretty easy to describe, and yet one of the most powerful ones when used with any given model. In short, it can be described as: your chat application runs a few Google searches, feeds them to the model, and voila, there's now much more and fresher information to answer your question. This additional information can come in most any form: company documents, reports, emails, or spreadsheets — anything that you might supply to the model yourself, directly tokenized into its context window.
While broadly speaking most contemporary LLM chat applications run searches, activating RAG, usually triggered by selecting a "web search" switch or sometimes enabling "thinking" or "high effort" mode, will explicitly instruct the application to find as much data as it believes necessary to answer a query. Given that pure context is often key to answering many questions, and do so in an informational manner, RAG is among the most powerful tools available.
Fun fact: the search queries the application will search for are usually generated by a smaller, separate model that will, for example, say what web searches are bound to give the best results, or what to look for in a linked Office 365 account.
The main drawback is that it can be extremely computing-intensive, as the text for your questions and responses may consume, say, 10,000 tokens, yet the information in the retrieved webpages can take hundreds of thousands of tokens all on their own. For example, the Perplexity service was built with an emphasis on RAG usage, and judging from personal experience and user reports, it's usually much more competent and context-aware when answering questions, even though it's underpinned by the same models as everyone else.
Inference, Prefill and Decode
Inference is the act of using a trained model to generate outputs or tokens. It happens every time you send a prompt, and it's where all of the elements that we've discussed above come into play. Inference can be split into two primary parts: Prefill and Decode.
Prefill is the first phase of inference. Essentially, all of the input history (or your prompt) is tokenized and then processed by an AI model. This can include documents, code, and more. These inputs also dictate what gets put into your KV cache. Prefill is processed all at once in parallel, which often means that prefill times are often faster than overall outputs.
Prefill is a large part of the overall workload when measuring how long it takes for a specific chip or piece of hardware can take to output its first token, also known as "time to first token" (TTFT), a common AI benchmark, usually reported alongside prefill tokens per second. Longer prompts take longer to prefill, and context, KV cache, and everything else we've discussed are taken into account.
Decode is the second phase of inference. After a prefill has processed your input and has built the KV cache, the AI model then generates its response one token at a time, which must be done sequentially in order to determine the ones that come after, which means that the step cannot be performed in parallel, unlike prefill. Decode is usually also dictated by context, and reads from a model's KV cache during this step. Decode is usually limited by memory bandwidth, instead of raw compute, as streaming single tokens from weights and reading the KV cache is a bandwidth-intensive task, meaning memory speeds matter more. You'll usually see Decode speeds referred to as tokens-per-second (TPS).
Speculative Decode is a technique that makes those single tokens in the decode step stream faster, without changing the overall output. A drafting mechanism guesses several upcoming tokens, and then the model attempts to verify them in a parallel pass (almost like an additional prefill step). The model then verifies the pass itself; if the guesses are good, then the model's outputs are indeed correct, you get tokens for less of a computational cost during a given decode pass, and when they're bad, they are rejected by the main model during verification, since the main model's output is always what's kept.
Multi-token prediction (MTP) attempts to predict the next set of tokens at once, rather than only serving the next token. This is often built into AI models when they are trained with multiple steps. This can serve as the built-in drafting mechanism required for speculative decode.
This is a non-exhaustive list of concepts critical to understanding how AI models and LLMs work, but it is by no means complete. We will continue to update and refine this article as we add more.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Geekom's Air12 Lite is the cheap mini PC I’d set up for browsing and email
articles.text:
The Geekom Air12 Lite is the kind of tiny, low-cost PC I’d set up for basic browsing and email — and it’s $269 at Best Buy
A Windows 11 Pro mini PC built for day-to-day tasks
When it comes to our testing, Geekom has a strong track record in mini PCs. The range runs from high-performance machines for content creation and heavy workloads to compact machines built for general office duty, browsing, streaming, and other undemanding tasks.
The Geekom Air12 Lite, currently $269 (was $599) at Best Buy, falls into the latter camp. If you need a small, cheap PC for a kitchen counter, a kid’s homework desk, or a living room TV, the Air12 Lite covers the basics without taking up any space.
• Best for: anyone who needs a simple, compact computer for web browsing, email, documents, and streaming video.
• Why we like it: a tiny, quiet design, a quad-core Intel N95 processor that handles everyday tasks, a 256GB SSD, and Windows 11 Pro preinstalled.
• What you need to know: The Intel N95 is a low-power chip that’s built for browsing, email, office documents, and streaming, but it will feel sluggish with lots of tabs open or more demanding software.
A compact mini PC with a quad-core, four-thread Intel Processor N95 boosting to 3.4GHz, integrated Intel UHD graphics, 8GB of DDR4 memory, a 256GB SSD, and Windows 11 Pro. Sold and shipped by Geekom through Best Buy’s marketplace.
Why we recommend it
Geekom has built a solid reputation for well-made mini PCs, and the Air12 Lite is its entry-level model, designed for light everyday tasks rather than heavy workloads. We haven’t tested it ourselves, so this pick rests on Geekom’s track record and the specs. We have, however, tested the improved Air12, which features DDR5 RAM and Wi-Fi 6 connectivity. We scored that machine 4 stars in our review, and for general office tasks, expect performance to be about the same.
Price Context & Historical Value
Ignore the $599 comparison price, since that’s far more than an N95 mini PC with 8GB of RAM has ever been worth, and budget machines with this chip have typically sold for well under $300. Rising memory prices have pushed up the cost of mini PCs this year, so $269 is a reasonable price today rather than a steal. Buy it if you need a basic PC now, but don’t expect much more than browsing and email from it.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Geekom Air12 Lite if... you need an inexpensive, compact PC for browsing, email, documents, and streaming, you want Windows 11 Pro preinstalled, or you’re setting up a simple machine for a family member.
❌ Skip the Geekom Air12 Lite if... you plan to multitask heavily or run demanding apps, since 8GB of RAM and the N95 chip will feel limited; you want to play games; or you’d rather spend a bit more for a mini PC with a faster processor.

articles.title: EA chose Battlefront over BioWare
articles.text:
A new report revealed more of the factors behind the Electronic Arts (EA) decision to shut down beloved Canadian developer BioWare.
According to Bloomberg, EA shut BioWare down after learning about an opportunity with Disney’s Lucasfilm to develop a third Star Wars Battlefront game. Meanwhile, the publisher faced financial pressure after a $55 billion buyout by a Saudi Arabian investment fund took the company private and saddled it with $18 billion in debt.
After reviewing its portfolio, the company saw that it had two sci-fi action games that would cost in the hundreds of millions to develop: Star Wars Battlefront III and a new Mass Effect (which had its trailer leaked, btw). In the end, the company chose to invest in the former and shut down BioWare.
Interestingly, Bloomberg pointed out that Star Wars Battlefront III hasn’t even begun development yet, but execs saw it as a less risky investment and more predictable than a new Mass Effect title (essentially betting on the blue chip), with Bloomberg adding that the company has always been more comfortable with shooters than RPGs.
Bloomberg also added that other factors contributed to the shutdown, mainly the low reception of BioWare’s last few games: 2017’s Mass Effect: Andromeda, 2019’s Anthem, and 2024’s Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which reportedly missed sales expectations by 50 per cent.
Corporate politics could also have played a role, after an executive reshuffling saw EA Sports veterans David Tinson and Cam Weber promoted, while Laura Miele, a BioWare and Mass Effect advocate, was sidelined.
Interestingly, NDP leader Avi Lewis posted to Bluesky that he wants BioWare developers to run the studio with financial backing from the federal government, writing: “The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio. They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity – and the federal support – to buy it and run it themselves.”
Source: Bloomberg

articles.title: Mischief 1, un modèle vidéo « dérivé de neurones vivants » : pardon ?
articles.text:
Il y a des communiqués qu’on lit trois fois pour être sûr d’avoir compris, surtout quand ils sont publiés, une fois n’est pas coutume, dans le tumulte d’un flux sur X. « Depuis quatre ans, nous faisons pousser de vraies cellules cérébrales sur des électrodes pour comprendre comment elles calculent », a écrit Alex Ksendzovsky, cofondateur et patron de TBC, le 30 octobre 2026. Avant d’annoncer que ces découvertes donnaient naissance à… un modèle de génération vidéo, disponible pour un demi-centime la seconde sur la plateforme fal.ai. Le lancement tombait la veille d’Halloween, d’où le nom (« mischief » désigne les petites farces de la Mischief Night).
Rassurez-vous déjà, si vous avez envie de tester le modèle : quand vous générez une vidéo avec Mischief 1, aucun neurone de rat ne travaille pour vous.
Le produit, au fond, est assez banal (si on considère banal le fait de pouvoir envoyer 3 lignes de texte à un ordinateur, générer une image et avoir une vidéo de qualité en retour, bienvenue en 2026). Mischief 1 est un modèle « image vers vidéo » : on lui donne une image de départ et une description de ce qui doit se passer, et il renvoie un clip de trois ou cinq secondes, en 480p ou 720p. Il est accessible par API sur fal, pour 0,5 centime de dollar la seconde en 480p et 1 centime en 720p, soit 5 centimes le clip de cinq secondes en 720p. TBC le présente comme le moins cher de sa catégorie.
Mischief 1 n’est pas un modèle conçu de zéro. Il repose sur Wan 2.2, un modèle vidéo open source développé par Alibaba qu’il est possible d’installer sur votre ordinateur. TBC y ajoute une petite couche logicielle, qui pèse moins de 0,1 % du modèle d’origine et s’insère entre ses blocs de calcul. Résultat revendiqué : des vidéos de qualité équivalente, générées au moins cinq fois plus vite et pour un coût de calcul inférieur de 80 %. Sur sa page produit, la start-up affiche 12 secondes de génération contre 142 secondes pour Wan 2.2 seul.
Et les neurones dans tout ça ?
TBC n’est pas une startup d’IA comme les autres. Fondée par deux neurochirurgiens, Alex Ksendzovsky et Jon Pomeraniec, elle cultive dans ses laboratoires de San Francisco et Baltimore des neurones de rat et des neurones dérivés de cellules souches humaines, posés sur des grilles d’électrodes. L’équipe traduit un problème informatique (des pixels, par exemple) en stimulations électriques, enregistre la réponse des neurones, et cherche dans leur activité des motifs de calcul récurrents. Ces motifs sont ensuite transposés en équations, intégrées dans des réseaux de neurones artificiels classiques.
Tout le challenge est d’approcher l’efficacité du cerveau humain. Notre cerveau fonctionne en effet avec une vingtaine de watts, quand un datacenter d’IA en consomme des centaines de millions. Si la nature a trouvé des façons de calculer plus efficaces, autant aller les observer directement.
TBC n’est pas seule sur ce créneau : l’australienne Cortical Labs vend déjà un « ordinateur biologique » à base de neurones humains, et la suisse FinalSpark loue l’accès à ses organoïdes cérébraux. Mais TBC est la première à transformer ces recherches en produit commercial grand public, tournant sur des GPU tout ce qu’il y a de plus classiques.
La start-up reste très évasive quand il s’agit d’expliquer comment l’activité de neurones de rat devient une ligne de code. Or des accélérations d’un modèle open source de cet ordre ne sont pas inédites. On sait déjà rendre Wan 2.2 plusieurs fois plus rapide grâce à des techniques de distillation, qui réduisent le nombre d’étapes de calcul nécessaires. Impossible, sans article scientifique étayé, de savoir si la « recette neuronale » fait mieux, ou si elle fait la même chose avec une meilleure histoire.
La société, qui a levé 52 millions de dollars, a de toute façon des ambitions bien plus larges : elle dit avoir appliqué sa méthode au modèle Cosmos de Nvidia pour la robotique, et travaille, à plus long terme, à remettre de vrais neurones dans la boucle de calcul.

articles.title: AI PCs Explained: Do Small Businesses Need the New Chips or Just Better Habits? - Tech Guide
articles.text:
The Rise of AI PCs in the Business World
Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from a futuristic concept to a core part of modern computing. One of the latest advancements is AI PCs-computers equipped with specialized chips designed to accelerate AI-driven tasks such as machine learning, data analysis, and natural language processing. These processors promise to transform business operations by enabling faster decision-making, automating routine tasks, and enhancing cybersecurity.
For small businesses, the key question is whether investing in these cutting-edge AI chips is necessary or if improving operational habits and IT practices could yield similar benefits. Understanding the advantages and potential drawbacks of AI PCs will help small business owners make informed decisions that align with their goals and budgets.
AI PCs are not just about raw power; they represent a shift in how computing resources are allocated and optimized. The dedicated AI chips embedded in these machines can process vast amounts of data in real time, enabling functions that were previously only feasible in large enterprise environments. This means tasks like customer sentiment analysis, inventory forecasting, and fraud detection can be executed faster and more accurately, potentially giving businesses a competitive edge.
What Makes AI PCs Different?
Traditional PCs rely on central processing units (CPUs) and graphics processing units (GPUs) that handle a variety of tasks but aren’t optimized specifically for AI workloads. AI PCs incorporate dedicated AI chips-sometimes called neural processing units (NPUs)-that process AI algorithms more efficiently and at lower power consumption. This results in faster data processing and real-time analytics capabilities that were once limited to large-scale enterprise systems.
This hardware innovation is accompanied by software improvements, such as AI-enhanced operating systems and applications that automate repetitive tasks, improve communications, and predict customer behavior based on data patterns. For example, AI-powered customer relationship management (CRM) tools integrated into AI PCs help small businesses tailor marketing campaigns more effectively by analyzing customer preferences and buying habits.
Moreover, AI PCs often include enhanced security features that leverage AI to detect unusual network activity or potential cyber threats in real time. This proactive cybersecurity approach is especially valuable for small businesses that may lack dedicated security teams but face increasing risks from cyberattacks.
The adoption of AI PCs aligns with broader digital transformation trends. A recent study found that 55% of small businesses are actively looking to adopt AI technologies in the next two years to improve operational efficiency. 
Are AI PCs a Must-Have for Small Businesses?
Despite these benefits, small businesses must consider their unique needs before investing heavily in AI PCs. Many operate on tight budgets where every dollar counts. For some, the cost of upgrading to an AI PC might not justify the immediate return on investment, especially if their current setups already meet operational demands.
Some organizations find that optimizing existing technology infrastructure and adopting better IT habits can significantly improve efficiency without new hardware. Streamlining workflows, enhancing cybersecurity protocols, and training employees on digital best practices often yield measurable gains.
It’s also worth noting that according to a recent survey, 42% of small businesses plan to increase their IT budgets in the next year, but only 18% intend to invest specifically in AI-related hardware, indicating a cautious approach to adopting new AI technologies. 
Small businesses also face challenges related to AI technology complexity. Deploying AI PCs requires not only hardware investment but also training staff to effectively use AI-powered tools. Without proper knowledge and integration strategies, the benefits of AI PCs may not fully materialize, leading to underutilized resources.
Leveraging Expert IT Support
One effective strategy for small businesses is partnering with managed IT service providers who understand technology adoption nuances and can tailor solutions accordingly. For instance, businesses trust Sterling Ideas can help companies evaluate whether AI PCs would be beneficial or if other IT improvements would be more cost-effective.
These providers often assist with cybersecurity enhancements, data management, and cloud integration-areas where many small businesses struggle but which can dramatically improve operational resilience and productivity without the latest hardware. They conduct comprehensive IT audits to identify bottlenecks and recommend cost-effective upgrades or process changes that maximize existing investments.
Similarly, companies working with Thriveon in Orlando have reported improved system uptime and better IT strategy alignment with business goals, demonstrating the value of expert guidance in navigating technology investments. These partnerships also provide ongoing support, ensuring businesses stay current with software updates and security patches—critical for maintaining system integrity.
By relying on expert IT support, small businesses can avoid costly missteps and ensure any move toward AI PCs or other technologies is strategically sound and aligned with operational priorities.
When Do AI PCs Make Sense?
Despite potential gains through better IT habits, certain scenarios make AI PCs a game-changer. Businesses relying heavily on data analytics, real-time customer interaction, or AI-driven automation may find traditional hardware limits growth potential.
For example, retail firms using AI-powered recommendation engines or professional services companies employing AI for predictive analytics benefit from AI chips’ speed and efficiency. In industries where milliseconds matter-such as finance or logistics-AI PCs provide a competitive edge.
Moreover, as AI integrates deeper into software, businesses without AI-optimized hardware may face compatibility issues or slower performance, eventually necessitating upgrades. This is especially relevant as AI-driven applications become more complex and resource-intensive.
Industries with strict compliance requirements may find AI PCs help automate and enforce regulatory adherence more efficiently. For instance, healthcare providers using AI for patient data analysis can improve accuracy and reduce human error, benefiting from AI chips’ specialized processing power.
Balancing Cost and Capability
AI PCs currently cost more than standard machines due to specialized chips and the need for compatible software ecosystems. Small businesses must evaluate if expected productivity gains or new capabilities justify the expense.
Considerations include AI workload scale, business process complexity, and staff readiness to leverage AI tools effectively. The total cost of ownership-maintenance, training, and potential downtime during transitions-should factor into decisions.
A phased approach might be best. Starting with pilot projects or limited AI-enabled applications helps assess real-world impact before committing to widespread AI PC deployment. This cautious method reduces financial risk and provides valuable insights into organizational readiness.
Additionally, leasing options or cloud-based AI services offer flexible alternatives to purchasing AI PCs outright, allowing businesses to scale usage based on demand without heavy upfront costs.
Building Better Habits: The Foundation for Success
Regardless of AI PC investment, cultivating better digital habits is critical. Effective data management, regular software updates, employee training, and sound cybersecurity practices form the backbone of a resilient IT environment.
Statistics show that 60% of small businesses experiencing a cyberattack go out of business within six months, underscoring the importance of robust IT practices over just hardware upgrades.
Small businesses often underestimate consistent IT hygiene’s value. Simple measures like strong password policies, multi-factor authentication, and regular backups can prevent costly disruptions. Employee awareness training is equally important since human error is a leading cause of security breaches.
Focusing on process improvements and leveraging expert IT consultants can enhance efficiency and security, making technology investments more impactful. This foundation protects current operations and prepares organizations to adopt advanced technologies like AI PCs more effectively.
The Future Outlook for Small Businesses and AI
Looking ahead, AI integration is expected to deepen, with 75% of small businesses planning to incorporate some form of AI technology within the next three years. This trend suggests that while immediate large-scale investment in AI PCs may not be widespread, the adoption curve is steepening. 
Small businesses that prepare now-by improving digital workflows and engaging knowledgeable IT partners-will be better positioned to adopt AI PCs when the time is right. Technology readiness will be as important as hardware itself.
As AI technology becomes more accessible and affordable, the gap between early adopters and latecomers may narrow, making it critical for small businesses to stay informed and agile. This includes tracking emerging AI applications relevant to their industries and continuously evaluating how technology supports strategic objectives.
Conclusion: A Thoughtful Approach to AI Adoption
AI PCs represent a significant technological leap with the potential to revolutionize business operations, but they are not a one-size-fits-all solution for small businesses. While the promise of faster AI processing and automation is enticing, many small companies will benefit more from smarter IT management and strategic partnerships with service providers before committing to expensive hardware upgrades.
By carefully assessing business needs, budget constraints, and growth plans, small businesses can decide whether to adopt AI PCs now or focus on optimizing current systems and digital habits. Either way, embracing AI thoughtfully will position companies to thrive in an increasingly digital marketplace.
Ultimately, the decision to invest in AI PCs should be driven by a clear understanding of business objectives, operational demands, and potential return on investment. Combining technology upgrades with disciplined IT practices and expert guidance ensures small businesses maximize AI’s benefits while mitigating risks and costs.

articles.title: Un estudio explica por qué en España 1 GW de centros de datos no se solucionará instalando simplemente 1 GW de renovables
articles.text:
Que los centros de datos necesitan una cantidad ingente de electricidad no es ninguna sorpresa. Estos “vampiros energéticos” suponen uno de los principales retos a los que se enfrentan los países que los van a albergar. En España, el Gobierno ha intentado abordar este desafío vinculando la expansión de los centros de datos a la generación renovable, de manera que no supongan un peaje altísimo que obligue al sistema eléctrico a recurrir a más generación fósil o a incrementar la presión sobre los precios.
Sin embargo, y aunque se ha presentado recientemente un nuevo borrador mucho más suave, este nuevo texto sigue insistiendo en la misma idea de fondo sobre la exigencia de renovables. Y según un informe de la consultora EY, de cumplirse los planteamientos que propone el decreto, se necesitaría la instalación de casi 50 GW adicionales de energía solar y eólica y de baterías, para abastecer únicamente 3,5 GW de centros de datos.
Los centros de datos trabajan todo el día, las renovables no. Tanto el borrador que se presentó en agosto como la revisión que se ha hecho estos días contemplan que los centros de datos tendrán que ir acompañados de nueva generación renovable. Se mantiene el objetivo de cubrir, como mínimo, el 80% del suministro eléctrico con energía solar o eólica (adicionalidad renovable), y que el 80% del consumo esté respaldado hora a hora (correlación horaria). Es decir, no basta con producir muchísima energía renovable en el conjunto del año: hay que tener generación suficiente para cubrir el consumo en las horas complicadas.
Pero ¿qué pasa cuando no hay generación renovable? Las renovables llevan asociada una característica fundamental y es que son intermitentes. No se produce la misma energía un día soleado de verano a las 15 horas, cuando hay mucho recurso solar, que una noche sin viento, cuando no hay recurso ni solar ni eólico. Para cubrir esas horas en las que no hay suficiente producción renovable, los centros podrán recurrir a una combinación de generación adicional y almacenamiento.
Unas cifras enormes para la demanda esperada. El problema aparece cuando intentamos hacer coincidir ambas curvas: la demanda continua de un centro de datos y la producción variable de las renovables. El análisis de EY concluye que, bajo sus supuestos, la forma de garantizar esa cobertura obliga a sobredimensionar enormemente la cartera de generación y almacenamiento. Según esa línea, cumplir las exigencias energéticas del proyecto de real decreto para los 3,5 GW de demanda de centros de datos contemplados para 2030 requeriría, bajo los supuestos de su simulación, una cartera de 49,8 GW de solar, eólica y almacenamiento. De esa cifra, 26,8 GW corresponderían a la solar fotovoltaica, 8,8 GW a la eólica y 14,2 GW al almacenamiento en baterías. Unas cifras que resultan enormes comparadas con la demanda que se pretende cubrir.
De este modo, y según el estudio, la capacidad resultante de la simulación de EY multiplicaría por 14 la potencia eléctrica de los centros de datos contemplados. Dicho de forma sencilla, en el escenario analizado por EY, por cada GW de demanda de centros de datos habría que desplegar unos 14,2 GW de energía solar, eólica y baterías para cumplir las condiciones planteadas.
La otra cara que apunta el estudio. El análisis de EY también advierte de que este sobredimensionamiento de la generación renovable para garantizar el suministro a todas horas puede conllevar algunos efectos indeseados. Por ejemplo, el modelo de EY calcula 19.742 GWh de excedentes anuales y estima que los vertidos del sistema aumentarían al menos un 16%. Según la consultora, esto podría reducir la rentabilidad de las instalaciones renovables que ya existen.
Otra de las consecuencias que prevé la consultora en el escenario analizado y que recoge El Periódico de la Energía es que los costes de suministro de los centros de datos podrían llegar a alcanzar los 133,07 euros/MWh, frente a los 55 euros/MWh que tiene el mercado de futuros para ese año. Es decir, un coste 2,4 veces superior que podría llegar a repercutir en los servicios digitales que dan los centros de datos y hacerlos menos competitivos. Tanto es así que el sector, a pesar de la revisión reciente de la normal, sigue pensando en recurrir el proyecto por vías legales.

articles.title: DoorDash Cuts Grocery Reorder Latency from 16 to 2 Seconds with AI Agents
articles.text:
DoorDash cut latency in its AI-powered grocery reorder flow from about 16 seconds to 2 seconds by precomputing recurring purchase needs instead of rebuilding them with each request. The change doubled shopping list views and increased the flow’s order rate by approximately 34%. The implementation builds on DoorDash’s shared agent platform and grounded shopping interface, which provide reusable agent infrastructure and let consumers modify shopping lists directly.
The implementation combines batch large language model (LLM) inference, deterministic validation, and live product catalog resolution within Ask DoorDash, the company’s conversational shopping assistant. Previous InfoQ coverage described how Ask DoorDash uses specialized agents and tools to support conversational discovery and shopping. For grocery reordering, DoorDash processes 90 days of purchase history alongside consumer profile signals. Batch LLM inference identifies likely recurring purchases, while deterministic validation checks the generated results before storing reusable shopping list data.
DoorDash’s grocery reorder architecture (Source: DoorDash Blog Post)
The serving path retrieves this prepared data and resolves each item against the current catalog. It first tries to match the original store item, then a catalog product identifier, and finally a search term. This allows the system to accommodate changing listings and unavailable products without repeating historical reasoning for every request.
The shared platform provides orchestration, memory, model access, tracing, evaluation infrastructure, and rollout controls. Domain teams retain ownership of agent instructions, skills, tools, and evaluation criteria. DoorDash reports that adding its Reservations agent took one week, approximately ten times faster than building its initial domain agents.
Ask DoorDash shared agent platform architecture (Source: DoorDash Blog Post)
Twisha Jain, a DoorDash engineer, described the design rationale in a LinkedIn post:
Better agentic systems aren’t always about more reasoning; they’re about deciding what belongs in the agent loop and what can happen ahead of time.
Moving recurring purchase analysis offline reduces the work required during a live request while retaining current catalog information for product selection. The system still invokes the Grocery agent for requests requiring additional reasoning, such as finding cheaper alternatives based on current prices, promotions, package sizes, inventory, and consumer preferences. Simpler operations, including changing quantities or removing products, update the shopping list directly without another LLM round trip.
A DoorDash engineering post about its shopping interface states:
A consumer’s direct edit is authoritative: the next agent turn starts from the edited list, not from what was said earlier.
The design treats the shopping list as a structured artifact that both the consumer and agent can update, rather than relying solely on conversational history. Other grocery platforms also use AI to personalize shopping. Instacart’s AI shopping assistant supports meal planning, list creation, and product discovery using consumer preferences and local grocery offerings. DoorDash’s implementation focuses specifically on reducing reorder latency by separating historical purchase analysis from live product resolution.

articles.title: Anthropic expected to receive high 'junk' rating from credit agencies following IPO, FT report says | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anthropic is expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit rating agencies following its initial public offering, according to a report from the Financial Times.
The FT says the investment giant Blackstone, the anchor investor in a recent $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic’s chips, told investors in the deal that it expects the AI lab to receive a “high” junk rating after its IPO. Previously, the FT notes, Blackstone had said the opposite: that the Claude maker would receive an investment-grade rating (indicating low risk for lenders) before 2027 rolls around.
Now Blackstone expects double B range rating, the top tier of speculative “junk” grade, according to the reporting.
TechCrunch reached out to Anthropic and Blackstone but both declined to comment.
Blackstone’s forecast is just a prediction, but naturally, a high junk rating would make it more difficult and costlier for Anthropic to raise the money to keep funding its massive spending that has undergirded its business. The lab has been on a spending spree, racking up large compute power deals throughout the past 12 months, which has worried investors.
Anthropic officially filed to go public earlier this week, kicking off a wave of speculation about how the massive IPO would impact the broader AI industry.

articles.title: OpenMouse Launches Open-Source Customization for Logitech, Razer, Wooting, and SteelSeries Keyboards
articles.text:
Friday, October 30th 2026
OpenMouse Launches Open-Source Customization for Logitech, Razer, Wooting, and SteelSeries Keyboards
Not too long ago, the developers behind OpenMouse, the open-source, community-driven alternative mouse configuration suite, revealed that they were working on supporting keyboard customization alongside the myriad gaming mouse models the suite now supports. As per a recent announcement on the project's Discord server, the latest OpenMouse beta release has added support for a number of gaming keyboards from Logitech, Razer, SteelSeries, and Wooting. Initial support also appears to be in development for Wuque Studio and the Kochi Hummingbird 68. 
So far, actual feature support also appears to be limited, and the implementation is very much still in beta, with the app connecting correctly to a Wooting 80HE in a brief test but failing to load the proper keymap and failing to adjust the settings correctly. However, the planned feature set appears to be competitive with most proprietary keyboard customization tools, with HE features like adjustable actuation, rapid trigger, toggle key, mod tap, SOCD, and DKS, all present in addition to robust RGB customization and support for layers and profiles. What is notably absent is the ability to remap keys, however.OpenMouse also now allows users to install the Bridge app to create custom per-game profiles for compatible gaming mice, and it appears as though the same functionality will eventually be added for supported keyboards. It's not clear when keyboard support will leave the beta testing phase, but the development team has called on gamers to participate in the beta test.

articles.title: London, Ontario is Canada's number one city for partying: report
articles.text:
According to a recent report by Uber, Ontario is home to Canada’s top partying destination, but it’s not Toronto that holds the honour.
Releasing its fifth annual Nightlife Index on Wednesday, Oct. 28, the ridesharing app revealed that, of all places, London, Ontario, is the number one city in the country for partying.
It makes sense, given the city’s substantial student population, but a city’s got to be really good at partying to dethrone one like Toronto, which boasts a population nearly 10 times the size.
This marks the fourth time the Ontario city has landed the first-place slot, after being dethroned just once by Toronto in 2024.
Toronto didn’t even manage to land in the top three Canadian cities for partying, as it turns out. Winnipeg secured a second-place finish, while Lethbridge, Alberta, came in third.
Toronto ended up in fifth place, sandwiched between Kitchener-Waterloo in fourth and Halifax in sixth. And as someone who has lived in both Halifax and Toronto, I’d argue that those two positions ought to be swapped.
Since the list was created using aggregated and anonymized data from Uber and Uber Eats, such as late-night trips and food orders, I guess I stand corrected.
The study also showed that New Year’s Eve, Halloween Night and Halloween Weekend are the three biggest holidays for partying (no surprise there), and that, on average, Canadians stay out the latest on Halloween.
As for hangover cures, Canadians have been ordering those in spades, too. The most popular? None other than classic hot coffee, followed, as it so often is, by hash browns, breakfast wraps, bagels, and iced coffee.
Here’s to another year of partying, Canada!

The Boulies EP200 is our best-value office chair pick — now the 'archetypal office chair for most people' drops in price in an early Black Friday sale
All-day comfort and a sturdy build for the price
The Boulies EP200 isn't the fanciest office chair to ever pass through our testing grounds. But it is one of the most reliable value picks you can get - far superior. It's been our office furniture editor's daily driver for home-working for since February 2025, and it's as good as the day he got it. It is, he said "the archetypal office chair for most people."
Now, as part of the company's early Black Friday sale, the Boulies EP200 is down to $220 (was $310) in the US, while the UK sees the chair discounted to £210 (was £280). If your home office chair leaves your back aching by mid-afternoon, the Boulies EP200 offers proper ergonomic support without the premium price tag.
• Best for: home and office workers who want a comfortable, supportive mesh chair for long days at the desk on a modest budget.
• Why we like it: an airy mesh back that keeps you cool, adjustable lumbar support and headrest, adjustable seat depth and armrests, and a sturdy, professional-looking build.
A mesh office chair with adjustable lumbar support, a removable adjustable headrest, four-level seat-depth adjustment, 3D padded armrests, a multi-tilt mechanism with recline up to 120 degrees, a Class 4 gas lift, and a five-star base. It comes in black or green, ships free in the US, and includes a two-year limited warranty and a 14-day return window.
UK price: now £210 (was £280)
Why it's worth a look
In our Boulies EP200 review, our office furniture editor Steve found it supremely comfortable and breathable, and said he felt no fatigue even after long sessions in it. He also praised its sturdy, stable build and clean, professional look, and his one-year follow-up confirmed it has held up well. His main complaints were that adjustability is more limited than on pricier chairs, which is to be expected, while the mesh back won’t suit anyone who prefers padding.
For more picks, including the Boulies EP200, see our guide to the best office chairs.
Price & Value Context
This is $90, or 29%, off the $309.99 list price. The EP200 dropped to about $200 around the time of our review, so this isn’t a record low, but it’s close. At this price, it’s an easy recommendation for anyone who wants a quality mesh chair without spending $300 or more.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Boulies EP200 if... you want a comfortable, breathable mesh chair for long workdays, you need adjustable lumbar support and a headrest, or you’re after quality ergonomics without a premium price.
❌ Skip the Boulies EP200 if... you need the fine-tuned adjustability of a high-end ergonomic chair, or you prefer a padded backrest to mesh.

articles.title: Motorola Signature 27 : la date de sortie se précise, mais attention au prix
articles.text:
Dévoilé en septembre dernier lors du Snapdragon Summit de Qualcomm (sans tarif ni date de sortie), le nouveau smartphone haut de gamme de Motorola, le Signature 27, va livrer ses derniers secrets le 5 novembre prochain, notamment autour de son prix, qui s’annonce encore plus salé que le Signature sorti en début d’année.
Un prix en fuite pour le Signature 27
Motorola donnera les dernières informations autour de son Signature 27 la semaine prochaine, mais le site MegaPC a déjà référencé le smartphone à 1 594,90 euros pour sa version équipée de 12 Go de RAM et de 512 Go de stockage. À titre de comparaison, le Motorola Signature a été lancé à 1299 € (ce qui était plus élevé que les 999 € annoncés lors de sa présentation au CES 2026).
 Now that’s a nice touch.
motorola signature 27: elegantly crafted for comfort.
See for yourself on November 5.
#MotorolaSignature #SignatureStatement https://t.co/hG9ZjNY08h
— motorola (@Moto) October 29, 2026
Ce prix est évidemment à prendre avec des pincettes dans la mesure où une boutique en ligne peut tout à fait publier un prix provisoire en attendant le tarif officiel du constructeur pour la commercialisation. La page en question présentait le coloris Pantone Coal Smoke et signalait le produit comme étant en rupture de stock, sans indiquer de date particulière.
Un smartphone clairement haut de gamme
Du côté des informations officielles dont nous disposons, le téléphone embarque le processeur Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, une puce gravée en 2 nanomètres qui intègre un nouveau système de refroidissement « ArcticMesh » qui combine un gel thermique et une chambre à vapeur plus grande. Cela pourrait résoudre les problèmes de chauffe que nous avions pointés sur le Motorola Signature. Pour la partie photo, le Signature 27 mise sur un capteur principal Sony Lytia 910 de 50 mégapixels et un téléobjectif périscopique avec un capteur de 200 mégapixels qui offre un zoom optique 5x.
Pour ce qui est du suivi logiciel, la marque promet sept mises à jour majeures d’Android et de sécurité. Enfin, le volet audio bénéficie pour la première fois de réglages signés Bang & Olufsen. Un partenariat qui vient remplacer le précédent partenariat avec Bose.

articles.title: This art festival reveals why the creative economy is as much about audiences as creators
articles.text:
This art festival reveals why the creative economy is as much about audiences as creators
In this photo essay, we showcase more highlights from the Contemporary Now arts festival in Chennai, along with director insights.
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,025 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.
Chennai recently hosted the third edition of the art festival 'Contemporary Now', with collaboration from art galleries of Kolkata, Ahmedabad, New Delhi, and Mumbai as well. A diverse range of artworks was exhibited in 10 venues across the city, as shown in this photo essay.
The artist lineup included Ashwini Bhat, Prajakta Potnis, Khageswar Rout, Amitesh Shrivastava, Sandeep Mukherjee, Saju Kunhan, Pratap Morey, Benitha Perciyal, Natasha Preenja, and many others.
“Now is a good time to be in art. Aspiring artists as well as audiences today are much more connected to art, thanks to social media,” mixed-media artist Benitha Perciyal tells YourStory.
Earlier, art catalogues and visits to a few galleries were the only available options. “You had to simply wait to get access and exposure, or travel to other cities, which was quite expensive,” she recalls.
“Today, online access is immediate and global. But at the same time, too much online exposure can be confusing or intimidating,” she cautions.
Digital platforms and AI make things much easier and faster now for art. “But it also takes away from the satisfaction of finding or creating something after a lot of effort,” Perciyal says.
The art festival’s directors are Ashvin Rajagopalan and Priyanjoli Basu. Both express satisfaction with the event’s achievements for the art community of Chennai and beyond.
“We had collectors who usually have not come out much, but engaged with us at the festival. We had many art fans and students who could see what was happening in the rest of the country thanks to our institutional partners in other cities,” Rajagopalan says.
There are plans to have more editions of the festival. “We may end up having two or three editions of Contemporary Now. One, of course, in Chennai, but others could be in Ahmedabad, Baroda or Shantiniketan,” he adds.
“The festival’s level of contemporary artwork has probably not been shown in Chennai earlier. A lot of feedback I got was that there are major art events in Delhi and Mumbai but not as much in Chennai,” Basu observes.
The art community felt this event should happen more often in Chennai. “It should not be a once-a-year thing. The displayed artworks should be shown elsewhere also, to continue the conversation,” she adds.
As trends in the art market in India today, she points to more appreciation of art about politics, gender and climate change. “People are trying to engage with a new narrative, a new trend. The works of a lot of young women artists are also being collected,” Basu says.
“Many contemporary artists have been responding to what is happening around the world. Art collectors are also responding to such art because it makes them feel something and moves them. Knowledgeable collectors are able to find more artists making such work,” Rajagopalan adds.
Both directors see a growing importance for the role of art today, as well as a need for more art appreciation in society. “Artists voice the world’s uncertainty and conflict for us. Engaging with such art reflects your concern about such issues,” Rajagopalan says.
Basu calls on audiences to discuss art with people they meet, attend art events, and visit art galleries. “When you go on holiday, make sure you see a city’s art galleries also,” she suggests.
“And of course, if you are traveling abroad, it is very important to go and see their museums. That is how we can improve art appreciation and knowledge of art right here in India,” Basu signs off.
Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?
(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at 'Contemporary Now' venues in Chennai.)

articles.title: C'est déjà le Black Friday : voici les premières vraies offres tech à saisir en DIRECT ce samedi — Frandroid
articles.text:
C’est Halloween et bientôt la fin des premières vacances scolaires dans l’Hexagone, mais ce samedi 31 octobre 2026 marque également le premier week-end des offres du Black Friday. En effet, le célèbre vendredi noir qui permet de faire de bonnes affaires comme à aucun autre moment de l’année ne se limite plus à quelques jours ou à une semaine, mais à tout un mois.
Si vous recherchez un nouveau smartphone, tablette, TV, PC portable, casque ou écouteurs sans fil, des objets connectés ou tout autre objet Tech à bon prix, vous êtes au bon endroit. Cet article sera régulièrement mis à jour, au rythme des ventes flash, n’hésitez donc pas à revenir y faire un tour plus tard si vous ne trouvez pas votre bonheur la première fois.
Black Friday 2026 : les meilleures offres en avant-première
ECOVACS Winbot W2S Omni
Le Winbot W2S Omni est un robot laveur de vitres autonome qui embarque sa propre batterie dans une station mobile – pas besoin d’une prise à proximité pour nettoyer fenêtres, miroirs ou parois de douche. Avec 8 000 Pascals d’aspiration et un réservoir de 80 ml couvrant jusqu’à 65 m², il fait franchement le taf sur les grandes surfaces vitrées.
- Station mobile avec batterie intégrée, aucune prise nécessaire
- Détection des bords, obstacles et du vide pour éviter les chutes
- Compatible vitres, miroirs et parois de douche, 68 dB en fonctionnement
Le Winbot W2S Omni est en promotion à 379 euros chez Boulanger, au lieu de 499 euros habituellement.
Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8
Le Galaxy Z Flip 8 est l’un des derniers smartphones pliablesde Samsung. Il pèse seulement 8 grammes de moins que son prédécesseur et offre une FlexCam de 50 mégapixels avec un petit écran externe (FlexWindow) qui gagne en autonomie d’usage.
- FlexCam 50 Mpx avec mode portrait sans les mains
- Performances solides et mises à jour logicielles garanties 7 ans
- Petit écran externe FlexWindow plus exploitable qu’avant
Noté 8/10 dans notre test, il est actuellement en promotion à 865 euros sur Amazon, au lieu de 1 499 euros au lancement, dans sa version avec 512 Go de stockage.
Ninja Foodi 11-en-1
Le Ninja Foodi est un multicuiseur 11-en-1 qui regroupe autocuiseur, friteuse à air, grill et mode vapeur sous un seul couvercle à curseur – une bonne option si vous cherchez à remplacer plusieurs appareils encombrants.
- 11 fonctions de cuisson accessibles via un simple curseur SmartLid
- Cuisson sous pression jusqu’à 70 % plus rapide que les méthodes traditionnelles
- Grande cuve de 6 litres pour nourrir jusqu’à 4 personnes
Le Ninja Foodi est disponible en promotion à 149 euros sur Amazon, contre 329,99 euros habituellement. L’offre est valable jusqu’à ce soir seulement.
Asus ROG Keris II Origin
La ROG Keris II Origin est une souris gaming sans fil de 65 grammes, pensée pour les longues sessions : switch remplaçable sans outil, capteur optique de 42 000 dpi et triple connectivité (2,4 GHz, Bluetooth, USB).
- Capteur ROG AimPoint Pro : 42 000 dpi avec tracking sur verre
- Switch ROG Micro II garanti 100 millions de clics, remplaçable sans outil
- Connexion sans fil jusqu’à 8 000 Hz avec le ROG Polling Rate Booster
La ROG Keris II Origin est disponible à 89,99 euros sur Amazon, au lieu de 149,99 euros.
Asus ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless
Le ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless est un clavier mécanique au format 96 %, qui conserve le pavé numérique et les touches de fonction dans un encombrement à peine plus large qu’un 80 %.
- Triple connectivité : Bluetooth (3 appareils), 2,4 GHz ROG SpeedNova et USB filaire
- Switches NX Snow linéaires pré-lubrifiés et remplaçables à chaud
- Mousse d’insonorisation intégrée pour une acoustique de frappe plus feutrée
Le ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless est disponible en promotion à 129,80 euros sur Amazon, au lieu de 149,95 euros.
JBL Live 775 NC
Le JBL Live 775 NC est un casque circum-aural avec réduction de bruit active qui mise avant tout sur l’endurance : jusqu’à 65 heures d’autonomie.
- Jusqu’à 65 heures d’autonomie, 50 heures avec l’ANC activé
- Charge rapide USB-C : 5 minutes pour 4 heures d’écoute
- Multipoint Bluetooth 5.3 et mode conversation sans retirer le casque
Le JBL Live 775 NC est disponible à 99,99 euros sur Boulanger, au lieu de 179,99 euros.
Hisense 75E8S
Avec sa dalle XXL 4K Mini LED, sa fréquence de rafraîchissement maximale de 144 Hz et ses multiples compatibilités, le TV Hisense 75E8S entend bien satisfaire les cinéphiles comme les gamers exigeants.
- Une dalle Mini LED de 75 pouces + 144 Hz
- Des compatibilités Dolby Vision, HDR10, HDR10+, HLG
- Quatre ports HDMI 2.1, le VRR et l’ALLM
Initialement affiché à 1 499,99 euros, le TV Hisense 75E8S est aujourd’hui disponible en promotion à 899,99 euros chez Carrefour.
Logitech MX Vertical
La Logitech MX Vertical est une souris ergonomique dont l’angle à 57° positionne la main en prise de poignée de main, ce qui réduit la tension sur le poignet et l’avant-bras. Franchement, pour qui passe ses journées devant un écran, c’est un investissement utile.
- Angle vertical à 57° pour une posture naturelle du poignet
- Capteur 4 000 PPP avec commutateur de vitesse instantané
- Autonomie de quatre mois, trois heures après une minute de recharge
La MX Vertical est disponible à 49,99 euros sur Cdiscount, au lieu de 99,99 euros habituellement.
Dreame R20
Le Dreame R20 est un aspirateur balai sans fil qui mise sur la légèreté (tube en fibre de carbone) et une autonomie de 90 minutes pour couvrir toute la maison sans s’arrêter.
- 90 minutes d’autonomie avec la batterie intégrée
- LEDs sur la tête de brosse pour repérer la poussière dans les zones sombres
- Puissance de 190 AW avec reconnaissance intelligente de la poussière
Le Dreame R20 est disponible en promotion à 190,83 euros sur Amazon, au lieu de 279 euros sur le site officiel de la marque.
Apple MacBook Air 13 M5
En juin dernier, Apple a augmenté le prix de son MacBook Air 13 M5, désormais affiché à 1 399 euros, pour faire face à la crise de la mémoire. Mais en ce moment, Joybuy le propose à 1 199 euros, soit son prix de lancement.
- Un ultraportable toujours aussi léger et fin
- Une puce M5 qui promet de solides performances
- Le support du Wi-Fi 7 et du Bluetooth 6 avec la puce Apple N1
Habituellement proposé à 1 399 euros depuis la hausse des prix, le MacBook Air 13 M5 (16+512 Go) est aujourd’hui disponible en promotion à 1 199 euros sur Joybuy, soit son prix de base.
Motorola Moto G67
Le Motorola Moto G67 est un smartphone 5G qui mise sur un écran OLED de 6,78 pouces, 256 Go de stockage et une batterie de 5 200 mAh pour tenir la journée sans stress.
- Écran OLED 6,78 pouces, résolution 2772 x 1272 pixels
- Stockage de 256 Go, extensible jusqu’à 2 To via microSD
- Batterie 5 200 mAh et résistance à l’eau et à la poussière
Habituellement affiché à 299,99 euros, le Motorola Moto G67 est actuellement disponible en promotion à 199,99 euros chez Auchan et Boulanger.
Garmin Venu 4
La Garmin Venu 4 (45 mm) est une montre de sport et santé en acier inoxydable, avec un écran AMOLED lumineux, une lampe LED intégrée et plus de 80 activités suivies – notre test lui a attribué 9/10.
- Boîtier en acier inoxydable avec lampe LED intégrée
- GPS fiable et paiement sans contact au quotidien
- Suivi santé complet : Body Battery, sommeil, stress, VFC
Habituellement affichée à 449,99 euros, elle est en promotion à 339,99 euros sur Amazon grâce à une remise de 50 euros et une réduction supplémentaire de 15 % appliquée directement au panier.
MSI Cyborg 15 Max
Le MSI Cyborg 15 Max C2WG-001FRNN possède une fiche technique séduisante : une RTX 5070, un Intel Core 7 240H dans un format 15 pouces, le tout avec 350 euros de remise.
- Son châssis de 2 kg, transportable au quotidien
- Son écran 15,6 pouces rafraîchi à 144 Hz
- Sa RTX 5070 8 Go GDDR7
Affiché à 1 599 euros, le MSI Cyborg 15 Max (C2WG-001FRNN) est en ce moment proposé à 1 249 euros sur Darty grâce au code promo INFO100.
HP Victus 15,6″
Le HP Victus 15,6″ embarque une RTX 5060 avec 8 Go de GDDR7 et un Ryzen AI 5 340, ce qui en fait une option sérieuse pour le jeu en Full HD sans exploser le budget. Si vous cherchez un PC portable performant, il mérite un coup d’œil.
- RTX 5060 avec DLSS 4 et 8 Go de GDDR7 pour le jeu en Full HD
- Écran IPS 15,6″ Full HD 144 Hz avec dalle antireflets
- Charge rapide : 50 % de batterie en 30 minutes
Le HP Victus 15,6″ est disponible en promotion à 1 099,99 euros chez Boulanger, au lieu de 1 299,99 euros habituellement.
Honor MagicPad 4
Le Honor MagicPad 4 est actuellement disponible en pack avec son clavier magnétique, ce qui en fait une tablette Android polyvalente taillée aussi bien pour regarder des vidéos que pour travailler. Avec ses 4,8 mm d’épaisseur et son écran OLED 165 Hz, c’est l’une des références les plus sérieuses face à l’iPad Pro – noté 9/10 dans notre test.
- Dalle OLED 12,3 pouces à 165 Hz, particulièrement lumineuse
- Snapdragon 8 Gen 5, 12 Go de RAM et 256 Go de stockage
- 8 haut-parleurs intégrés et 6 ans de mises à jour garantis
Le pack Honor MagicPad 4 avec clavier est disponible en promotion à 599 euros chez Boulanger, au lieu de 799 euros habituellement.
Philips NeoPix 560 Smart
Léger, compact et capable de projeter des images Full HD jusqu’à 120 pouces, le Philips NeoPix 560 Smart est un picoprojecteur qui cumule les bons points.
- Un poids plume
- Des images en Full HD jusqu’à 120 pouces
- Google TV intégré
Initialement affiché à 348,29 euros, le Philips NeoPix 560 Smart est aujourd’hui disponible en promotion à 259,71 euros chez Boulanger.
iRobot Roomba Plus 675 Combo
L’iRobot Roomba Plus 675 Combo entretient efficacement votre intérieur grâce à son aspiration puissante et son nettoyage des sols boosté par l’intelligence artificielle.
- Pour son système de nettoyage efficace en deux temps
- Une forte puissance d’aspiration de 30 000 Pa
- L’AutoWash Dock se charge de l’entretien
Sur le site de Boulanger, vous pourrez acheter l’iRobot Roomba Plus 675 Combo pour 599 euros alors qu’il est habituellement vendu à 799 euros.
Koorui G2721E
Le Koorui G2721E est un écran gaming 27 pouces qui associe une dalle IPS QHD (2560 x 1440) à un taux de rafraîchissement de 320 Hz – une combinaison qu’on retrouve habituellement sur des références bien plus onéreuses.
- Dalle IPS QHD 27 pouces avec 320 Hz de rafraîchissement
- Temps de réponse de 1 ms et compatibilité Adaptive-Sync
- Hauteur réglable et support VESA 75 x 75 mm
Le Koorui G2721E est disponible en promotion à 169,99 euros sur la Fnac, au lieu de 259,99 euros.
Google Pixel Watch 4
La Google Pixel Watch 4 a apporté une nette évolution par rapport à la Google Pixel Watch 3 à bien des égards, notamment au niveau de l’écran et de la puce qui l’anime. Avec aussi un cheval de bataille en matière d’intelligence artificielle puisqu’on passe de l’assistant Google à Gemini, avec notamment la fonction « lever pour parler » qui permet de ne pas avoir à donner de mot déclencheur.
- Pour son écran Actua 360 lumineux et 10 % plus grand
- Pour ses finitions impeccables avec son boîtier en alu recyclé
- Pour la fiabilité de son capteur de suivi cardiaque
Au lieu de 449 euros, la Google Pixel Watch 4 version 45 mm est actuellement en promotion à seulement 249 euros chez Boulanger. Fnac s’est depuis aligné à son concurrent pour proposer la montre au même prix.
ECOVACS Deebot X12 Pro Omni
Le Deebot X12 Pro Omni fait partie des aspirateurs robots haut de gamme qui combinent aspiration puissante et lavage des sols – on l’a d’ailleurs intégré à notre sélection des meilleurs modèles. Sa station gère seule le vidage de la poussière, le remplissage en eau propre et le séchage du rouleau-brosse, ce qui réduit au minimum les interventions manuelles.
- Aspiration à 22 000 Pa avec rouleau anti-emmêlement pour poils d’animaux
- Station autonome : vidage, remplissage et séchage du rouleau automatiques

Le Deebot X12 Pro Omni est disponible à 599 euros chez Boulanger, au lieu de 749 euros habituellement.
Asus ROG Strix 18
L’Asus ROG Strix 18 est un laptop parfait pour jouer. Outre sa configuration compétitive, il possède un grand écran de 18 pouces avec un affichage en QHD.

L’Asus ROG Strix 18 est actuellement disponible à 2 199,99 euros au lieu de 2 499,99 euros sur le site de Boulanger grâce au code GAMER100.
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra
Le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra est l’un des derniers pliables de la marque sud-coréenne, le plus fin de sa lignée, à retrouver en ce moment avec plus de 700 euros de réduction.
- Un écran interne de 8 pouces AMOLED LTPO
- Seulement 4,1 mm d’épaisseur déplié et 215 grammes sur la balance
- Un capteur grand-angle de 200 mégapixels et de la vidéo 8K
Lancé à 2 199 euros, le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra tombe aujourd’hui à 1 485 euros pour les membres Amazon Prime et à 1 499 euros pour les autres.
Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G
Le Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G mise tout sur l’endurance avec sa batterie silicium-carbone de 8 340 mAh, un écran de 3 500 nits et une certification d’étanchéité complète – noté 7/10 dans notre test, c’est la version 8 Go + 512 Go qui est en promotion aujourd’hui.
- Batterie silicium-carbone de 8 340 mAh, jusqu’à 2,4 jours d’autonomie

- Étanchéité totale à l’eau et à la poussière, charge rapide 67 W
Le Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G (8 + 512 Go) est disponible en promotion à 399 euros sur Amazon, au lieu de 553 euros habituellement.
Sony WH-1000XM4C
Le 7 septembre, Sony a officialisé son WH-1000XM4C. Il s’agit d’une mise à jour de son XM4, sorti en 2020, qui restait encore intéressant six ans plus tard. Le casque revient ainsi au catalogue, dont il avait disparu en juillet, avec quelques nouveautés comme un son retravaillé.
- Une réduction de bruit qui n’a pas pris une ride

En entrant le code AUDIO10 sur le site de Boulanger, vous pourrez profiter du Sony WH-1000XM4C pour 224,99 euros au lieu de 249,99 euros.
Samsung TQ75QN82H

- Une grande dalle Neo QLED de 75 pouces

- Tizen OS
Initialement affiché à 1 499 euros, le TV Samsung TQ75QN82H est aujourd’hui disponible en promotion à 1 299 euros chez Boulanger.
Philips 55PQS9011/12
Le Philips 55PQS9011/12, un TV QLED 4K de 55 pouces équipé de l’Ambilight, est proposé à un super prix en cette avant-première du Black Friday, mais les stocks sont très limitées.

- HDMI 2.1, VRR jusqu’à 144 Hz et FreeSync Premium pour jouer

iiyama X2491H-B1

- Dalle IPS 120 Hz avec temps de réponse de 1 ms
- Luminosité de 350 cd/m² et contraste de 1500:1

L’iiyama X2491H-B1 est disponible à 76,91 euros sur Joybuy, au lieu de 99,99 euros.
TP-Link Deco BE22
Le Deco BE22 est un kit mesh Wi-Fi 7 en deux points d’accès, conçu pour couvrir jusqu’à 130 m² avec un débit maximal annoncé de 2 882 Mbps – de quoi encaisser sans sourciller le streaming 4K, les jeux en ligne et les appareils connectés en simultané.
- Wi-Fi 7 avec débit jusqu’à 2 882 Mbps sur la bande 5 GHz
- Réseau maillé pour une couverture jusqu’à 130 m² sans rupture
- Contrôle parental, pare-feu et compatibilité WPA3 intégrés
Le TP-Link Deco BE22 (pack de 2) est disponible en promotion à 99,99 euros chez Boulanger, au lieu de 199,99 euros.
Garmin fenix 8
Taillée pour les sportifs exigeants, la Garmin Fenix 8 reste une montre connectée très performante et tout à fait recommandable, même deux ans après sa sortie.
- Une montre robuste
- Une dalle Amoled lumineuse de 1,4 pouce
- Un suivi GPS précis et suivi de fréquence cardiaque fiable
Lancée à 999,99 euros, mais affichée à 799,99 euros sur le site officiel de la marque, la montre connectée Garmin Fenix 8 (47 mm, acier) est actuellement disponible en promotion à 559 euros chez Joybuy.
Sony Bravia Theatre Quad

articles.title: Sam Altman (OpenAI) préfèrerait que la RAM de votre PC aille dans ses datacenters
articles.text:
Il y a des phrases qu’il vaut mieux ne pas prononcer quand on est en partie responsable du problème. Sam Altman, patron et fondateur d’OpenAI, peut-être légèrement saoul, bière à la main, en a prononcé une dans le podcast Cheeky Pint publié le 29 octobre 2026.
Vers la 29e minute, la discussion porte sur ces internautes qui font tourner des modèles d’IA open source en local, sur des PC qu’ils possèdent déjà ou qu’ils montent pour l’occasion. Le patron d’OpenAI n’est pas fan du tout de la pratique.
Pourquoi ?
Avoir tout ce monde qui garde une partie de l’offre mondiale limitée de DRAM, c’est « assez terrible », explique-t-il, puisque cette mémoire dort dans des machines utilisées 5 % du temps. Dans le cloud, au contraire, on cherche l’utilisation maximale. Et d’ajouter, un brin étonné, que l’intuition de beaucoup de gens va dans le sens inverse.
Une RAM qui coûte désormais un bras
Le contexte rend la sortie savoureuse. Un kit de 32 Go de DDR5, qui se trouvait autour de 119 euros en octobre 2025, s’affichait vers 414 euros à la mi-octobre 2026 selon les relevés de Hardware Cooking. Dans notre guide mis à jour et sur les tarifs européens, on suggère 16 Go de RAM pour 288 €. Et on peut vous dire qu’on a cherché. Le tout, avant l’arrivée massive de la robotique dans l’équation, qui pourrait faire encore augmenter les prix..
La cause est connue : les fabricants de mémoire (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) réservent leurs lignes de production aux puces destinées aux serveurs d’IA, bien plus rentables, au détriment des barrettes grand public. Parmi les plus gros clients, on trouve évidemment OpenAI, qui avait signé fin 2025 avec Samsung et SK Hynix des accords pour sécuriser une part considérable de la production mondiale de DRAM, dans le cadre de son projet Stargate. Bref, oui, Sam Altman juge que votre RAM est mal utilisée tout en étant l’un de ceux qui vous empêchent d’en acheter.
Sur le fond, on va se faire taper, mais l’argument d’Altman n’est pas idiot. C’est la logique de l’autopartage ou des robotaxis appliquée au silicium : une voiture reste garée 95 % du temps, et une barrette de RAM dans un PC de bureau ne fait pas grand-chose la nuit. Mutualiser les ressources dans des datacenters qui tournent jour et nuit est, sur le papier, plus efficace pour la planète comme pour le portefeuille.
Sauf que l’efficacité n’est pas le seul critère pour l’Humanité (ça se saurait). La RAM d’un PC ne sert pas qu’à l’IA : elle fait tourner des jeux, du montage vidéo, des dizaines d’onglets de navigateur. Et faire tourner un modèle en local, c’est garder ses données chez soi, ne dépendre d’aucune panne de serveur, d’aucune hausse de tarif ni d’aucun changement de conditions d’utilisation. Bref, posséder son outil plutôt que le louer. Les commentateurs de Tom’s Hardware, qui a relayé l’interview, ne s’y sont pas trompés : pour beaucoup, Altman défend avant tout son modèle économique, celui de modèles fermés qui ne tournent que dans ses serveurs et se paient au mois.
Le raisonnement suppose aussi que la construction de datacenters ne ralentira jamais, et que la capacité ainsi mutualisée finira par profiter à tout le monde à prix raisonnable. Pour l’instant, la mutualisation se traduit surtout par des abonnements à 20 dollars par mois (minimum) et des barrettes à 500 euros.
Notez enfin que le podcast est particulièrement intéressant, au-delà de cette sortie, et mérite largement l’écoute.
