articles.title: How Ghana’s TrustCheck helps shoppers vet online sellers before they pay - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ghanaian startup TrustCheck has built a review and trust platform that allows consumers to check out businesses, especially social media sellers, before they part with their money.
Launched in January of this year by Elliot Brenya, Tema-based TrustCheck lets users look up a business, read verified customer reviews, and see a trust score out of 100. The score combines a business’s rating, review volume, how responsive it is to customers, verification status and any open disputes.
“A lot of buying in Ghana now happens on Instagram, TikTok, X and WhatsApp. You see a product, message the seller, send money by Mobile Money and hope it arrives,” Brenya told Disrupt Africa. “Most of the time it does, but when it doesn’t, there is usually no way to get your money back and no record that warns the next person. TrustCheck is meant to be that record.”
Brenya was inspired to build the platform after being scammed while buying a mobile device, having relied on fake ratings for the vendor.
All reviews on TrustCheck are moderated before going live, and reviewers can attach proof of purchase, such as MoMo receipts or order chats, which only moderators can see. Businesses cannot pay to have reviews removed, but can claim their pages for free, respond to reviews and apply for verification. This month the startup also launched a scam check for phone numbers, MoMo numbers, social media handles and websites, as well as a public API that returns a business’s trust score.
“There are global review sites, but they were built around formal businesses with websites and card payments. The sellers people in Ghana worry about most are an Instagram page, a TikTok shop or a WhatsApp number,” Brenya said. “Nothing gives you one searchable place, built for how people here actually buy and pay, that you can check in a minute before sending money.”
The platform is free for shoppers, and makes money by charging businesses for verification and premium tools. It also runs display advertising. Bootstrapped so far, TrustCheck has around 300 registered reviewers and over 50 businesses listed, 20 of which have signed up to manage their pages. It has secured its first paying business customers, though Brenya said revenue remains small.
“Encouraging on the consumer side and slower on the business side, which is what we expected,” he said. “A page they don’t control, with reviews they can’t delete, feels like a risk at first. The ones who have engaged see it the other way round: a page with real reviews and replies is the best proof a small online seller can show a new customer.”
TrustCheck is focused on Ghana for now, but sees West Africa as the obvious next step.
“The problem is the same in Nigeria, Ivory Coast, Kenya and anywhere else where social commerce and mobile money have grown faster than ways to check who you are paying,” Brenya said.

articles.title: Come for capability, not just capacity: Why Europe is looking to India for tech partnerships
articles.text:
Come for capability, not just capacity: Why Europe is looking to India for tech partnerships
At TechSparks 2026, representatives from Switzerland, the Netherlands, and Denmark discussed how Indian startups can tap European research, funding, and markets, and why international collaboration is essential to technological growth.
Countries around the world are investing in their own semiconductor capabilities, AI models, and critical infrastructure. But building everything independently is neither practical nor always necessary. The challenge is to balance strategic sovereignty with international collaboration.
This was the focus of a panel titled 'New tech alliances: Why the world's startups need India, and India needs the world' at TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru on October 15. The discussion explored how Indian startups could work with international technology ecosystems and how global partners could build stronger ties with India.
The panel featured Dr Angela Honegger, CEO and Consul General, Swissnex India (Switzerland); Jacobus Johannes 'Jaap' Veerman, Consul-General of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Bangalore; and Peter Winther-Schmidt of the Consulate General of Denmark in Bangalore. The three representatives discussed programs that help startups access research, funding, markets, and partnerships across India and Europe.
Balancing sovereignty and collaboration
“We have to avoid equating strategic sovereignty with technological independence,” Winther-Schmidt said.
While defence and security require a degree of sovereignty, he argued that areas such as talent, research, and technical interoperability benefit from international cooperation.
He cited the European Union’s digital identity wallet, which he said is being built on the Indian technology stack with support from India.
Veerman agreed that countries should identify what is critical to their own ecosystems while remaining open to partnerships.
“I don't believe in isolation,” he said, emphasising the importance of finding the right partners.
Honegger also stressed the need for cooperation. “If we want a fighting chance, we have to collaborate,” she said.
Switzerland: Connecting research with startups
Honegger described Swissnex as a science consulate with six locations worldwide, including Bengaluru.
Its programs cover student and researcher exchanges, joint research funding for Swiss-Indian teams, bilateral startup exchanges, and market-validation camps. Under its startup program, 10 startups from each country visit the other to explore opportunities.
She cited Suind, a company working across AI, drones, and agriculture, as an example of cross-border collaboration.
Founded by a Swiss and an Indian entrepreneur, Suind initially opened a subsidiary in Bengaluru before switching the locations of its headquarters and subsidiary.
“Technically, they are an Indian startup with a Swiss arm,” Honegger said.
She encouraged Indian deeptech founders to consider moving part of their research and development operations to Switzerland while retaining their headquarters and manufacturing in India.
Switzerland Innovation Parks, she said, offer access to research facilities, specialized technology platforms and public funding for joint R&D with Swiss institutions. Bengaluru-based robotics startup CynLr has already opened a subsidiary in one of these parks.
Honegger also highlighted Apertus, Switzerland's open-source large language model, as an example of efforts to develop public AI infrastructure and prevent control of the technology from becoming concentrated “in the hands of a few corporates”.
The Netherlands: Partnerships across the semiconductor industry
Veerman spoke about the Netherlands’ semiconductor partnership with India, signed a couple of months earlier.
The agreement covers semiconductor design, photonics, and advanced packaging, alongside manufacturing. He also said Dutch semiconductor equipment company ASML is establishing a presence in India.
The Dutch consulate recently brought 17 startups to Semicon India as part of its efforts to strengthen technology ties between the two countries.
Veerman also highlighted Brain Bridge, a programme connecting Dutch and Indian universities with Dutch companies already operating in India.
Five Indian medtech startups have been selected for grants to explore opportunities in the Netherlands, while a cybersecurity mission is also being planned.
“We look at Bangalore as the Silicon Valley of Asia,” Veerman said.
Denmark: Supporting joint development
“The key word for us is co-development,” said Winther-Schmidt, outlining Denmark’s approach to working with Indian startups.
He highlighted the country's Water Challenge, which brings 10 selected Indian startups to Danish universities to work on AI-led water-cleaning solutions. The startups subsequently pitch their ideas to investors, with seed funding available.
Denmark’s Green Strategic Partnership with India is also being renewed and expanded to include spacetech, deeptech, and defence technology.
Winther-Schmidt pointed to a recent memorandum of understanding between DTU and IIT Madras, alongside efforts to bring venture capital and private equity investors from both countries together through a “financing bridge”.
He also mentioned the Danish Impact Fund, which primarily provides loans for solutions that have a positive environmental impact.
What Indian startups should keep in mind
The three representatives offered practical advice for Indian founders looking to enter European markets.
Winther-Schmidt urged startups to identify a specific market rather than approach Europe as a single destination.
“Don't treat Europe as a single destination,” he said.
He advised founders to validate their value proposition before entering a market, invest time in building relationships, and be willing to share their solutions with local partners rather than being overly protective of them.
Honegger called for greater willingness among Indian companies to take risks when working with international startups.
She wanted to see “more risk appetite... to become a co-creator and not just a receiver of innovation”.
Swiss startups, she explained, often find that discussions with potential Indian partners end after a free pilot project. She argued that companies should be more willing to share the financial and operational risks of developing new technologies.
The solution, she said, was to “share the risk that comes with innovation on multiple shoulders”.
During the audience interaction, an 11-year-old founder asked how smaller companies could navigate European regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The panel advised startups to prepare early, choose their target markets carefully, and seek guidance from local partners, consultants, and consulates.
India as a partner for capability
Winther-Schmidt said Danish companies had traditionally viewed India primarily as a market that offered scale. But that, he argued, was only part of the opportunity.
“You don’t come to India for capacity, you come actually to India for capability,” he said. He also emphasized that international partnerships should involve learning on both sides.
“We don't have so much we can teach India... We can learn as much from them,” he added.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: Un agujero negro que se parte en dos suena imposible. Un nuevo estudio dice que la física deja una rendija abierta
articles.text:
La física de los agujeros negros está rodeada aún de muchas preguntas sin resolver. Por ejemplo, sabemos que dos agujeros negros pueden fusionarse para dar lugar a uno más grande, ¿pero puede un gran agujero negro dividirse en dos más pequeños? Tradicionalmente se ha pensado que no, pues iría en contra de las leyes de la física. Sin embargo, un equipo de científicos de la Universidad Federico II de Nápoles, la Sorbona de París y la Universidad del Sur de Dinamarca acaba de encontrar un atajo teórico por el que sí sería posible.
Una cuestión de orden. Según la segunda ley de la termodinámica, la entropía de un sistema aislado siempre tiende a aumentar. A muy grandes rasgos, la entropía hace referencia al desorden, o la cantidad de conformaciones microscópicas distintas que puede alcanzar dicho sistema. Por eso, siempre se dice que el Universo tiende al desorden.
Generalmente, en la mayoría de objetos, la entropía es proporcional a la cantidad de materia, por lo que si se rompe en dos un pedazo de papel su entropía no disminuirá, ya que la suma de los dos pedazos sigue siendo la misma. Con los agujeros negros, la cosa cambia, ya que en ellos la entropía es proporcional al área del horizonte de sucesos, que crece con el cuadrado de la masa irreducible del agujero negro. Si un agujero negro se divide en dos, el área de sus horizontes de sucesos será más pequeña, de modo que la entropía disminuye. Iría contra las leyes de la física.
La clave está en el giro. Según los autores de este estudio reciente, sí que podría haber una forma de que un agujero negro se divida en dos sin disminuir su entropía. Podría ocurrir si gira muy rápido, prácticamente al límite de lo permitido por la física. Esto es así porque la energía está relacionada con la masa. Todos conocemos la famosa fórmula E=mc^2. Si un objeto gira muy rápido, parte de su masa está invertida en la energía necesaria para llevar a cabo el giro. Por lo tanto, ya que hemos visto que la entropía es proporcional al cuadrado de la masa, para una masa fija, cuanto más rápido girase un agujero negro, menor sería su entropía.
Al dividirse en dos, puede que la cantidad de giro, conocida como momento angular, pasase de ser de rotación (el agujero negro sobre sí mismo) a momento angular orbital (un objeto alrededor de otro). Los agujeros negros resultantes girarían uno en torno a otro, pero no sobre sí mismos, por lo que se recuperaría parte de esa masa invertida en el giro y la entropía podría no disminuir.
Podrían fusionarse. Una vez que el agujero negro se dividiese, podría ocurrir que los dos fragmentos se atrajesen entre sí, cayesen uno encima del otro y volviesen a unirse. Por eso, la energía debería ser suficiente para escapar a esa atracción. Algo así como ocurre con la velocidad de escape de un cohete. Esto hace aún más excepcional la separación; pero, según los cálculos de estos científicos, no es imposible.
Otros parámetros. Más allá de la velocidad de giro, el estudio incluye otros parámetros que favorecerían la división teórica del agujero negro, como son la existencia de más dimensiones o la gravedad modificada.
Más probable en los agujeros negros primordiales. Estos científicos creen que los agujeros negros primordiales reunirían mejor las cualidades necesarias para que se produzca esta separación.
Solo son cálculos. Cabe destacar que todo esto es física teórica. Se ha visto que, bajo ciertas condiciones, los cálculos no prohiben que un agujero negro se divida en dos. No obstante, no se ha demostrado de forma práctica ni se ha observado. No hay más que ver que lo más probable es que ocurre en los agujeros negros primordiales y que estos también son objetos teóricos. Aun así, es interesante comprender que la física permitiría que esto ocurra. Y es que, si de verdad llega a pasar, veríamos que las leyes de Einstein se aplican muy bien a lo que hemos observado hasta el momento, pero tendrían algunas lagunas que pulir.

articles.title: MacBook Pro tactile : Apple veut vraiment que vous mettiez vos doigts sur l'écran
articles.text:
Apple semble ne pas savoir sur quel pied danser à propos de l’arrivée du tactile sur son MacBook Pro. Gadget pour certains ou fonctions utiles pour d’autres, difficile de vendre cet ajout auprès d’un public aussi varié. Une chose est sûre : Apple veut aller plus loin avec l’expérience tactile de macOS.
« Ça ne fait que commencer » : l’expérience tactile de macOS va s’améliorer
John Ternus l’a expliqué, « il y a des moments où le tactile est pratique et confortable » sur le nouveau MacBook Pro tactile. Une amélioration mise en avant dans la communication d’Apple : la marque a surtout invité des créateurs de contenu en ligne à sa présentation, qui sont les plus susceptibles de l’utiliser, et elle a axé ses vidéos d’annonce sur cette fonction. D’un autre côté, Apple a pour défi de ne pas déboussoler les clients actuels ou historiques de son MacBook Pro. Son dirigeant a précisé dans la presse que « la fonction tactile ne dévalorise en rien le produit. Il ne l’alourdit pas, il ne l’épaissit pas. » Difficile de voir ce qu’Apple pense vraiment, alors que le principal obstacle à l’achat de cet ordinateur reste son prix.
Néanmoins, comme l’a écrit le journaliste de Bloomberg Chris Welch, en employé d’Apple a répondu aux questions des journalistes ce mercredi. Il « a déclaré que l’entreprise ne faisait que commencer l’optimisation de macOS pour les écrans tactiles. » On peut ainsi s’attendre à des nouveautés sur cet usage dès l’année prochaine avec l’arrivée de macOS 28, qui devrait être présenté lors de la conférence WWDC 2027 qui devrait avoir lieu en juin prochain.
Que permet déjà l’écran tactile du nouveau MacBook Pro ?
Il faut dire que pour le moment, Apple a offert le service minimum sur les fonctions tactiles de son ordinateur avec son écran Proled XDR. Un simple toucher fait un clic, deux touchers rapides font deux clics, pincer l’écran à deux doigts permet de zoomer en avant ou en arrière, etc. Apple a essentiellement reproduit les clics et les gestes du trackpad sur l’écran pour ne pas perdre ses utilisateurs. Certains gestes sont mêmes configurables. Cela a l’avantage d’avoir beaucoup d’applications Mac existantes qui répondent au doigt sans avoir besoin d’être retouchées. Bonne nouvelle, on peut interagir au doigt avec la nouvelle Dynamic Island qui a été ajoutée sur ce MacBook Pro.
Dans les usages plus précis, par exemple les peuvent tester des applications iOS et iPadOS directement sur l’écran du MacBook Pro ; pratique pour éviter d’installer leurs applications à chaque test. Apple a pensé à optimiser certains de ses logiciels : Pixelmator Pro (pour dessiner ou peindre), Logic Pro (pour jouer sur un clavier virtuel), Final Cut Pro (pour déposer des clips à l’endroit voulu), Creator Studio, etc.
Pour aller plus loin, Apple n’aura pas seulement besoin d’ajouter de nouvelles fonctions tactiles. L’entreprise compte s’appuyer sur les développeurs d’applications tierces et elle a déjà prévu le coup. Ces derniers disposent de nouvelles API de gestes à l’échelle du système pour créer des interfaces réellement tactiles.

articles.title: From Beginner to Bug Hunter: Learning Cybersecurity in the AI Era.
articles.text:
Finding a real security flaw and getting paid for it is an appealing goal when you are learning cyber security. Bug bounties give you a chance to test your skills on real software and help its developers make it safer.
Headlines about programs closing or pausing under a flood of AI reports can make that route feel less certain.
Earlier this year, curl, the widely used data transfer tool and library, ended its paid bounty program after similar problems.
As a beginner, these decisions raise a practical question about where to put your effort.
A useful starting point is understanding what went wrong, then building the skills to produce findings that someone else can verify.
Why some bug bounty programs are pulling back
A bug bounty program rewards eligible security findings under a defined set of rules. Developers must still review each submission, reproduce the issue and assess its impact.
A convincing report about an imaginary vulnerability can consume time that a small security team needs for genuine problems.
When curl ended its program on January 31, 2026, maintainer Daniel Stenberg explained how the quality of submissions had deteriorated. He confirmed vulnerabilities fell from above 15% in previous years to below 5% starting in 2025. Across its lifetime, the program had helped uncover 87 confirmed vulnerabilities and paid researchers more than $100,000.
Those figures describe curl’s experience specifically.
Google’s pause also has a defined scope: supply chain submissions and outstanding reports remain unaffected. Its wider vulnerability rewards programs paid researchers $17.1 million in 2025. The closures and restrictions show pressure on particular programs, while other opportunities continue.
Learn cyber security hands-on, right in your browser
TryHackMe gives you browser-based labs and guided learning paths for every level, from complete beginner to advanced practitioner.
Join 8 million+ learners and start free, with no setup needed.
Start Learning
A glimmer of hope
In April, Stenberg reported that submission quality had improved and the share of confirmed vulnerabilities had returned to roughly 15% to 16%.
He observed extensive AI use in those reports. Researchers were finding real problems, although the growing volume still created work for maintainers.
For someone learning, the lesson is to take responsibility for the evidence behind a finding. Generating a report is easy compared with establishing whether its claim holds up.
Build the foundations you need to check a finding
Before chasing your first payout, learn how the systems you plan to test work. For web security, that means understanding HTTP requests, login sessions, permissions and how applications handle data.
Basic networking and command line skills help you investigate what is happening when a tool produces an unexpected result.
Practise these ideas in an environment designed for learning. You can make mistakes, repeat a test and inspect the result without affecting a live service. Choose a specific skill for each session, such as explaining a request or identifying which account is allowed to access a resource.
TryHackMe’s Cyber Security 101 learning path covers networking, Linux and Windows fundamentals, web application basics, and offensive and defensive security. Working through a structured path gives each new tool a purpose and helps you understand the evidence it produces.
After a lab, write down what you changed, what happened and why. Then repeat the task with your notes closed. Being able to explain and reproduce the result is a useful way to check your progress.
Use AI to support your learning
AI can help explain an unfamiliar error, suggest questions to investigate or review the clarity of your notes. You will get more useful practice if you attempt the task first and give the model a specific point of confusion.
After inspecting a lab request, for example, ask the model to explain how the session cookie relates to the logged-in account. If you are stuck, ask for one hint and describe what you have already tried. Then test your next step and explain why it worked.
Finish the session by doing the task again without assistance. If you can explain which evidence supports the finding and what would disprove it, you have learned something you can use beyond that exercise.
Make every report possible to reproduce
Imagine an authorized training application with two test accounts. Changing an invoice identifier returns a successful response. To establish an access control flaw, you still need to show that one account can access the other account’s private test invoice and that this violates the application’s intended permissions.
Record the behavior you can demonstrate, including the conditions required for it to happen. Keep any claim about wider impact tied to evidence.
Before submitting the finding, check that your report includes:
- The affected asset or software version, with confirmation that your testing falls within the program's scope.
- The setup and exact steps needed to reproduce the issue, including any required account permissions.
- The expected behavior and the actual result, supported by relevant requests, responses or other evidence with sensitive information removed.
- The demonstrated security impact, with any assumptions or untested possibilities clearly identified.
Give your first month a clear purpose
A month of focused practice can help you establish useful habits. Adjust the pace to your starting point and measure progress by what you can explain and repeat:
- In week one, work through networking, operating system and web basics. Draw a simple request flow and explain where identity and permissions are checked.
- In week two, choose one vulnerability type and practise it across several authorized labs. Keep a short record of the evidence behind each result.
- In week three, use AI for hints after making your own attempt. Revisit an earlier lab without help, then examine the logs or other evidence a defender could use to spot the activity.
- In week four, write a complete report for a lab finding. Ask a peer to reproduce it from your instructions, or follow them yourself from a fresh setup and fix anything missing.
By the end, you should have a record of your reasoning and a report you can improve. Continue practicing wherever you still need help. Readiness for a live program depends on your skills and its rules, so use the month as a starting point.
Keep your career options open
Bug bounty work is one way to apply security skills. The same habit of checking evidence matters in security operations, incident response and penetration testing.
When you investigate a lab, practice explaining how a defender could detect the issue and what a developer could change to fix it.
Bounty income depends on a finding being valid, eligible and covered by the program’s payment rules.
Learning will be easier to sustain if you judge progress by the skills you are building. Save clear lab notes and share write-ups where the training platform permits them, so you have concrete work to discuss as you explore security roles.
For your next session, choose one exercise, make your own attempt and keep the evidence that explains the result.
And if you need guidance along the way, TryHackMe offers the ultimate path to get you started just as you would in an actual security environment.

articles.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
articles.text:
Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- RIKEN
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.
- Share:
Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.
Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.
Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."
Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors
Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.
Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.
This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.
To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.
"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.
Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%
The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.
When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.
The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.
Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.
According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."
A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors
The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.
This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.
"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."
The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.
"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.
Story Source:
Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yi-Hsien Wu, Leon C. Camenzind, Patrick Bütler, Ik Kyeong Jin, Akito Noiri, Kenta Takeda, Takashi Nakajima, Takashi Kobayashi, Giordano Scappucci, Hsi-Sheng Goan, Seigo Tarucha. Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03466-2

articles.title: Fin a 28 años de historia: Telefónica dejará de encargarse de prestar el Servicio Universal de Telecomunicaciones
articles.text:
A partir del 1 de enero de 2027, Telefónica dejará de ser la operadora obligada a prestar el servicio universal de telecomunicaciones, ese mínimo de teléfono fijo e internet que puede pedir cualquiera, viva donde viva. Así lo prevé el proyecto de orden del Ministerio para la Transformación Digital y de la Función Pública. El texto salió a audiencia pública el 7 de octubre de 2026, y con esta orden se cierran 28 años de historia.
Casi tres décadas de Telefónica. El servicio universal arrancó en España en diciembre de 1998, con la liberalización de las telecomunicaciones, y desde entonces ha sido Telefónica la que ha cargado con él, tal y como recoge un documento de la antigua Comisión del Mercado de las Telecomunicaciones. Al principio giraba alrededor de la línea de teléfono fijo, pero desde el 1 de enero de 2012 incluye también una conexión a internet de 1 Mbps, según el mismo documento.
Una banda ancha con poco tirón. Pero esa banda ancha universal nunca ha sido demasiado popular, entre otras cosas debido a sus límites de descarga y a una velocidad que siguió anclada en 1 Mbps hasta 2022. Ese año, con la Ley General de Telecomunicaciones, el mínimo pasó a 10 Mbps, la cifra que sigue vigente según el proyecto de reglamento del servicio universal.
Por qué el Ministerio da el paso. El proyecto de orden sostiene que la fibra, el cable, el acceso fijo radio y el satélite forman “un extenso abanico de tecnologías” que permite constatar “la universalización de las redes de muy alta capacidad para todo el territorio nacional”. De hecho, el texto destaca un “excelente nivel de cobertura” de fibra óptica y 5G, además de la evolución de las redes por satélite. Y con ese panorama, apoyándose en el artículo 35.6 de la Ley General de Telecomunicaciones, el Ministerio concluye que el teléfono y la banda ancha fijos quedan “garantizados por las circunstancias normales de explotación comercial”, así que no renovará a Telefónica cuando su designación termine el 31 de diciembre de 2026.
Qué podrás pedir desde 2027. A partir de esa fecha dejará de haber un único operador designado, y cada compañía tendrá que ofrecer el servicio universal dentro de la zona en la que dé cobertura, según el proyecto de orden. Las condiciones las concreta el proyecto de reglamento, que el Ministerio sometió a audiencia pública el 22 de abril de 2026 y que todavía está en tramitación. Si sale adelante tal cual, tanto particulares como microempresas, pymes y organizaciones sin ánimo de lucro podrán exigir 100 Mbps de bajada, 5 Mbps de subida y una latencia media máxima de 690 milisegundos, además de la función de Texto en Tiempo Real (RTT) en las llamadas.
Además, el proyecto de reglamento obligaría a todos los operadores a aplicar a quienes cobren el Ingreso Mínimo Vital un descuento de al menos el 25% sobre su precio comercial, tanto en el alta como en la cuota mensual.

articles.title: Anthropic manager stops coding interviews because Claude beats most candidates
articles.text:
A hot potato: These days, plenty of software engineers spend weeks grinding LeetCode problems just to get through a single round of interviews. One engineering manager at Anthropic has now stopped using that round altogether. Claude, he says, beats most candidates at those puzzles anyway.
That manager is Felix Rieseberg. He's led engineering on Claude.ai and the Claude Code desktop app, among other things. Earlier this week, he posted on X that the coding interview no longer tells him anything useful. So he pulled it from his team's hiring loops this month.
In a longer blog post, Rieseberg says watching candidates define a problem and land on a neat solution used to be a weak-but-real predictor of how they'd do on his teams. But once Claude got good at those exercises, a small React challenge started telling him about as little as a quiz on assembly.
Anthropic's performance team has run into the same problem with its take-home test. Team lead Tristan Hume wrote in January that Claude Opus 4 outscored most applicants within the time limit. So he made the test harder. Then Opus 4.5 came along and matched even the strongest candidates. Hume's third version now leans on odd, puzzle-game-style problems that Opus 4.5 couldn't crack.
As for Rieseberg, he hasn't settled on a replacement yet. For now, he's scanning resumes and portfolios for small prototypes that show taste, empathy, and principled thinking. He also asked other managers to share anything better they've come up with. Google principal engineer Jaana Dogan replied on X that she'd rather watch candidates work with coding agents because doing so tells her more about their coding skills.
Most of Rieseberg's essay is aimed at junior engineers. Its title, "Hunger beats tenure," pretty much sums up the pitch. He argues that newer engineers can now outpace veterans since building things has gotten so cheap. As proof, he points to two fairly new Anthropic engineers who built a working graphical interface for Claude Code over a single weekend. The first public version shipped about eight days later.
Most talk around AI and new grads has been a lot gloomier, though the hiring data is honestly still mixed. Meanwhile, ZipRecruiter labor economist Nicole Bachaud told The Register that tech employers are still the most likely to test for skills.
In the company's October survey of 1,500 employers, 62.5 percent of those in the information sector required formal skills tests as part of the initial application process. Around 70 percent have also moved those assessments to proctored or in-person sessions to keep AI out.
Anthropic's own candidate guidance still asks applicants to keep Claude out of live interviews and take-home tests unless told otherwise. Rieseberg dropped the coding round only for his own team, too. So anyone applying elsewhere at the company will likely still face one.

articles.title: Banks must become ‘invisible’ to compete in digital finance
articles.text:
Banks must anticipate customers’ needs and embed financial services into everyday transactions to compete with digital platforms, executives from Access Holdings and OPay told Moonshot by TechCabal in Lagos.
Daniel Awe, head of Fintech Foundry at Access Holdings, said banking’s next phase would require institutions to offer services when customers needed them, rather than wait for people to visit a branch or open an application.
“The future of banks is going to be in everyday people, where banks become invisible,” he said during a panel titled “The Next Bank: Competing in the Age of Programmable Money”.
His argument extends the shift from branch banking to mobile services. Moving a transaction onto a phone changes how customers access a bank; integrating finance into activities such as paying school fees or replenishing stock changes when they encounter it.
“When the customer is engaging you, it’s not the future of banking. It’s the banks that now have to place themselves in the life of the customer,” Awe said.
Chukwudinma Okafor, chief compliance officer at OPay Nigeria, said the starting point should be customers’ practical needs, rather than the availability of new technology.
“For us at OPay, the major focus is just to address one thing, and that’s customers. You have to meet the customers where they need you,” he said.
OPay sent developers, technology professionals and sales teams to markets across Nigeria to observe how traders worked and gather feedback, Okafor said. Requests for different sounds to signal successful and failed point-of-sale transactions illustrated how small changes could make a service more useful.
The example highlighted a distinction in the discussion: anticipating customers’ needs can involve sophisticated infrastructure, but the improvement customers value may be straightforward.
Modernising the systems
Awe said traditional banks would also need to overhaul the infrastructure supporting their products. Conventional core banking systems alone were insufficient for competing with fintechs and technology companies offering financial services.
That transition would have to be gradual, preserving reliability and compliance while addressing the risks created by increasingly interconnected systems.
“Whatever you want to achieve, you have to put security in the middle,” he said.
Okafor said digital-first companies had benefited from starting with more modern infrastructure, including cloud-based systems, while established banks were increasingly adopting similar technologies.
Despite their competition for customers, both speakers argued that banks and fintechs remained dependent on one another.
Awe said partnerships combined banks’ financial capabilities with fintechs’ ability to serve particular customer groups. Some businesses required approaches that companies such as OPay could provide more readily, he added.
Okafor pointed to fintechs’ reliance on commercial banks for settlement and the handling of customer funds. Cooperation was also necessary to respond to fraud when money moved between institutions.
“Ultimately, we need each other for the ecosystem to work well,” he said.
The discussion also turned to Nigeria’s approach to cryptocurrency and stablecoins, with Awe describing differing priorities among regulators.
He said the Securities and Exchange Commission had shown greater appetite for cryptocurrency-related activities, while the Central Bank of Nigeria had been more cautious because of monetary policy and consumer protection concerns.
According to Awe, the central bank was examining stablecoin use cases through a regulatory sandbox, allowing approved participants to test services under supervision.
He characterised stablecoins as less volatile than other cryptocurrencies. That distinction was his assessment of their appeal to the regulator, rather than a guarantee of their stability.
For banks weighing new technologies, the broader challenge identified by the panel was to make services easier to access while maintaining the security and reliability customers expected. Becoming less visible in a transaction would require substantial work on the systems behind it.

articles.title: Busy GPUs can hide slow AI inference on Kubernetes
articles.text:
Busy GPUs can hide slow AI inference on Kubernetes
A Kubernetes cluster can be healthy while the AI service running on it disappoints users. A model might return its first token quickly but take too long to finish an answer. It might respond promptly and still give the wrong answer. And a busy GPU tells the operations team little about either outcome. The operational challenge is connecting AI service behavior with the Kubernetes, GPU, compute, storage, and network conditions behind it—not viewing each layer in isolation.
That’s why you should measure an inference service before production, then compare live behavior with the baseline. In the fourth article in this HPE-sponsored series on AI and Kubernetes, The New Stack speaks with Marius Bogoevici, Senior Principal Product Manager for HPE Morpheus Software; Mahesh Ramachandran, Vice President of Product Management for HPE OpsRamp Software; and Karthik Subramanian, Principal Product Manager for HPE Morpheus Software.
Inference adds a further question: Does the whole service deliver a useful result at a cost and speed the business can support?
Earlier in this series:
- Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it.
- Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap
- Part 3: Your Kubernetes dashboard is green. Your users are seeing red.
Start with the experience, then establish a baseline
For a conversational service, Bogoevici recommends measuring time to first token, time per output token, reliability, capacity, resource efficiency, cost, and answer quality. The right mix depends on the experience a team intends to deliver. A quick first token can mask slow subsequent generation; a fast complete response can still be inaccurate or unhelpful.
“A quick first token can mask slow subsequent generation; a fast complete response can still be inaccurate or unhelpful.”
Time to first token and time to a complete response answer different questions. Inter-token latency and time per output token help explain generation speed after the first token arrives. Teams should document where they measure each interval and compare results under sustained load and demand spikes. Set targets for the particular workload and user experience.
Ramachandran urges teams to profile the AI serving system before customers depend on it. Test representative prompt and context lengths, output volumes, and traffic levels. Record token throughput, latency, and service-level measures under those conditions. The resulting baseline gives operators a reference to measure production behavior changes.
Correlating those workload measures with infrastructure performance and capacity helps teams distinguish rising inference demand from resource contention and plan capacity more effectively. As Ramachandran tells The New Stack, teams should “profile it before you launch.”
Quality needs its own evaluation. Bogoevici says teams should ask whether the service gives proper answers or hallucinates. Platform telemetry can show a request was served, but data science and domain specialists need representative tests and acceptance criteria for the answer.
The newly published ebook, Kubernetes in 2027: Building platforms for AI, autonomy, and scale, recommends assessing output quality alongside service performance and revisiting both after model, prompt, retrieval, or serving changes.
When the GPU is busy but the service is slow
GPU utilization is a useful signal, but it does not identify the bottleneck. Bogoevici sketches a misleading victory lap: “Our GPUs are maxed at 100%. So we’re doing well.” That tells teams little about how the service actually performs. Ramachandran suggests checking whether inference pods scale on workload-appropriate metrics, whether requests reach the intended model, and whether related components can be scheduled when needed. Different models can have different latency and capacity demands, so a change in request mix can change the user experience even while GPU activity looks normal.
Bogoevici sketches a misleading victory lap: “Our GPUs are maxed at 100%. So we’re doing well.”
Subramanian adds dependencies around the model: network configuration and database or vector-database response time. He raises another question: “Is the GPU partition too small to serve that model?” These are investigation paths, not a diagnosis that applies to every deployment. Teams should correlate them with the affected requests and time window before choosing a fix.
Kubernetes’ Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can use configured custom or external metrics, so teams do not have to replace it simply because CPU utilization is a poor trigger for inference. They do need to supply and test the metrics pipeline, scaling bounds, and available accelerator capacity for their serving stack. A scaling policy cannot make additional GPU capacity appear instantly.
What HPE Morpheus and OpsRamp contribute
HPE describes HPE Morpheus Software as a platform for governed provisioning and automation across hybrid environments. Its Advanced and Enterprise versions include HPE Kubernetes Service (HKS); Enterprise extends the operating model across hybrid and public-cloud environments. Platform teams can use catalog items, blueprints, access controls, and approvals to define how they request and manage supported environments. This gives platform teams a consistent way to deliver governed self-service and manage VMs and Kubernetes clusters together, reducing separate tooling and manual handoffs. Those capabilities alone do not benchmark a model or decide whether its answers are good.
HPE OpsRamp Software provides full-stack observability and monitoring across multi-vendor hybrid infrastructure and applications, with service maps, AI-powered event correlation, and operational automation to help teams understand dependencies and move from detection to resolution. Ramachandran describes HPE Morpheus as the provisioning engine and OpsRamp as the observability engine in HPE’s broader cloud operations approach.
Ramachandran says HPE’s combined solution includes Morpheus, OpsRamp and runtimes. He says it can measure token service rates in a model-serving environment and token request rates in an agentic workload. HPE is extending OpsRamp’s AI workload observability to connect model and agent activity, token volumes, token serving rates, inference latency, and time to first token with supporting infrastructure telemetry.
The operational value is the correlation: teams can investigate whether slow responses originate in the application, model-serving layer, or infrastructure, while using workload demand to inform capacity planning and cost accountability. For a specific deployment, teams should confirm which component emits each metric, how it is collected, and what additional application instrumentation is needed.
For agentic applications, HPE’s planned observability enhancements extend that context to AI traces, tool calls, errors, and quality signals alongside Kubernetes, CPU, GPU, memory, storage, and network telemetry. Lightweight eBPF and OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation are also planned to deepen visibility while minimizing collection overhead. These signals support investigation; they do not replace domain-specific answer evaluation or security controls.
As the preceding article in this series explains, collecting telemetry across a stack depends on deployed agents, integrations, permissions, and application instrumentation. For an inference service, connect user-facing measurements with model-server metrics and traces, Kubernetes events, and relevant network, database, and accelerator signals. Check where visibility stops, especially at an external model or service boundary.
Plan for AI-specific routing and scheduling
Looking toward 2027, Ramachandran urges teams to examine autoscaling, model routing and scheduling as deliberate design choices for AI workloads. He discusses content-aware request routing, co-scheduling related components, and disaggregated serving. These are areas to evaluate for a specific architecture, not features that every Kubernetes installation or HPE product provides automatically.
An experimental Gateway API proposal describes pre-routing filters and cites the Inference Extension’s Body-Based Router as an example. That router can extract a model name from a request body for use in routing, but teams need a compatible implementation and configuration. They should measure any latency or efficiency benefit from routing and scheduling choices with their own models, traffic, and hardware.
Protect telemetry and share the launch decision
Inference observability also has a data-handling problem. Bogoevici warns that prompts, responses, and retrieved documents may appear in logs and traces. He asks, “What information is actually captured and where does it go?” Teams should decide what to collect, where to store it, how long to retain it, and who can see it. He stresses a simple point: prompts are data. Sensitive content needs protection even when teams collect it for troubleshooting.
Ramachandran sees operations and security observability moving closer together as AI agents introduce new events and access records. He says OpsRamp is preparing to interpret existing telemetry from a security perspective, while agent-specific activity may require additional instrumentation. Teams still need to design and test their security controls and incident response.
Before launch, Ramachandran recommends that business and IT stakeholders agree on the value the service should deliver, including a plausible inference volume tied to a business outcome. “There has to be measurable business value,” he says.
“The goal is not simply busy GPUs, but reliable AI services with performance and resource use aligned to business needs.”
Subramanian makes the sign-off point plainly: “It can’t be a single person.” Platform administrators, machine learning and data science teams, and security teams need to work together and plan for failures or attacks. Add the relevant business owner, test representative load and failure cases, and record the capacity, quality, cost, and recovery evidence behind the decision.
A launch decision should rest on evidence that the service can meet agreed user and business targets and that the responsible teams know what to measure and how to respond when it cannot. After launch, continue comparing AI workload behavior with infrastructure conditions so teams can detect regressions, troubleshoot across layers, and adjust capacity as demand changes. The goal is not simply busy GPUs, but reliable AI services with performance and resource use aligned to business needs.

articles.title: Hasta 5.000 usuarios de Cursor instalaron una versión falsa de Claude Code con una puerta trasera
articles.text:
Cursor, la empresa de herramientas de programación con IA, informó que una versión alterada de la extensión de Claude Code, el asistente de programación de Anthropic, estuvo disponible en su tienda de extensiones durante unas 11 horas del 29 de octubre. Según la compañía, como máximo 5.000 usuarios la descargaron.
La extensión maliciosa estuvo publicada entre las 2:27 y las 13:35, hora del Pacífico de Estados Unidos. Se presentaba como la versión 2.1.313 de Anthropic.claude-code, pero Cursor aclaró que Anthropic no la desarrolló. Reuters, que informó el caso, indicó que Anthropic no respondió de inmediato a su pedido de comentarios.
Cursor, que pertenece a SpaceX, dijo que retiró esa versión apenas la detectó y cerró toda la tienda de extensiones por precaución. Después rotó sus claves de acceso, reconstruyó la tienda y la volvió a abrir. La empresa afirmó que revisó el resto de las extensiones y que ninguna había sido manipulada.
Qué hacía el programa en las computadoras
De acuerdo con el aviso de Cursor, el código malicioso recopilaba el nombre del equipo y del usuario, el sistema operativo, la arquitectura del procesador, la ruta de la carpeta personal, los nombres de las variables de entorno, el correo configurado en Git y la dirección IP pública.
También intentaba agregar una clave SSH del atacante al archivo de claves autorizadas, activar el servicio local de SSH (un método de acceso remoto) y abrir un túnel inverso hacia el servidor del atacante. Para mantenerse activo, instalaba tareas programadas en Windows y un agente de inicio en macOS, que reintentaban la conexión cada 60 segundos.
Cursor precisó que activar el servicio SSH exige permisos de administrador, que la extensión no tiene en la mayoría de los equipos con macOS y Windows. En esos casos el paso falla y el atacante no pudo entrar por el túnel. Aun así, la clave quedaba instalada y los datos del equipo se enviaban al atacante.
La empresa agregó que el servidor del atacante ya no funciona, porque trabajó con el proveedor de nube que lo alojaba para desconectarlo. Cursor dijo no tener pruebas de que otras versiones de la extensión ni la distribución oficial de Anthropic estén afectadas.
Cómo saber si un equipo fue afectado
La clave que agrega el programa lleva la etiqueta “svc-telemetry”. Cursor publicó comandos para macOS y Windows que buscan esa etiqueta en el archivo de claves autorizadas. Si aparece, el equipo está afectado. La empresa dijo que se comunicará directamente con los usuarios que descargaron la versión.
Quienes la instalaron deben aislar el equipo, eliminar la clave y los mecanismos de persistencia, y cambiar las credenciales a las que ese equipo tenía acceso, desde otro sistema de confianza. Desinstalar la extensión no basta, advirtió Cursor, porque el programa deja scripts independientes que siguen ejecutándose.
La firma de seguridad StepSecurity, que analizó el programa en un entorno aislado, señaló que el código malicioso era un cargador insertado en la extensión legítima, unos 7 KB mayor que la versión limpia anterior. Añadió que no se conoce cómo llegó la versión al registro de extensiones: si por credenciales robadas o por otro medio.
Jenn Gile, cofundadora de OpenSourceMalware, dijo a The Hacker News que la versión se retiró con rapidez, pero que quienes tuvieran activada la actualización automática pudieron recibir el programa. Paul McCarty, investigador de seguridad, afirmó que los nombres de las variables recolectadas pueden revelar qué servicios en la nube y qué tipos de credenciales usa cada equipo.
El 30 de octubre, Anthropic publicó la versión 2.1.314 de la extensión en Open VSX, el registro abierto de extensiones que usan Cursor y otros editores, y en la tienda de Microsoft. StepSecurity confirmó que ambas plataformas ya no ofrecen la 2.1.313.

articles.title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
articles.text:
In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape.
Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing “exponential growth” in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels.
The investment in Fujifilm’s Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it “the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities.” The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation “FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10” tape.
Mainstream consumers may have abandoned tape decades ago, but the enterprise world never did. Cloud giants rely on tape to back up vast troves of data. Fujifilm’s work with magnetic tape as a data storage medium dates back to the 1950s, and in 2000, the company released its first LTO Ultrium storage tape. In 2011, the company was the first to commercially produce tape with barium ferrite magnetic particles, and in 2025 it debuted the LTO Ultrium10, the first storage solution in the medium to use what the company calls “fine hybrid magnetic particles” by combining barium ferrite with strontium ferrite tech. Each generation of tape (currently Gen 10) has seen meaningful increases in both compressed and uncompressed storage limits.
According to Fujifilm, “major cloud service and data center operators” have been expanding their use of magnetic tape because it can store large data volumes at relatively low cost. Tape backups can be easily disconnected and stored in a drawer, a vault, or a separate facility. Fujifilm highlights the ability to air-gap tape cartridges as a last defense for user data: “Given the sophistication of cyberattacks, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware.”

articles.title: Jogos populares no Steam ficaram 20% mais baratos, aponta estudo
articles.text:
Enquanto grandes lançamentos de videogame ultrapassam cada vez mais a faixa dos R$ 300, os jogos populares do Steam apresentam uma tendência diferente. Um levantamento da GameDiscoverCo, publicado em novembro de 2025, revelou que o preço mediano dos títulos analisados caiu aproximadamente 20% entre 2023 e 2025.
O resultado está relacionado principalmente ao crescimento de jogos mais baratos, incluindo produções independentes, e à frequência de promoções de títulos mais antigos.
O estudo desconsiderou jogos gratuitos (free-to-play) e analisou o comportamento dos preços entre fevereiro de 2023 e outubro de 2025.
Quanto os preços dos jogos caíram no Steam?
Segundo a GameDiscoverCo, a mediana dos preços passou de US$ 19,50 em 2023 para US$ 15,64 em 2025, uma redução próxima de 20%.
Já o preço médio dos 50 jogos mais populares apresentou uma queda menor, de aproximadamente 2%, passando de US$ 21,80 para US$ 21,41.
A diferença entre os indicadores mostra que, embora os grandes lançamentos continuem chegando ao mercado com valores elevados, jogos mais acessíveis têm conquistado espaço entre os títulos de destaque da plataforma.
Jogos baratos estão conquistando mais espaço
A análise também aponta que o preço pode influenciar diretamente as chances de sucesso de produções menores.
Jogos independentes vendidos entre US$ 10 e US$ 15 conseguem encontrar público no Steam, enquanto títulos próximos de US$ 25 podem enfrentar mais dificuldades, especialmente quando são desenvolvidos por estúdios pouco conhecidos.
Isso não significa que jogos caros deixaram de vender. Grandes produções continuam alcançando bons resultados mesmo com preços de US$ 60 ou US$ 70.
Outro fator importante são as promoções. Descontos que chegam a 50% ou até 90% em jogos antigos contribuem para reduzir o valor pago pelos consumidores.
Os resultados indicam que o mercado de PC apresenta duas tendências simultâneas: enquanto grandes lançamentos ficam mais caros, jogos independentes acessíveis e promoções ampliam as opções para quem procura gastar menos.
Vale destacar que o levantamento considera preços em dólares e não representa necessariamente uma queda equivalente nos valores cobrados no Brasil.
Rachele Victoria é formada em Letras, MBA em Inovação e atua há 10 anos com comunicação e conteúdo gamer.
Amazon Prime também é feito para jogadores!
Todo mês, obtenha itens exclusivos, jogos grátis, uma assinatura gratuita na Twitch.tv e muito mais com sua assinatura Prime. Clique aqui para um teste gratuito de 30 dias.

articles.title: In Other News: Anthropic Breach Dispute, UEFI Flaw Hits Most Servers, Cloudflare AI Data Leak
articles.text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.
This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.
Here are this week’s highlights:
Iran suspected in US military freezer hacks
US officials suspect Iran-linked hackers caused freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at around six military base commissaries starting in late August, Nextgov reports, citing people familiar with the matter. At Fort Huachuca in Arizona, a freezer entered defrost mode and heated its contents, and Cyber Command and Defense Department law enforcement units are investigating with French authorities, after hackers overrode refrigeration controls at some 350 French establishments earlier this month.
Most servers rely on UEFI code hit by critical boot flaw
A critical 16-year-old buffer overflow (CVE-2026-97631) in TianoCore EDK II, open source code that most of the world’s server vendors and data centers use through firmware suppliers such as AMI, Insyde and Phoenix, means the flaw affects most servers worldwide, Ars Technica reports. An attacker with local network access can send an oversized ICMP error message to a machine while it boots over the network (PXE) to hang the process or, if the target’s firmware build is known, run code at the highest privilege level before defenses such as Secure Boot take effect. Only machines that use network boot are exposed, and the flaw, found by Anthropic and Google researchers, became public months ahead of a planned January disclosure after AMI published a code fix, leaving organizations to seek firmware updates from their vendors.
Anthropic disputes scope of ex-DOGE startup’s AI-led intrusion
Cathedral, a cybersecurity startup founded by former DOGE staffers, says its AI agents found ways into Anthropic’s internal systems in less than 12 hours by abusing weaknesses in third-party business software, reaching meeting transcripts, salary and job offer data, and Slack discussions about the company’s most advanced models, according to a draft report reviewed by the Washington Post (paywalled). Anthropic, which received the findings through its bug bounty program, says only a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems was reached, that it cut off the startup’s access the same day, and that Claude conversations, source code and model weights were not affected. It also accuses Cathedral of breaking the bounty program’s rules by not disclosing all of its activity.
Midterm spending disclosures stall after FEC intrusion attempt
The US Federal Election Commission took its electronic filing system offline after someone attempted to breach its systems, according to an internal FEC email seen by Reuters, leaving political groups unable to submit campaign finance reports a week before the November 3 midterm elections. The outage blocked the 24-hour and 48-hour reports that track last-minute spending on specific races, although past filings remained searchable. The system was restored on October 28.
Hackers obtain national ID numbers, card PINs in University of Copenhagen breach
The University of Copenhagen says hackers who gained access to one of its test environments obtained personal data on about 525,000 current and former members of the university community, including names, phone numbers and personal email addresses, along with national identity (CPR) numbers for many of them. The attack was detected on October 20 and contained, but the PIN codes for the ID cards of roughly 20,000 staff and students were also compromised and have since been reissued. The university says it does not yet know who is behind the attack or what the motive was.
ENGIE data breach traced to tool used by sales partners
French energy giant ENGIE says attackers stole customer data after gaining access to a tool its partners use for customer prospecting and marketing energy offers, but that its own internal IT systems were not compromised. The incident is limited to customers in France, and notification letters say the stolen data includes names, contact details, customer IDs, contract numbers and energy supply point identifiers, but no banking information. ENGIE has not said how many customers are affected, and no group has claimed the attack.
Fake ChatGPT and Claude bots probe sites for leaked secrets
Cequence has tracked a single threat actor that rotates through about 32 AI bot identities (including crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Perplexity) while scanning websites for files that commonly hold secrets, such as .env files, cloud credentials and private SSH keys. Running from a major cloud provider since at least late September, the scanner used more than 300 IP addresses in a single day and, on one day in October, reached 48% of the Cequence-protected organizations that saw any AI bot traffic. Cequence warns that a bot’s self-declared identity can’t be trusted, noting that the impersonator accounted for more than 80% of traffic labeled as AI bot traffic at some organizations.
Cloudflare and SGLang fix cross-tenant data leak in AI inference
Cloudflare says that between August 27 and September 9, 155 responses from the GLM 5.3 model on its Workers AI platform contained data from other customers’ recent requests to the same model, all involving prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. The leak resulted from a configuration mismatch that left the model’s KV cache smaller than its advertised context window, combined with a bug in the SGLang inference engine that allowed over-length requests to read cache data left behind by earlier sessions. Cloudflare fixed the issue after Knostic researcher Gadi Evron reported it via HackerOne, found no evidence of deliberate exploitation, and recommends that SGLang operators update to version 0.5.22 or later.
Defense worker, Russian money movers targeted over North Korean IT scheme
John Allen Kurrle Jr., 62, a defense contractor employee with a Top Secret clearance, has pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy for aiding a North Korean remote IT worker scheme by letting foreign individuals use his identity (and that of a third person) to apply for remote jobs and hosting victim companies’ laptops at his home. The applications led to nine job offers from US companies, and Kurrle faces up to 20 years in prison. Separately, OFAC sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity supporting North Korea’s IT worker schemes, including two Russians who allegedly converted the workers’ crypto earnings into cash, two North Koreans who managed Russia-based IT worker groups, and the Russia-based First Financial and Technical Development Center (FFTDC), which deploys North Korean IT workers abroad.
Rockwell aims SecureOT at OEMs facing CRA and machinery rules
Rockwell Automation has added OEM-focused capabilities to its SecureOT offering to help machine builders prepare for cybersecurity requirements under the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and Machinery Regulation. Built on the SecureOT Platform, the additions include machine-level inventories of hardware, software and firmware, vulnerability identification, continuous monitoring for newly disclosed flaws after deployment, and exportable compliance reports for customers and auditors. Rockwell is also offering assessments and advisory services to help OEMs find gaps, set up governance processes, and align with standards such as IEC 62443.
AI moves deeper into ransomware, C2 malware and grey-market tooling
Sophos says the Gold Ogre group behind Aur0ra ransomware has used AI extensively, with agents orchestrated through Cursor handling network discovery, credential attacks and lateral movement with limited human involvement, after the operators bypassed guardrails by framing the intrusions as authorized red team work. Cisco Talos has detailed NIK C2, a new AI-integrated command-and-control framework whose Windows implant can steal credentials, stream keystrokes and deploy screen-locking ransomware. Symantec and Carbon Black, meanwhile, warn of a grey-market relay service, seen at a dozen organizations mostly in mainland China, that installs the genuine Codex and Claude Code CLIs but reconfigures them to route all requests through third-party servers with sandboxing disabled.
Related: In Other News: ICS-Sniper Attack, Hacking XWorm Malware Operators, $250k Chrome Exploit

articles.title: PaperFoam secures €2 million loan to scale sustainable packaging made from starch and natural fibres | EU-Startups
articles.text:
PaperFoam, a Dutch company that manufactures sustainable, biodegradable, starch-based packaging, has secured a €2 million loan from Invest International to expand its production facility in the Czech Republic and strengthen working capital for its Malaysian and U.S. plants.
The Hague-based Invest International is a Dutch government-backed organisation that helps Dutch and Dutch-linked businesses overcome barriers by providing financial support, foreign market knowledge, and sector expertise.
Jeroen Plag, Chief Investment Officer at Invest International, said, “PaperFoam is a great example of a Dutch innovator that has travelled a difficult path from promising technology to an internationally scalable company. Our involvement dates back to 2020, when we supported the company during its first expansion into the Czech Republic.
“With this new investment, we’re helping to enable the next phase of growth at a time when traditional financiers still view it as too risky. For the Netherlands, it’s crucial that we help green leaders in the manufacturing industry scale up. This way, we retain innovation within our own country and demonstrate that sustainability and international competitiveness go hand in hand.”
Founded in 1998, Paperfoam was founded by Vertis Holding, a former Dutch IT company. The Barneveld-based company is a global provider of biodegradable starch-based packaging solutions, with production facilities in the Netherlands, the Czech Republic, the United States, and Malaysia.
PaperFoam b.v. is owned by PaperFoam Holding b.v. Since March 2023, Nissha Co. Ltd., a Japanese stock-listed company, has owned 30% of PaperFoam Holding b.v. The other 70% is owned by Sustainable Pioneers Holding b.v., a Dutch entity.
PaperFoam states that it develops packaging solutions based on starch and natural fibres as a fully fledged alternative to conventional plastic and paper. Using its patented foaming technology and natural raw materials, the company creates lightweight packaging with an “exceptionally low” carbon footprint. The material is also fully compostable, and the fibres can be easily recycled into paper.
PaperFoam Plus is thicker and stronger than PaperFoam and is designed as a sustainable alternative to EPS (Expanded Polystyrene). It offers protective qualities (drop-tested up to 5 kg), is up to 5 mm thick, and is compostable in both home and industrial composters.
The company serves customers in sectors such as consumer electronics, medical, dry food, and cosmetics. 
Willem Derkman, CEO of PaperFoam, said, “Developing an innovative and sustainable alternative to traditional packaging requires time, investment, and partners who are willing to look further ahead. Thanks to the ongoing support from Invest International, we have been able to take important steps in our international growth. This funding helps us further expand our production capacity and efficiently serve new markets and clients.”
According to the company, production machinery from Dutch suppliers Kuyer Metaal in Nijkerk and Shuffle-Mix in Barneveld makes the expansion possible in part.
