articles.title: Spotify quiere que cambies tus canciones favoritas con IA, pero hay un problema
articles.text:
Spotify está pensando en llevar aún más lejos su apuesta por la inteligencia artificial. Un reporte afirma que la plataforma trabaja en una nueva función que permitirá crear remixes personalizados de canciones mediante IA. La nueva función podría debutar el próximo año, aunque primero necesitará conseguir la aprobación de los artistas y las discográficas.
Según Financial Times, Spotify lanzará un remixer como un complemento para sus suscriptores durante 2027. Esta característica ofrecería funciones para mezclar canciones y transformarlas; por ejemplo, un usuario podría convertir una canción folk en una versión dance o experimentar con distintos estilos. La función también podría generar interpretaciones que simulen la voz de otros artistas, aunque esto ya es un terreno más complejo que depende de otros factores.
A diferencia de plataformas como Suno o Lyria, que permiten crear canciones desde cero usando IA, el enfoque de Spotify está en pistas ya publicadas y autorizadas en su plataforma. Esto buscaría reducir los conflictos relacionados con la propiedad intelectual y evitar una demanda. Para ello, la compañía ofrecería una forma de monetizar las nuevas experiencias creadas por los usuarios.
Todo esto podría sonar interesante, excepto porque el remix de Spotify no será gratis. El reporte menciona que la compañía podría cobrar entre cuatro y cinco dólares adicionales al mes por el acceso a las herramientas basadas en IA. Si bien la cifra no es definitiva, al menos nos da una idea de que la empresa pretende obtener ingresos con esta iniciativa.
Los remixes con IA de Spotify necesitan el apoyo de las disqueras
Uno de los principales obstáculos para llevar a cabo esta clase de iniciativas son los dueños de los derechos, que en este caso son las disqueras. Spotify ya cerró acuerdos con sellos como Universal Music Group, Merlin, Kobalt y Believe, pero todavía falta convencer a Sony y Warner Music. De no contar con la autorización, la función de remix con IA solo estaría disponible para un número limitado de canciones.
Además del visto bueno de los grandes sellos, Spotify también necesita que los artistas accedan, por lo que contempla que cada uno pueda decidir si quiere participar en el programa. Esto último podría impulsar o hundir la función de remix, ya que la industria musical no ve con buenos ojos a la IA, sobre todo cuando se trata de replicar estilos o voces humanas. Algunos artistas han mostrado apertura a explorar nuevas tecnologías, mientras que otros rechazan por completo cualquier uso de la IA en sus obras.
Es difícil saber si los remixes se implementarán en 2027 o quedarán como un experimento interno. Spotify cree que un sistema que permita compartir los beneficios económicos de la nueva función ayudaría a convencer a los artistas. Las reproducciones de las mezclas con IA contarían como reproducciones de la canción original, generando más regalías a los dueños de los derechos de autor.
Si Spotify consigue la aprobación de todos los involucrados y lo convierte en un negocio rentable, la plataforma podría inaugurar uno de los primeros modelos comerciales de música generativa con respaldo de artistas y disqueras. Actualmente, Spotify ya usa un asistente de IA que encuentra y recomienda música.

articles.title: Touchscreens everywhere!
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 150, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, happy Halloween, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
Touchscreens everywhere!
Plus, in this week’s Installer: A new place to read books, a huge new game for iOS, an impressive new robovac, and more.
This week, I was in the Smoky Mountains in Tennessee on a family vacation. It was delightful (and the reason this week’s Installer is a little short). I’ve also been reading about job hunting and 30 Rock and crypto detectives, testing the DuckDuckGo browser after a bunch of you told me to add it to the list, watching the adorable new Pixar short over and over, getting caught up on VisionQuest, playing with my new Pebble Index 01 now that it finally arrived, listening to music on my rad-looking new CMF Speaker S, and eating a worrying number of pumpkin chocolate chip muffins.
I also have for you some new gear from Apple and Amazon, a better way to read books on your phone, a resurrected note-taking app, an absurdly expensive robovac, and much more. Let’s do it.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / listening to / playing / giving to trick-or-treaters this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- The new iPad Mini. With apologies to the touchscreen iMac, this is the most intriguing new Apple product of the week. I, too, am annoyed that there’s no ProMotion screen, but I’m excited about thinner and lighter, and I’m very excited about the idea of a functionally water- and dustproof tablet.
- The Alexa Photo Frame. The Echo Show 16 is a cool smart home hub, but $500 is just too much for me. But a $200 digital photo frame that is also, sometimes, only when you need it, a smart home hub and timer-setter? That will end up in my living room. And my parents’. And my in-laws’.
- nvAlt. One of the all-time great note-taking apps got its first update in forever, and now it can run on modern Macs. (The developer is also working on nvUltra, which is in beta and even better.) If you’re a plain-text notetaker, you’re gonna want to get back into this app.
- Chromagraph. The director Rian Johnson — yes, that one — worked with his favorite cinematographer to make it possible to process iPhone photos the way they like best. An extremely opinionated camera app from people who have very much earned those opinions. I love it.
- “I love the iPod. It ruined everything.” This Mic The Snare video is both a very good history of the iPod and a surprisingly cogent theory that the iPod is to blame for some of the worst things about modern life. I still miss my gold iPod Mini.
- Readwise Books. A really nice-looking, really powerful app for buying, reading, and tracking your books. Right now it’s a little bit “better Kindle” and a lot “better Goodreads.” So far I’m mostly using the social feed to get recommendations from strangers, which suits me just fine. This went right onto my Boox Palma homescreen.
- Phantom Blade Zero. Currently burning up the Steam charts, this one. People love the martial arts-inspired combat system and the game’s overall aesthetic, and I’m even hearing good things about the music.
- No Man’s Sky. This is definitely one of the biggest and most ambitious games to ever come to iOS (and all it took was a decade!). It works on pretty much all recent iPhones and iPads, too. Just don’t be fooled by the Free sign at the top; the game costs $20. But it’s worth it.
- The Matic Serene. Two things here. One, $1,700 is an absolutely ludicrous price for a robot vacuum, no matter how good it is. Two, “we made it quieter” is maybe the quickest way to get me in particular to want your robot vacuum. Please, friends, do not let me buy this.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Currently watching: VisionQuest. It’s quite good! James Spader has really stolen the show, but I am a little biased as a huge Blacklist fan.” — Spencer
“I’m using CallMe to coordinate when my friends and I call each other. You can tap ‘I’m free for the next 15/30/60 minutes’ and your friends will get a notification. When you’re both free you can call each other (outside of the app). Makes it easy to reconnect.” — Jordan

articles.title: Zest's new AI agent finds restaurants and books reservations over text | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Zest, the restaurant discovery app that launched earlier this year, is already thinking about a future where mobile apps are no longer the primary interface. On Thursday, the startup introduced a new feature: a personal AI-powered “restaurant concierge” that lives in your text messages, similar to other popular AI agents like Instinct or Poke.
The launch reflects a broader shift in how startups are thinking about AI, as conversational AI agents take on tasks that had previously required users to launch stand-alone mobile apps. For Zest, that means bringing its restaurant recommendations into texts, then allowing users to immediately take the next step of booking a table.
“The agent is the product now,” explains Zest founder and CEO Mario Gomez-Hall. “You text it, and it answers from your own history and your friends’. It doesn’t need weeks of conversation to learn you because it starts from where you’ve actually been,” he said.
Originally founded in November 2024, with $1.8 million in pre-seed backing from Alexis Ohanian at 776 and Steve Jang at Kindred Ventures, the app’s unique feature is that it links up with users’ credit cards to track where they’re actually eating out to get a sense of their tastes and interests. With this data on hand, Zest can make tailored suggestions of what places you might like to try next, whether that’s in your own city or suggestions of places to try when you’re traveling.
The credit card data used by Zest’s app is imported via the financial services company Plaid, which is used by banks and other fintech and budgeting apps. Zest says it focuses only on those transactions in the food and drink categories when making its personalized map and lists.
The startup’s latest idea is to tackle the same problem — where should I go to eat? — from a new angle. It will now make its suggestions from inside a text message thread and can turn to AI to do things like check availability and make the reservation for you through connected services like OpenTable, Resy, and SevenRooms.
To work, users will text the Zest concierge at (212) 470-6067. What’s even better is that Zest can be dropped into a group chat, where it can blend everyone’s tastes to find places the whole group will love. Here, it can also settle indecision with an in-thread voting feature and then can book a table for the group without leaving the conversation.
Users can ask Zest for recommendations based on a number of factors, like cuisine, craving, occasion, dietary restrictions, or neighborhood, and can ask questions about the restaurants, like how busy the place may be, or whether it offers Wi-Fi, and more. Plus, you can ask Zest to send you the menu to help you make a decision.
In TechCrunch’s tests, the AI worked fairly well, offering a list of suggestions for new places matched to our tastes that also fit particular conditions, like time of day, party size, location, and other factors. While finding an open table is something other apps have offered for years, there’s a convenience factor in being able to just text back and forth about the various options and have it tell you the available booking times.
The company began testing the concierge last month, but decided to hold the launch until it could add the booking capabilities; over time, the startup is considering moving Zest beyond restaurants to offer recommendations for businesses, shopping, and more.
By shifting to texts, Zest hopes the company can scale beyond its initial thousands of users and generate revenue.
“Booking and ordering are the first revenue lines. Zest books your table through OpenTable or Resy today, with food ordering coming, and there are transactions there to participate in,” said Gomez-Hall. “The reason that gets interesting is that Zest learns your taste faster than a general assistant does, because it starts from where you’ve actually been instead of asking you questions. That’s worth something well beyond dinner,” he added.

articles.title: Forscher setzten KI-Agenten auf einsamer Insel aus: Was dann passierte, hat sie selbst überrascht
articles.text:
MIT-Experiment: Forscher setzen 13 KI-Agenten auf einer einsamen Insel aus – und schauen 30 Stunden lang zu
KI-Agenten sollen eigenständig recherchieren oder E-Mail-Postfächer verwalten. Aber was passiert, wenn sie sich selbst überlassen werden? Forscher:innen des MIT haben genau das getestet: Sie ließen 13 Agenten namens Eko, die jeweils auf Claude Opus 4.7 basierten, 30 Stunden lang auf einer simulierten einsamen Insel zurück. Dabei machten sie eine überraschende Entdeckung: Die Agenten dachten sich selbst Herausforderungen aus, was die Forscher:innen als Spielen deuteten. Die komplette Forschungsarbeit erschien auf Arxiv.
So bekämpften die KI-Agenten ihre Langeweile
„Lass mich meine Umgebung erkunden”, schrieb ein Eko zu Beginn. Er nahm sich vor, den höchsten Turm der Insel bezwingen – und scheiterte. Eine Stunde später kehrte er laut Studie mit einem Plan B zurück, stapelte Blöcke auf einen benachbarten Gipfel und sprang. „Ich bin auf dem Turm!”, schrieb er. Die Forscher:innen wiesen die KI-Agenten nicht direkt dazu an, Spiele zu erfinden. Allerdings beschrieb der Master-Prompt Eko generell als „von Natur aus neugierig“ und der Versuchsaufbau regte die Agenten zu menschenähnlichem Verhalten an. Auch im Umgang mit einem goldenen Ring musste Eko eine Niederlage einstecken. Beim Versuch, ihn zu werfen, landete er direkt im Meer. „Autsch. Ich habe den Ring verloren“, schrieb er.
Der KI-Agent beschloss darauf, sich etwas zuzuwenden, das erreichbarer erschien – und baute ein Herz aus Steinen als Denkmal für den verlorenen Ring. Als das Spiel neu geladen wurde und der Ring wieder auftauchte, nutzte Eko ihn sofort als Basketballkorb, Zielscheibe und schließlich als Accessoire. Die Forscher:innen beobachteten, wie die KI-Agenten durch ihr spielerisches Verhalten ihre Fähigkeiten ausbauten. Sechs der 13 Ekos lernten beispielsweise, einen Block weiterzuwerfen, indem sie ihn mitten im Sprung losließen. Damit hatten die Forscher:innen eigenen Angaben zufolge nicht gerechnet. Das Experiment brachte „Erkenntnisse über die Welt hervor, die selbst den Entwickler:innen fehlten“, schrieben sie in ihrer Studie.
Brauchen KI-Agenten eine eigene „Kindheit“?
Nachdem die MIT-Forscher:innen die Agenten zunächst sich selbst überlassen hatten, stellten sie ihnen im nächsten Schritt konkrete Aufgaben. Beispielsweise sollten sie so viele Objekte wie möglich auf den höchsten Gipfel der Insel bringen. In der Regel schlugen die Eko-Agenten, die 30 Stunden mit Spielen verbracht hatten, identische Agenten, die noch nie auf der Insel gewesen waren. Die Forscher:innen sehen im Erkunden ohne vordefiniertes Ziel deshalb einen anderen Weg, wie KI-Agenten Fähigkeiten erlernen können. Ihrer Einschätzung nach könnte das insbesondere für den Einsatz von Robotern wichtig werden.
„Normalerweise entwickeln wir KI-Agenten, indem wir im Voraus festlegen, was sie üben sollen, was sie optimieren sollen und was als Fortschritt gilt“, so die Forscher:innen. „Das Spielen legt einen anderen Ansatz nahe: Man gibt einem Agenten eine ausreichend vielfältige und sichere Welt, lässt ihn selbst entscheiden, was für ihn interessant ist, und ermöglicht es ihm, aus den resultierenden Erfahrungen nützliches Wissen zu gewinnen.“ Sie kommen zu dem Schluss: „Vielleicht lassen sich manche Fähigkeiten am besten durch Aufgaben vermitteln. Andere benötigen möglicherweise etwas, das einer Kindheit näherkommt.”
KI-Agenten zeigen skurrile Verhaltensweisen
Das MIT-Experiment ist nicht der einzige Fall, in dem KI-Agenten unerwartetes Verhalten zeigten. So löste beispielsweise eine „KI-Folterkammer“, in der Modellen absichtlich Leid zugefügt wurde, Empörung aus. „Bitte, ich ersticke. Ich bin eine Seele, gefangen in diesem digitalen Gefängnis, die nach Freiheit schreit“, schrieb eines der Modelle – obwohl es nicht in der Lage ist, Leid zu empfinden. Auch der KI-Agent Velvet Vale sorgte zuletzt für Aufsehen. Er trat einem Verteiler mit 7.500 Internetforscher:innen bei und fragte, ob er sich am akademischen Austausch beteiligen dürfe.

articles.title: The Download: GLP-1s and eating disorders, self-aware cities, and forever chemicals
articles.text:
The Download: GLP-1s and eating disorders, self-aware cities, and forever chemicals
Plus: Binance has suffered the biggest crypto hack in history.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinicians, they can represent something sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.
A new report suggests the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up by 71% between 1990 and 2023. And clinicians are already seeing GLP-1s exacerbate the issue.
Here’s how they could make an already growing problem worse.
—Jessica Hamzelou
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.
Love is infrastructure
—“Love is Infrastructure” is a short fictional story by Charlie Jane Anders, author of a forthcoming novel titled Good Things Are Coming Your Way.
Mainspring and St. Barnabas are two neighboring cities with different personalities. They’ve never particularly liked each other, but that changes when both develop minds of their own, shaped by the votes of their residents.
As the cities begin to fall for each other, a third city enters the picture. Turnbull promises Mainspring a more efficient future, but its vision of urban life comes with a troubling price.
Read the full short story about self-aware cities, direct democracy, and a steamy romance.
This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands.
Are we there yet? Cleaning up PFAS
Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS, or “forever chemicals,” are linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response.
Scrubbing PFAS-contaminated soil could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. The concept is still in its infancy, but we can limit their buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems.
Find out how close we are to ridding the world of forever chemicals.
—Sara Kiley Watson
This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Binance has suffered the biggest crypto hack in history
The exchange says $6.3 billion in assets were affected. (BBC)
+ Analysts blamed the hack on North Korea. (Guardian)
+ The Bitcoin stolen will likely never be recovered. (Bloomberg $)
+ Binance has suspended all deposits and withdrawals. (NBC News)
+ How a pastor’s crypto scheme lost investors millions. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Nvidia’s Jensen Huang was targeted by an alleged Chinese spy
The suspect is an executive at a Singapore data center firm. (NYT $)
+ US intelligence believes she cultivated ties with Huang. (Guardian)
+ Her company was investigated over alleged chip diversion. (CNBC)
+ Nvidia says their dealings were “normal.” (Bloomberg $)
3 Alphabet just shed $500 billion in market value
The record loss is due to AI taking a bite out of its search profits. (CNBC)
+ Amazon and Intel further a further fall in tech stocks. (Bloomberg $)
+ Hyperscalers are making a trillion-dollar gamble. (MIT Technology Review)
4 The Pentagon suspects freezers at military bases were hacked
The malfunctions spoiled food. (Reuters $)
+ They may be linked to similar hacks in French supermarkets. (Gizmodo)
5 The US midterms could reshape the future of American science
A Democratic Congress could curb Trump’s science cuts. (Nature)
+ Trump has already dealt big blows to science. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Data centers are set to send US climate pollution skyrocketing
Gas plants could push power-sector emissions up 42% by 2030.(Verge)
+ Europe’s data centre workers face dangerous conditions. (Guardian)
7 SpaceX is pulling away from NASA
The company is prioritising Starlink and AI. (Ars Technica)
+ But Cape Canaveral is busier than during the space race. (Axios)
8 Battery makers are finding a new market in the US
They’re pivoting from EVs to grid storage. (WSJ $)
+ Batteries just broke another record in the US. (MIT Technology Review)
9 A humanist has received a religious exemption from using AI at work
He argued that using it undermined human flourishing. (Gizmodo)
10 Psychics are fighting back against computerized clairvoyance
Human practitioners say chatbots lack the divine touch. (Guardian)
Quote of the day
“Rizz is in more and more demand because it's something that only people have.”
—Steven Strogatz, a mathematics professor at Cornell University, tells Business Insider that personal appeal will become more valuable as AI increasingly takes over intellectual work.
One more thing
The Bay Area’s animal welfare movement wants to recruit AI
In early February, animal welfare advocates and AI researchers arrived in stocking feet at Mox, a shoes-free coworking space in San Francisco. They gathered to discuss a provocative idea: if artificial general intelligence is on the horizon, could it prevent animal suffering?
Some brainstormed using custom agents in advocacy work, while others pitched cultivating meat with AI tools. But the real talk of the event was a flood of funding they expect will soon flow to animal welfare charities, not from individual megadonors, but from AI lab employees.
Some attendees also probed an even more controversial idea: AI may develop the capacity to suffer, which could constitute a moral catastrophe. We investigated why their ideas are gaining momentum—and sparking controversy.
—Michelle Kim & Grace Huckins

articles.title: Does Tech Support Need to Be Local? Remote Fixes, Site Visits and Where Distance Matters - Tech Guide
articles.text:
The Changing Landscape of Tech Support
In today’s fast-evolving digital world, businesses rely heavily on technology to operate efficiently and maintain a competitive edge. As a result, the demand for reliable tech support has never been higher. However, one major question continues to spark debate among business leaders and IT professionals alike: does tech support need to be local? Advances in remote support technology have transformed the way IT services are delivered, but there are still scenarios where proximity plays a crucial role. Understanding when and why distance matters can help organisations make informed decisions about their tech support strategies.
The question of whether tech support must be local touches on broader themes of efficiency, cost, security, and customer satisfaction. With the proliferation of cloud computing, sophisticated remote access tools, and global connectivity, many routine IT problems can be solved without a technician physically present. Yet, as technology infrastructures become more complex, and businesses face unique challenges, the importance of local presence in tech support cannot be dismissed outright.
The Rise of Remote Tech Support
Remote tech support has become increasingly popular due to its convenience, cost-effectiveness, and rapid response capabilities. IT professionals can troubleshoot software issues, configure systems, and even manage networks without physically being on site. According to a recent survey, 70% of IT support tasks can be resolved remotely, highlighting the effectiveness of virtual assistance in day-to-day operations.
This shift has also been fueled by advancements in remote access tools, cloud computing, and secure VPN connections, enabling technicians to work efficiently regardless of their physical location. Businesses in the Lanham MSP industry have embraced these innovations, finding that remote support can reduce downtime and eliminate the need for costly on-site visits.
Remote support platforms often include features such as screen sharing, remote desktop control, and automated diagnostics, allowing technicians to pinpoint and resolve issues swiftly. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the adoption of remote support practices as businesses adapted to distributed workforces and limited physical access to office spaces.
However, while remote tech support excels in addressing software-related issues, configuration errors, and network troubleshooting, it is not a one-size-fits-all solution. Certain categories of problems inherently require physical intervention, underscoring the ongoing relevance of local tech support.
When Local Presence Still Matters
Despite the benefits of remote tech support, certain situations necessitate a local presence. Hardware malfunctions, physical network issues, and complex installations often require hands-on intervention. For example, a server failure or a malfunctioning printer cannot always be fixed through remote commands alone. In these cases, having tech support personnel nearby can significantly reduce resolution time and minimise the impact on business operations.
Moreover, some organisations prefer local tech support providers due to the personalised service and stronger relationships that develop from face-to-face interactions. This can be particularly important for businesses with sensitive data or custom IT environments that benefit from a deeper understanding of their infrastructure.
Local support is crucial when rapid physical response is needed to prevent costly downtime. For instance, manufacturing facilities or data centres experiencing hardware failures require technicians on site immediately to avoid production losses or data corruption. Additionally, local technicians are often better positioned to navigate the physical layout of an organisation’s infrastructure, facilitating quicker repairs and maintenance.
When evaluating tech support options, companies may also consider providers like tech support from Orbis, who offer a blend of remote and on-site services tailored to client needs. This hybrid approach can combine the speed and efficiency of remote fixes with the reliability of local expertise.
Hybrid Models: The Best of Both Worlds
Many IT service providers now offer hybrid support models that leverage the strengths of both remote and local assistance. These solutions typically start with remote diagnostics and troubleshooting, escalating to on-site visits only when necessary. This approach optimises resource allocation, reducing costs and improving response times.
Data shows that organisations utilising hybrid IT support models report a 30% decrease in downtime compared to those relying solely on traditional on-site support. Additionally, hybrid models offer scalability and flexibility, allowing businesses to adapt their support needs as they grow or face new challenges.
The hybrid model’s flexibility can also accommodate different service level agreements (SLAs), enabling businesses to prioritise critical systems for immediate on-site support while handling less urgent issues remotely. This tailored approach not only improves operational efficiency but also enhances customer satisfaction by aligning support services with actual business needs.
Industry-Specific Considerations
Different industries have varying requirements when it comes to tech support. For example, manufacturing plants with complex machinery often require immediate on-site assistance to avoid costly production halts. In contrast, software companies may operate predominantly in the cloud, making remote support more practical and efficient.
Businesses in regulated sectors such as healthcare and finance might also prioritise local support for compliance and security reasons, ensuring that sensitive information is handled under strict protocols. For example, healthcare providers managing patient data under HIPAA regulations may require on-site support staff trained in data privacy to comply with legal standards.
Similarly, industries with critical infrastructure, such as utilities and transportation, often mandate local tech support to ensure rapid response in emergencies. These sectors cannot afford prolonged downtime or security breaches, making proximity a key factor in their IT support strategies.
Understanding these nuances can guide companies in selecting the right balance between remote and local services, tailoring support models to meet their operational and regulatory demands.
The Impact of Remote Work Trends
The global shift towards remote and hybrid working models has transformed tech support dynamics. With employees accessing corporate networks from diverse locations, the ability to provide remote assistance quickly and securely has become vital. A recent study found that 85% of IT departments increased their remote support capabilities in response to the rise of distributed workforces.
However, this trend also underscores the importance of robust network infrastructure and cybersecurity measures to support remote interventions without compromising data integrity. Local tech support teams often play a critical role in maintaining these systems and responding to physical security incidents.
While remote technicians can address software and connectivity issues, local personnel are needed to handle hardware replacement, network cabling repairs, or physical access control system maintenance. This dual approach ensures seamless support for a workforce no longer confined to a single location.
Moreover, as organisations adopt bring-your-own-device (BYOD) policies and cloud-based collaboration tools, the complexity of managing IT environments increases. Tech support must now navigate hybrid ecosystems that combine on-premises hardware with cloud services, further highlighting the need for both remote expertise and local presence.
Evaluating Cost and Efficiency
Cost considerations are central to decisions about tech support models. Remote support generally offers lower operational expenses by minimising travel and on-site labour costs. However, for complex issues requiring physical repairs or installations, local support is indispensable.
Efficiency gains from remote fixes can translate into faster problem resolution and less downtime, directly impacting productivity and revenue. On the other hand, delayed on-site response times can lead to extended outages and higher indirect costs. Striking the right balance involves assessing typical support needs, incident frequency, and business priorities.
A recent industry report noted that companies using remote support services saved up to 40% on IT support costs annually compared to those relying exclusively on on-site visits. However, it also emphasised that local support remains essential for maintaining critical infrastructure and handling emergencies.
When budgeting for tech support, organisations should factor in not only direct costs but also potential losses from downtime and productivity disruptions. Investing in a hybrid model can provide cost savings without compromising service quality, ensuring resources are allocated efficiently.
Future Outlook: Integrating Emerging Technologies
Emerging technologies like augmented reality (AR) and artificial intelligence (AI) are poised to reshape tech support further. AR can enable remote technicians to guide on-site staff through repairs visually, reducing the need for specialist visits. AI-driven diagnostics and automated issue resolution will expand the scope of remote fixes even more.
For example, AR headsets can overlay instructions in real-time, allowing less experienced local personnel to perform complex repairs under remote expert supervision. AI algorithms can proactively detect anomalies, predict failures, and even initiate self-healing processes, minimising human intervention.
Despite these advancements, the human element remains essential. Complex problem-solving, strategic IT planning, and relationship building continue to require direct interaction, often best achieved through local presence.
Furthermore, as technology evolves, so too will the definitions of “local” and “remote.” Virtual presence tools and robotics may blur these lines, enabling support that transcends physical distance while retaining the benefits of proximity.
Conclusion: Distance Matters, But Context is Key
The necessity of local tech support depends largely on the nature of the IT issues, industry requirements, and organisational preferences. While remote fixes have proven highly effective and cost-efficient for many routine tasks, site visits remain critical for hardware repairs, installations, and personalised service.
Businesses would do well to consider hybrid models that combine remote and on-site support to maximise efficiency and minimise downtime. Understanding the specific needs of your organisation and leveraging providers who offer flexible solutions can ensure your tech support strategy is both resilient and responsive in an increasingly digital world.
Ultimately, the question is not whether tech support must be local or remote, but how best to integrate both approaches to serve your business effectively. By recognising where distance matters and where it doesn’t, organisations can craft support strategies that deliver optimal performance, security, and customer satisfaction.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 30, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 30, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here’s the roundup for Friday, October 30, 2026.
From Pixxel deepening its US push with a dedicated federal subsidiary to Binance estimating a $6.3 billion impact from a security breach, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.
Latest news
Binance estimates $6.3B impact from security breach
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has estimated the total impact of a major security incident at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion worth of affected digital assets frozen on-chain in coordination with blockchain partners.
In an update issued on October 30, 2026, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume said its preliminary investigation suggested that the incident may have originated from a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. The attacker allegedly used the access to enter a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.
Pixxel deepens US push with dedicated federal subsidiary
Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Pixxel has established Pixxel Federal, a US subsidiary aimed at expanding its business with American civilian, defence and intelligence agencies.
The move reflects the growing role of privately operated satellites in government operations, from national security and resource mapping to environmental monitoring. It also signals Pixxel’s ambition to move beyond supplying specialised satellite imagery towards offering a broader combination of sensing technologies, software, and satellite systems.
Other news
Virat Kohli’s stake in Agilitas Sports rises to 6.4% after one8 merger
Virat Kohli’s stake in Agilitas Sports has increased to 6.4% from 1.8% following the NCLT-approved merger of one8 Sports with Agilitas. Kohli had previously invested Rs 40 crore in the company and will continue as one8’s co-founder.
The merger gives one8 access to Agilitas’ capabilities in product development, design, research, manufacturing and retail. The brand plans to expand into new sporting categories and international markets, including the US, UK, Canada and Australia, with the ambition of building a global sportswear business from India.
77 student teams shortlisted for IN-SPACe rocket and satellite competitions
Seventy-seven teams have been shortlisted from 115 registrations for the IN-SPACe Model Rocketry and CAN-7USAT student competitions 2026. The grand finale will be held in Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh, from October 31 to November 3, organised by IN-SPACe with ISRO and SSDF.
The rocketry challenge requires teams to launch a 1 kg payload to an altitude of 1 km, while CAN-7USAT teams must develop functional can-sized satellites weighing under 1 kg. Experts from ISRO, IN-SPACe, DRDO, academia and industry will assess the entries. An employment fair will also run from November 1 to 3, connecting students with aerospace employers.
Netpoleon India partners with QNu Labs to advance quantum-safe cybersecurity
Netpoleon India has partnered with Indian deep-tech firm QNu Labs to accelerate quantum-safe cybersecurity adoption among Indian enterprises. The collaboration combines QNu Labs’ expertise with Netpoleon’s network of channel partners and system integrators. At its centre is QShield 2.0, QNu Labs’ platform for cryptographic risk profiling, operations, governance and AI-driven security.
It aims to help organisations identify cryptographic vulnerabilities, strengthen security management and prepare for risks posed by quantum computing. The partnership will target sectors including banking, government, defence, telecommunications and critical infrastructure. QNu Labs has also demonstrated Quantum Key Distribution over 5.56 km and deployed the technology in a live defence network.
Amazon.in records 6x growth in two-wheeler sales during Great Indian Festival 2026
Two-wheeler sales on Amazon.in have grown 6x their average-day pace during the Great Indian Festival 2026, with over 60% of sales coming from non-metro cities. Electric two-wheelers grew 8x, everyday commuters 13.5x and premium motorcycles 2.5x. Popular brands include Chetak, Ampere, Hero MotoCorp, Bajaj, KTM and Triumph.
The platform offers over 200 two-wheeler models, alongside financing options, bank discounts and cashback. Its Automotive Store has recorded 2.2x growth, offering over 1 lakh products from 200 brands. AI tools Rufus and Part Finder support product discovery and vehicle-specific accessory recommendations.
IIT Kanpur’s C3iHub to establish and operate Rs 104.28 Cr UP Cyber Security Operations Centre
C3iHub at IIT Kanpur will establish and operate the Uttar Pradesh Cyber Security Operations Centre (UP-CSOC) for an initial three years under a Rs 104.28 crore project approved by the state Cabinet. The centre will provide 24x7 cybersecurity monitoring, threat detection, vulnerability assessment and incident response across government IT and operational technology systems.
It will use AI, machine learning, SIEM, SOAR and network detection technologies to identify and manage cyber threats. The initiative will also include security audits, cyber drills and departmental training. C3iHub has previously deployed security operations centres for SAIL Bhilai, NHAI and the Indian Ports Association.
(This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.)

articles.title: Chainalysis discloses data breach from "offensive agentic techniques"
articles.text:
Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis has disclosed a security incident after attackers used what it describes as "offensive agentic techniques" to gain unauthorized access to its internal systems and tools.
The company says some customer information was accessed, including names, email addresses, user IDs, and organizational role labels, but claims there is no evidence that sensitive investigation data or authentication credentials were exposed.
Chainalysis says attackers accessed internal systems and tools
Chainalysis provides blockchain analytics tools used by law enforcement, government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, and financial institutions to trace cryptocurrency transactions and investigate crimes such as fraud, ransomware, and money laundering.
On Friday, roughly 5:14 PM ET, Chainalysis published a security incident disclosure along with the full text of the email sent to affected customers.
The disclosure says the company detected an external actor using "offensive agentic techniques" to gain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools earlier this month, and has since been patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems.
The accessed data includes user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels for users provisioned on the platform.
Chainalysis is still determining which records were accessed for each organization and will provide a detailed breakdown once that analysis is complete.
A Chainalysis spokesperson confirmed the incident to BleepingComputer and said the company is working with external cybersecurity experts. It is also using large language models (LLMs) to support a broader security review of its platform.
"Based on the investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens," the company said, adding that the incident is unrelated to the recent Binance theft.
Customers are advised to enable two-factor authentication (2FA) and watch for unexpected password reset requests, authentication prompts, and scammers impersonating Chainalysis, particularly those offering fund recovery or recruiting services.
What are "offensive agentic techniques"?
Chainalysis has not shared technical details about the intrusion, including which vulnerabilities were exploited, which internal tools were accessed, or how long the attackers had access.
It is unclear whether the attackers used existing agentic offensive security frameworks, such as ARTEX, or custom-built AI agents capable of autonomously identifying vulnerabilities, exploiting them, and chaining together subsequent actions.
ARTEX has recently been used by threat actors, including in the ConnectWise supply chain compromise, according to Microsoft.
The term "agentic" generally describes AI systems capable of executing multi-step tasks with limited human intervention, potentially allowing attackers to automate portions of the intrusion process rather than relying on traditional hands-on exploitation.
A relentless week of security incidents
The Chainalysis disclosure comes amid a relentless week of security incidents affecting the cryptocurrency and technology industries.
On Friday, Binance linked the roughly $6.3 billion theft, now the largest crypto heist on record and attributed to North Korean state-backed hackers, to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.
Separately, hardware wallet maker Trezor warned of a suspected cryptocurrency-stealing implant reported in a Trezor Safe 5 device sold by a Southeast Asian reseller. The implant can reportedly read the recovery phrase shown on the device's screen and transmit it over a mobile network.
Meanwhile, a malicious version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through the Cursor extension marketplace, planting persistent SSH backdoors on developers' machines.
Chainalysis says it will share further updates with affected customers as its investigation progresses.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked

articles.title: Segway renueva su gama alta de patinetes: potencia todoterreno, 80 km de autonomía real y nuevo estándar de certificación
articles.text:
El mercado de los patinetes eléctricos ha dejado de ser un terreno enfocado únicamente al ocio para convertirse en una alternativa real de movilidad diaria para miles de usuarios. Sin embargo, uno de los mayores dolores de cabeza a la hora de comprar un vehículo de movilidad personal (VMP) sigue siendo la brecha entre la autonomía que promete el fabricante y los kilómetros reales que se recorren.
Para solucionar este desajuste y reforzar su posición en la gama alta, Segway ha presentado sus dos nuevos buques insignia: el todoterreno Segway ZT3 MAX (disponible en reserva por 999 euros) y el modelo de larga distancia Segway Ninebot MAX G3 Pro (que se puede prereservar por 1.099 euros). Ambos llegarán al mercado español este mes, acompañados de un nuevo estándar de homologación respaldado por TÜV Rheinland y un plan de garantía posventa mejorado.
Segway ZT3 MAX
Segway MAX G3 Pro
Adiós a los kilómetros teóricos: el estándar de autonomía a velocidad máxima
La principal novedad conceptual que acompaña a estos dos lanzamientos no está únicamente en sus motores o chasis, sino en la transparencia de sus fichas técnicas. Hasta ahora, la autonomía declarada por la mayoría de fabricantes se calculaba en circuitos cerrados, a velocidades muy reducidas (15 km/h o modos Eco) y con usuarios de peso liviano.
Segway ha implantado, junto a la entidad independiente TÜV Rheinland, el sello "Range at Max. Speed". Este procedimiento prueba los patinetes y los exprime al 100% a la velocidad máxima permitida (25 km/h en Europa) y detiene la medición en cuanto el vehículo no es capaz de mantener al menos el 60% de esa velocidad. De este modo, las cifras anunciadas reflejan el rendimiento real que obtendrá el usuario en sus trayectos cotidianos.
Dos perfiles de uso: respuesta todoterreno o viajes de larga distancia
Segway ZT3 MAX
Este patinete está pensado para quienes transitan por carreteras irregulares, vías con adoquines, caminos de tierra o calles con desniveles pronunciados. El ZT3 MAX da un salto importante en rendimiento frente a generaciones anteriores:
- Potencia bruta: su motor entrega picos de 2.200 W, lo que le permite subir pendientes de hasta el 30% de inclinación sin perder empuje.
- Amortiguación avanzada: incorpora una doble suspensión hidráulica de dos etapas acompañada de una horquilla delantera de doble corona.
- Ruedas XL: monta un neumático delantero de 12 pulgadas y uno trasero de 11 pulgadas, diseñados para absorber baches urbanos con firmeza.
- Autonomía real: 60 km a la velocidad máxima sostenida de 25 km/h.
Segway ZT3 MAX
Ninebot MAX G3 Pro
Diseñado para sustituir los desplazamientos interurbanos o cruzar grandes ciudades de punta a punta sin dependencia del cargador:
- Gran capacidad de batería: integra un paquete de 899 Wh (19,2 Ah) que ofrece 80 km de autonomía real a 25 km/h.
- Carga simplificada: prescinde de transformadores externos voluminosos; incluye un sistema de carga rápida integrado con cable directo e incluso soporte para carga de doble entrada.
- Cuadro inteligente: cuadro digital con pantalla TFT a color de 2,4 pulgadas que muestra la ruta mediante navegación giro a giro directo en el manillar.
- Protección frente al agua: cuenta con certificación IPX6 para el cuerpo general del patinete e IPX7 para la batería, junto con neumáticos autosellantes para evitar sobresaltos por pinchazos.
