articles.title: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
articles.text:
MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- MIT engineers have built a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light, allowing it to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough could pave the way for tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that ordinary machines cannot safely navigate.
- Share:
A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.
The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.
By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.
In experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.
"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," says study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. "
A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle
The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.
Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.
"Currently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," says Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's new bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself."
The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.
From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot
The new swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.
For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.
When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.
The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.
"People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny."
For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.
They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.
The earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could quickly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.
To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.
"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman says. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells."
Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot
Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.
The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.
This alignment was important because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.
The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.
By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.
Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.
The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.
The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.
How Light Makes the Living Robot Swim
With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.
The finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.
Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.
"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap."
To test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.
As the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.
Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.
The researchers now plan to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.
"Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments."
The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Jennifer Chu. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Maheera Bawa, Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, Seanbiron Johnson, Ritu Raman. 2D Skeletal Muscle Thin Film Actuators Enhance Efficiency of Biohybrid Robots. Advanced Functional Materials, 2026; DOI: 10.1002/adfm.78065

articles.title: Microsoft Retires Azure Deployment Environments with No Replacement Product
articles.text:
Microsoft is retiring both halves of its Azure developer-environment offering. Azure Deployment Environments goes on February 22, 2027, with no successor product. Microsoft Dev Box follows on September 18, 2028, pointed at Windows 365, which Microsoft states plainly is not an equivalent.
The Deployment Environments retirement guide lists alternatives, and none of them is a product. Microsoft suggests "direct infrastructure-as-code deployment with Azure Resource Manager templates or Bicep," reusable Azure verified modules "when teams need standardized, governed building blocks," and CI/CD workflows "when environment provisioning can be integrated into repositories and pipelines." On the partner ecosystem it is blunter: "None of the third-party solutions we identified directly support a Bicep or ARM lifecycle. Use Bicep or ARM directly in Azure for deployment."
That is a hyperscaler leaving the environment-as-a-service category and telling customers to hand-roll what the product did. Microsoft says nothing about why it is withdrawing.
InfoQ covered the general availability in May 2023, when Microsoft launched the service at Build as the answer to exactly that problem. Senior program manager Sagar Chandra Reddy Lankala wrote then that "by enabling self-service deployment for developers, Azure Deployment Environments also benefits platform engineers," who could publish a catalog of standardized, pre-approved templates instead of provisioning environments one by one.
The service itself was free, with customers paying only for the Azure resources their environments created.
Self-service from a governed catalog is the capability going away, and it is the one the retirement guide does not replace. Bicep, verified modules, and pipelines rebuild the provisioning. They do not rebuild the catalog, the role rules, or the developer-facing portal. That territory belongs to Backstage, Port and Humanitec now.
Engineer Ikiru Yoshizaki, posting in Japanese as guitarrapc_tech, made the same objection from the user side when the retirement guide appeared. The advantage, he wrote, lay in the areas that could not be done easily with Bicep, Terraform or Pulumi. He did not spare the product either, adding that right to the end the API was unstable and the documentation sparse, and calling it sad that the value was never recognized.
Teams have sixteen months. Microsoft’s instruction is to inventory "ADE environments, definitions, catalogs, environment types, projects, dev centers, deployment subscriptions, identities, and role assignments," using the Azure Advisor Service Retirement workbook to find them, then validate a replacement for each scenario and move users and automation across. What happens on the date is only partly specified: "ADE create, deploy, redeploy, and other write operations are expected to be blocked. Inventory, read, log, and delete operations are planned to remain available for a time-bound cleanup period." How long that period runs is not stated.
Dev Box has a longer runway, though its clock started earlier than the headline date suggests. The service "starts its closing-down period at 16:00 UTC on 14 September 2026," more than a month ago, before full retirement at 17:00 UTC on 18 September 2028.
Microsoft’s own FAQ is unusually direct about what the move involves. Asked whether Windows 365 is a one-to-one replacement, the guide answers: "No. Windows 365 is the recommended path forward, but architecture, licensing, management, networking, image delivery, and developer self-service can differ. Validate each workload and don’t assume complete feature parity." Developer self-service is on that list, and it is the capability that made Dev Box a developer-platform product rather than managed desktops.
InfoQ covered the Dev Box general availability in July 2023, when that model ran on three roles: infrastructure admins handled security and networking, dev team leads built pools per project, and developers took boxes from enabled pools themselves. Amanda Silver, then corporate vice president in the Developer Division, said more than 10,000 Microsoft developers were using it internally.
There is no migration tool either. Teams should "provision the target Cloud PCs, recreate required policies and configurations, deploy applications, and transfer user data through approved processes." And the consequence of missing the date is stated without hedging: "Microsoft Dev Box won’t be available after retirement. Expect deletion of remaining customer workloads."
Windows 365 is a Microsoft 365 product rather than an Azure service, managed through Intune and licensed separately. Teams that adopted Dev Box as Azure infrastructure, billed and governed alongside the rest of their estate, are being moved to a different commercial surface. Azure Virtual Desktop, Microsoft’s Azure-native virtual desktop service, is not named anywhere in the retirement guide, though it remains under active development and reached a general availability milestone as recently as September.
The retirements are also entangled, since both products share dev center and project resources. The Deployment Environments guide warns against deleting shared dev centers "until you confirm that they have no remaining Microsoft Dev Box dependency."
Neither guide explains the withdrawal. The Dev Box notice says investment is going to Windows 365. For Deployment Environments there is no equivalent statement, only a list of things to build yourself.

articles.title: Pedro, conductor de autobuses: "¿Quién decidió que el asiento del autobús debía parecer un fondo de pantalla de los años ochenta?"
articles.text:
Los asientos de autobuses y autocares tienen una estética muy reconocible, con formas geométricas imposibles y colores chillones que parecen sacados de un catálogo de los años ochenta. Pedro, conductor de autobuses, se hace la pregunta con humor en un Reel de Instagram: “¿Quién decidió que el asiento del autobús debía parecer un fondo de pantalla de los años ochenta?”. Y es que, aunque parezca un capricho de diseño anticuado, la respuesta que da él mismo tiene mucho que ver con el mantenimiento.
Una tela pensada para durar. El vídeo lo ha compartido la empresa Autocares Grupo Benidorm en su cuenta de Instagram, y en él Pedro promete explicar por qué “estos estampados llamativos llevan décadas apareciendo en el transporte”. De hecho, la moquette, que es la tela de este tipo de asientos, llegó al transporte público londinense en los años veinte, según la historia que recoge el Museo del Transporte de Londres, y se eligió en parte porque es un tejido duro y duradero.
Mucho uso y normas de seguridad. Pero la tapicería de un autocar no es una tela cualquiera, ya que tiene que aguantar el paso constante de pasajeros que se sientan y apoyan mochilas o maletas, además de roces continuos y limpiezas frecuentes. “La tapicería del autobús debe soportar mucho uso, roces constantes, limpieza frecuente y unas exigencias de seguridad específicas. Por eso se utilizan tejidos de transporte diseñados para durar”, explica Pedro.
Entre esas exigencias está el comportamiento frente al fuego, que regula el Reglamento n.º 118 de la Comisión Económica de las Naciones Unidas para Europa (CEPE) para autobuses interurbanos y autocares, y que se aplica a los materiales del habitáculo, tapicería de los asientos incluida.
El estampado hace de camuflaje. Aun así, por muy resistente que sea el material, en un transporte que utiliza tanta gente el desgaste y las manchas acaban apareciendo, y ahí es donde entran los famosos dibujos. Las formas geométricas, las rayas superpuestas y los contrastes de color sirven para disimular la suciedad y el deterioro, algo que también señala el mismo museo londinense. Un tejido liso o de un solo color, en cambio, dejaría a la vista cualquier roce o mancha de líquido. Vamos, que el estampado está ahí para que no se note lo que el asiento ha vivido.
Identidad para el interior. Pedro añade otra función, ya que según él “los colores y patrones ayudan a dar identidad al interior y a mantener una apariencia uniforme durante años de servicio”. Y lo resume con una frase que lo engloba todo: “Ese estampado que parece aleatorio combina diseño, persistencia y mantenimiento”.
De esta manera, esas formas aparentemente aleatorias absorben a la vista las imperfecciones y permiten que el interior del vehículo mantenga un aspecto cuidado y limpio durante años de servicio continuado, o sea que esa estética que recuerda a los ochenta tiene una razón muy práctica detrás.

articles.title: Fini les allers-retours : Gemini permet enfin de modifier vos documents directement dans l'application
articles.text:
L’application Gemini intègre désormais de nouvelles fonctionnalités qui vont vous permettre d’éditer beaucoup plus facilement vos fichiers, qu’il s’agisse d’un document texte, d’une présentation ou de lignes de code. Il est désormais possible de modifier les fichiers générés directement dans l’interface de conversation de Gemini, ce qui évite de faire des allers-retours entre différents logiciels.
Nouveaux outils et formats pris en charge
Sur le chat de Gemini, vous pouvez désormais agrandir les documents en mode plein écran pour modifier plus facilement votre document, surligner du texte pour poser des questions ciblées, ou encore demander à l’intelligence artificielle de modifier le contenu ou les visuels. Dans l’exemple de la vidéo ci-dessous, Google montre qu’il devient par exemple possible de sélectionner un tableau pour que Gemini le transforme en graphique.

En revanche, les autres formats comme les documents Google Docs, les feuilles de calcul Google Sheets, les présentations, les fichiers Markdown, les fichiers TXT ainsi que le code sont pour l’instant réservés à la version web.
Disponible pour tous les utilisateurs de Gemini
Ces nouveautés de Gemini sont déployées dès aujourd’hui pour tous les utilisateurs de l’application, dans toutes les langues où le service de Google est disponible. articles.title: The Elder Scrolls 6 is reportedly titled "Sentinel," and a reveal might come soon
articles.text:
In brief: Bethesda has provided virtually no substantial information about The Elder Scrolls VI since officially announcing it more than eight years ago. If recent reports are to be believed, that might be about to change. While the game's release window remains unclear, the upcoming anniversary of its immensely popular predecessor could give parent company Microsoft an opportunity to renew enthusiasm for its gaming business.
Sources familiar with Bethesda's inner workings have informed The Verge that The Elder Scrolls VI will be subtitled "Sentinel," and that Microsoft will reveal the title next month. The game may still be years away, and Microsoft is reportedly considering an Xbox-exclusive launch.
The upcoming open-world RPG will center on Hammerfell, a region of the Elder Scrolls universe featured in The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard and The Elder Scrolls Online but not in a mainline title since The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall, released in 1996. Sentinel is a major city in Hammerfell and the capital of the kingdom of Sentinel. The area is home to the Redgarruds, one of several races that appear throughout the series.
Any announcement from Microsoft would likely happen on November 11, the 15th anniversary of the previous entry, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. Skyrim is one of the best-selling RPGs of all time and maintains one of the industry's biggest modding communities.
It remains unclear whether Microsoft might try to use the follow-up to lift sagging Xbox sales or release it on PlayStation as well, as Bethesda did with prior titles before Microsoft acquired the studio. A reveal next month, likely without gameplay footage, might also be seen as an attempt to show proof of life amid ongoing layoffs affecting thousands of Microsoft employees.
New Xbox CEO Asha Sharma recently teased The Elder Scrolls VI by revealing that its subtitle has eight letters. Sentinel immediately became one of the most widely guessed titles, and fans have long speculated that the next game would feature Hammerfell.
Bethesda technically announced The Elder Scrolls VI at E3 2018 but showed only the title and a brief landscape shot. Since then, studio head Todd Howard has only provided scant details.
Earlier this year, he said the game will resemble its predecessor more than other recent games from the studio like Fallout 76 and Starfield. Starfield, which launched to a mixed reception, provided a learning experience, and Bethesda has since optimized its production pipeline on Creation Engine 3, which will power Elder Scrolls VI.

articles.title: What worries Entire co-founder Thomas Dohmke about the future of tech?
articles.text:
What worries Entire co-founder Thomas Dohmke about the future of tech?
Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke is taking on his old company. His startup, Entire, launched a GitHub alternative this week, replacing traditional pull requests with Trails, a review system that uses AI agents to evaluate code changes while developers oversee the work.
A month before that launch, The New Stack asked Dohmke what excites him most about technology’s future and what worries him. He welcomed the ability to turn more of his ideas into working software. His concern was about learning.
“What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding,” Entire’s co-founder and CEO told TNS at WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San Jose in September. “I think it’s fundamental for every kid out there to not only learn math and biology and geography, but also understand the basics of computer science.”
“What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding.”
Dohmke was one of several people we posed those questions to at the conference. Their answers reveal enthusiasm for what more people can now build, along with some concerns about understanding, safety, and access to these new tools.
For Josh Bentley, SAP’s senior director of community advocacy, broader access to technology means people can build things in hours or days that once took weeks or months. His concern: Whether that speed comes with enough understanding.
“People are getting recognized as a builder when they really don’t understand the context of what they’re building,” Bentley said.
Darko Mesaroš, distinguished developer advocate at AWS, was similarly excited about more people being able to build software. He also worried about bad code and “AI slop.”
“I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally.”
“I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally,” Mesaroš said.
For Mark Cavage, Docker’s president and chief operating officer, the concern was whether the industry could quickly establish the safeguards and efficiencies needed around AI agents.
“The thing that worries me about it, of course, is that actually we as an industry don’t figure out quickly enough how to bring ourselves new efficiencies and trust and safety around it,” Cavage said.
Cassidy Williams, GitHub’s senior director of developer advocacy, was excited that people can ask a machine to help turn an idea into something real. She also raised concerns about safety guardrails and the cost of participating.
Williams wants people to have accessible tools and “not be priced out from being able to be a part of the future.”
The pace of change itself was a source of excitement for Matt Hobbs, head of Cloud, Engineering, Data, and AI at PwC.
“Everything that I just built, I could rebuild again and do it better, do it faster, do it safer, do it more ready for enterprise scale,” Hobbs said.
Frederic Branczyk, vice president of data engineering at Dash0, described his outlook as cautiously optimistic. He was excited about what AI enables his company to offer customers and how it uses the technology internally, while acknowledging the uncertainty ahead.
“None of us really have the answers to all the problems that we’re facing together,” Branczyk said.
The conversation is part of The New Stack’s six-video Inside WeAreDevelopers series. The other five videos explore what developers should learn next, what teams are building, and what brings people together:
- What should every developer get hands-on with right now? — Speakers make the case for experimenting with GPU programming, local AI models, agent frameworks, and sandboxes.
- What people missed at WeAreDevelopers — From technical debates to unexpected career connections, attendees explain what happens beyond the stage.
- What tech industry experts enjoy most about developer events — Hallway conversations, old friends, and extended debates offer something a recorded session can’t.
- Exciting releases for developers — Speakers share updates on agent tools, Git infrastructure, observability, and cloud sandboxes.
- What tech leaders are focused on right now — Teams discuss agent development, engineering guardrails, infrastructure, and data privacy.

articles.title: Warren advierte que la salida a bolsa de Anthropic obligará a fondos de jubilación a comprar sus acciones
articles.text:
La senadora demócrata Elizabeth Warren advirtió en una carta a Anthropic que la salida a bolsa de la empresa obligará a los fondos indexados con ahorros de jubilación de los estadounidenses a comprar sus acciones, aunque el precio sea volátil o esté sobrevalorado. La carta se hizo pública el 28 de octubre.
Warren, la principal legisladora demócrata del Comité de Banca del Senado, dirigió el texto al director ejecutivo de Anthropic, Dario Amodei. Le pidió respuestas a diez preguntas antes del 3 de noviembre.
Según el comunicado de la senadora, los proveedores de índices bursátiles eliminaron este año los períodos de espera que retrasaban el ingreso de las empresas nuevas en los grandes índices. Por eso las acciones llegan más rápido a las cuentas de jubilación.
“Esto significa que los fondos indexados que invierten los ahorros de jubilación de los estadounidenses se verán obligados a comprar acciones de Anthropic aunque la acción sea volátil o esté sobrevalorada”, escribió Warren.
Dos riesgos: seguridad pública y estabilidad financiera
La carta cita pasajes del formulario S-1, el documento que Anthropic presentó ante la SEC, el regulador bursátil de Estados Unidos, el 26 de octubre. De sus más de 90 páginas de factores de riesgo, la senadora destacó que la empresa admite que sistemas de IA avanzados podrían representar “riesgos catastróficos o existenciales para la humanidad”.
Warren sostiene que una inyección masiva de capital público acelerará el desarrollo de esa tecnología en pleno debate sobre su seguridad. También afirma que, por su tamaño, las variaciones del precio de la acción podrían sacudir a los mercados desde el primer día.
La senadora cuestionó además que la empresa necesite “un flujo insaciable de capital” y planteó que eso no justifica exponer a los ahorristas comunes a sus riesgos. Según el diario The Wall Street Journal, que vio la carta, también pregunta por los vínculos con socios como Amazon y Broadcom y por cómo se justificaría una valuación cercana a los USD 2 billones.
Una pérdida de USD 80.748 millones, casi toda contable
El S-1 muestra ingresos de USD 16.286 millones en el primer semestre de 2026, frente a USD 1.163 millones en el mismo período de 2025. La pérdida neta fue de USD 80.748 millones, frente a USD 12.969 millones un año antes.
La revista Fortune precisó que USD 72.400 millones de esa pérdida responden a un cargo contable por el mayor valor de los bonos convertibles que la empresa emitió. La pérdida operativa fue de USD 693 millones, y la compañía informó que, con una medición ajustada, tuvo una ganancia operativa de USD 1.600 millones.
El formulario indica que Anthropic tenía USD 131.651 millones en efectivo e inversiones de corto plazo al 30 de junio. Planea cotizar en el mercado Nasdaq con el símbolo ANT.
Una valuación de hasta USD 2 billones, según la prensa
Medios como Fortune y CNBC informan que la empresa busca una valuación de entre USD 1,5 y 2 billones. Reuters, citado por TipRanks, indicó que los inversores habían hablado recientemente de unos USD 1,5 billones para una salida prevista a mediados de noviembre. La cifra superaría los USD 1,77 billones de SpaceX en su debut de junio.
Anthropic no respondió de inmediato a la consulta de Moneywise sobre la carta. La fecha límite que fijó Warren para recibir sus respuestas es el 3 de noviembre de 2026.

articles.title: Analysts find looming launch crisis is "more severe" than anticipated
articles.text:
A new report from the analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years.
The firm estimates that between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled.
“What we wanted to get at is to understand how severe this launch crisis is and when will it be resolved,” said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space. “What we learned is that the launch crisis is more severe than we thought and that it will not go away this decade for sure, and it might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s.”
The report tallies a number of familiar factors that have gone into this crisis: the war in Ukraine taking Russian rockets off the Western market; Amazon Leo demand; developmental delays in a new generation of rockets, from New Glenn and Vulcan to Neutron, Terran R, and Nova; and more recently, the retirement of the Falcon 9 as a rocket for commercial service.
At a time when the supply of commercial rockets is contracting, demand for satellite launch is soaring, from megaconstellation operators such as Amazon to a flurry of small satellite startups. The report estimates the crunch will become most acute in 2028 but should then slowly improve.
“How should people react and plan around this?” Henry asked. “To be honest, I don’t have a good answer. If you haven’t booked your launch already, and you need one, you’re late.”

articles.title: Google hit with criminal probe over unapproved AI data center deforestation — 816 acres of forest destroyed in Finland as wolves flee into local villages, facility threatens 40% power bill hikes
articles.text:
Google hit with criminal probe over unapproved AI data center deforestation — 816 acres of forest destroyed in Finland as wolves flee into local villages, facility threatens 40% power bill hikes
The local Fins have a reputation for their low propensity for data center protests, but they are being tested.
A criminal investigation into the environmental damage caused by Google’s Finnish subsidiary has been launched. Tuike Finland Oy is being investigated after five complaints were received regarding the Muhos data center project, according to an official police statement published today [machine translation].
The police say that the investigation is backed by Finland’s Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV). Google/Tuike Finland Oy is accused of suspected breaches of environmental law and environmental damage. Other lesser criminal offenses related to ambiguities and shortcomings in the drainage and water management are also being investigated.
Since Google representatives have previously publicly apologized for the unauthorized forest clearings near Muhos, which have turned 816 acres of forest into an expanse of mud, there seems little doubt it is guilty of some wrongdoing. Rather, it is the scale of the punishment and any proposed remedies that will probably be of most concern to execs from the tech giant now.
As well as the awful mess Google has made near Muhos, it seems to have also jumped the gun and plowed ahead with data center development by clearing 500 acres of forest near Otanmäki.
Though the horse has already bolted, Reuters reports that a Google rep said the company would cooperate with the police investigation and continue to focus on maintaining compliance at its sites. Maintaining?
Last week we reported that wolves had descended on Finnish villages after their habitats had been destroyed to make way for the Google AI data centers. Data center developments were already a thorny issue with locals. Potential construction and operating noise, pollution, utility competition, and environmental damage concerns were overshadowed – for some – by the presence of wild animals that had moved out of the forest.
Google sees Finland as an attractive location for data center development with its cool climate, affordable power, and government endorsement of AI projects. It has also benefitted from being able to develop in low population density areas and from a populace with a low propensity for protest. However, Google is testing the Finnish public with its trampling of the environment. The wolves, pollution, potentially 40% higher electricity bills, and other impacts weren’t helping its case, even before this criminal investigation.

articles.title: IPVanish finally launches a dedicated IP — and it fixes one of the VPN's biggest gaps
articles.text:
IPVanish finally launches a dedicated IP — and it fixes one of the VPN's biggest gaps
The new feature gives IPVanish users a static IP address that belongs to them alone
- IPVanish has launched a dedicated IP, a feature reviewers have long flagged as missing.
- It gives you a fixed VPN IP address that no other user shares, with five locations at launch.
- It's aimed at people who need reliable logins and remote access, but there's a privacy trade-off to weigh up.
IPVanish has launched a dedicated IP, an optional add-on that fills one of the most noticeable gaps in its feature list.
Until now, the provider only offered shared, dynamic IP addresses. Reviewers have repeatedly pointed to the missing option as a weak spot, particularly for remote workers and small businesses, and as recently as last week, rivals were still listing it as something IPVanish couldn't do.
NordVPN and Surfshark have offered dedicated IPs for years, so the launch brings IPVanish closer in line with the best VPN services on the market.
How IPVanish's dedicated IP works
When you connect to a VPN normally, you share an IP address with everyone else on that server, and you might get a different one each session. A dedicated IP flips that: it's a unique address assigned to a single user, and it stays the same every time you connect.
This stops you from getting locked out of your accounts when service providers get suspicious of your ever-changing IP address, and you can also add it to your allowed lists for remote work networks, staging servers, or a home NAS.
The add-on launches in five locations: New York, London, Paris, Frankfurt, and Tokyo. It supports WireGuard, OpenVPN, and IKEv2, and works across IPVanish's Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, Android TV, Fire TV, and Apple TV apps.
You buy and manage it through the IPVanish account portal, after which it appears under a Dedicated IP tab in the app's Locations menu. You're not locked in, either. You can switch between your dedicated IP and the regular shared servers at any time, so you only use the fixed address when you need it.
The privacy trade-off
This isn't an always-on feature, however. Shared IPs let you blend into a crowd, while a dedicated IP makes it easier for trackers to build a profile of your activity.
For everyday browsing, a shared IP remains the more private choice, which makes the option to easily switch back a welcome touch. But if endless verification checks or locked accounts have been driving you up the wall, the new feature is worth a look.
It also rounds out a busy year for the provider, following the launch of Threat Protection Pro and its ongoing move to RAM-only servers by 2027.

articles.title: Google's first data center satellite is online and writing poetry | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.
After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus:
Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core. ✨
Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite.
A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally.
The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.
Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.
If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links.
Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively. Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites.
Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX. And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable.
In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles. 
Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s. Getting there, however, may depend on how the rest of the company responds to the pressures and opportunities of AI in the near term. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, saw its stock plunge this week after reporting that efforts to insert AI into its search businesses are hurting ad revenue growth.
Correction: The Suncatcher prototype satellite has four TPUs onboard, but can only operate one at a time.

articles.title: Passkeys Are Better Than Passwords. But They Are Not Enough.
articles.text:
For decades, passwords have been one of cybersecurity’s most persistent weaknesses. Users forget them, reuse them, share them, and surrender them to convincing phishing sites. Attackers steal credentials, automate credential stuffing, and increasingly use artificial intelligence to make social engineering more effective.
What are passkeys?
Passkeys promise to eliminate much of this problem.
Built on public-key cryptography, passkeys replace shared secrets with cryptographic credentials. There is no password for an attacker to steal, intercept through phishing, or reuse against another service. Properly implemented passkeys are also phishing-resistant because authentication is bound to the legitimate service.
That represents a significant improvement over passwords and many traditional forms of multi-factor authentication (MFA). But it does not answer a more fundamental question: Just because someone successfully authenticated, should we continue to trust that identity?
Passkeys strengthen authentication. They do not eliminate identity risk.
What Passkeys Get Right
Traditional authentication frequently relies on passwords combined with one-time passcodes, SMS messages, or push notifications. While stronger than passwords alone, these methods remain vulnerable to phishing, adversary-in-the-middle attacks, MFA fatigue, SIM swapping, and social engineering.
Passkeys fundamentally change that model. Instead of presenting a reusable secret, the user’s device holds a private cryptographic key while the service retains the corresponding public key. The private key is not transmitted during authentication.
This provides meaningful protection against phishing, credential stuffing, password database theft, and other attacks built around stealing reusable credentials. Passkeys can also improve usability because users no longer need to remember complex passwords or repeatedly retrieve authentication codes.
Organizations should welcome that transition. The mistake would be assuming that stronger authentication solves the broader identity security problem though.
Authentication Is Not Identity
When passkey authentication succeeds, the system has strong cryptographic evidence that a credential associated with an account completed the authentication process.
But was the account legitimately established? Has the underlying identity been compromised? Is the device trustworthy? Is an attacker operating through an authenticated session?
A perfectly functioning authentication mechanism cannot compensate for an identity that should never have been trusted.
If an attacker establishes or takes control of an account before a passkey is bound to it, the organization may subsequently perform highly secure authentication of the wrong person. The stronger the authenticator becomes, the more important the integrity of enrollment becomes.
What Happens When the Device Changes?
Legitimate users also do not always authenticate from the same device. Phones are lost, stolen, damaged, or replaced. Employees receive new laptops. Consumers switch technology ecosystems.
Passkey synchronization addresses many of these scenarios by making credentials available across supported devices. But organizations still need to accommodate legitimate users who arrive without access to the expected passkey.
At that point, the challenge shifts from authentication to recovery and re-establishing trust. How does the organization determine whether someone requesting access from an unfamiliar device is the legitimate account owner?
If the fallback relies on a password, SMS code, email link, knowledge-based question, or help desk process, attackers may target that weaker recovery path.
The passkey has not been compromised. The attacker has gone around it.
Organizations therefore need a secure way to re-establish identity trust before associating a new authenticator or device with an existing account.
Authentication Is Only One Moment
Another gap emerges after authentication. Many identity architectures effectively operate according to a simple sequence: Authenticate, grant access, and trust the resulting session.
Modern identity-based attacks do not necessarily stop at the login screen. Attackers can hijack authenticated sessions, compromise trusted devices, abuse privileges, manipulate account attributes, or conduct anomalous transactions. In these situations, the authentication mechanism may have worked exactly as designed.
The question cannot simply be, “Did this user authenticate successfully?” It must also be, “Do we still have sufficient evidence to trust this identity and its activity?”
Layer Identity Threat Detection on Top
This is where identity threat detection complements passkeys.
Instead of treating successful authentication as a permanent declaration of trust, organizations can continuously evaluate identity risk. Device characteristics, identity attributes, behavioral anomalies, network intelligence, account changes, transaction context, and threat indicators can help determine whether an identity remains trustworthy.
This does not require adding friction to every interaction. A risk-based model can allow legitimate users to proceed normally while escalating controls when risk changes.
A known user authenticating from an established device and behaving normally may require no additional intervention. The same account attempting recovery from an unfamiliar device, changing critical account attributes, or conducting anomalous activity could trigger additional identity verification.
The model changes from authenticate once and trust thereafter to establish trust, continuously evaluate risk, and respond when trust changes.
The Future of Identity Security Must Go Beyond Authentication
Passkeys and identity threat detection address distinct parts of the identity attack surface.
Passkeys reduce risks associated with passwords, credential theft, credential stuffing, and phishing. Identity threat detection addresses risks surrounding authentication, including enrollment, recovery, device changes, session compromise, and anomalous activity.
As organizations eliminate passwords, attackers will adapt. Instead of attacking the authenticator directly, they will look for opportunities around it.
That does not mean passkeys failed. It means they succeeded in making one part of the attack surface harder.
Passkeys answer an important question: Does this user possess a legitimate credential required to authenticate?
Identity threat detection addresses the question that matters throughout the identity lifecycle: Should we still trust this identity?
Organizations need to answer both.

articles.title: European SpaceTech recieves a €560 million injection to promote European sovereignty | EU-Startups
articles.text:
A new partnership between Deutsche Bank and the European Investment Bank (EIB) is set to mobilise a €560 million investment towards European SpaceTech, helping businesses scale, bring new tech to market, and strengthen Europe’s independent space capabilities.
This will directly support companies across the space supply chain, from component manufacturers and launch technology developers to satellite applications and in-orbit services.
“This new partnership between the EIB and Deutsche Bank will help unlock investment in Germany and across Europe – backing the companies, supply chains and technologies that will make Europe’s space sector stronger, more competitive and ready to scale,” said Nicola Beer, European Investment Bank Vice-President.
The agreement follows a series of SpaceTech financing announcements across Europe in 2026.
In Germany, Munich-based The Exploration Company secured €387 million, HyImpulse Technologies raised more than €50 million, ATMOS Space Cargo attracted €25.7 million and deltaVision received €10.2 million.
Elsewhere, Finland’s ICEYE raised €450 million in primary funding, Spain’s PLD Space extended its Series C to €288 million and France’s UNIVITY secured €27 million.
Alongside further announcements involving AIRMO, Hydrosat and Arkadia Space, these financings exceeded €1.3 billion, independently of the proposed Deutsche Bank–EIB investment mobilisation.
EU-Startups previously reported on the EIB’s separate €30 million venture-debt loan to PLD Space in April 2026.
“Europe has the engineering talent to lead in space. Our job is to help finance its next stage of growth,” added Marc Mueller, Global Head Trade Finance & Lending at Deutsche Bank. “Working with the EIB, we can offer space businesses the long-term financing they need to invest, expand production and compete internationally.”
Agreed ahead of the European Space Agency (ESA) Space Investor Forum in Munich, this operation also builds on cooperation between the EIB and European Space Agency to address the financing needs of Europe’s space sector. ESA provides market intelligence and sector expertise to support the development of financing solutions that reflect the needs of space SMEs and Mid-Caps and enable the space sector to access finance.
It also helps connect these financing opportunities with the European space ecosystem, raising awareness among eligible companies and facilitating outreach to potential beneficiaries.
The initiative will support investment in technologies including reusable launchers and spacecraft, advanced propulsion systems, satellite manufacturing and Earth observation. These technologies underpin services ranging from communications and navigation to wildfire detection, pollution monitoring and security.
The financing will have a pan-European reach, with around half of investment expected in Germany and the remainder elsewhere in the EU.
“This partnership with Deutsche Bank will help companies across Europe’s space sector invest in the technologies, production capacity and supply chains needed to scale up and compete globally. In doing so, we are strengthening Europe’s capacity to deliver essential space services more autonomously,” said Robert de Groot, European Investment Bank Vice-President.”
Space businesses often face long development cycles, complex technologies and uncertain commercial returns, making conventional bank lending harder to secure. The partnership aims to give Deutsche Bank long-term funding and flexible financing structures to support commercially viable companies investing in their next stage of growth.
The partnership forms part of Space TechEU, the EIB’s dedicated space financing programme launched in November 2025, designed to mobilise an estimated €1.4 billion in investment with commercial banking partners.
The idea is that this will compliment broader EIB Group support through direct investment loans, venture debt, equity investment and advisory services. By combining these instruments with commercial bank lending, the Group aims to help European space companies secure financing at successive stages of development – from innovation to industrial expansion.
“Europe has a growing number of space companies with outstanding technologies that are ready to scale,” said ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher. “The next step is ensuring they have access to the capital they need to grow. This initiative can help open that path, enabling European space companies to scale up, compete and succeed.”

articles.title: Disney Plus stellt wieder scharf – aber wohl nur temporär
articles.text:
Tech-Trick mit Haken: Disney Plus bringt HDR zurück – aber Millionen schauen in die Röhre
Nach einer einstweiligen Verfügung wegen der Verletzung von Patenten im November 2025 hatte Disney Plus zunächst die High-Dynamic-Range-Formate Dolby Vision und HDR 10 Plus sowie 3D-Filme aus seinem Streamingangebot gestrichen. Ein weiterer Gerichtsentscheid sorgte Mitte Juni 2026 dafür, dass Nutzer:innen bei Disney Plus auch auf 4K UHD und HDR verzichten müssen.
Patentstreit um Videocodec HEVC
Konkret geht es bei dem Patentstreit um die angeblich widerrechtliche Nutzung des Videocodecs HEVC durch den Streaminganbieter. Die Patente beansprucht das US-Technologieunternehmen Interdigital für sich. Im September 2026 hatte Interdigital Disney wegen ausgebliebener Lizenzgebühren auf einen Schadenersatz in der Höhe von 101,7 Millionen Euro verklagt.
Disney Plus war derweil ins Visier von Verbraucherschützer:innen geraten, weil es die Technologien zwar gestrichen, seinen Kund:innen aber keinerlei Entschädigung dafür angeboten hatte. Jetzt versucht der Streaminganbieter, das Problem technisch zu lösen, wie hdtvtest.co.uk berichtet.
Disney Plus setzt auf Workaround
Demnach setzt Disney Plus jetzt auf die HEVC-Alternativen VP9 und VP9-2. Dem Unternehmen zufolge sollen mittlerweile alle Titel in 4K-Auflösung mit VP9 statt HEVC zur Verfügung stehen. Das Gleiche soll mit HDR 10 via VP9-2 geschehen sein. Dolby Vision fehlt bei dieser Lösung aber weiterhin.
Ein Problem an dem Workaround ist, dass Millionen TV-Geräte und Media-Player die Codecs VP9 oder VP9-2 nicht unterstützen. Das gilt sowohl für Samsung-, Panasonic- und LG-Geräte sowie Apple TV 4K oder Spielkonsolen wie Nvidia Shield. Unterstützt werden die Codecs dagegen von neueren Android-, Amazon-Fire- und Google-TV-Geräten sowie Hisense-Fernsehern.
Weiteres Gerichtsurteil droht
Darüber hinaus könnte es sein, dass Disney Plus diesen Tech-Trick bald wieder aufgeben muss. Denn Interdigital ist auch im Besitz von Patenten, die die beiden VP9-Codecs betreffen – und soll schon eine entsprechende Beschwerde eingereicht haben. Käme es zu einem weiteren Gerichtsentscheid pro Interdigital, könnten die Premium-Inhalte erneut verschwinden.

articles.title: No tiene rival: la cámara del nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max es lo mejor que hay ahora mismo en el mercado
articles.text:
Hay algunas verdades absolutas: el sol sale por el este, una hora está compuesta de 60 minutos, que el agua hierve a 100ºC y desde ayer, que el nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max tiene la mejor cámara que existe en el mercado. Posiblemente muchas personas piensen que estamos exagerando pero sólo tienes que echar un vistazo a la galería que figura más abajo para que veas de lo que es capaz.
La nueva serie vivo X500 fue presentada oficialmente ayer martes, pero nosotros llevamos probando el modelo Pro Max varias semanas. Nos hemos ido a China con él, hemos recorrido las calles de Madrid y Barcelona con él y el resultado, en todos los escenarios, siempre ha sido sobresaliente.
La realidad es que vivo lleva años sacando flagships con una cámara magnífica, siempre de la mano de ZEISS. Ya el modelo del año pasado, la serie vivo X300, era para muchos la mejor cámara, aunque es cierto que todavía podía existir alguna duda. Este año esas dudas quedan disipadas.
Además del modelo vivo X500 Pro Max hemos probado el kit de teleobjetivo y lo que ha conseguido vivo es sencillamente increíble. Hay otros teléfonos que posiblemente se acerquen mucho, como el Oppo XFind 10 Pro Max, pero en la foto finish, es vivo el que se lleva el título.
La importancia de una buena cámara
En general, como teléfono, el nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max es muy bueno. El nivel que han adquirido los teléfonos Android hoy en día es magnífico, y más aún si le metes un procesador como el MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro. El resultado es un teléfono que funciona de manera muy fluida y que derrocha potencia en todo momento. A eso le añades baterías de cada vez más capacidad, en el caso del vivo X500 Pro Max una de 6.750 mAh con carga rápida de 90W y una capa de personalización propia a cargo de OriginOS 7, y tienes un teléfono sencillamente perfecto.
Por eso, en los últimos años, el foco especial está puesto en la cámara, donde los fabricantes pueden poner toda la carne en el asador. Sensores más grandes, estabilizadores ópticos, mayor resolución… Y es precisamente en la cámara donde más se nota la diferencia entre dos teléfonos de gama alta.
Durante este año hemos visto como grandes fabricantes, como Samsung o incluso el propio iPhone, han introducido pequeñas mejoras en su cámaras, pero siempre hay aspectos donde se notan las costuras. En escenarios de poca luz o interpretando una imagen tras usar el zoom.
vivo ha solucionado eso y el salto de calidad que ha dado entre el modelo del año pasado a este se nota bastante. Hemos puesto su cámara a prueba en multitud de escenarios y el resultado ha sido siempre sobresaliente.
Qué secretos esconde la mejor cámara del mercado
Si nos fijamos a nivel de hardware y especificaciones, el módulo de cámaras del nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max se compone de: una cámara principal TrueDynamic de 50 megapíxeles, un teleobjetivo de 200 megapíxeles, un ultra gran angular de 50 megapíxeles, todo ello co-desarrollado con ZEISS. A esto le añadimos un sensor de enfoque láser.
Sobre el papel muy bien pero, siendo honestos, muy pocas personas entienden la repercusión que tiene un sensor u otro en el resultado de una fotografía. O que más megapíxeles no es automáticamente sinónimo de mejores fotografías. Por eso, vamos a ver en detalle cómo funciona en conjunto el módulo de cámaras y lo que es capaz de hacer.
Por ejemplo, tiene un sistema de estabilización profesional que funciona a la perfección sin importar el mal pulso del fotógrafo. Esto no es sólo importante a la hora de grabar vídeo sino también en esos momentos donde se necesita dejar el teléfono quieto en tiempos prolongados de exposición, por ejemplo haciendo fotos de noche.
También tiene un sistema de seguimiento de objetos, llamado Lock-On Subject que lo que hace es mantener el enfoque en la persona, incluso si sale momentáneamente del plano. Esto cobra también especial importancia en la parte de vídeo, donde puede granar enfocando hasta en 60 fps. Esto se complementa con las funciones Pro AF Tracking Video en 4K a 120 fps y Auto Framing Video, que permiten realizar un seguimiento preciso de los sujetos y mantenerlos correctamente encuadrados.
Acercando lo que está lejos, muy lejos
Para cualquier persona que prueba la cámara la primera vez, uno de los aspectos que más sorprende es la capacidad del zoom de la mano de su teleobjetivo ZEISS APO, con una distancia focal equivalente a 85 mm. Pero llama mucho, muchísimo, más la atención el extensor de teleobjetivo ZEISS, que permite alcanzar una distancia focal equivalente a 400 mm. Coges el teléfono, le pones la carcasa especial y ya puedes acoplar el teleobjetivo e incluso un disparador que sirve también como agarre, para que sea mucho más cómoda la experiencia de fotografiar.
No importa lo lejos que se encuentre. Durante estos días, hemos intentado llegar a sitios muy lejanos y el nivel de detalle es increíble. Además, donde no llega (por razones obvias de distancia) las capacidades del teleobjetivo, lo completa el uso de la Inteligencia Artificial, que recompone la imagen cargándola de detalles pero de manera muy realista.
Además, gracias al buen detalle de las imágenes, puedes hacer recortes muy concretos que cuando se amplíen, apenas perderán detalle.
Qué maravilla de grabación de vídeo
En nuestro día a día tenemos que grabar cantidad de recursos para redes sociales. Hasta ahora, solíamos usar una cámara réflex profesional y decidimos probar a salir sólo con el vivo X500 Pro Max. Nos encomendamos a la cámara principal ZEISS TrueDynamic, que ofrece todo lo necesario tanto para creadores de contenido como para todas aquellas personas que quieren obtener un resultado perfecto en sus grabaciones de vídeo. La manera en la que ajusta el rango dinámico, las condiciones de luz, el tratamiento de color… es lo más cercano a la realidad que hemos podido ver hasta ahora.
Uno de los modos que más nos ha gustado es el Cinematic Pro Log Video, que permite capturar más detalles tanto en las zonas iluminadas como en las sombras, ofreciendo una mayor flexibilidad creativa en la edición, similar a la que proporcionan las cámaras de cine profesionales. Es una cámara muy polivalente, que se adapta a la perfección a la situación y a las condiciones.
También nos ha gustado mucho el modo 4K Cinematic Portrait Video, que combina calidad de imagen cinematográfica con mejoras inteligentes para los retratos en vídeo. Y para los que necesitan editar después, el nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max puede grabar en resolución 4K a 240 fps.
Como curiosidad, nos llevamos también el nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max a un concierto para poner a prueba el modo Escenario 3.0.
Esto es sólo la teoría de una experiencia que nos ha dejado boquiabiertos, pero en los próximos días verás vídeos en nuestras redes sociales sobre aspectos relacionados con la cámara. No te pierdas nada de lo que publiquemos durante los próximos del ya considerado: mejor cámara en un teléfono.

articles.title: Apple Intelligence is finally coming to China with iOS 27.3
articles.text:
Apple will launch Apple Intelligence in China with iOS 27.3, the company announced on its Chinese newsroom website, as reported by MacRumors. The Apple Intelligence features will be available first in an iOS 27.3 beta that’s set to launch on November 4th, with a full iOS 27.3 release scheduled for December.
Apple Intelligence is finally coming to China with iOS 27.3
Apple is launching an iOS 27.3 beta next week that will bring some of the initial Apple Intelligence features to the Chinese market.
This launch doesn’t bring the new Siri AI to China. Instead, Apple is launching several of its earlier Apple Intelligence features like notification summaries, real-time translation, rewriting and proofreading tools, visual intelligence, and removing objects from photos. Apple also says it has worked with Ailbaba to add support for its Qwen chatbot in some experiences, which sounds similar to iOS’s integration with OpenAI’s ChatGPT that launched in 2024.
Apple Intelligence was approved in China in July, which signalled that the launch of the AI tools was getting near. Apple trained its own LLM specifically for China, Reuters reported in August.

articles.title: Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
articles.text:
Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
Emerging evidence suggests some people with eating disorders are misusing weight-loss drugs.
GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.
A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%. By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders.
What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders. And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue.
Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years. She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says.
Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health. They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others.
It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset. That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny. Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson.
Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the heroin chic era springs to mind). To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world. The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps.
That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023. They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one DALY represents a year of healthy life lost).
The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling. Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found. Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too. In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai.
Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise. In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people.
It gets worse. Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study. The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says.
Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth). So how did we get here?
Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study. Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says.
Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or “fitspiration” content. But users with eating disorders appear to be more likely to engage with this content—and to be fed more of it as a result.
When researchers at the University of Melbourne investigated this phenomenon a couple of years ago, they found that the algorithms of TikTok users with eating disorders delivered 4343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” than those of users who didn’t have the disorders. They also got more content focused on dieting or exercising. Many were fed over 1000 problematic videos per month. Bulik describes social media as “quicksand” for people with, or at risk of, eating disorders.
The covid-19 pandemic—and the social isolation that accompanied lockdowns—also appears to have contributed to the rise in eating disorders. Research conducted in 2021 found that the number of people hospitalized with eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020.
Researchers don’t yet have good data on how trends in eating disorders might have progressed since 2023. But anecdotally, things seem to be getting even worse. “There are more eating disorders, more severe eating disorders… and we’re seeing earlier ages of onset,” says Levinson. “We’re seeing eight- and nine-year-olds with eating disorders.”
“From what I’m hearing and seeing, I am not going to be surprised if that number isn’t at least doubling again,” she adds.
Levinson particularly worries about the impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, which have exploded in popularity in recent years. A Gallup survey conducted earlier this year suggested that 15% of Americans had used one of these drugs for weight loss. And they’re becoming more accessible—drug companies are working on new formulations that are both easier to take and more effective, and many people can buy versions of these drugs from compound pharmacies or dubious online sources.
In a small study published earlier this year, Levinson and her colleagues found that 30% of people with eating disorders had used GLP-1 drugs. The drugs might benefit some of those people. But 10% appeared to have misused the drugs. And Levinson thinks that figure is also an underestimate.
Levinson says she and her colleagues have seen children develop eating disorders after being prescribed GLP-1s for medical reasons. They’ve seen others—even children as young as 11—buy versions of these drugs over TikTok.
“We’re very concerned that GLPs will lead to even faster and more extreme weight loss in people with anorexia nervosa, and that patients will come to us in even more advanced stages of illness that become difficult to reverse,” says Bulik.
Both Bulik and Levinson are continuing to study the impacts of these drugs in eating disorders. In the meantime, both urge medical professionals to consider the risks GLP-1s might pose to people with those disorders. Bulik contributed to a set of research and clinical guidelines, published earlier this month, that recommends doctors screen for eating disorders before prescribing the drugs, for example. The guidelines also recommend more patient education and more robust monitoring of people who take GLP-1s.
If you think you or someone you know might have an eating disorder, you can find information and support at the National Eating Disorders Association.
