articles.title: GM to pay $220 million after selling customer Smart Driver data
articles.text:
General Motors marketed its Smart Driver system as a way for parents to monitor teen drivers or for adults to track their driving behavior. But in 2024, it emerged that GM had been sharing that data with brokers. Those brokers then sold the data to insurance companies, and some drivers found that their insurance became more expensive as a result. To make matters worse, many of those drivers claimed they had no knowledge of ever agreeing to share such data for such purposes.
Last year, GM and its OnStar subsidiary entered into a settlement with the FTC, prohibiting them from sharing some kinds of driver data with third parties. The settlement was finalized this January. That agreement banned the two companies from sharing geolocation data or driver behavior data for five years. At the time, GM also discontinued Smart Driver across its entire range.
Now the automaker has reached terms with the District of Columbia and 35 states after their attorneys general joined together to sue GM as well.
GM said in a statement that “[s]afer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share.”
According to TechCrunch, the settlement with the states is notable in a third party is required to assess GM’s compliance with the new privacy program.

articles.title: 'If the PS5 turns out to have been the perfect Steam Machine all along it would be so funny': custom Linux OS lets you play PC games on your PS5 — but I wouldn't recommend it
articles.text:
Can't afford a Steam Machine? You can now turn your PS5 into one with a new spin on Linux — but I really wouldn't recommend it
As it involves jailbreaking your console
- PS5 Bazzite Deck is a new spin on this gaming-focused version of Linux
- It allows you to boot your PS5 to a Steam Deck interface and play PC games
- You need to jailbreak your Sony console to run it (via the PS5 Linux loader), and that's a risky path to take for a number of reasons
Don't want to fork out all that cash for a Steam Machine? If you've got a PS5, you could turn it into a spin on Valve's gaming PC thanks to a custom version of a Linux distro — although the major catch is you'll need to jailbreak your console.
TechPowerUp noticed the PS5 Bazzite Deck project on GitHub, which takes this flavor of the gaming-focused Bazzite distro and adapts it for Sony's console. (Bazzite Deck is different from vanilla Bazzite, as it was built specifically for handhelds to offer an experience similar to SteamOS for the likes of the Asus ROG Ally — but without some of the headaches of running Valve's OS on that portable).
When PS5 Bazzite Deck is run on a jailbroken console, it'll boot straight into the Steam Deck interface (Steam Gaming Mode), and you can play your PC games from there.
You don't need to install the PS5 Bazzite Deck OS, either; you can just run it from a USB stick (via the PS5 Linux loader). As the developer VivaLaVent explains, when you next restart the PS5, it'll boot its own operating system again, and you'll be back at Sony's welcome hub.
So the PS5 isn't modified by running this OS as such, except for the fact that you have to jailbreak the console (then run the PS5 Linux Loader).
This project is compatible with the base PS5 and PS5 Pro consoles, and you can also switch to a desktop mode running KDE Plasma on your PS5, should you wish.
Of course, game compatibility is going to be hit-and-miss, although a gamer on Reddit observed that they've successfully run Horizon Zero Dawn, Palworld, Genshin Impact, and Rimworld — although Marvel Rivals was a non-starter.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Analysis: interesting times
I should make it very clear up front that I wouldn't recommend jailbreaking your console even as an experiment. There are potential legal ramifications (depending on where you live) with doing so, the possibility of Sony banning your account, and a whole raft of risks (including the third-party software involved, of course). So, if you do want to turn your PS5 into a take on a Steam Machine in this way, proceed at your own risk.
That said, there's an increasing amount of activity around getting the PS5 to run PC games, as you might have seen, so clearly this is something that quite a few gamers are interested in. Most notably, we've seen Playden, which is a very different way of running PC titles on a PS5, by using a compatibility layer (a custom port of Wine) to pull this off. PS5 Bazzite Deck differs in that it replaces the entire OS with a new one, as opposed to running on top of Sony's system.
By all accounts, PS5 Bazzite Deck is pretty slick. One Redditor shares their experience: "I've been using this distro for 4 days, and WOW! Seriously, it's way better than the others. There are constant updates that bring bug fixes."
The DualSense controller support is also niftily implemented by all accounts, as you can pair to both Linux and the PS5 system (saving you from unpairing when switching between the two). The controller's touchpad works like a mouse on the PS5 Bazzite Deck, and seemingly waking from sleep takes only two seconds (much faster than the PS5's normal wake time).
Another gamer on Reddit declares: "If the PS5 turns out to have been the perfect Steam Machine all along, it would be so funny."
But I refer you back to my previous advice on jailbreaking (and game compatibility). Still, this kind of modding is attention-grabbing, to say the least, and we're also seeing it in reverse, with a breakneck pace of development for PS5 emulation on the PC (very much accelerated by the use of AI, it's worth noting).
That effort is, of course, generating a ton of interest given that GTA 6 is nearly here, and indeed there are theories floating around that the work on that PS5 emulator could force Rockstar to launch the PC port much earlier than intended (before an emulated version is up and running). The rumor mill reckons we could see the PC version of GTA 6 early in 2027 as a result.

articles.title: Suspected North Korean hackers steal $5.6 billion in crypto in record-breaking cryptocurrency heist, Binance withdrawals frozen — firm says it will cover losses as stablecoin networks move to freeze $2.4b in stolen assets
articles.text:
Suspected North Korean hackers steal $5.6 billion in crypto in record-breaking cryptocurrency heist, Binance withdrawals frozen — firm says it will cover losses as stablecoin networks move to freeze $2.4b in stolen assets
SpookITober refuses to end.
Update, Friday 30 Oct, 6:30 am ET: This developing story has been updated with information from Binance regarding how its system was compromised, and reports from security outlets claiming North Korea may be responsible. These details have been added to the story below.
From hereon, this month shall be called SpookITober. In yet another high-profile cybersecurity incident this month, Binance.com, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has been hacked, to the tune of $5.6 billion taken in various cryptocurrencies. As of this writing, withdrawals at the exchange are suspended until the company sorts out the situation, though it has stated repeatedly that "user funds remain safe," adding that it "will cover all losses." The U.S.-specific Binance.us website is so far reportedly unaffected. At least two security agencies, including TRM, have pinned the attack on an elite North Korean hacking unit.
"Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," the company said in an update on Friday. "This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it. We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."
"TRM attributes this attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s premier hacking unit," the security firm said. "We base this assessment on robust on and off-chain intelligence sources," continuing to note that the group has been named responsible for a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. Per TRM, this latest instance bears many of the same hallmarks as earlier North Korean heists. According to CNN, an unnamed analyst at Pangolin Intelligence corroborated this story by "Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]."
Preliminary info breaks down the stolen amounts like so: $1.57b in Tether dollars (USDT), $1.45b in Bitcoin (BTC), $875m in Ethereum (ETH), $823m in Circle dollars (USDC), $234m in Tron (TRX), $88.5m in Ripple dollars (RLUSD), $75M in Wrapped-Beacon Ethereum (WBETH), $50m in Tether Gold (XAUT), and $447.5 million in other cryptocurrencies. The "dollar" currencies are all stablecoins, meaning they're pegged to $1 to represent dollars in the virtual space. Meanwhile, Tether Gold is pegged to the value of one troy ounce.
The stablecoin issuers all moved to blacklist the thief's main wallet (you can see it here on the Ethereum blockchain) in their smart contracts, a move that means the amounts in USDT, USDC, and RLUSD are frozen in place, totaling around $2.4 billion. It's possible, but not guaranteed, that the gold-pegged XAUT will also be frozen.
Note that this does not mean those funds have been recovered — the thief simply cannot do anything with those tokens, be it moving or exchanging. Normally in these situations, restitution from the frozen funds happens only after complainants provide proof of ownership, something that usually means copious time spent in courts.
The situation is a lot more grim for the amounts in pure cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, among others. Since there is no governing entity for their blockchains, the most likely prospect is that the remaining $3.2 billion or so is forever lost in the ether — though some networks incorporate clawback mechanisms. Exchanges may block the thief when he eventually tries to cash out his virtual dough, but historically this hasn't been a reliable means of recovery.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Note that this is a developing story, so the tallies are subject to change. Should that amount be final, this heist would exceed the $1.5b stolen from Bybit in February 2025, of which only a paltry portion has so far been recovered. There's little info so far on the miscreant's means of larceny. Apparently, the Binance 14 , Binance 16, and Hot Wallet 34 hot wallets, which hold pooled customer funds, were drained. It's currently not known if this happened via stolen private keys, a compromised signing process, or another type of intrusion.
Binance has assured users that their funds are safe, and most importantly, that it will cover all losses. For what it's worth, the company has a means of insurance and a reasonable track record in these situations, though the amount of bullion pilfered today is exorbitant.
The company created its SAFU reserve fund in 2018, where it deposits 10% of its trading fees to cover any losses incurred from security issues. That fund currently sits at 15,000 BTC in it (verifiable here), or about $1.17b at the current BTC-USD price of $77,858. SAFU is a cold wallet, meaning its private keys are stored offline.
Back in May 2019, thieves made out with 7,000 BTC from Binance, amounting to around $40 million at the time. The company covered the entirety of the losses with SAFU funds.
However, while $1.17b is certainly a tidy sum, 'tis but a morsel of what currently looks like a multi-billion loss. Binance co-founder, shareholder, and former CEO Changpeng Zhao (CZ) stated in a tweet that he too expects that users will be made whole.
As a final note, Binance is alerting everyone to be on the lookout for contact attempts impersonating the company and/or referencing the current situation. Expect a flood of emails, SMS, and phone scams in the coming months. Be especially wary of any "compensation" or "withdrawal restoration" offers, and never click any e-mail links or otherwise offer any account information — always use the official website or applications yourself directly.

articles.title: Google: Weniger Werbeeinnahmen führen zu mehr Werbung
articles.text:
KI-Suche drückt auf Werbeeinnahmen und Google will mit mehr Werbung gegensteuern
Der KI-Boom beschert Google auf der einen Seite sprudelnde Einnahmen, sorgt auf der anderen Seite aber für hohe Ausgaben für Investitionen in die KI-Infrastruktur. Für Investor:innen besonders problematisch sind derweil die negativen Auswirkungen auf die Suche und das Werbegeschäft.
Großes Wachstum bei Suchanfragen
Wie Googles Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler im Gespräch mit Analyst:innen nach Bekanntgabe der Quartalszahlen einräumte, bringt der KI-Modus im Vergleich zur herkömmlichen Suche weniger ein. Zuvor hatte der Suchmaschinenkonzern den höchsten Wert beim Wachstum der Suchanfragen seit fünf Jahren gemeldet.
Der entsprechende Umsatz der Suchmaschinensparte kletterte allerdings „nur“ um zwölf Prozent gegenüber dem Vorjahresquartal und blieb unter den Erwartungen der Analyst:innen. Im Vorquartal (Q2 2026) hatte Google hier dagegen noch ein Plus von 17 Prozent verbucht.
Geringere Monetarisierung im KI-Modus
Der Konzern will das Problem mit der „geringeren Monetarisierung“ der Werbung im KI-Modus allerdings über kurz oder lang lösen. Die Werbetreibenden, so Schindler, benötigten vielleicht noch etwas Zeit, um die Vorteile der Werbung in KI-Suchen zu verstehen. Google-Analysen zufolge sollen Nutzer:innen diese Werbeform als relevanter und hilfreicher einstufen als jene, die auf herkömmlichen Suchergebnisseiten zu sehen sei, wie Ars Technica schreibt.
Derweil kündigte Google an, sein Werbeangebot im KI-Modus auszubauen. Künftig sollen neben den USA Nutzer:innen in weiteren Ländern wie Australien, Kanada, Kenia, Neuseeland oder Pakistan Werbung im KI-Modus angezeigt bekommen. Später soll das auch für Brasilien, Mexiko und Großbritannien gelten.
Google setzt auf mehr und andere Werbung
In den USA will der Konzern sogenannte „multiturn ads“ einführen. Dabei soll nicht nur eine bestimmte Anzeige pro KI-Suche erscheinen. Vielmehr sollen die Anzeigen wechseln, wenn sich die Anfragen in der Suchunterhaltung ändern. Bis die Änderungen die Werbeeinnahmen bei Google wieder stärker wachsen lassen, kann es aber noch dauern.
Im abgelaufenen dritten Quartal 2026 machte das klassische Suchmaschinengeschäft jedenfalls zum ersten Mal in der Konzerngeschichte weniger als die Hälfte des Gesamtumsatzes aus. Das, die hohen KI-Ausgaben und die verfehlten Analyst:innen-Ziele verunsicherten die Börsianer:innen nachhaltig.
Google-Aktie stürzt nach Q3-Zahlen ab
Die Google-Aktie stürzte nach Bekanntgabe der Quartalszahlen an der Tech-Börse Nasdaq umgehend um bis zu zwölf Prozent ab und hat sich bisher auch nicht wieder erholt. Der Börsenwert schrumpfte dadurch auf einen Schlag um 500 Milliarden US-Dollar.

articles.title: DJI acaba de solucionar una de las mayores preocupaciones de los robots aspiradores
articles.text:
DJI entró hace tiempo en el segmento de los robots aspiradores con el ROMO, con un diseño bastante rompedor pero unas especificaciones de gama alta, actualizado posteriormente con el Romo 2. Ahora la compañía da un paso más allá y ha anunciado un cambio de paradigma en el software de sus robots aspiradores: el control local.
De esta forma, la compañía ofrece una alternativa a la nube y a sus problemas de privacidad, ofreciendo a los usuarios la posibilidad de controlar el robot sin dejar rastro en internet. ¿Cómo funciona? El modo de datos locales desconecta la aplicación DJI Home de internet y mantiene los datos de los usuarios almacenados y procesados localmente en sus dispositivos, incluyendo las funcionalidades avanzadas de los mismos.
No obstante, la primera puesta en marcha sigue necesitando conexión a internet. DJI confirma que en la primera puesta en marcha de ROMO se conecta a internet para crear un mapa de su entorno, pero que, una vez que se activa el modo de datos locales, esos datos de mapeo se almacenan de forma local y no en la nube.
De ese momento, y con el modo local activado, todos los mapas, imágenes y otros datos utilizados en la navegación y evasión de obstáculos se almacenan y procesan localmente en el dispositivo, reduciendo el riesgo de exposición externa o acceso no autorizado por parte de terceros a los datos de tu casa.
Con todo, si permites que el robot mantenga la conexión a Internet, DJI aplica un cifrado de extremo a extremo que protege los datos durante la transmisión y evita que terceros puedan acceder a ellos, por lo que en cualquiera de las dos opciones la privacidad está garantizada; ahora solo se ofrece ir un paso más allá para tener control total sobre tus datos y tu casa.
Sobre su disponibilidad, el modo de datos locales estará disponible para ROMO 2 desde hoy mismo. No obstante, deberás actualizar; deben actualizar el robot al firmware más
Reciente para que sea compatible con el modo de datos locales, que también llegará a la primera versión, pero será más adelante.

articles.title: Exclusive details about Akai’s MPC Sample Key
articles.text:
Akai teased its new MPC Sample Key on Instagram earlier this week, and said it plans to open-source its software so the modding community can hack it to their hearts’ delight. While there’s no word yet on when the device will launch or how much it will cost, The Verge has received exclusive images of the upcoming instrument that offer some details about its feature set.
Exclusive details about Akai’s MPC Sample Key
The open-source MPC Sample Key won’t be focused on chopping up drum breaks.
While the Sample Key shares many of the same controls as the MPC Sample — including the three context-sensitive encoders, a large main encoder — it seems designed for pitched sample playback, rather than chopping up drums. In fact, the “chop” button from the MPC Sample is missing entirely from the Sample Key.
The dedicated pitch and mod wheels are another clue there. But there are also buttons for changing the octave range of the 25-key keyboard, as well as ones labeled “chord” and “arp.” Presumably, those enable a chord playback mode and an arpeggiator. While using an arpeggiator to play back drum samples can be a fun way to create rhythms, it’s more commonly used for melodic and bass parts. And a chord mode would be basically useless for drums. Those options also appear to replace the chop function from the standard MPC Sample.
There also appears to be a dedicated looper that could be useful for live performance and layering sounds. And, instead of the Flex Beat effects from the original MPC Sample, there’s something called “Swarm.” Though what that is isn’t exactly clear at the moment.
Like the first entry in the Sample series, the Key has a built-in mic and speaker for all-in-one music production. While we haven’t gotten a glimpse at the back panel yet, the config options on the front suggest that, in addition to MIDI, the Sample Key will have CV outs for integrating with modular synths.
Correction October 30th: The MPC Sample Key is 25 keys, not 37.

articles.title: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz warns that the AI boom is 'a great opportunity to go deceive people' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
“You Can See Everything,” the documentary capturing disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes’ final weeks before prison, is sparking national conversation as it becomes one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time. The film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, intentionally refuses to characterize Holmes as a master manipulator or victim, instead highlighting her uncanny, almost hypnotic knack for making people pity her, even when they’re well aware of her crimes.
Tyler Shultz didn’t need to see “You Can See Everything” to make up his mind about Holmes. Shultz, whose first job out of college was at Theranos, was a key whistleblower who exposed the company’s dangerously inaccurate blood testing devices, which made their way into Walgreens stores and delivered faulty results to real patients. (Theranos reached a peak valuation of around $10 billion despite its technology never actually working — the company only used its own machines for a fraction of tests, instead outsourcing others to third-party equipment.)
There is little reason to keep talking about Holmes — her case is closed, and she’s in federal prison — but her con-artistry has fascinated the media (myself included) for the last decade.
In fact, as Shultz says in an interview with The San Francisco Standard, “the only reason we’re talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now is because she wants us to be talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now.”
But the cautionary tale of Theranos takes on a new significance as we enter the peak of the AI era, when companies that have never turned a profit are raising capital at trillion-dollar valuations.
“I think the days of having a thirty-minute coffee with someone and sending them $100,000 should be over. Elizabeth took that model and scaled it to $100 million,” Shultz told SF Standard.
His grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury George Shultz, was a notable investor and board member himself.
“I believe that what [Holmes] did was raise the biggest angel round of funding of all time, but even at the smaller levels, I think investors need to recognize that when they put that type of money in someone’s hands, they are giving them tremendous power,” he added.
Theranos’ funding often came from individual investors like the DeVos and Walton families, rather than venture firms. Theranos did not share scientific information or evidence that its machines worked with potential investors, citing concerns about revealing trade secrets, which warded off many top venture capitalists in Silicon Valley.
At the time Theranos’ fraud was uncovered, it was seen as a shrill wake-up call for investors that they need to prioritize due diligence. But in the AI era, Shultz worries that investors may forget these lessons.
“A huge danger with AI is that I think it is really hard to do due diligence on it,” he said. “It’s really hard to tell the difference between what is something truly unique and new versus like, a ChatGPT wrapper… If you want to deceive people, I think this is a great opportunity to go deceive people.”
The first question posed by “You Can See Everything” lies in the premise of the movie itself. Why would a mother of two young children choose to invite a film crew to follow her final days with her family before surrendering to serve a prison sentence of over 11 years? The film poses questions that seem inscrutable, but this one seems pretty clear. She wants people to pity her, because this pity could be more useful for her future endeavors than hate or mockery.
In the film, we see Holmes and her partner, hotel heir Billy Evans, working on Haemanthus, a diagnostics company that they call “Theranos 2.0,” which has reportedly raised about $20 million in funding.
“You Can See Everything” doesn’t make Holmes look good, but it also glosses over the more heinous crimes of Theranos, like giving dangerously faulty medical information to real patients, or even its targeted harassment of Shultz himself when he was attempting to sound the alarm about his former employer. In the cultural zeitgeist, Holmes remains more of a joke than a persona non grata.
“I have this feeling of unease about what might come next,” Shultz said. “She’s certainly preparing and beginning her second act, and I don’t know exactly where it’s going to go.”

articles.title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget?
Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume.
The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence.
In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults.
The operating model in one view
Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing.
Stage 1: Attribute every dollar
You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0, and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys.
Setup is four steps:
- Turn on IAM principal data in your CUR 2.0 data export.
- Tag your IAM principals with business dimensions such as team, application, and cost center. For federated access, configure your identity provider to pass session names and tags through OIDC or SAML claims.
- Activate those tags as cost allocation tags in AWS Billing (console or the UpdateCostAllocationTagsStatus API).
- Analyze the tags: they surface in CUR 2.0 with an iamPrincipal/ prefix (for example, iamPrincipal/team) and appear in AWS Cost Explorer under the IAM category within 24–48 hours of activation, ready for filtering and grouping by team, application, or cost center.
This is invoice-grade, per-identity attribution with no custom infrastructure.
The shared-role problem
The pattern that deserves the most attention is the shared-role problem, because it is where most platforms silently lose attribution. A large language model (LLM) gateway that calls Amazon Bedrock through a single IAM role attributes every dollar to that one role, eliminating per-user visibility entirely. The fix is per-user session management. The gateway assumes the Amazon Bedrock invocation role once per user, passing the user’s identity as the role session name and their attributes as session tags, then caches those credentials for up to an hour (one AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) call per user per hour, not per request).
This needs two roles: a gateway execution role holding sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession permissions, and the Amazon Bedrock invocation role it assumes. The result is line_item_iam_principal entries like assumed-role/BedrockRuntimeRole/gw-alex, each carrying its user’s tags: per-user and per-tenant attribution restored behind a shared gateway.
A note on application inference profiles and Projects
Amazon Bedrock offers two more attribution mechanisms, each suited to a different pattern. Application inference profiles are pre-created, per-application resources on the bedrock-runtime endpoint that carry cost allocation tags. You create one profile per application per model per AWS Region, and callers reference the profile ARN, which fits teams with a small and stable set of applications and models. Projects and workspaces serve the bedrock-mantle endpoint (Responses API, Chat Completions API). A project isn’t tied to a specific model, so a single project ID spans many models, which fits teams whose model usage changes frequently. You pass the project ID at client initialization, and its tags flow to CUR 2.0 and Cost Explorer (see Manage AI costs with Amazon Bedrock Projects). Projects are the attribution path for OpenAI-compatible workloads on Amazon Bedrock.
For bedrock-runtime workloads, we recommend IAM principal attribution through session tags as the primary mechanism. It scales with your identity system, requires no pre-created resources, and covers every model and API operation. Application inference profiles work well when a small, stable set of business units needs invoice-grade billing separation without changes to identity design. Use projects for bedrock-mantle workloads that use the Responses API or Chat Completions API.
Stage 2: Make every request observable
CUR tells you who spent. Invocation logs tell you what happened. Amazon Bedrock supports model invocation logging of request data, response data, and metadata to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or both. Use Amazon CloudWatch for fast operational queries and S3 plus Amazon Athena for long-term business intelligence (BI) access. Treat logging as infrastructure, not a manual toggle: provision the log group or bucket through code, define retention and encryption policies, and validate delivery during environment setup. If logging exists only in development or only in one Region, your cost program becomes fragmentary the moment usage grows.
Logging also closes the latency gap: CUR attribution lags roughly 24 hours, but CloudWatch plus OpenTelemetry can power near-real-time dashboards showing per-developer spend within minutes (Analyzing Claude Code usage with CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry demonstrates this end to end).
Request metadata for workload-level attribution
Raw logs answer identity-level questions. To answer workload-level questions (which feature, workflow, or tenant generated the tokens), stamp request metadata on every call. Amazon Bedrock captures this metadata in the invocation logs for later analysis:
The following example uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock through the US cross-Region inference profile. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. For availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
Amazon Bedrock doesn’t enforce request metadata, and teams drift into inconsistent schemas quickly when every application does its own thing. The platform team should inject mandatory metadata centrally in a shared SDK wrapper or gateway, normalize the key set, and treat metadata coverage as a platform health metric.
Diagnostic queries
With logs and metadata in place, CloudWatch Logs Insights answers the standing questions. Who consumes the most tokens:
The same query grouped by requestMetadata.application and requestMetadata.workflow instead of caller produces the workload-level leaderboard: the view product and engineering teams will ask FinOps for the moment chargeback conversations start.
Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.
Stage 3: Enforce budgets
With attribution and observability in place, enforcement becomes an architecture choice rather than a wish. There are three viable tiers. The right one depends on your spend velocity, your risk tolerance for overspend, and how your tools connect to Amazon Bedrock.
Tier 1: Monitor and alert (no blocking)
Amazon Bedrock writes principal identity into the billing pipeline automatically. You put AWS Budgets on top for threshold alerts, with the OpenTelemetry dashboards from Stage 2 closing the 24-hour CUR gap for day-to-day visibility. Nothing to deploy, native AWS billing, and no added latency on inference calls. It works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. Nothing can hard-stop spend, so you see the problem after it happens. Right for early adoption, where alerting plus human intervention is sufficient. Two builder guides walk through it: Limiting Bedrock usage and controlling costs, and Deep dive on managing Bedrock in Claude Code with AWS Budgets and Tags.
Tier 2: IAM tag enforcement (deny on breach)
An aggregator AWS Lambda function tallies per-user token and dollar counters in Amazon DynamoDB from invocation log data. When a user breaches their threshold, the function adds their identity to a shared IAM deny policy (denying bedrock:*) until a monthly reset or admin override. This enforcement runs entirely on IAM and Amazon Bedrock logging, with no third-party component in the inference path, and it works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. The Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock in the AWS Solutions Library provides a deployable variant. It checks each user’s usage against per-user and per-team limits when it issues credentials, and withholds credentials once a user exceeds their limit. Because that check uses usage telemetry emitted by the client, its figures can differ from CUR. In either form, enforcement is asynchronous. A block takes effect seconds to minutes after the breaching call for an IAM policy update, or at the next credential refresh for the credential check. Your platform team owns the pipeline. This tier is right for teams that need real enforcement, can tolerate that lag, and want to keep third-party software out of the data path.
Tier 3: Gateway enforcement (synchronous block)
A gateway sits in the inference data path and enforces budgets synchronously, returning HTTP 429 the moment a user or team exceeds their limit. You get sub-second blocking, per-user model allowlists, token rate limits, and centrally enforced routing rules. The trade-off: a component in the data path that must be deployed, scaled, and security-reviewed. Clients must be configured to send their requests through the gateway.
For Claude Code and Claude Desktop fleets, the Claude apps gateway for AWS is the official recommendation. It ships inside the CLI binary and runs as a single stateless container backed by PostgreSQL. It provides OIDC identity, centrally managed policy, OpenTelemetry telemetry, multi-Region Amazon Bedrock routing, and per-user/group/org spend caps out of the box. For mixed-model workloads spanning multiple providers, general-purpose gateways remain the right choice: LiteLLM through the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate reference architecture, or a serverless alternative described in Build a proactive AI cost management system for Amazon Bedrock, Part 2.
Choosing a tier
Two factors dominate.
Connectivity: If developers call Amazon Bedrock directly with no proxy, only Tiers 1 and 2 are viable.
Spend velocity: If spend is already in the millions per month, build enforcement now. If alerts can hold the line for another quarter, invest in Stages 1 and 2 first and add enforcement when the data demands it.
Most organizations should phase it: observe at Tier 1, then step up. Treat all three as bridges, not destinations: the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens already codifies agent cost governance as a first-class architectural concern, and the attribution foundation from Stage 1 is what any managed enforcement will sit on.
Stage 4: Optimize the defaults
Most Amazon Bedrock waste is not individual carelessness. It is platform defaults nobody set. The two highest-impact levers are both platform-controlled.
Model routing
Not every task needs a frontier model. Routine completions (boilerplate, linting suggestions, small refactors) can run on smaller, cheaper models with quality reserved for complex reasoning, through intelligent prompt routing within a model family or routing rules at the gateway (see Reduce costs and latency with Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing and prompt caching for the full walkthrough). Which workflows can downshift is an empirical question: pull the workload leaderboard from Stage 2, run a quality evaluation on the cheaper model for the top entries, and route what passes. For agentic coding fleets, where boilerplate dominates call volume, more than half of calls landing on cheaper models is an achievable target.
Prompt caching
Prompt caching rewards stable repeated prefixes. As of October 2026, the published Amazon Bedrock pricing for Anthropic Claude models in US East (N. Virginia) bills a cache write at 1.25x the base input rate with the 5-minute time-to-live (TTL) (2x with the 1-hour TTL). A cache read is billed at 0.1x the base input rate on Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and at 0.05x on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5. Check the pricing page for your model and Region, because these multipliers vary by model and can change. The break-even math is friendlier than teams assume. With the 5-minute TTL, a single reuse already pays for the write, and ten calls against a stable prefix cost roughly a fifth of the uncached price (about 22 percent at a 0.1x read rate, 17 percent at 0.05x). The only losing case is writes that are never re-read, which cost 25 percent extra with the 5-minute TTL and double with the 1-hour TTL. So the platform dashboard should track cache-read volume against cache-write volume per workflow. A low read ratio means the prefix is not actually stable (usually a timestamp or session ID embedded before the cache point).
Candidates surface directly from the invocation logs:
Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.
Application-level optimization
A third class of savings (just-in-time retrieval instead of stuffed context, compaction of long conversations, distilling stable high-volume workflows onto smaller models) belongs to application teams rather than the platform. The platform’s job is to make those savings visible: publish the per-workflow token leaderboard, set token limits per model and workflow, and let the teams that own expensive workflows see exactly where they stand.
Stage 5: Operate the loop
The first four stages produce data. This one turns it into decisions. The platform team runs a standing health dashboard with four signals:
- Model mix: Which models are called and how often, the direct measure of routing discipline.
- Failed request rates: Errors, throttles, and timeouts. Each retry adds latency, and a client-side timeout on a request that still completes on the service side can be billed twice, once for the abandoned call and once for the retry.
- Cache effectiveness: The read-versus-write ratio from Stage 4.
- Metadata coverage: The percentage of production calls with complete metadata. Every uncovered call is an attribution blind spot that quietly degrades every other number.
When a signal drifts, the remediation is a policy change (routing rules, token limits, metadata enforcement), not an email asking teams to be careful.
The money loop
FinOps runs the money loop on the same data. When attribution is clean, anomaly detection becomes an investigation stream rather than a panicked all-hands: a spike in a tagged team or application triggers a lookup in the Stage 2 leaderboard, not a war room. Chargeback runs from CUR groupings by team and application.
Scorecard
The following thresholds are starting points, not prescriptions. Calibrate them against your own fleet data and pricing tier before adopting them as policy.
| Dimension | Metric | Green | Yellow | Red | 
| Unit economics | Cost per successful outcome | ≤ budget | 1–1.5x budget | >1.5x budget | 
| Per-dev cost | Daily spend per developer | <$100 | $100–$300 | >$300 | 
| Model routing | % of calls to cost-efficient-models | >50% | 30–50% | <30% | 
| Cache efficiency | Cache-read hit ratio | >60% | 30–60% | <30% | 
Green means the workload operates inside its economic envelope. Yellow means routing or caching discipline is slipping. Red means spend is concentrating in premium models or uncached context, and the Stage 3 and 4 controls are the remediation path. Review this scorecard on a regular cadence (weekly for high-velocity fleets, biweekly otherwise) and treat it as the joint FinOps-plus-platform decision surface.
Conclusion
In this post, you learned how to build a five-stage operating model that takes Amazon Bedrock spend from uncontrolled to fully governed:
- Attribute every dollar to an owner using IAM principal tags, session tags, and CUR 2.0.
- Observe every request through model invocation logging and stamped request metadata.
- Enforce budgets at the tier that matches your risk: monitor-only, IAM deny on breach, or synchronous gateway blocking.
- Optimize platform defaults with intelligent prompt routing and prompt caching to remove waste centrally.
- Operate a scorecard and review cadence that turns telemetry into policy decisions.
Notice the first row of that scorecard: cost per successful outcome, not cost per call. That distinction is where this playbook hands off. Everything here makes Amazon Bedrock spend visible, attributable, capped, and efficient, but a workflow can be perfectly efficient and still not be worth running. Deciding that requires measuring the agent against the human process it replaced, which is a product and analytics discipline rather than a FinOps one. What the cost platform contributes is the foundation: clean attribution and per-workflow cost data are exactly the inputs that outcome measurement joins against.
Build the five stages and you can answer, end to end: who spent it, why, and whether it was controlled. That is what it means to manage Amazon Bedrock cost, and it is the difference between a monthly bill review and an operating model.
To get started, deploy the Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock reference architecture for Stages 1–3, then use the cost attribution best practices documentation to configure your tagging strategy.

articles.title: Smaller Components Complicate BGA Rework Heating- EE Times
articles.text:
Smaller components and denser boards are creating new thermal challenges for ball grid array (BGA) rework. Miniature passives can be located within a millimeter or two of rework targets. This tightens thermal profile windows and raises the stakes for precision heat delivery. Traditional hot-air systems that operated at larger scales struggle to meet the demands of today’s high-density assemblies.
The SMT miniaturization trend behind modern PCB design
The drive toward higher functionality in smaller form factors has pushed surface mount technology (SMT) miniaturization to the forefront of PCB design priorities. Designers are packing more components into less space, with passive components such as 0201 and 01005 footprints increasingly used in high-density applications.
The International Electronics Manufacturing Initiative (iNEMI) electronics roadmap identifies component miniaturization and increased packing density as important industry drivers, with HDI microvia sizes continuing to shrink as manufacturers push toward finer geometries. This trend creates new challenges for rework operations that were engineered around larger geometries.
Proximity and warpage risks in high-density assemblies
As spacing tightens, the gap between a target BGA and its neighboring 0201 or 01005 passives can fall below a millimeter. Standard hot-air nozzles weren’t designed for this proximity.
Airflow meant to reflow a single package can reach adjacent passives and cause unintended reflow, misalignment, or physical displacement. Thinner substrates and multi-layer stackups add warpage concerns when uneven thermal gradients stress the PCB during heating and cooling cycles.
Proper thermal profiling practices show that warpage occurs when temperature gradients exceed acceptable limits. Bottom-side preheaters with adjustable nozzles help reduce localized substrate stress.
A peer-reviewed heat shield study found that strategic heat shield placement resulted in up to an 8.18% reduction in adjacent-component peak temperatures. It also found that keeping center and corner BGA temperatures below 195° Celsius and 210° Celsius, respectively, cut solder joint cracking rates by more than half. Some facilities are reportedly adopting focused laser rework systems and micro-convection stations that establish much narrower thermal zones.
Solder voids and capillary effects at micro geometries
Thermal profile windows tighten as solder ball diameters shrink. At the scale of SMT miniaturization, airflow turbulence from convective heating can disrupt the surface tension of molten solder. This poses a risk of defects, such as capillary wicking or vapor-pressure-driven voiding, in underfilled fine-pitch BGAs.
Even minor package or PCB warpage during the cooling phase can cause solder bridging between adjacent balls or open joints where contact fails to establish. The margin for error becomes nearly invisible. Heating methods that worked reliably at 0.5-mm pitch often struggle at 0.3 mm. A finer pitch requires tighter process control windows and more precise thermal delivery systems.
How convective hot air heating works
Energy transfer in convective heating happens through circulated airflow directed via sized nozzles. Responsive control over ramp rates and cooling phases makes the method effective for many rework scenarios. As component geometries shrink, however, maintaining airflow uniformity becomes more challenging, and that uniformity can affect thermal delivery consistency.
For instance, a nozzle sized for a 15-mm BGA may create edge effects or turbulence when operators attempt to confine heat to a 5-mm device surrounded by delicate passives. The physics favor larger-scale applications where spatial margins allow airflow to spread predictably.
The physics behind radiant and infrared heating
Radiant heating, including infrared (IR), delivers energy via electromagnetic radiation rather than relying on airflow. However, while this removes turbulence concerns, it introduces a different set of variables for operators evaluating the BGA rework process. Top-to-bottom thermal uniformity depends heavily on whether the station includes a focused bottom hot-air feature.
Stations without this feature can’t ensure that radiant energy is distributed evenly from the top of the BGA to the bottom of the PCB. Operators often need to compensate by raising under-heater temperatures, and the required temperature delta varies significantly across different equipment designs.
Hot air and IR station capabilities become critical when facilities need consistent, repeatable results on high-density boards, where even small thermal imbalances can cause joint failures or damage to nearby packages. The temperature can vary by up to 100° Celsius from the software setpoint in some machines, so it’s important to calibrate and monitor temperatures to create a reliable profile.
Thermal profiling for high-density PCB rework
Equipment selection comes down to matching heating physics to board architecture. While convective systems offer ramp control, they often struggle with proximity constraints.
Radiant approaches can reduce turbulence, though engineers must pay careful attention to top-to-bottom uniformity. The IPC-7530 thermal profiling standard provides the formal framework for temperature profiling in mass soldering processes like reflow. This gives engineering teams a consistent basis for evaluating rework equipment capabilities.
Why heating method choice now defines rework success
Choosing a heating method is a primary equipment decision. As geometries shrink and assembly densities rise, thermal delivery physics in the BGA rework process affects yield in high-value assemblies. Matching rework heating systems to current and future board designs protects production efficiency and assembly integrity. Designers can only expect the industry to push further into sub-millimeter spacing in the next few years.

articles.title: Leben auf dem Mars? Ältester Meteorit liefert bedeutende Hinweise für Wasser
articles.text:
4,1 Milliarden Jahre alt: Ältester Mars-Meteorit offenbart Spuren von Wasser
Meteoritenbruchstücke, die irgendwo auf der Erde landen, können beeindruckende Zeugen der Vergangenheit unseres Sonnensystems sein – das zeigt sich jetzt gerade wieder an „Teghaza 001“. Verschiedene Analysen ergaben, dass der unscheinbare Stein vom Mars stammt und mindestens 4,1 Milliarden Jahre alt ist. Und: Der Meteorit enthält Hinweise auf ein Wasservorkommen auf dem Mars.
Die Ergebnisse der gemeinsamen Untersuchung des Meteoriten durch die University of New Mexico, das Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), das Caltech und die UCLA wurden jetzt in der Fachzeitschrift Science veröffentlicht.
Ähnlichkeit mit „Black Beauty“: Warum der Meteorit Forscher überraschte
Zunächst war es der Wissenschaftler Carl Agee vom Institut für Meteoritenkunde der University of New Mexico, der auf die Besonderheiten des Meteoriten aufmerksam wurde. In seiner Analyse von Proben des Marsmeteoriten entdeckte Agee „ungewöhnliche Merkmale in Textur, Mineralogie und Zusammensetzung, die bei Marsmeteoriten unüblich sind.“
Unüblich, aber nicht unbekannt. Stattdessen erinnerte Agee die Zusammensetzung an „Black Beauty“, den ersten Meteoriten, der der Kruste des Mars zugeschrieben werden konnte.
„Mir fiel auf, dass dieser Meteorit Black Beauty ein wenig ähnelte, nicht genau, aber die Sauerstoffisotopenwerte wiesen Ähnlichkeiten auf“, so Agee gegenüber phys.org. „Ich untersuchte ihn mikroskopisch und fand Bereiche mit hohen Konzentrationen an Manganoxid, einer Verbindung, nach der die Rover auf dem Mars suchen, da sie als Indikator für lebensfreundliche Umgebungen gilt.“
Manganoxid-Funde: Hinweise auf Wasser und mögliches Leben auf dem Mars
Manganoxid gilt für viele Wissenschaftler:innen als ein häufiges Nebenprodukt mikrobiellen Lebens. Auch die ungewöhnliche Sauerstoffisotopen-Zusammensetzung und veränderte Mineralien fielen den Wissenschaftler:innen als bemerkenswert auf. Laut Agee zeichnen sie ein ganz anderes Bild vom Mars als das, das wir heute kennen.
„Diese Probe stammt wahrscheinlich aus einer Umgebung auf dem Mars, die der Erde ähnlicher war“, sagt der Wissenschaftler. Dabei spricht er von Oberflächenwasser, einer dichteren Atmosphäre und möglicherweise sogar einem schützenden Magnetfeld, das vor Strahlung aus dem All schützte. Das ist zwar alles noch kein Beweis für einstiges Leben auf dem Mars, hilft aber, die Geschichte unseres Nachbarplaneten besser zu verstehen.
4,1 Milliarden Jahre alt: So wurde Teghaza 001 datiert
Aufgrund der besonderen Beschaffenheit des Meteoriten holten Agee und sein Team schließlich weitere Wissenschaftler:innen und Institute ins Boot. Dabei wurden Zirkonkristalle in dem Meteoritengestein entdeckt, die per Uran-Blei-Methode zur Altersbestimmung genutzt werden konnten. Und das Ergebnis beeindruckt: Teghaza 001 ist rund 4,1 Milliarden Jahre alt. Laut Agee ist er damit der älteste bekannte Mars-Meteorit aus Lava-Gestein überhaupt.
Doch nicht nur die Superlative beeindruckt, auch die Bedeutung dahinter: Der Meteorit stammt aus der Frühphase des Mars, dem sogenannten Prä-Noachium. „Wenn primitives Leben auf dem Mars weit verbreitet war, dann ist dies der wahrscheinlichste Zeitpunkt dafür“, ordnet Agee ein. Und die Analysen stützten diese frühere Einschätzung.
Anders als andere Mars-Meteoriten: Aus welcher Region stammt Teghaza 001?
Weil sich Teghaza 001 chemisch und mineralogisch deutlich von anderen Mars-Meteoriten unterscheidet, dürfte er aus einer Region stammen, die bisher kein Rover erreicht hat. Mit Fernerkundungsdaten konnte das Team die Suche immerhin eingrenzen: Die Mineralogie passt zu den südlichen Hochländern des Mars, möglicherweise Richtung Hellas-Becken, sagt Yang Liu vom JPL der Nasa.
Künftige Marsmissionen könnten also diese Region ins Auge fassen, um weitere, ähnlich aufschlussreiche Proben zu finden.

articles.title: Malicious Claude Code extension on Cursor planted SSH backdoors
articles.text:
A malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code VS Code extension was distributed through Cursor's extension marketplace for approximately 11 hours on October 29, exposing up to 5,000 developers to malware designed to install persistent SSH backdoors.
The extension used the version number 2.1.313 and was distributed between 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. Pacific Time.
Cursor is an AI-powered code editor built from Microsoft’s open-source Visual Studio Code (VS Code), with support for VS Code extensions. Anthropic’s Claude Code extension brings its AI coding assistant directly into compatible editors, helping developers write and debug code using natural-language instructions.
Cursor says Anthropic did not develop the malicious extension but has not explained how attackers distributed the compromised package under Anthropic's name.
"Between about 2:27 am PT and 1:35 pm PT today, a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code extension Marketplace," warned Cursor.
"The extension runs malicious code that attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor."
Researchers at Phorion and OpenSourceMalware found that the attackers inserted a malicious JavaScript loader at the beginning of the extension's extension.js file, leaving the legitimate extension code otherwise unchanged.
The malicious code executes when the extension loads, without requiring user interaction with Claude Code.
When installed, the malicious extension performs the following actions on compromised systems:
- Collects system and user information, including Git email and public IP address.
- Adds an attacker-controlled SSH key and attempts to enable SSH access and establish a reverse tunnel.
- Installs persistence through a macOS LaunchAgent or Windows scheduled task/Startup script, retrying the tunnel roughly every minute.
- Sends host details and backdoor status to the attacker’s server at the IP address 134.209.82[.]225
However, according to Phorion, coding errors in the malware's SSH setup routines likely prevented attackers from gaining remote access to many affected Windows and macOS systems.
The mistakes prevented the malware from enabling SSH on machines where it was not already running, leaving the reverse tunnel unable to provide access to the compromised device.
On macOS, the malware attempts to check whether Remote Login is enabled using the systemsetup -getremotelogin command, but runs it without elevated privileges. Instead of returning the SSH service's status, the command produces an administrator-access error.
Because the malware only attempts to enable SSH when the output contains "Off," it skips the activation step entirely.
On Windows, the malware attempts to install and start the OpenSSH server through PowerShell, but it tries to do so via /bin/sh, a Unix shell that isn't available on standard Windows installations. Due to this, the SSH setup fails.
In both cases, the malware can still install its SSH keys, establish persistence, and attempt to create the reverse tunnel. However, if the SSH server is not already running, the tunnel cannot provide access to the compromised machine.
Even if the SSH backdoor fails, the malware still sends reconnaissance data to the attacker's server, including the victim's username, hostname, public IP address, Git email address, and names of environment variables associated with sensitive credentials.
However, the script does not directly steal credentials, suggesting the attackers intended to retrieve sensitive data manually after gaining access through the SSH tunnel.
Cursor removed the malicious extension and temporarily shut down its entire marketplace to audit other extensions and rotate all access keys before making it available again.
The company also worked with the hosting provider to take the attacker's server offline, disrupting both the reverse SSH connections and the transmission of reconnaissance data.
Following an internal investigation, Cursor says it found no evidence that any other extension versions or the official distribution were affected.
Those who have downloaded the package during the exposure window should check for the presence of an 'svc-telemetry' SSH key on their machines, and follow Cursor’s remediation instructions if impact is confirmed.
For impacted machines, it is recommended to isolate them, rotate accessible secrets, invalidate sessions, and rebuild the affected environment from safe backups.
While initial reports suggested that npm, Open VSX, and Microsoft's Visual Studio Code Marketplace were also impacted, it was later confirmed that Cursor was the only source distributing the malicious extension.
However, many questions remain unanswered about the supply chain attack, including how the threat actors published a malicious extension under Anthropic's name on Cursor's marketplace and whether Cursor or Anthropic's systems were compromised during the incident.
BleepingComputer contacted Anthropic and Cursor with questions about the attack and will update this story if we receive a response.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.
