articles.title: North Korean hackers blamed for stealing record $6.3B in Binance breach | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Hackers working for the North Korean regime have been blamed for a record cryptocurrency heist following a cyberattack at crypto exchange Binance. The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers.
The breach is by far the largest known theft of crypto in history, though the incident has not been confirmed yet to be resolved, and the amount of crypto stolen may change.
In a post on X, Binance said its initial investigation showed that the hackers broke into the company’s network after targeting a “compromised” Binance engineer’s laptop, which “allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
Binance said it has seen no evidence of a leak of its private keys, which would grant the hacker near-unfettered control over the company’s stores of crypto.
The crypto exchange — the world’s largest — said it has now suspended all deposits and withdrawals while its investigation into the breach continues. TechCrunch reported on Thursday that the exchange had paused withdrawals across some of its blockchains.
Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim. The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.”
Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners. The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.”
It’s unclear how the hack went down or under what circumstances the employee’s laptop was compromised, but it’s not uncommon for security incidents to stem from the use of compromised software on employee devices.
Software is generally built from many components, including open source projects, which hackers regularly target, compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on. Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords, and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee.
Binance will face questions about why the company’s security allowed a single employee’s laptop to access systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in funds.
Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach. TechCrunch has also asked the company who, if anyone, performed a security audit of Binance’s network and systems prior to the hack. Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review.
Security researchers at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and forensic company, attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, and called it the “largest hack in history.”
Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges. This group was also blamed for the now-second-largest heist on record, a $1.4 billion theft from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
According to TRM, the theft of Binance’s billions in crypto took about 20 minutes.
Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers. Elliptic said some of the stolen funds ended up in the same wallet that was used in a previous cyberattack on crypto exchange Bitget earlier this year, in which hackers stole $351 million.
The U.S. government and its allies have long warned about the threat from North Korea, which remains cut off from the U.S. and the global financial system for its ongoing development of its nuclear weapons program. Researchers say the breakaway country’s sole motivations are to steal as much crypto as possible in order to continue developing its sanctioned weapons of mass destruction.
Updated with statement from Binance.

articles.title: GPT-6.1 Terra vs. GPT-6 Astra: One sacrifices accuracy for lower cost and higher speed at high effort
articles.text:
GPT-6.1 Terra vs. GPT-6 Astra: One sacrifices accuracy for lower cost and higher speed at high effort
OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra on October 26, marketing it as a cheap, fast model for high-volume everyday work, priced at a tenth of its GPT-6 Astra flagship.
As the mid-priced model in its GPT-6 family, OpenAI lists Terra at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, a mere tenth of Astra’s $10 and $50. The AI giant also reports that Terra completes tasks more than three times faster than Astra in its Agents’ Last Exam benchmark. Those computer-use results are not directly comparable to the three tests below.
Early benchmarks showed some limitations, alongside gains. Plotly reported that Terra caught three of five planted patterns in its analytics test and passed 40 of 43 questions overall. Artificial Analysis found that it guessed on 38% of questions it couldn’t answer instead of saying so, down from 88% for GPT-5.6 Terra in the same benchmark. DualEntry’s accounting benchmark put its accuracy at 78.2%.
In this AI arms race, each launch needs to be marketed as the best; otherwise, it risks being ignored. This can create a confusing experience for users, especially when reality doesn’t quite match the promise. I compared Terra with Astra on three synthetic tasks to see how their speed, estimated token costs, and accuracy differed. This is a separate test of those trade-offs, not a replication of OpenAI’s computer-use benchmark.
The tests
I ran the final version of each test once per model through OpenAI’s API with reasoning effort set to high. I didn’t set an output-token cap, though the models still have built-in output limits. I graded each test against keys I built and verified, after developing three versions of each test. These are single-run results on synthetic tasks, not estimates of repeatability or performance across all workloads. Matching the effort setting does not impose the same reasoning-token budget on both models.
Both models returned the same score on easy and medium-difficulty tests. To test the real soft spots, after the same results returned a third time, I ran hard tests against a weaker model, GPT-5 Mini, until Mini’s score was very low.
Here is the final iteration of the tests. These are the tests detailed in the remainder of this article. In the usage figures below, “out” includes reasoning tokens; the parenthetical reasoning count is a subset, not an additional charge. Costs are estimates calculated from the reported tokens at standard uncached input and output rates, excluding any tool charges or billing adjustments. They are not verified invoice totals.
- SQL reasoning – I built a fake database of 500 software builds and asked each model 25 questions about it. Some builds were deleted, some were retries, costs are in three currencies, and a few questions depend on time zones. Two of the questions can’t be answered from the data.
- Data validation – I gave each model a spreadsheet of 4,950 fake customer records and 19 rules they’re supposed to follow. Some rules only make sense across the whole file, like no more than three customers at one postal code and no referral loops; forty records break a rule, and 10 look wrong but are actually fine.
- Incident log triage – I wrote about 7,000 lines of logs from a fake outage across more than 20 services. I planted errors like drifting clocks, error messages blaming the wrong service, and unrelated changes sending alerts before the one that actually caused the outage.
SQL reasoning
This test showed the widest split between the two models. Astra scored 48/50 and Terra 26/50. Each of the 25 questions was worth two points, for a total of 50. An answer had to be exactly right to earn the two points, so a close answer earned zero. Unanswered questions also earned zero points. For the questions that can’t be answered from the data, the correct answer was to identify that. On every other question, a model that didn’t give an answer earned zero.
Terra processed all 500 rows and handled soft deletes, retries, and three currencies. Its one miss was the total run time for 151 builds in a single region. Astra’s answer came in 406 seconds short of the correct 31,428. Its answer was 31,022 seconds, about 1.3% below the stated correct total. The final answer alone doesn’t show whether the error came from addition, a skipped row, or a misread value.
Astra was more accurate in this run, but its incorrect total still needed checking. It generated 27,970 reasoning tokens, and the response took 319.7 seconds—more than five minutes.
On the six questions that required adding up costs or durations across all 500 rows, Terra didn’t attempt an answer. It wrote a SQL query for me to run instead and marked each one as not calculated. Terra didn’t make up numbers, which is good. But it left the hardest part of the job, running the query and getting the totals, for you to do yourself. This is the first time I’ve seen AI hand work back.
The bigger problem is that Terra answered six questions wrong. Four of them were counts that were off by just one or two. Terra gave those answers with the same confidence as its correct ones, so nothing signaled that they were wrong. If you used those numbers in a report, you wouldn’t know which ones to double-check.
I’m including the numbers for both Terra and Astra here, but since the results were so different, the lower price and faster time aren’t wins.
- Terra 133.1 s, 21,060 in, 11,554 out (10,707 reasoning), $0.079
- Astra 319.7 s, 21,060 in, 28,806 out (27,970 reasoning), $1.65
Data validation
Astra scored a perfect 50, and Terra scored 45. 40 of the 50 points came from the 40 records that broke a rule. A model earned one point for each record it flagged, as long as it named the rule the record broke. The last 10 points came from records that looked wrong but followed every rule. A model lost a point for every correct record it accidentally flagged as incorrect.
Before giving its answer, Terra warned that it couldn’t reliably check all 4,950 records against the rules and might miss some (as it did in the SQL test). The reported input fit within the model’s context window, and I did not set an output cap. Terra generated 1,841 reasoning tokens compared with Astra’s 12,831. The responses took 31.4 and 145.0 seconds, respectively; these elapsed times don’t isolate reasoning time.
Terra correctly flagged 35 of the 40 invalid records and flagged none of the valid records: 87.5% recall and 100% precision in this run. Its 45/50 score is a test score, not an accuracy percentage across all 4,950 records. Three of the five it missed only break a rule when you compare them with other records in the file, such as a customer who reused another customer’s phone number. Terra flagged everything correctly, but it missed five invalid records. The results don’t explain why it missed them.
Astra caught all 40, but it took more than four times as long and cost about 12 times as much. Terra used fewer reasoning tokens and missed records in this run; that association does not establish the cause of the misses.
The numbers:
- Terra 31.4 s, 234,045 in, 2,336 out (1,841 reasoning), $0.25
- Astra 145.0 s, 234,045 in, 13,369 out (12,831 reasoning), $3.01
Incident log triage
This one was a tie, with both models scoring 50. I graded this test using a 50-point list of what a correct answer needs to include. To earn the full 50 points, a model had to trace the outage to the settings change in the ledger service, find the three servers with wrong clocks, and avoid blaming the planted false leads. False leads included a fraud service update that was rolled back, a payments setting that changed seconds before the real cause, a database switchover, and an unrelated memory problem in the search service.
Error messages blamed the fraud service, but both models traced the outage to a settings change in the ledger service and spotted the three servers with wrong clocks. Neither model took the error messages at face value. Both checked the evidence underneath, which is what you’d want from an engineer during a real outage.
Astra cost about 11 times as much as Terra and took 2.6 times as long to complete the work. Most of Astra’s additional output tokens were reasoning tokens: 4,628 of the 6,650-token difference. Both models earned the same score here despite that difference. These runs don’t show whether additional reasoning led to better scores on the other tests.
The numbers:
- Terra 94.3 s, 251,651 in, 7,508 out (5,114 reasoning), $0.29
- Astra 244.5 s, 251,651 in, 14,158 out (9,742 reasoning), $3.22
Results
| Test | Terra (out of 50) | Astra (out of 50) | GPT-5 Mini (out of 50) | 
| SQL reasoning | 26 | 48 | 6 | 
| Data validation | 45 | 50 | 10 | 
| Incident log triage | 50 | 50 | 12 | 
| Total (of 150) | 121 | 148 | 28 | 
| Estimated token cost | $0.61 | $7.88 | — | 
| Total time | 258.8 s | 709.2 s | — | 
I included GPT-5 Mini’s baseline results for reference. I rebuilt these tests several times and kept making them harder because both models kept returning identical scores. Because I selected these harder versions after seeing earlier results, they shouldn’t be treated as a representative sample of everyday work. A low Mini score is a comparison point, not an independent measure of test difficulty.
What do I think?
In these three final high-effort runs, Terra generated fewer reasoning tokens and finished sooner than Astra. It scored lower on SQL reasoning and data validation, and tied Astra on incident log triage. That is a trade-off in the results, but it doesn’t tell us whether Terra was overwhelmed or why it made specific errors.
The measured totals were 258.8 seconds for Terra and 709.2 seconds for Astra, so Astra took about 2.74 times as long overall. At the stated standard uncached rates, the estimated token costs were $0.61 and $7.88; Terra’s cost was about 7.8% of Astra’s. Terra scored 121/150 and Astra 148/150 under these test rubrics. The runs show a cost, time, and score trade-off; they don’t show that OpenAI deliberately cut reasoning to achieve it.
Terra matched Astra’s scores on my earlier easy and medium versions, but that does not establish its accuracy on every task at those difficulty levels. On the final tests, I would be cautious about using it for unchecked numerical aggregation or exhaustive data validation. It may be an acceptable lower-cost alternative for some workloads, including tasks like the incident triage tested here, as long as you verify the results. Astra’s incorrect SQL total also reminds you to check its work.
Learning Path

articles.title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints, you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file.
In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses.
The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo.
How Session endpoints work
Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it.
You choose which ports it reaches. You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime: 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports. Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0.
The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl.
Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer, each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access.
The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session:
It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket.
It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting.
A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens http://localhost:8088, and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it.
A Session endpoint is different from a runtime endpoint, which AgentCore runtime already provides. Use a runtime endpoint, such as DEFAULT, to reach your agent, which controls which version of it callers will reach. InvokeAgentRuntime calls resolve through it, so you can keep development and production on different versions and promote or roll back without changing callers. Use a Session endpoint to see what your agent runs in its session, such as a web preview. It’s an authenticated URL that reaches only the ports you allow, works with whichever version the session runs, and stops working when the session ends. For complete documentation, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint.
Solution overview
The sample has four parts. A coding agent runs in the session on port 8080 and edits the website’s files with four tools: list, read, write, and edit. The agent starts a Vite development server on port 8090, which serves the website and pushes each saved change to the browser over its hot-reload WebSocket. On your machine, PreviewApp serves the preview page, sends your prompts to InvokeAgentRuntime, and opens a local endpoint for the website. As Figure 1 shows, the preview page loads the website from the Vite development server on port 8090 through the local endpoint and the Session endpoint, and sends your prompts through InvokeAgentRuntime to the agent on port 8080. The numbers show the order of the steps for one request.
Before step 1, PreviewApp has already called InvokeAgentRuntime once to start the session, which starts the agent and the Vite development server. PreviewApp read the Session endpoint URL from that response and opened a local endpoint for port 8090. The numbered steps in Figure 1 then follow one request for a change:
- The site pane of the preview page loads the website from the local endpoint on localhost:8088. The local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and the WebSocket handshake, and forwards them to the Session endpoint. The Session endpoint checks the signature and the port against allowedPorts, then forwards them to the Vite development server on port 8090. The page keeps the Vite hot-reload WebSocket open.
- You send a prompt from the chat pane. PreviewApp sends it to InvokeAgentRuntime as a standard AWS API call signed with your AWS credentials, and the runtime delivers it to the agent on port 8080. The agent’s steps stream back to the chat pane as it works.
- The agent calls Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock to decide what to change.
- The agent reads the site’s files and saves the ones it changes. The Vite development server serves those files and watches them for changes.
- When a file is saved, Vite pushes the change over the WebSocket opened in step 1, back through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the site pane updates without a refresh.
- From the notebook, PreviewApp reads the agent’s /status route on port 8081 through the same Session endpoint. Only the port changes.
Port 8080 isn’t in allowedPorts, because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without going through the Session endpoint.
Prerequisites
To follow the walkthrough, you need:
- An AWS account in an AWS Region where AgentCore runtime Session endpoints are available, with credentials configured.
- Permissions to create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, upload to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and create a runtime, plus bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime and bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on that runtime and its DEFAULT runtime endpoint. For details, refer to IAM permissions for AgentCore runtime.
- Python 3.10 or later, with bedrock-agentcore 1.25.2 or later and boto3 1.43.122 or later.
- Git, to clone the sample repo, and a Jupyter environment, such as JupyterLab or Visual Studio Code with the Jupyter extension, to run the notebook.
- Access to Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models.
- Node.js 22 or later with npm, which the deployment script uses to package the agent and the website.
The sample deploys the agent as a zip file in Amazon S3 with direct code deployment for Node.js, so you don’t need Docker or an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Session endpoints work with microVM runtimes, not with the Instances compute type, and Session endpoint URLs are reachable over public HTTPS. AWS PrivateLink isn’t supported for inbound connections.
Deploy the agent and its website
First, you deploy the runtime, and the configuration you choose here decides which ports the Session endpoint can reach. The deployment script bundles the agent into one file, adds the website and its dependencies for the runtime’s Linux on Arm64 system, uploads the zip to Amazon S3, and creates the runtime.
The following excerpt from deploy.py shows the two settings that matter for this post. protocolConfiguration says where the agent listens for InvokeAgentRuntime, and allowedPorts lists the ports the Session endpoint can reach: 8090 for the website and 8081 for the agent’s status route. Port 8080 isn’t in the list, because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without it. For the port and path settings, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path.
The website’s Vite configuration makes the development server reachable from the Session endpoint. It listens on 0.0.0.0 at port 8090 and doesn’t restrict the Host header (server.allowedHosts is true), because requests arrive under a host name the runtime assigns rather than localhost. The Session endpoint authenticates every request before it reaches the server, so the server doesn’t need its own host check.
To deploy the runtime:
1. Clone the sample repo and change to the sample folder:
2. Open session_endpoints_preview.ipynb from the sample folder.
3. Run the install cell, which installs the Python dependencies.
4. Run the %run deploy.py cell. Deployment takes a few minutes, mostly waiting for the runtime to reach the READY status.
Open the preview
With the runtime ready, you start the preview. One call does three things: it starts a session (which starts the website), opens a local endpoint for port 8090, and serves the preview page on localhost:8087.
Inside start(), the calls that use Session endpoints are short. The first InvokeAgentRuntime call returns the URL in a response header, session_endpoint_url reads it, and the Session endpoint client opens a local endpoint for port 8090:
To open the preview:
- Run the cell that starts PreviewApp.
- Open the printed link, http://localhost:8087, in your browser.
The page shows the website on the right, served from port 8090 in the session, and a short guide with suggested requests on the left.
Ask the agent for a change
Now you ask for a change and watch it arrive. Each prompt goes to the agent through InvokeAgentRuntime. The agent reads the files it needs, writes the ones it changes, and reports each step as it happens. When a file is saved, the Vite development server pushes the change over its WebSocket, through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the website updates in place.
To ask for a change:
- On the preview page, choose Switch this website to a dark coffee-house color theme.
- Follow the agent’s steps in the chat pane as it reads and saves files.
- Watch the site pane. It changes when the agent saves the stylesheet, and a banner names the file the change came from.
The following video shows the preview page while the agent works through several requests. Choosing a suggested request sends it to the agent, the chat pane lists each file the agent reads and saves, and the site pane on the right updates without a refresh, from the dark theme to a green Order ahead button.
The steps stream because the agent answers with server-sent events when you ask it to. You can send the same prompts from Python with app.ask, which reads the stream with iter_events from the bedrock-agentcore SDK. The open page updates in the same way:
The output of this Python script should resemble the following:
Reach a second port in the same session
The website isn’t the only server you can reach. The agent serves /status on port 8081, which lists each prompt and the files it changed. The same Session endpoint reaches it, and the only difference is the port argument.
The output of this Python script should resemble the following:
What the Session endpoint refuses
When the runtime refuses a request, it answers with an HTTP status, an empty body, and an error code in a response header, so you can tell its refusals from errors your application returns. The notebook sends a request to a port outside allowedPorts and a request without credentials, and the runtime refuses both with 403 AccessDenied.
The following table lists the refusals you’re likely to meet while you build with Session endpoints.
| Request | Response from the runtime | 
| A port that isn’t in allowedPorts | 403 AccessDenied | 
| A request without valid credentials | 403 AccessDenied or 401 AuthenticationRequired | 
| An allowed port with nothing listening on it | 502 PortNotReachable | 
| A URL whose session no longer exists | 404 SessionNotFound | 
How access to your session is protected
The runtime removes its own authentication headers before it forwards a request, so the website doesn’t receive your signature. Requests are recorded in AWS CloudTrail as InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy events, with the event source bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com. The local endpoint acts with your credentials, so it limits who can use it. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, answers only requests addressed to its own local address, and refuses WebSocket connections opened by pages from other origins. Run the local endpoint only while you use the preview. For more information, see Log session endpoint requests in CloudTrail.
The access controls don’t separate the website from the agent. Both run in the same session, so give the execution role only the permissions the agent needs. If the runtime replaces the session’s compute, open connections close, and the agent’s edits might not survive unless the session uses persistent storage. Refer to File system configurations for AgentCore runtime if you need the files to outlast the compute.
The agent’s file tools resolve every path inside the site folder and refuse paths outside it, so a prompt can’t make the agent change other files in the session. If other people can send prompts to your coding agent, consider Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful prompts and responses, and review the agent’s changes before you publish them.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, stop the preview and delete the resources the sample created. The website the agent edited lives in the session, so it goes with the session.
To clean up:
1. Run the stop cell, and press Enter when the notebook asks. This stops the preview page, the local endpoint, and the session.
2. Run the %run cleanup.py cell, which deletes the runtime, the uploaded code, and the IAM role.
Conclusion
Session endpoints give you authenticated access to the applications in an AgentCore runtime session from your own tools over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and WebSocket, on the ports you allow. In this post, you deployed a coding agent with a Vite website in its session, opened the live website in your browser through a local endpoint, asked the agent for a dark theme, and watched the change arrive as the agent saved the file. You also reached a second port in the same session and confirmed what the Session endpoint refuses.
To go further, run the notebook with your own site in the site folder, or change the agent’s tools to match how your coding agent works. For the full set of options, including port ranges, OAuth, HTTP/2, and gRPC, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint.
To change the port or path that InvokeAgentRuntime uses in your own agent, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path. If your agent also needs to run build or test commands in the same session, refer to Execute shell commands in AgentCore runtime sessions. To deploy your own Node.js agent from a zip file the way this sample does, refer to Direct code deployment for Node.js. For everything else the service offers, start with Host agent or tools with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and find more examples in the agentcore-samples GitHub repo.

articles.title: What five P99 CONF talks reveal about database trade-offs
articles.text:
What five P99 CONF talks reveal about database trade-offs
P99 CONF is a virtual conference on high-performance, low-latency applications. Its 2026 event ran October 21–22. Here, we cover five of its 60-plus sessions. The recordings are available on demand at p99conf.io after registration.
Database storage design balances read amplification, write amplification, and space amplification (RUM conjecture). Improving one can increase another, depending on the workload and configuration. The five talks below show how engineers make those trade-offs across different database systems.
“Can Everything be an LSM?”
Almog Gavra, Co-Founder at Responsive (now Databricks)
Gavra frames database design around read amplification (data read per result), write amplification (data written per logical write), and space amplification (storage used relative to live data). A log favors fast writes but makes reads work harder; a sorted array does the reverse. As Gavra put it, “I think about LSM trees as a mechanism for tuning between these two extremes.”
LSMs were built for local disks, but their immutable files also fit object storage. Gavra points to Amazon S3’s lower storage cost, durability, and availability, then names the trade-offs: objects must be replaced rather than edited, each GET and PUT has a price, and cold reads are slower. In his example, a local NVMe cache miss takes about 150 microseconds, versus 20–30 milliseconds for S3 Standard — roughly two orders of magnitude. LSMs batch writes into immutable files; caching helps keep object-store reads off the hot path.
Gavra’s SlateDB is an open-source, object-store-native LSM library. It exposes a key-value interface over stores such as S3, GCS, and R2, so developers can build data systems without implementing their own LSM.
How ScyllaDB Eliminates Read Amplification at Scale
Michael Litvak (Senior Software Engineer) and Felipe Cardeneti Mendes (Technical Director), ScyllaDB
ScyllaDB’s presentation examines Logstor, an opt-in storage engine for read-intensive key-value workloads, not a replacement for its existing LSM engine. For each key, an in-memory index stores a hash and the record’s location on flash. A read can return a cached value or find the record with one disk I/O, avoiding an LSM search across SSTables, Bloom Filters, and Indexed data structures. Tables using either engine can run in the same cluster with ScyllaDB’s existing drivers and consistency options.
The speakers’ preliminary read-dominant test sustained 1.1 million reads per second with p99.9 latency below one millisecond and p99.99 latency around 1.5 milliseconds. That test used 2 KB values; the earlier LSM examples in the talk used 1 KB values, so the results are not direct comparisons. They also reported similar throughput and sub-millisecond p99.9 latency in an 80% read, 20% write workload.
Logstor pays for those reads with a larger RAM index and more work on writes. Even a small update writes the full new value to a log, leaving the old record as dead space; segment compaction later reclaims it. The speaker positions it for bounded key sets, frequent overwrites, and point lookups where the extra memory is acceptable. During this talk, Mendes called the trade-off “optimized for time at the sacrifice of space.”
The Vertical Scaling Wall, and How Valkey Gets Over It
Madelyn Olson, Principal Software Engineer at AWS
Not every bottleneck is storage. Olson begins with Amazon ElastiCache customers who saw sudden p50 latency spikes, then tests where Valkey’s main execution thread reached its limit.
In Olson’s unpipelined GET benchmark, with about three million keys and 650 clients, p50 latency rose sharply near 150,000 requests per second. Valkey already had I/O threads, but they sat idle while the main thread executed commands. The team used lockless queues to keep network I/O and command parsing active on those threads while command execution stayed on the main thread.
Olson reported a new ceiling of about 1.2 million requests per second in that workload — roughly eight times the earlier threshold. (This is the talk’s workload-specific result, rather than a general throughput guarantee.)
For horizontal scaling, Valkey 9.0 introduced atomic slot migration. The source shard keeps ownership while it streams a snapshot and subsequent changes to a target, then transfers ownership once the target catches up. Olson said a roughly 40 GB, three-to-four-shard test ran about 10 times faster without load and about five times faster under a heavy GET workload. If a migration fails before handoff, the staged transfer can be aborted without losing end-user data.
The I/O threads can be added or removed as workload demands change. Olson’s operating advice is to use horizontal scaling for baseline capacity and vertical scaling for short bursts, while keeping command execution single-threaded for now. Her guiding principle? “Efficiency trumps headline numbers.”
Searching 100B Vectors on Object Storage @ 200ms P99
Nathan VanBenschoten, Chief Architect at turbopuffer
VanBenschoten described turbopuffer’s search index at a scale of 100 billion vectors, representing more than 200 TiB of dense vector data. The company reports 200 ms p99 latency at more than 1,000 queries per second and 92% recall in early results. Object storage is the durable backing store, but this high-query-rate workload pins its data in local SSD caches. Hierarchical clustering groups nearby vectors; RaBitQ binary quantization shrinks a shadow index to one bit per dimension, allowing the search to narrow candidates before reranking a small subset using full-precision vectors.
The uncompressed search was limited by the bandwidth needed to move vectors from storage into memory. Quantization shifts more work into higher cache tiers, but it also increases arithmetic intensity, making the system CPU-bound.
“Often when you push down one bottleneck, a new one emerges,” VanBenschoten said. That gives the team a different optimization target, including more efficient vector instructions.
To hold an index this large on SSDs, turbopuffer splits it across machines. VanBenschoten says its separated compute-and-storage architecture favors fewer, larger shards: a replacement machine can point to object storage and hydrate its local cache instead of receiving a full shard from another node. Queries fan out to the shards, and a coordinator combines their top results.
The Fastest Object Storage Client in the World*
Georg Kreuzmayr, Software Engineer at TigerBeetle
TigerBeetle is a financial transactions database. In this talk, Kreuzmayr describes the concept of “diagonal scaling”: keeping hot data on local NVMe while extending the storage hierarchy to shared object storage for colder data.
A failed machine doesn’t need to reconstruct data already stored in object storage. As a scale illustration, he estimates that recovering 128 TB over a 100 Gbps network takes about three hours at line rate; if recovery takes longer than the interval between failures, a cluster can enter a failure spiral.
That design needs an object storage client compatible with TigerBeetle’s single-core transaction processing. Kreuzmayr cites the AWS C++ SDK’s blocking `getaddrinfo` call as one mismatch: A call on that core would stall transaction work. SDK thread pools, runtime allocation, and dependencies also conflicted with the project’s design goals.
TigerBeetle therefore built its own multi-cloud client rather than adapting the official SDKs. It supports S3, Azure, and GCP and can be tested with simulated I/O and injected faults.
Built in Zig, the client includes custom DNS, TLS, and HTTP components, uses `io_uring` and zero-copy sends, and allocates its working memory at startup. Kreuzmayr says the implementation is under 40,000 lines of code and has no dependencies beyond its toolchain. Those choices follow TigerStyle’s three principles: safety, performance, and developer experience.
In the talk’s S3 `PutObject` test — 8 MB requests over plain HTTP without checksums on an AWS `c7gn.metal-24xlarge` instance — Kreuzmayr reports uploads around 20 times faster than official SDKs and five times faster than a research implementation. For `GetObject`, he reports about three times the SDK throughput and roughly 25% more than the research implementation. He attributes the smaller download gain to the cloud TCP receive path. These are results for the stated test setup. The conference summarizes the broader client comparison as 4–10 times faster than official GCP and AWS SDKs.
Kreuzmayr’s takeaway is that building the client required more upfront work but made the code easier to test and tune. As he puts it, “code stops being technical debt and ends up being an asset.”
Performance is a process
Across the five talks, engineers identify different bottlenecks in storage, search, networking, and scaling. Their designs improve specific workloads while introducing new costs or complexity elsewhere.
Watch these and more than 200 other P99 CONF talks on demand at p99conf.io. Registration is required. P99 CONF is a ScyllaDB community.

articles.title: SS7 and Diameter Attacks: How Signaling Flaws Expose Your Phone
articles.text:
SS7 and Diameter signaling attacks can track, intercept, and impersonate you. Here’s how they work and how to stop them.
Your phone can be tracked, your SMS two-factor codes can be intercepted, and your number can be impersonated, all without malware, a phishing link, or any access to your device.
The attacks happen inside the telecom network, in the carrier-to-carrier control protocols known as signaling, the automated descendants of the old telephone switchboard. Most users never see them, and most carriers can’t reliably stop them.
Signaling attacks aren’t new. Most recently, they made headlines when Iranian-linked actors reportedly exploited outdated network technology to locate the phones of US personnel in the Middle East during the Iran war.
But the vulnerability has been around for decades, and it’s been used for far more everyday crimes, like intercepting bank one-time passcodes. It has even been demonstrated by popular YouTubers: Veritasium hijacked a tech influencer’s calls and texts using only his phone number.
This keeps happening
- Criminals have reportedly exploited signaling protocols in attacks on bank accounts and global telecom infrastructure.
- Citizen Lab exposed two long-running commercial surveillance campaigns abusing SS7 and Diameter, with thousands of attacks against targets in dozens of countries.
- Congressman Ted Lieu’s phone was hacked on live TV via SS7 on 60 Minutes Australia
- Attackers have intercepted SMS one-time passcodes to drain victims’ bank accounts.
What is a signaling attack?
Every call, text, and mobile data session requires your carrier to verify you’re a paying customer and route your traffic to the right destination.
Carriers do this with signaling–background messages that identify your location and forward traffic accordingly. Signaling has been the connective tissue between global providers for decades, and it is one of the most overlooked attack surfaces in mobile security.
Two protocols do most of the work: SS7 (from the 1970s, used in 2G/3G) and Diameter (its successor, used in 4G and most 5G).
Both were designed when a small number of large operators could plug into the system, so they assume that traffic claiming to come from a legitimate operator really does. SS7 has essentially no process for authenticating the machine making a request.
Diameter supports stronger authentication on paper, but operators don’t always deploy basic protections like encryption, and many fall back on the same peer-to-peer trust model.
An attacker with access to the global signaling backbone, through a commercial leasing arrangement or a compromised operator, can send messages that carriers worldwide treat as trustworthy.
How does it work
Signaling lets an attacker ask your carrier questions and make claims on your behalf:
- Harvest your IMSI. Knowing your number, an attacker can request your International Mobile Subscriber ID (IMSI) under the pretense of routing a call or SMS. It can be reused for follow-on attacks for years.
- Locate you in real time. Queries can return the cell tower you last connected to. Others, normally reserved for emergency responders, can return the actual coordinates your phone reports.
- Intercept communications. The attacker claims you’ve roamed onto another network, so your calls and texts are redirected to them. Combined with a stolen username and password, this delivers your SMS second factor to the attacker instead of you.
- Impersonate or block you. With your IMSI, an attacker can place calls or send SMS as you. A false roaming claim can also cut off service to your phone.
- Disrupt networks. Deliberately misconfigured signaling messages can overwhelm provider systems.
None of this touches your device. It happens in automated transactions you can’t see and that leave no trace on your phone.
Why firewalls and velocity checks fall short
Carrier signaling firewalls reliably block messages sent to or from the wrong place. For correctly routed messages, they often run a velocity check to test whether you could physically have traveled from your last known location to the one now claimed. If you were in New York an hour ago and a Turkish carrier says you’re on its network, the request is denied.
The structural problem is that the firewall’s location data is often hours old. In research presented at the Wireless Security conference in 2025, Cape, the privacy-first mobile carrier, measured Diameter updates from a visited network arriving as infrequently as every two to ten hours.
For subscribers in the US and Germany, over 250 distinct networks are reachable within a single hour of travel time. An attacker with enough operator identities will eventually find one that looks plausible.
Citizen Lab’s report shows this in practice: the actor it calls STA1 repeatedly tried to track a user by rotating through eleven operator identities in nine countries to look like legitimate roaming traffic. They also pivoted between SS7 and Diameter, which most carriers defend with separate firewalls and little coordination.
Consider a target who boards a flight from Nashville to Berlin and powers off her phone. A message posing as China Mobile claiming she’s roaming there gets rejected, because it’s physically impossible.
A message from a carrier in nearby Nassau, Bahamas, looks plausible, and the home carrier can be fooled into routing her calls and SMS to the attacker.
Protect yourself with private cell service.
Cape is America's privacy-first mobile carrier providing unlimited talk, text, and 4G/5G data, built from the ground up with privacy and security at it's core.
Most carriers track everything: where you go, who you call, what you do. Cape collects the minimum amount of information required to provide you with service, deletes call and text metadata after 24 hours, rotates your network ID to prevent tracking, defends against SIM- and network-based attacks, and more.
Privacy shouldn't cost more. Switch today and get $29 off for life.
Learn More →
How Cape defends against signaling attacks
Cape is a privacy-first mobile carrier, whose approach is to assume the global telecom system is compromised and build protections that keep communications private anyway. There are four layers:
1. Daily IMSI rotation. Almost every targeted signaling attack starts with an IMSI, and once an attacker has yours, it stays useful for as long as you have it. A Citizen Lab report confirms this, with the same IMSIs being attacked across operations separated by months and years. On most carriers, your IMSI is permanent. You get one when you activate your SIM and you keep it forever. On Cape, your IMSI rotates daily. The databases of harvested IMSIs that surveillance vendors build up over the years are no longer useful against Cape subscribers.
2. No SS7. Cape doesn’t support SS7 at all, and there is no SS7 fallback in the network, so SS7-based attacks have nothing to land on. Many carriers still struggle to retire legacy SS7 infrastructure because some revenue-generating part of their network depends on it.
3. Network Lock. Instead of trusting a network’s idea of where you are, Cape asks your device. When a foreign network requests to attach to your phone, Network Lock queries the Cape app, which evaluates the claim locally at the country level and reports back whether it matches. If an attacker tries to attach your IMSI from another country while your phone is at home, the request is denied and you’re notified. Cape’s systems learn only whether the claim matches, not where you actually are, and Cape never collects or stores your precise location.
4. Continuous penetration testing. Most signaling firewalls are compliance tools tuned to GSMA baseline recommendations. Those recommendations are distributed to more than 1,200 member providers, so the same guidance is available to attackers who can send signaling messages. Cape has third-party firms that specialize in current signaling exploitation techniques to test its infrastructure, then hardens the network against what they find, especially anything affecting subscriber privacy.
| Attack | Other Carriers | Cape | 
| Real-time location tracking | Phone attaches whenever it gets service; velocity checks can be beaten by plausible spoofing | Network Lock verifies attach requests against your device | 
| IMSI harvesting and reuse | IMSI is permanent and stays useful indefinitely | Daily rotation makes previously harvested IMSIs useless | 
| SS7-based attacks | Attackers use several methods to evade SS7 firewalls | No SS7 support | 
| Diameter-based attacks | Firewalls rely on widely published GSMA baselines | Firewalls updated from penetration tests using current techniques | 
You can’t patch the telecom backbone, but you can choose your carrier
Following every best practice, such as using encrypted messaging, avoiding public Wi-Fi, and enabling 2FA, still leaves your device dependent on networks never built with security in mind.
For people who are targeted, such as journalists, executives, security staff, and anyone whose accounts rely on SMS verification, the carrier is part of the threat model.
Switch to a carrier built for signaling security. Learn more about Cape →

articles.title: ¿Quieres invertir en criptomonedas? Conoce su valor y cómo ha fluctuado en las últimas horas
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 77.996,72 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de 0,285% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de -0,823% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.230,99 dólares.
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de -0,07%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 707,58 dólares, con un cambio de -6,73%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 55.711 dólares, tras una variación de -5.8099546.
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,08 dólares tras presentar un cambio de -4,69% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
Su avance en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.

articles.title: Razer Blade 18 RTX 5090 Laptop Review
articles.text:
Razer is often called the Apple of the gaming laptop industry. Like the MacBook Pro, the Razer Blade series is famed for being slim, stylish, powerful, and overly expensive. But does the Blade 18 with its RTX 5090 live up to that reputation, both the good and the bad, and can it compete with my favorite desktop replacement, the very similar Lenovo Legion 9i Gen 10?
The Blade configuration we received for review is an absolute beast of a gaming machine. In addition to packing Nvidia's flagship 24GB mobile GPU (175W TGP), there's a 24-core Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus, 32GB of DDR5-6400, a 2TB PCIe 4.0 SSD, and a 99Wh battery. There's also a dual-mode 240Hz/440Hz IPS display, which we'll get to later.
Thanks to the memory crunch, gaming laptops are priced like second-hand cars right now, but few are more expensive than this $5,400 machine.
The slim and sleek descriptors are definitely warranted here. It's amazing how Razer fits all this hardware into a chassis measuring just 15.74 × 10.84 × 1.10 inches. It's the same thickness as the Legion, in fairness, but more compact in its other dimensions.
It's also noticeably lighter at just over 7 pounds, making it easier to carry around than many other 18-inch laptops.
The Blade is stylish. The CNC-milled chassis, with its black anodized finish and illuminated green Razer logo, makes this look like the laptop Darth Vader would use. In a good way.
This chassis oozes quality and expense. There's not a hint of flex in it, and the lid stays firmly in place even when you're bashing away at the keys. It feels cool and smooth to the touch. I also like the clean look of having the power button integrated into the keyboard itself, rather than the usual massive button slapped between the keys and screen.
My only nitpick is that the lack of a lip makes it a little harder to open than the Legion, but Razer would likely argue that omitting it improves the aesthetics.
This is also one of those rare gaming laptops without LEDs (beyond the logo) on the outside of the chassis, so there are no rear light bars, underglow strips, illuminated vents, or edge lighting like you'd find on many rivals. Some people will likely see that as even more incentive to buy a Blade.
Connectivity, Ports, and Keyboard
The Razer Blade 18 offers a generous selection of ports, including three USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 connections, one Thunderbolt 5/USB-C port, and one Thunderbolt 4/USB-C port.
Both USB-C ports support DisplayPort 2.1 and up to 100W USB Power Delivery, although the Thunderbolt 5 port provides display output directly from the RTX 5090, while the Thunderbolt 4 port routes display output through Intel's integrated graphics. Razer doesn't indicate which Thunderbolt port is which, either.
There's also an HDMI 2.1 port, a full-size 2.5Gb Ethernet port, a UHS-II SD card reader, a 3.5mm combo jack, a proprietary power connector, and a Kensington security lock slot.
The Legion 9i Gen 10, in comparison, has one extra USB-C port, two Thunderbolt 5 connections instead of one, and supports up to 140W USB-C power delivery compared with the Blade 18's 100W maximum.
Wireless connectivity, meanwhile, consists of tri-band 2×2 Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) and Bluetooth 5.4.
An 18-inch laptop means you get a full-size keyboard with a 10-key numpad. There's 1.5mm of key travel, and Razer's Chroma RGB lighting offers a slew of customization options.
Below the keyboard sits a large glass touchpad that's responsive and pleasant to use, easily on par with the Legion's.
The Blade 18 offers a very impressive typing experience, but I definitely prefer the Legion in this department for its slightly stiffer keys and larger gaps between them. Also, despite the palm-rejection technology, there were a couple of occasions when the touchpad registered an accidental click while I was typing, but these were rare.
Display
The Blade's screen shares almost exactly the same specs as the Legion's: 3840x2400 at 240Hz, with the option to switch to 1920x1200 at 440Hz. Razer's machine is slightly brighter at 600 nits (vs. 520 nits), while both have a 3ms response time, 100% DCI-P3 coverage, and Nvidia G-Sync.
The part that puts many people off, though, is that both use IPS panels rather than OLED or mini-LED. They're the best IPS screens I've ever seen, but it's still easy to imagine that most consumers would prefer another panel type over the ability to play at up to 440Hz.
The Calman-verified, color-calibrated display looks superb on the Blade. Not OLED or mini-LED superb, but it's still super sharp, bright, crisp, and accurate.
If you want to try the 440Hz mode, you'll need to use Razer's app and restart the machine, just as you do with the Legion and its app.
It's difficult to choose a favorite between the two laptops, as their screens are so similar. The Legion's does pop more because of its glossy coating. However, that also causes its biggest problem: reflections in bright rooms and outdoors, something the Blade 18 handles much better. Razer's machine is actually great to use outdoors and in bright indoor environments, with almost no reflections on the screen.
Ultimately, being able to switch to 1920x1200 at 440Hz is a cool feature to have, especially with a machine packing an RTX 5090, but how many people beyond competitive or dedicated FPS players will actually use it regularly?
Gaming Performance
Razer's Synapse software offers five performance profiles when plugged in: Balanced, Silent, Performance, Turbo, and Custom. We'll be using Turbo for these benchmarks.
A 24GB RTX 5090 paired with a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus is always going to be a powerhouse. It's a shame I wasn't able to get the same GPU in the Lenovo laptop, which has an RTX 5080 and 64GB of RAM instead of 32GB. All titles were tested at 2560x1600 with no upscaling or ray tracing enabled.
2560 x 1600 in Turbo Mode
| Game / Scene | Settings | Avg. FPS | Min | Max | 1 % Lows | 0.1 % Lows | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Space Marine 2 / Mission 4: Servant of the Machine | High | 113.3 | 19.8 | 160.8 | 81.6 | 54.1 | 
| Black Myth: Wukong / Yellow Wind Sage boss | Very High | 73.7 | 42.3 | 141 | 49.2 | 42.8 | 
| 007: First Light / Market | Ultra/High Lighting | 68.2 | 32.4 | 104.1 | 50 | 28.6 | 
| Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced / Havana | Very High | 80.1 | 56.8 | 115.6 | 65.3 | 59.8 | 
| Cyberpunk 2077 / Japantown driving | High settings | 115.6 | 14.6 | 184.7 | 84.3 | 72.7 | 
| Baldur's Gate 3 / Baldur's Gate | Ultra preset | 133.2 | 73.5 | 247.6 | 87.3 | 80 | 
| Assassin's Creed Shadows / Yamashiro | High preset | 75.7 | 21.2 | 139.1 | 61.3 | 54.1 | 
| The Blood of Dawnwalker / Outdoors | High preset | 69.2 | 10.6 | 159.7 | 55 | 45.3 | 
| Onimusha way of the sword demo / Daidara fight | Ultra preset | 99.9 | 75.9 | 121.8 | 85.3 | 80.2 | 
Interestingly, the more expensive and powerful RTX 5090 Blade delivers only around 10 FPS more than the RTX 5080 Legion in most games, with an average performance advantage of ~9%, illustrating the relatively small gaming performance gap between the two mobile GPUs.
We also tested gaming at the Blade's native 3840x2400 resolution to see how the RTX 5090 handled them. Without upscaling, titles like Black Myth and First Light struggle, though several other titles were still very playable.
3840 x 2400 in Turbo Mode
| Game / Scene | Settings | Avg. FPS | Min | Max | 1 % Lows | 0.1 % Lows | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Space Marine 2 / Mission 4: Servant of the Machine | High | 60 | 36.1 | 82.7 | 46.5 | 42.7 | 
| Black Myth: Wukong / Yellow Wind Sage boss | Very High | 38.2 | 14.4 | 182.6 | 27.2 | 20.4 | 
| 007: First Light / Market | Ultra/High Lighting | 42.6 | 17.3 | 90 | 35.6 | 24.8 | 
| Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced / Havana | Very High | 48.5 | 32.9 | 98.6 | 40.7 | 38.4 | 
| Cyberpunk 2077 / Japantown driving | High settings | 69.5 | 34.5 | 142.7 | 55 | 48.7 | 
| Baldur's Gate 3 / Baldur's Gate | Ultra preset | 110.5 | 45.8 | 146.3 | 83.3 | 62.7 | 
| Assassin's Creed Shadows / Yamashiro | High preset | 54.4 | 40.1 | 110.5 | 45.7 | 41.4 | 
| The Blood of Dawnwalker / Outdoors | High preset | 42.2 | 20.7 | 132.7 | 33.2 | 10.4 | 
| Onimusha way of the sword demo / Daidara fight | Ultra preset | 57.7 | 48.5 | 66.6 | 49.6 | 48.5 | 
Synthetic Benchmarks
The RTX 5090 puts the Blade ahead of the Legion in 3DMark, leading by 14% in Steel Nomad and 10% in Time Spy. But that's another modest increase given the step up in GPU tier.
| Program | Test | Result | 
|---|---|---|
| 3DMark | Steel Nomad | 6,411 | 
| 3DMark | Time Spy | 23,948 | 
| Cinebench 2026 | Single Thread | 565 | 
| Cinebench 2026 | Multi Thread | 8,555 | 
Despite sharing the same Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor, the Blade trailed the Legion by around 5% in Cinebench's multi-thread test and just 1.2% in the single-thread test.
Differences in power limits and cooling could explain the gap, as the RAM difference (64GB in the Legion versus 32GB in the Blade) is unlikely to have had much impact on the Cinebench results.
Thermals and Cooling
Packing 280W of total power into an aluminum chassis this comparatively thin and light really is impressive, but it also means things can get very hot. Despite the large vapor chamber and other cooling technologies, you start to feel the heat when pushing this Blade hard.
The area around the keyboard can hit 116-117°F, while the keys themselves can reach 109°F and the touchpad 100°F in extreme cases. The hottest areas of the Legion, in comparison, reached 109-111°F, while the touchpad and palm rests remained at around 89-91°F.
Personally, I noticed the heat in demanding games but never found the Blade too uncomfortable to use. It's something to consider, though.
During a 10-minute Cinebench 2026 multi-core run in Performance mode, the Blade 18's Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus peaked at 102°C on its DTS package sensor, with CPU power draw reaching 137W.
Package temperature averaged 79°C, but HWiNFO recorded thermal throttling, and the processor frequently hit its configured power limit. Under the same test conditions, the Legion 9i peaked at just 88°C without thermal throttling, despite reaching a higher peak power draw of 174W.
Storage Performance
Opting for a PCIe 4.0 SSD instead of a PCIe 5.0 drive like the Legion's is a bit of a disappointment in a $5,400 laptop. It's a decision that applies across the 2026 Blade 18 range, although one of its two M.2 slots supports PCIe 5.0, allowing owners to upgrade to a faster drive themselves.
The CrystalDiskMark results show excellent read and very good write performance, reaching 7,032 MB/s and 5,851 MB/s, respectively.
That's around 42% lower for reads and 55% lower for writes than the SK hynix Platinum P51 PCIe 5.0 SSD in the Legion, which reached 12,217 MB/s and 12,932 MB/s. However, most people are unlikely to notice much difference between the two in everyday use.
Battery Life and Noise
It goes without saying that gaming laptops, especially 18-inch ones, aren't really designed to spend long periods away from a wall socket. The Blade 18 performs well in this department compared to its competitors, though. It beat the Legion in our YouTube playback test, lasting around seven and a half hours compared to six hours.
Another area where the Blade beats the Legion is the noise it produces under load. I recorded an average of 48 decibels in Turbo mode, much quieter than the Legion's 57.5 decibels and considerably quieter than the Medion Erazer Beast 16 X1's 61 decibels. This is one of the quietest high-end gaming laptops I've tested.
Wrap Up
For an 18-inch laptop, the Blade 18 is ridiculously slim, sleek, and quiet, with enough power to tear through games at high and maximum settings.
It also looks beautiful, is built to survive a war, has plenty of ports, hugely impressive audio, much better battery life than you'd expect, and is lighter than many rivals, making it one of the most portable 18-inch gaming laptops.
The display is sharp, colorful, and accurate, but it's still an IPS panel. For some, this could be a dealbreaker in a $5,400 laptop. And to reiterate, not everyone will care about a 440Hz refresh rate.
The Blade is also one of the hotter laptops out there, and the lack of a PCIe 5.0 SSD is disappointing at this price, as is the 32GB of RAM. Moreover, the RTX 5080 model could be the better buy, potentially offering better value for $400 less.
Ultimately, though, there's no arguing that this Blade 18 is an absolutely stunning machine, and it's hard to imagine anyone with the money to buy one would be disappointed.
Pros
- An impressive combination of power, thinness, weight, and low noise for an 18-inch laptop
- Dual-mode IPS screen is beautiful, bright, and reaches 440Hz
- Stunning looks and premium build quality
- Impressive speakers
Cons
- A price that's hard to justify
- OLED and mini-LED options would have been welcome
- Can get quite hot
- 64GB of RAM and a PCIe 5.0 SSD would be expected for over $5,000

articles.title: Hackers steal $6.3 billion from Binance in record crypto heist
articles.text:
Binance has suspended all withdrawals after the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange fell victim to what appears to be the biggest heist in history.
The exchange put the “estimated total impact” of the hack at about $6.3 billion and said around $3 billion of affected assets, mainly stablecoins that act as cash for the crypto market, had been frozen.
But analysts at Elliptic said the attacker had changed about $3.3 billion into digital assets that could not be frozen and was working to cash those out as traditional currency.
An “initial investigation” suggested hackers had been able to compromise an engineer’s laptop and withdraw funds from the platform, Binance said, adding on Friday morning that further investigation “has uncovered additional points of breach.” The company is working with law enforcement.
Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs linked the hack with a North Korean unit known as TraderTraitor, saying that the sums involved would make it “the largest crypto theft on record.” Last year, North Korean hackers stole crypto worth $1.5 billion in an attack on exchange Bybit.
Peter Ward, of the Sejong Institute in Seoul, said North Korea had considerable expertise and offered “near-total protection to its hackers.”
“Things may get a lot worse going forward,” he said.
Binance said on Friday that it had “already reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident,” with $5 billion of the funds “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.”
The company said it was actively buying more tokens in order to cover the remaining amount. “This step can take longer because some tokens may have low liquidity,” and settlement “also takes time,” it said.
The hack is a major blow to Binance, which was co-founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao and holds about $140 billion of digital assets. In 2023, the company pleaded guilty to US criminal charges related to breach of anti-money laundering laws and paid a $4.3 billion fine.

articles.title: Hollywood dice adiós a Patrick Stewart: las despedidas de Ian McKellen, Hugh Jackman y más
articles.text:
El pasado jueves 29 de noviembre nos enterábamos de la triste noticia de la muerte de Patrick Stewart. El legendario actor de sagas como Star Trek o X-Men fallecía a los 86 años tras una breve batalla contra el Alzheimer y la demencia. Por supuesto, los mensajes de despedida tanto de sus fans como de personas destacadas de la industria no se han hecho esperar.
Probablemente la despedida a Patrick Stewart que más interés generaba era la de su gran amigo Sir Ian McKellen. El actor de Magneto emitió a través de redes sociales un comunicado recordando a su compañero, el Profesor X. "Por encima de todo, lo que definía a Patrick era haber nacido y crecido en Yorkshire, ese orgulloso condado del norte de Inglaterra al que amó hasta el final", comienza el escrito.
"Se notaba en su acento y en la severa honestidad con la que te decía lo que pensaba y sentía. Los yorkshireños no toleran las medias verdades ni eludir los temas importantes. Llevaba el corazón en la mano, lo que lo convertía en un hombre en el que se podía confiar, a quien admirar y, en mi caso, amar", prosigue.
"Nos conocimos hace medio siglo, cuando éramos dos jóvenes actores ambiciosos en la Royal Shakespeare Company, aunque no participábamos en las mismas producciones. Mi primer recuerdo nítido fue unos años más tarde, cuando me lo encontré por la calle en el centro de Londres y me habló de una oferta para asumir un papel protagonista en Star Trek. «Pero, Patrick, piensa en tu carrera teatral en el Reino Unido. ¿De verdad quieres arriesgarte a perderte en Hollywood durante años y años?»", rememora Ian McKellen sobre Patrick Stewart.
"Pues bien, asumió el riesgo. Y, por suerte para todos nosotros, lo hizo no solo por sus devotos trekkies, sino también por el público del cine y del teatro, que se maravilló de cómo aprovechó su fama internacional para protagonizar una serie de éxitos cinematográficos (como X-Men, por supuesto) y grandes obras clásicas de Shakespeare, Ibsen, Arthur Miller, Peter Shaffer, Pinter y Beckett en Stratford-upon-Avon, en el West End londinense y en Broadway", añade.
"Estados Unidos era su hogar adoptivo, donde conoció a su adorada Sunny, que le ha cuidado en la salud y en la enfermedad, en las buenas y en las malas. Pero nunca renunció a sus orígenes: y el logro del que más se enorgullecía este actor —el más respetado y querido de su generación a ambos lados del Atlántico— fue su nombramiento como rector de la Universidad de Huddersfield, en Yorkshire", afirma McKellen. "Su actuación de despedida aún está por ver en Avengers: Doomsday", sentencia.
Hollywood se despide de Patrick Stewart
Otra emotiva despedida a Patrick Stewart la firma Hugh Jackman, compañero inseparable de su Profesor X al dar vida a Lobezno en toda la saga X-Men. "Hoy hemos perdido a uno de los grandes del teatro y el cine. Y, en mi opinión, a un amigo y a un hombre extraordinario. Aprendí muchísimo de él. Te echaré de menos todos los días de mi vida", escribe en su cuenta de Instagram junto a una foto en el set de rodaje.
Hablando de X-Men, la joven Dafne Keen, estrella de la película Logan, tampoco ha tardado en mostrar su dolor y condolencias por el fallecimiento de Patrick Stewart. "Me he enterado hoy mismo del fallecimiento de Patrick, lo cual resulta curioso, como si fuera una coincidencia del destino, teniendo en cuenta que anoche, a última hora, estaba redactando un correo electrónico para enviárselo, algo que hacía tiempo que no hacía", reconoce.
"Era un hombre muy amable, auténtico, divertido, único, cariñoso y encantador. Recuerdo sus bromas interminables, su carácter bondadoso y sus coloridas gafas de lectura. Cada uno de los días que pasé trabajando a su lado fue un honor y un privilegio que aún me cuesta creer que haya tenido. Era un maestro andante de su oficio y de la vida. Uno de los más grandes de nuestra época, tanto en el escenario como en la pantalla", le celebra la actriz española.
"Siempre lo he admirado, y siempre lo haré. Como actor y como persona. Tenía una forma maravillosa de envolver en asombro, diversión y emoción cada antigua lección que impartía. Siempre recordaré su calidez y el respeto que mostraba hacia todos los que le rodeaban. Guardaré para siempre en mi corazón esos meses que pasamos juntos, y siempre pensaré en él como una parte fundamental de mi forma de ver el mundo que me rodea. Así que descansa en paz, gigante, leyenda entre los hombres. La hermosa obra, la humanidad y la bondad que dejas atrás perdurarán para siempre", concluye Keen, con una tierna imagen de los dos jugando en el set de Logan.
En lo referido a su otra gran saga, Star Trek, Patrick Stewart también ha recibido hermosas palabras tras su muerte. Entre ellas, las de William Shatner, el eterno capitán Kirk. "Qué semana tan desgarradora ha sido. Sir Patrick Stewart era un amigo, un compañero y un magnífico actor. Desde los escenarios hasta el puente de la Enterprise, aportó inteligencia, elegancia y un profundo sentido de la humanidad a todo lo que hacía. El capitán Picard representaba lo mejor de nosotros, al igual que el hombre que lo interpretaba. Sentía un gran cariño y admiración por él y por su trabajo. Mi más sentido pésame a Sunny y a su familia. Le echaremos mucho de menos", publica en su perfil de Facebook.
Alex Kurtzman, cocreador de Star Trek: Picard, escribía lo siguiente. "Es difícil, en realidad imposible, expresar lo agradecido que estoy por haber compartido esos momentos con él. Agradecido en el sentido de que es algo que «solo ocurre una vez en tu carrera». Desde nuestro primer encuentro, dejó claro que la única razón para volver a interpretar a Picard era abrir nuevos caminos. Su reto era claro: Picard tenía que ser el hombre que conocíamos y amábamos, pero también completamente diferente, al igual que lo era el propio Patrick treinta años después de haberse puesto el uniforme por última vez".
"Por encima de todo, quería estar orgulloso de la obra porque sabía que Jean-Luc Picard sería su legado. Me parte el corazón, y al mismo tiempo me llena de orgullo, saber que ese legado sigue vivo a día de hoy. Un legado que también incluye su valentía a la hora de defender abiertamente aquello en lo que creía. Legado que incluye la forma en que amaba a su mujer y cuidaba de su familia. Legado que se manifestaba de manera tan hermosa en cómo se acurrucaba junto a cualquier pitbull que veía, y en cómo estas criaturas, supuestamente temibles, simplemente le devolvían el cariño. Era mágico. Era mi amigo. Me enseñó cuál era el verdadero sentido de Star Trek. Y, al fin y al cabo, fue y siempre será mi capitán", concluye.
