articles.title: Grey targets dollar-free payments for African businesses
articles.text:
Grey, the Y Combinator-backed cross-border payments company, says it has built direct currency conversion routes to help African businesses pay suppliers across borders without first converting their money into US dollars, as it expands its services for businesses trading across the continent.
Speaking at a media briefing with journalists on the sidelines of Moonshot by TechCabal 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria, on Thursday, Idorenyin Obong, Grey’s co-founder and chief executive officer, identified payment reliability and foreign exchange (FX) liquidity as two major challenges businesses face when making international transactions.
Payments between African countries can involve multiple currency conversions. For instance, a Nigerian business paying a supplier in Kenya may need to convert naira into US dollars before exchanging it for Kenyan shillings, adding another step to an already complicated transaction.
“Most times, if you’re trading within Africa, there’s always some form of intermediary currency,” Obong said. “We’ve built out these currency pairs, these exotic currency pairs, such that you never have to go in between to the USD.”
Obong said Grey has invested in payment infrastructure that allows customers in Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana to collect and send money, supported by liquidity arrangements across multiple currencies.
The company said the infrastructure enables real-time settlement in several supported currencies, reducing the need for businesses to source FX through multiple intermediaries.
The problem extends beyond Grey’s customers. In October, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the global bank for central banks, said that many payments between African countries still pass through correspondent banking networks outside the continent, increasing costs and exposing businesses to operational risks.
Other payment providers are also trying to address the problem. The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), developed by Afreximbank in partnership with African institutions, has been expanding local currency payment infrastructure.
In February, it partnered with Kenya’s Pesalink network to connect regional payments with Kenyan banks and mobile money providers.
Reducing currency conversion steps is only one part of the problem for Grey. Businesses also need assurance that payments will reach suppliers within an expected timeframe, particularly when delays can disrupt procurement and trading relationships.
Obong said customers moving amounts as little as $50, and larger amounts reaching $1 million, can experience uncertainty over whether funds will reach their destination when needed. To address this, Grey provides estimated payment delivery times and says it has invested in infrastructure to improve the reliability of its international payouts.
“We spent the last six years building the infrastructure to ensure that we’re delivering at the last mile at 99.99% to our customers,” Obong said.
In February, Grey expanded into payments and settlement for businesses, as its consumer transaction volumes grew. During the briefing, Obong disclosed that the company had processed more than 40 million transactions and nearly $5 billion in payments since inception.
Grey Business, its multi-currency platform for startups and small businesses, has processed nearly $100 million since launching in February, according to the company. By June, the company said that the platform had processed $61.4 million in its first four months, partly driven by demand for stablecoin-based payments.
The company has also expanded payouts to China, allowing businesses to pay overseas suppliers in Chinese yuan.
Beyond business payments, Grey is trying to solve another problem: what happens after individuals receive money from abroad.
Obong said the company initially launched in 2020 as a currency exchange service but expanded into foreign currency accounts after discovering that customers struggled to receive international payments in the first place.
Remote work accelerated demand for those services, especially among professionals earning foreign currencies while living in African markets.
“Most of our customers were using Grey to receive their foreign salary. And so we decided to build what I would call simply a salary account for these customers,” he said.
That insight led the company to build Paycheck, the salary product Grey launched on Wednesday. The service allows professionals earning in dollars, pounds, and euros to receive and manage their salaries, with features designed to separate money intended for spending and saving.
Obong said Paycheck also integrates with Pouch, Grey’s savings feature, which allows customers to set aside money for goals such as education, travel, or major purchases. The company is exploring additional benefits, including credit and lifestyle rewards.
The push reflects Grey’s ambition to build services around customers’ financial activities rather than simply helping them receive or transfer money.
Grey also faced questions at the briefing about difficulties some customers encounter when accessing foreign currency accounts and obtaining support.
The company said it offers round-the-clock digital assistance and has a physical office, although it considers online support more effective for routing customer issues to its distributed teams.
Grey’s next challenge is proving that its expanding range of services can solve these problems consistently.

articles.title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money.
Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion.
In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results.
The challenge
In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories:
- Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record.
- Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price.
- Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote.
Each exception triggered a five-step manual process:
- Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing.
- Research the root cause in vendor records.
- Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details.
- Wait for a response.
- Execute the resolution in the TMS.
With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth.
Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework.
From assessment to production
In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months.
How it works
The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable.
Agents
When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute:
- Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up.
- Pricing Variance Agent compares the carrier’s charge against the contracted rate and determines whether the difference is valid.
- Accessorial Validation Agent checks whether unexpected fees (such as residential delivery or liftgate charges) are supported by the actual delivery events.
Each agent pulls specific carrier billing rules and policies before making a recommendation. After the exception is resolved, the system generates a plain-language note explaining what was found and what action was taken.
Each custom agent has an instruction prompt (defining its role, decision boundaries, and output format), a set of actions (integrations into SpeedShip), and access to carrier-specific knowledge bases. By using Amazon Bedrock, each agent accesses a suitable foundation model through a single API while inheriting existing AWS governance. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
Actions
The agents connect to SpeedShip through the same APIs that analysts use. That means the AI sees exactly what a human reviewer would see (contract rates, shipment details, delivery proof) and writes its resolution into the same workflow. SpeedShip has APIs on AWS, so the agents wire into the same endpoints as other existing systems.
Carrier knowledge base
Every carrier has different billing rules, fee definitions, and dispute procedures. Worldwide Express stores each carrier’s documentation: tariff rules, surcharge definitions, dispute steps, and variance thresholds. When an agent processes an exception, it retrieves that specific carrier’s policies and standard operating procedure (SOP) documents before deciding, so each decision is grounded in the carrier’s own rules. The same three agents handle all carriers without any carrier-specific code.
Human-in-the-loop
The approval step was necessary for FinOps adoption during the initial rollout. Initially, a human reviewer would use the existing SpeedShip UI to approve recommendations before they’re finalized. Eventually when accuracy exceeded 99 percent, bulk approval became the default.
Observability
Worldwide Express’s team built dashboards tracking automation rate by carrier, error rate by exception type, resolution time, and human override frequency. When a reviewer rejects a recommendation, the system logs the feedback. The team refines instruction prompts and knowledge bases based on rejection history, steadily increasing automation coverage.
End-to-end flow
The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from exception detection through the three specialized agents to human approval. In the diagram, exceptions from the data sources (the SpeedShip TMS, a shipping system, an electronic data interchange (EDI) server, and carrier and vendor portals) are detected and routed to one of three agents. Each agent runs on Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling, uses an agent framework with its own prompt, tools, and carrier knowledge base, and calls Amazon Bedrock for model inference. The agents produce a resolution report. Cost finalization and an AI-written note then go to a human reviewer for approval in the SpeedShip analyst UI.
Results
Six months in, Worldwide Express has deployed the solution across over 40 LTL carriers. The agents currently close 10,000 (approximately 50 percent) exceptions weekly with a less than 1 percent error rate. This shifted the FinOps team’s time from routine resolution to complex, high-value disputes.
The impact shows up most clearly in the backlog of active exceptions, which fell from $15M in June 2025 to $4M six months later, a 75 percent reduction. Worldwide Express unlocked $10M in freed-up cash flow, over $1M in annual cost savings, and 60x first-year ROI. The company reports time-to-cash improving by four weeks.
        “With AWS, we’ve automated more than 40 percent of weekly billing exceptions, significantly reducing costs and accelerating billing cycles from days to minutes. Today, we release approximately $10 million more in customer billings each week at a speed that simply wasn’t possible before.”
— Nathanael Pearson, VP of FinOps, Worldwide Express
Looking forward
Worldwide Express is already expanding this approach to other parts of the Order-to-Cash cycle. For logistics companies managing high carrier volumes, the path forward is to start small. Automate the most repetitive exception type first, prove accuracy, then scale across the rest of the portfolio.
Conclusion
Worldwide Express’s exception automation shows what’s possible when agentic AI meets a well-scoped business problem. The combination of Amazon Bedrock, carrier-specific knowledge bases, and a human-in-the-loop approval design let Worldwide Express move from assessment to production in less than 6 months while maintaining financial controls. The company is now expanding automation to other Order-to-Cash processes.
To explore whether a similar approach might work for your organization, request a conversation with your account team or learn more about Amazon Bedrock. Partners like LTM can run a Proof of Value sprint with your own data.

articles.title: Build a Validated Kubernetes Runtime for NVIDIA Dynamo | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Teams building AI applications need a repeatable path from a model configuration to a working inference endpoint. NVIDIA Dynamo is a distributed inference framework that coordinates model serving across GPU workers. Deploying it on Kubernetes is only a first step. A successful model deployment requires more: GPU drivers, resource allocation, scheduling, networking, and monitoring must all work together. Resolving these dependencies takes time away from testing model behavior, serving performance, and application integration.
The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together technologies to help the ecosystem design, build, and operate more efficient AI factories, and Dynamo is one of them. To make management of those infrastructure dependencies easier, the platform contains NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR). It packages NVIDIA Dynamo and its supporting infrastructure into validated recipes. Each recipe defines a configuration for a specific environment and workload, including pinned component versions, compatibility constraints, and validation checks. AICR gives platform teams a repeatable way to deploy and check the runtime, providing developers with a consistent foundation for serving models and testing applications.
This walkthrough covers the infrastructure that supports Dynamo on Kubernetes, compares two routing options, and shows how to deploy and validate the runtime with AICR.
Why the underlying runtime matters for Dynamo
Running a model with Dynamo on Kubernetes starts with a DynamoGraphDeployment that specifies how vLLM, SGLang, or NVIDIA TensorRT LLM should run in pods on the cluster. But the graph is only the top of the stack. A production inference cluster also needs a runtime layer below it. It has to answer questions like:
- Is the NVIDIA GPU Operator installed with a driver stack that matches the nodes?
- Are GPU nodes labeled and discoverable?
- Does the cluster expose GPUs through the expected Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver?
- Can the scheduler place GPU workers with the required topology and gang scheduling semantics?
- Are node health signals available before workloads land on a degraded node?
- Is Prometheus reachable for Dynamo and accelerator metrics?
- Is the Gateway API / Endpoint Picker (EPP) path configured when the deployment should be Kubernetes-native at ingress?
AICR captures these runtime requirements in the recipe.
What AICR ships for Dynamo
An AICR Dynamo recipe packages both Dynamo and the cluster runtime components it depends on.
AICR ships version 1.4.2 of the dynamo-platform chart, which includes the Dynamo operator, Dynamo runtime images, and resources such as the nvidia.com/v1beta1 DynamoGraphDeployment CustomResourceDefinition (CRD). v1beta1 replaces the former v1alpha1 API version.
Table 1 lists the supporting infrastructure components included in the recipe.
| Prerequisite | Requirement | Component in the AICR recipe | 
|---|---|---|
| GPU driver stack | Driver and GPU software stack that matches the nodes | NVIDIA GPU Operator | 
| GPU discovery | GPU nodes labeled and discoverable for placement | Node Feature Discovery | 
| GPU allocation | GPUs exposed through Kubernetes-native Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) | DRA Driver for NVIDIA GPUs | 
| Scheduling | GPU workers placed with the required topology and gang scheduling | KAI Scheduler | 
| Inference Workload Orchestration | Multi-component serving graphs started, placed, and scaled as coordinated groups | Grove | 
| Node health | Health signals available before workloads land on a degraded node | NVSentinel and Nodewright, where supported by the selected recipe | 
| Metrics | Cluster, accelerator, and Dynamo service metrics collected | Prometheus stack | 
| Ingress | Gateway / EPP path configured when ingress is Kubernetes-native | agentgateway and Gateway API resources, described in the routing sections | 
In addition, the recipe pins component versions and records configuration values, node selectors, tolerations, checksums, and validation expectations to make deployment reproducible.
With Dynamo 1.4, frontends, workers, optional Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE) / Endpoint Picker Plugin (EPP) components, and other Dynamo services discover each other through Kubernetes resources. AICR’s default path therefore no longer uses NATS, and the dynamo-platform chart no longer installs it by default. NATS remains available as an opt-in for deployments that need it.
Agentic workloads repeatedly extend long token prefixes, including system prompts, tool definitions, conversation history, and tool results. If a turn reaches a worker without that prefix in GPU memory, the system reprocesses intermediate tokens instead of reusing cached results. Dynamo routes requests to workers that already hold the relevant KV blocks, either through its frontend router or through GAIE/EPP integration at the Gateway API layer.
Dynamo can also separate prompt processing (prefill) from token generation (decode), an architecture known as disaggregated serving. On KV-cache misses, all or part of the prompt must be reprocessed by the prefill pool. Decode workers then take over token-by-token generation, which has different GPU, memory, latency, and batching characteristics. The cache miss rate depends on the workload. Long-running agentic sessions behave differently from one-off chat requests. Disaggregated serving enables operators to scale and tune prefill and decode capacity independently for a given request mix.
The request plane and KV-cache event plane are separate. In Dynamo 1.4.2, the default AICR Kubernetes path uses TCP for requests and ZMQ for KV-cache events. Each vLLM worker engine emits raw KV-cache events through a local ZMQ publisher, for example, with the following vLLM configuration:
--enable-prefix-caching --kv-transfer-config \
  {"enable_kv_cache_events": true, "publisher": "zmq", "endpoint": "tcp://*:5557"}
Dynamo’s worker runtime then subscribes to that local vLLM event source, normalizes the events, and republishes them onto the Dynamo event plane. Both the native Dynamo Frontend router and the GAIE/EPP path use this Dynamo-managed KV-cache state to make routing decisions.
What are the Dynamo routing paths on Kubernetes?
Dynamo supports two routing paths on Kubernetes. The first uses the Dynamo Frontend router for worker selection. The second uses a Kubernetes Gateway API implementation for ingress and Dynamo EPP for endpoint selection. AICR ships and validates the Dynamo runtime for either topology.
Path 1: Dynamo Frontend router
The default path exposes a Dynamo Frontend behind a Kubernetes Service. Running with DYN_ROUTER_MODE=kv, the Frontend tokenizes each request, scores eligible workers using prefix overlap and current load, selects a worker, and dispatches the request through the Dynamo request plane, which uses TCP by default.
This path is suitable when an application team owns a model-specific endpoint or an existing edge proxy only needs to forward traffic to the Dynamo Frontend Service. It is the smallest topology for deploying and validating a Dynamo graph and is the most production-proven serving option. It does not require the additional gateway and EPP components used in Path 2.
Path 2: Gateway API Inference Extension and Dynamo EPP
This path integrates Dynamo with the Gateway API and Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE). In the AICR example, agentgateway resolves an HTTPRoute to an InferencePool. The Dynamo operator creates that InferencePool from the DynamoGraphDeployment: its selector identifies eligible worker pods, while its endpointPickerRef identifies the Dynamo EPP Service.
The gateway invokes the Dynamo EPP through GAIE’s endpoint-selection interface. The EPP tokenizes the request and uses Dynamo’s KV router to select an endpoint. It returns the selection and routing metadata to the gateway implementation, which is the actual HTTP proxy. In this mode, each routable worker pod includes a Dynamo Frontend sidecar that receives the request from the gateway and forwards it to the local worker container. The Frontend runs with --router-mode direct, so it applies the EPP selection without rerouting.
This path is suitable when the platform team manages shared Kubernetes ingress and needs to configure model endpoint worker selection, timeouts, retries, and fallback through Gateway API mechanisms. Note that both routing approaches can work behind a Gateway API HTTPRoute. The difference is which component manages the transport to the worker: the Dynamo Frontend or the Gateway itself.
Note: This post covers Dynamo’s operator-managed DynamoGraphDeployment integration with GAIE; the experimental standalone vanilla vLLM on-ramp is a separate integration. In Dynamo 1.4, this path uses GAIE’s Go EPP framework with Dynamo’s Rust KV router embedded through CGO and configured through eppConfig.
Outlook: Starting with Dynamo 1.5, a native Rust EPP replaces the Go/CGO bridge. It implements GAIE’s Lightweight Endpoint Picker (ext_proc) interface directly, runs the full Dynamo router in-process, and uses DYN_* environment variables in place of the eppConfig plugin and scheduling profiles. Aggregated and disaggregated routing are handled directly from the worker roles registered through Dynamo discovery. The surrounding Kubernetes topology remains unchanged. Removing the Go plugin framework and CGO boundary also reduces per-request EPP overhead.
A client request enters through a gateway, such as agentgateway, and matches an HTTPRoute backed by an InferencePool. The Gateway invokes the Dynamo EPP, which performs just the token-aware KV selection and returns the selected endpoint and routing metadata. The Gateway then forwards the request to the selected worker’s Frontend sidecar in direct mode, which sends it to the vLLM worker over the Dynamo request plane. Worker KV-cache state reaches the EPP through the Dynamo event plane, while the Dynamo operator creates the EPP and InferencePool from the DynamoGraphDeployment.
Choosing a path
The routing path depends on whether the Gateway or the Dynamo Frontend should handle the forwarding of requests to the workers, including timeouts, retries, and fallback management. Table 2 compares the Dynamo Frontend and Gateway API/EPP paths.
| Decision | Dynamo Router | GAIE / EPP | 
|---|---|---|
| Ingress owner | Dynamo Frontend Service | Gateway and HTTPRoute | 
| Worker selection | The Frontend selects and dispatches to a worker | The EPP selects an endpoint; the Gateway forwards the request | 
| Request path | Client → Frontend → worker | Client → Gateway → worker Frontend sidecar → worker | 
| Best fit | A model-specific Dynamo endpoint with the smallest serving topology | A shared Kubernetes ingress managed through Gateway API resources | 
| Additional infrastructure | None beyond the Dynamo frontend and workers | GAIE-compatible Gateway, InferencePool, EPP, and worker frontend sidecars | 
| KV-cache behavior | Dynamo KV-aware routing from worker-published cache and load state | The same Dynamo KV-aware routing at the Gateway layer | 
Both paths use worker-published KV-cache events for precise cache-aware placement. Dynamo can instead be configured to predict KV-cache state from where it sent each request. Prediction cannot see evictions, so the router’s view can drift from what each worker actually holds, and routing quality can degrade, especially under memory pressure. The AICR configuration in this post enables live events, so both paths route using the workers’ reported KV-cache state.
How the AICR recipe flow works
AICR separates runtime setup from application deployment. First, it captures the existing Kubernetes cluster and generates a matching Dynamo recipe. The runtime bundle is then rendered, deployed, and validated before the application’s DynamoGraphDeployment is installed and its inference endpoints are tested.
Step 1: Snapshot the cluster
The snapshot captures the cluster state that AICR uses for recipe selection and validation:
aicr snapshot \
  --namespace aicr-validation \
  --output snapshot.yaml
When no placement flags are specified, AICR automatically targets nodes labeled nvidia.com/gpu.present=true and tolerates GPU-node taints. The --node-selector and --toleration flags provide more specific placement when required by the cluster.
Step 2: Generate the Dynamo inference recipe
AICR uses the snapshot to identify the Kubernetes distribution, GPU accelerator, and GPU-node operating system. The command specifies the workload intent and platform:
aicr recipe \
  --snapshot snapshot.yaml \
  --intent inference \
  --platform dynamo \
  --output recipe.yaml
The generated recipe records pinned component versions, environment-specific configuration, compatibility constraints, and validation checks. For the Amazon EKS Dynamo inference recipe for NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems, AICR v1.0.0 selects the following Helm chart versions:
| Component | Version | 
|---|---|
| NVIDIA GPU Operator | v26.7.1 | 
| Node Feature Discovery | 0.19.0 | 
| cert-manager | v1.20.2 | 
| AWS EBS CSI Driver | 2.59.0 | 
| AWS EFA | v0.5.29 | 
| NVSentinel | v1.25.0 | 
| NodeWright Operator | v0.19.0 | 
| NVIDIA DRA GPU Driver | 0.5.0 | 
| KAI Scheduler | v0.16.9 | 
| Grove | v0.1.0-alpha.13 | 
| Dynamo Platform | 1.4.2 | 
| Agent Gateway | v1.5.0 | 
| Agent Gateway CRDs | v1.5.0 | 
| Kube Prometheus Stack | 84.4.0 | 
| Prometheus Operator CRDs | 28.0.1 | 
| Prometheus Adapter | 5.3.0 | 
| Kubernetes Ephemeral Storage Metrics | 1.19.2 | 
The AICR team tested these component versions together on the specified platforms and hardware. The following validation steps verify that the cluster meets the selected recipe’s requirements.
Optional offline check
Recipe selection already uses the cluster facts in snapshot.yaml, so validating the generated recipe against that same snapshot adds little. Offline validation is useful when testing a recipe against a different captured cluster snapshot without contacting Kubernetes. It evaluates declarative constraints, while behavioral checks are reported as skipped.
aicr validate \
  --recipe recipe.yaml \
  --snapshot candidate-snapshot.yaml \
  --no-cluster \
  --output dry-run.json
Step 3: Render the runtime bundle
AICR renders the recipe into deployment-ready Helm values and manifests:
aicr bundle \
  --recipe recipe.yaml \
  --accelerated-node-selector nodeGroup=gpu-worker \
  --accelerated-node-toleration dedicated=worker-workload:NoSchedule \
  --accelerated-node-toleration dedicated=worker-workload:NoExecute \
  --system-node-selector nodeGroup=system-worker \
  --system-node-toleration dedicated=system-workload:NoSchedule \
  --system-node-toleration dedicated=system-workload:NoExecute \
  --set-json agentgateway:allowedSourceRanges='["<your-cidr>"]' \
  --deployer helmfile \
  --output bundle
These placement flags reflect the test cluster used for this walkthrough. The flags can be adapted or omitted for clusters with different labels and taints. If the cluster has no default StorageClass, the command also requires --storage-class.
Step 4: Deploy the runtime
For a local deployment without an in-cluster GitOps controller, Helmfile provides a deployment option. With Helm and the helm-diff plugin available locally, the following commands inspect the AICR-generated release graph before applying it:
helmfile -f bundle/helmfile.yaml diff
helmfile -f bundle/helmfile.yaml apply
AICR encodes component dependencies in the generated Helmfile bundle. Helmfile processes those dependency tiers in order and applies independent components within a tier concurrently. Rerunning apply reconciles the installed Helm releases with the generated configuration.
If Helmfile is not available, the bundle can be regenerated with AICR’s default Helm deployer. Its generated deploy.sh script is a lightweight fallback for an interactive test drive:
aicr bundle \
  --recipe recipe.yaml \
  [... all the flags setting node selectors and tolerations ...] \
  --set-json agentgateway:allowedSourceRanges='["<your-cidr>"]' \
  --deployer helm \
  --output bundle-helm
chmod +x bundle-helm/deploy.sh
 ./bundle-helm/deploy.sh
For production, AICR also renders GitOps bundles with --deployer argocd, --deployer argocd-helm, and --deployer flux.
Step 5: Validate the installed runtime
After installation, deployment and conformance validation check the live cluster before the application workload is installed. Because no snapshot is supplied here, AICR captures the current cluster state before running the validator Jobs.
aicr validate \
  --recipe recipe.yaml \
  --node-selector nodeGroup=gpu-worker \
  --toleration dedicated=worker-workload:NoSchedule \
  --toleration dedicated=worker-workload:NoExecute \
  --phase deployment \
  --phase conformance \
  --output report.json
The application DynamoGraphDeployment is installed only after these checks pass. Performance validation runs separately because it deploys a temporary serving workload and consumes the GPUs under test.
What does AICR validation check?
AICR validates the installed runtime against the checks and constraints encoded in the selected recipe. Checks vary by recipe. For a Dynamo inference recipe, deployment and conformance validation typically cover the following:
| Area | What is checked | 
|---|---|
| Cluster baseline | Expected cluster resources, GPU allocatable capacity, and a functional nvidia-smi on accelerator nodes | 
| Platform health | GPU Operator health and version, plus Dynamo platform and operator health | 
| Accelerator access | DRA support and secure accelerator access | 
| Scheduling and scaling | Gang scheduling, pod autoscaling, cluster autoscaling, and robust controller behavior | 
| Observability | Prometheus-backed accelerator and AI service metrics | 
| Ingress | Gateway API and agentgateway readiness for Kubernetes-native ingress | 
These checks verify that the installed runtime meets the selected recipe’s requirements before an application is deployed.
AICR combines a versioned runtime configuration with checks that verify whether the cluster meets the selected recipe’s requirements.
Get Started
NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) and NVIDIA Dynamo are open-source components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform. Teams deploying Dynamo on Kubernetes can use AICR’s recipes and deployment examples to configure, deploy, and validate the infrastructure supporting their inference workload.
- Additional projects and community resources are available through the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub.
- Discussion is available in the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Slack community. The NVIDIA DSX OS AI Inference and Contributor Workshop provides hands-on experience with AICR during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America. Registration is required, as seating is limited.
- The NVIDIA booth #170 at KubeCon features Kubernetes deep dives and live demos.

articles.title: Tausende Android-User betroffen: Falscher PDF-Reader enthält Malware
articles.text:
Tausende Android-User betroffen: Falscher PDF-Reader enthält Malware
Wenn es Malware in den Google Play-Store schafft, verschleiert sie ihre wahren Absichten meist perfide. So wurde erst kürzlich ein Fake-Whatsapp von mehr als einer halben Million Android-User:innen heruntergeladen. Im Falle eines vermeintlichen PDF-Readers sind es zwar deutlich weniger Betroffene, doch könnten die Schäden für sie dennoch immens ausfallen.
PDF-Reader tarnt sich als Malware
Wie die Sicherheitsforscher:innen von Threatlabz herausgefunden haben, verbirgt sich nämlich in der Android-App „PDF Reader“ Malware. Sie wurde von mehr als 10.000 User:innen aus dem Play Store heruntergeladen, bevor Google das Problem erkannte und die App und den Account des Entwicklers „Duka Zuri“ aus dem App-Store warf.
Auf der Store-Seite versprach der PDF-Reader, eine Office-App zu sein, mit der User:innen „PDF-Dateien öffnen können, die lokal auf ihrem Smartphone gespeichert sind.“ Dabei würde die App sogar PDFs unterstützen, die mit einem Passwort geschützt wurden. Tatsächlich landeten nach dem Download aber nicht nur der PDF-Reader, sondern auch der Banking-Trojaner „Anatsa“ auf dem Smartphone der Android-User:innen.
Die besagte Malware ist schon seit Jahren im Umlauf und hat es auf Logins für Banking-Apps abgesehen. Sobald sie sich festgesetzt hat, kann „Anatsa“ das Einloggen einfach aufzeichnen oder die Oberflächen diverser Banking-Anwendungen täuschend echt nachahmen und über das richtige Interface legen. Dadurch geben die User:innen ihre Daten direkt an die Malware und deren Hinterleute weiter.
Während noch fraglich ist, wie die Malware es an den Sicherheitsmaßnahmen des Play Stores vorbeischaffen konnte, müssen Betroffene schnell handeln. Sie sollten die Anwendung deinstallieren. Dabei kann auch eine Antiviren-App helfen, um tiefer im System sitzende Schadsoftware zu entfernen. Im zweiten Schritt sollten Betroffene sämtliche Logins ändern, die sie seit der Installation genutzt haben. Zu guter Letzt sollten gerade Bankkonten im Blick behalten werden, um ungewöhnliche Transaktionen schnellstmöglich zu stoppen. Im Zweifel können sich Betroffene auch mit ihrer Bank in Verbindung setzen, bevor es dazu kommt, und den Vorfall schildern, um weitere Schritte zu besprechen.
„PDF-Reader tarnt sich als Malware“
Ja, wirklich schlimm…da will man sich eine Malware runterladen und bekommt ein PDF-Reader!
So weit ist es schon gekommen.

articles.title: Wikipedia pidió a un tribunal que la IA deje de reproducir sus artículos
articles.text:
La Fundación Wikimedia, la organización que opera Wikipedia, presentó un escrito ante el tribunal de Nueva York que juzga a OpenAI y Microsoft por el uso de artículos de prensa para entrenar IA. No toma partido: pide que entrenar modelos sea uso legítimo, pero que los chatbots no reproduzcan textos sin licencia.
El documento es un amicus curiae, que presenta quien no es parte del juicio para aportar argumentos al juez. Según The Verge, Wikimedia advierte que las posturas de ambas partes impulsan una aplicación “excesiva y simplificada” de la doctrina del uso legítimo, la excepción que permite emplear obras protegidas sin permiso en ciertos casos.
El litigio reúne las demandas a ambas empresas que presentaron The New York Times, el Daily News, The Intercept, el Center for Investigative Reporting, Ziff Davis y un grupo de autores de libros. El Times sostiene, por ejemplo, que OpenAI copió su sitio web para armar los datos de entrenamiento.
OpenAI y Microsoft responden que entrenar modelos de lenguaje es uso legítimo. La empresa dueña de ChatGPT dijo que la reproducción de textos es “un error poco frecuente”. Microsoft afirmó en un escrito de septiembre que, según un análisis de expertos, su asistente Copilot rara vez repite oraciones completas de las noticias.
Wikimedia plantea que los chatbots no pueden reproducir artículos
Wikimedia propone una salida intermedia. Según The Verge, que cita una publicación de la fundación, extraer datos de sitios web no debería considerarse infracción, y entrenar un modelo con obras protegidas y sin licencia debería ser uso legítimo cuando aporta “algo nuevo y diferente” respecto de las fuentes originales.
La excepción, de acuerdo con esa posición, son los sistemas que recuperan copias de un texto para responder a una consulta y lo entregan desplazando la lectura de la obra original. En ese caso, la fundación sostiene que corresponde pedir licencia, porque el resultado sustituye al original y no lo transforma lo suficiente.
Para Wikipedia, eso significaría citar la fuente original bajo su licencia Creative Commons, que también exige que cualquier adaptación se publique con la misma licencia. La fundación sostiene que servicios como ChatGPT reproducen texto de licencia libre sin respetar esas condiciones.
Cada extremo tiene un riesgo, según el escrito. Un triunfo total de los editores permitiría que los titulares de derechos bloqueen incluso usos innovadores. Un triunfo total de las empresas de IA sería “una luz verde para ignorar los términos de licencia y fragmentar el flujo de conocimiento” entre autores humanos y lectores.
Wikipedia, fuente de datos y también afectada
La fundación afirma en el escrito que sus sitios son una de las fuentes de datos más críticas para entrenar sistemas de IA. Esos mismos sistemas, agrega, desvían visitantes y debilitan a las comunidades de voluntarios que mantienen la enciclopedia.
El 5 de octubre, Wikimedia informó que agentes que cree operados por OpenAI hicieron millones de solicitudes automáticas a sus interfaces públicas y rastrearon millones de páginas, sobre todo de Wikidata y Wikimedia Commons. Según la fundación, ese tráfico pudo contribuir a una interrupción parcial del servicio de consultas en mayo.
Wikimedia también reconoce el valor de estos modelos: pueden ayudar a los editores a combatir el vandalismo, detectar violaciones de derechos de autor y publicación de datos personales, y encontrar artículos que necesitan mejoras.
“Un fallo que no aplique con cuidado los principios del uso legítimo podría amenazar la sostenibilidad del conocimiento libre”, dijo el asesor jurídico general de la fundación, Stephen LaPorte. La directora ejecutiva, Bernadette Meehan, afirmó que ampliar el acceso al conocimiento con IA es “un objetivo poderoso”, pero que debe respetar a quienes lo producen.
Wikimedia no es la única que intervino. El Gobierno de Estados Unidos presentó en septiembre un escrito a favor de OpenAI, según Reuters. Esta semana se sumaron escritos de la Asociación de Editores Estadounidenses, que respalda a los demandantes, y del profesor Matthew Sag, que no apoya a ninguna parte.
El juez Sidney Stein evalúa los pedidos cruzados de sentencia sumaria. Según Sag, su fallo será el primero del Segundo Circuito sobre si entrenar modelos con libros y artículos es uso legítimo, y el primero en el mundo que trate los reclamos de editoriales de noticias.

articles.title: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid: Drives like an EV, but there's no plug involved
articles.text:
Nissan has a new version of its bestselling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested in February. Most hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid.
That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V. Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars’ gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiasts irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for.
Series hybrids
Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher.
This charges a 1.67 kWh lithium-ion traction battery that has been optimized for its charge and discharge ability, which in turn powers a pair of electric motors. At the front axle sits a 202 hp (150 kW), 243 lb-ft (330 Nm) permanent synchronous magnet motor, at the rear another PSM providing 134 hp (100 kW) and 144 lb-ft (195 Nm), although given the battery’s limitations, combined power output is 225 hp (168 kW). And as you would expect, the motors will regeneratively brake under deceleration to return as much energy to the battery for reuse as possible.

articles.title: DoorDash said it's only received 'several hundred' orders from AI agents | TechCrunch
articles.text:
There’s a big uproar about AI agents taking over commerce and orders, but that might not be the case just yet. Delivery company DoorDash revealed during its third-quarter earnings call that it has only seen “several hundred” orders from third-party agents like Muse, Instinct, Fo, and others. For comparison, the company said in its 2025 report it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily.
“I would say that this [using agents to order] is something that is still a very dynamic area. And my take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity. But at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in an answer to an analyst’s questions about the topic. “What I mean by that is if you look at where AI agents are today, we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents,” he said.
Xu mentioned that users are still predominantly placing orders through DoorDash’s app. However, the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that, in the future, there could be an opportunity for it to advertise within these agents.
DoorDash has its own agents, including a text-to-order agent it launched in September, a CLI agent introduced in July, and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash it launched in June, which allows users to place orders through prompts and photos. The company also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering.
The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow them to access their content or not. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, but Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors.

articles.title: Moto elétrica ganha câmbio de duas marchas para melhorar desempenho e eficiência
articles.text:
A empresa britânica E-Motiv Shift Systems vai apresentar na feira EICMA, em Milão, um protótipo de moto elétrica com câmbio de duas marchas capaz de trocar de marcha sem interromper a entrega de potência. A tecnologia promete melhorar a aceleração e a eficiência do motor, combinando uma primeira marcha voltada ao desempenho e uma segunda otimizada para velocidades mais altas.
O projeto recebeu financiamento de £ 1 milhão do governo britânico e foi desenvolvido com participação da fabricante BSA, da Universidade de Bath e do instituto IAAPS.
Para quem tem pressa:
- A empresa britânica E-Motiv Shift Systems desenvolveu um protótipo de moto elétrica com câmbio de duas marchas, que será apresentado na feira EICMA 2026, em Milão;
- A primeira marcha foi projetada para melhorar a aceleração, enquanto a segunda busca manter o desempenho em velocidades mais altas. A troca ocorre sem interromper a entrega de potência do motor;
- O projeto recebeu £ 1 milhão em financiamento do governo britânico e ainda está em desenvolvimento. A previsão é concluir o protótipo em janeiro de 2027, quando também devem começar os testes.
Como funciona o câmbio de duas marchas?
A maioria das motos elétricas utiliza apenas uma marcha. Isso acontece porque os motores elétricos conseguem funcionar bem em diferentes velocidades sem precisar de várias relações de transmissão.
O protótipo da E-Motiv, porém, segue outro caminho. Ele conta com duas marchas: a primeira ajuda a moto a ganhar velocidade mais rapidamente, enquanto a segunda permite manter um bom desempenho em velocidades mais altas.
Outro diferencial é que a troca acontece sem interromper a potência atingida. Motocicletas convencionais geralmente perdem um pouco de força na troca de marchas, algo que a E-Motiv busca eliminar em sua moto.
Leia mais:
- 7 motos automáticas que dispensam a troca de marcha totalmente
- Essa moto voadora parece ter saído do universo Star Wars
- LUV1: nova moto elétrica pode ser personalizada e chega a 100 km/h
- Esta moto elétrica acelera como um carro e usa tomada comum
O projeto, chamado pela empresa de Demo 1, ainda está em desenvolvimento. A construção do protótipo conta com a participação da Envisage Group e do instituto IAAPS, ligado à Universidade de Bath.
A previsão da E-Motiv é finalizar a moto em janeiro de 2027, quando também devem começar os testes. Antes disso, a empresa apresentará a tecnologia na EICMA 2026, feira de motocicletas realizada entre 3 e 8 de novembro, em Milão, na Itália.
A tecnologia tem origem em um sistema desenvolvido para o automobilismo, que chegou a ser utilizado pela equipe Aprilia Racing na MotoGP. Agora, a empresa trabalha para adaptar a transmissão às necessidades das motos elétricas.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
articles.text:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually.
The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
The new control will allow publishers to apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers.
The shared “policy token” signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It will live within a website’s robots.txt file, which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can’t scrape a site — whether for search indexing, archiving, or AI training. Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company.
The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models. Some companies and organizations have attempted to combat unauthorized scraping, with the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard giving publishers the ability to charge crawlers that visit their sites, and Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default.
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing a site if they encounter the shared token. Meta communications head Andy Stone also signaled support for the new setting, but doesn’t say whether the company will honor it. “We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step,” Stone says. “And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry.”
Microsoft says it will offer granular controls that will give publishers the ability to opt out of AI training or AI grounding, the process of pointing an AI model to a verified source of information to reduce hallucinations. Microsoft notes that websites will still appear in Bing’s search results regardless of their preferences. Google previously implemented similar controls that allow sites to control whether their content appears in AI search features or is used for AI training, without impacting visibility in search.
While Anthropic has already adopted the signal, Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year. OpenAI says it will implement it in the “coming months.”
Update, October 30th: Added a comment from Meta.

articles.title: Drupal Commerce Core Vulnerability Exploited Against Online Stores
articles.text:
Drupal is urging online store owners to patch a highly critical access bypass vulnerability in the Commerce Core module, warning that it is being exploited in the wild.
Tracked as CVE-2026-118539, the issue affects a contributed module that adds e-commerce features to Drupal websites, including a shopping cart and checkout process. Drupal’s statistics show the module is used on more than 42,000 sites.
“The module doesn’t sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields, leading to an access bypass that may financially impact the vendor,” Drupal explains in its advisory.
The Drupal security team gave the issue a risk score of 21 out of 25. According to the score, unauthenticated attackers can exploit the flaw no matter how the module is set up.
Drupal has confirmed the attacks but has not said how the bug is being exploited, who is behind the activity, or how many sites have been targeted. It has also not said whether the vulnerability was exploited as a zero-day, before patches became available.
The vulnerability affects 3.x versions before 3.3.13 and earlier releases before 8.x-2.41. Administrators should update to one of the two fixed versions and review their store orders.
“Sites should audit their orders for inconsistencies as this vulnerability is being actively exploited,” the advisory reads.
The 38 other advisories Drupal published on October 28 address vulnerabilities in 21 contributed projects. Nearly a dozen are rated critical, including bugs that could lead to remote code execution, account takeover, or Commerce orders via Stripe being marked as paid without payment.
The CAPTCHA module also received a fix for a moderately critical bug that allows a protected form to be submitted again without solving a new challenge. Drupal’s rating indicates that exploit code for this bug exists in the wild, although the advisory doesn’t mention active exploitation.
Drupal’s ratings also indicate that proofs of concept exist for two information disclosure bugs, one in Commerce Core and one in Media Alias Display.
On October 14, Drupal announced fixes for two critical remote code execution bugs: CVE-2026-108097 in core’s Field UI module and CVE-2026-108099 in the Entity List module. Neither component exposes the flaws on its own, but certain other contributed modules or custom code make exploitation possible, in some cases without authentication.
Ahead of its October 14 security releases, Drupal cautioned that exploits might appear within hours or days. So far, however, there have been no public reports of the flaws being exploited in the wild.
CVE-2026-9082, a highly critical SQL injection issue in Drupal core’s database abstraction API that affects PostgreSQL-backed sites, did attract exploitation attempts in May.

articles.title: Cette compacte électrique premium voit son prix baisser de 6 000 euros quelques semaines après son lancement
articles.text:
Le groupe Volkswagen est en pleine offensive sur le marché des véhicules électriques en Europe. Si on a souvent abordé les nouveautés de Skoda, Volkswagen et Cupra avec des modèles citadins, Audi n’est pas en reste puisque la marque a relancé l’A2 en version électrique. L’Audi A2 e-tron est désormais éligible à la prime Coup de pouce CEE, ce qui devrait bien aider ses ventes en France.
Une voiture premium éligible à l’aide
Généralement, les voitures premium dépassent les critères pour profiter du bonus écologique, désormais appelé Coup de pouce CEE. Elles doivent rester sous un tarif de 47 000 euros, mais l’Audi A2 e-tron s’y maintient pour plusieurs versions. Mais ce n’est pas tout, il faut aussi valider l’éco-score, qui favorise les voitures produites en Europe. Parfait, l’Audi A2 e-tron est produite à Ingolstadt, en Allemagne.
Tous les feux étaient au vert pour l’obtention du bonus écologique. Et la publication au Journal officiel du 22 octobre 2026 valide son éligibilité à l’aide à l’achat d’une voiture électrique en France. De ce fait, elle profite d’une prime pour tous de 3 535 euros, de 5 890 euros si votre revenu fiscal par part est compris entre 11 251 et 16 880 euros et jusqu’à 6 145 euros si votre revenu fiscal de référence par part est inférieur à 11 250 euros.
Une voiture efficiente et relativement bien placée
Rares sont les voitures électriques premium à être éligibles au bonus écologique. Seules les versions d’entrée de gamme de la Mercedes CLA et du GLB électrique arrivent à rester sous les 47 000 euros. Du côté d’Audi, le choix de rester en 400 volts et la plateforme MEB commune avec la Volkswagen ID.3 Neo, permettent d’avoir des tarifs d’accès contenus.
La version de 170 chevaux avec batterie de 52 kWh débute à 38 600 euros au catalogue, pour une autonomie de 423 km WLTP. Ce qui réduit son prix pour tous à 35 065 euros avec l’aide du bonus écologique. Si cette autonomie vous semble trop juste, il est judicieux de s’intéresser à la version de 231 chevaux à propulsion, utilisant une batterie de 84 kWh pour une autonomie allant jusqu’à 646 km WLTP, grâce au très bon travail d’optimisation aérodynamique d’Audi sur l’A2 e-tron. En se contentant du premier niveau de finition, cette version dotée de la plus grande autonomie du catalogue est proposée à partir de 46 900 euros, ce qui la rend éligible au bonus et donc à un tarif de 43 365 euros pour tous.
Une bonne nouvelle pour Audi, qui va avoir fort à faire avec cette Audi A2 e-tron, qui arrive sur un marché très concurrentiel : celui des compactes électriques.

articles.title: Microsoft finally fixes VPN issues caused by September updates
articles.text:
Microsoft has resolved Always On VPN connection failures triggered after installing the September 2026 Windows 11 security updates.
The Always On VPN remote access solution runs in the background and establishes secure tunnels back to the user's corporate network when their devices connect to the Internet. It has replaced the legacy DirectAccess technology and supports domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID–joined devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server.
Microsoft has previously mistakenly flagged this known issue as fixed in the October 2026 Windows 11 cumulative updates.
The company first acknowledged it in a service alert sent to IT administrators in late September, saying the Always On VPN failures were triggered on Windows 11 systems by the September 2026 security updates when using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP.
On Wednesday, Microsoft confirmed that this issue has finally been fixed for users who installed this month's KB5127936 preview update.
"This update fixes an issue that affects Always On VPN connections after installing September security update," it said. "When automatic protocol selection or protocol fallback was configured, affected VPN connections could remain stuck in a Connecting state or fail to connect after an initial connection attempt failed. In some cases, subsequent connection attempts could display the error, 'The specified port is already in use.'"
Workaround also available
Microsoft also provides a temporary fix for users who don't want to install the preview update and would rather wait for next month's Patch Tuesday cumulative updates.
This requires admins to choose one of two tunneling protocols to prevent Always On VPN failures on affected devices.
"IT administrators can mitigate this issue by changing the Always On VPN profile from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, either SSTP only or IKEv2 only, depending on their environment and configuration," Microsoft said.
"Organizations should select the protocol based on their environment, security, and deployment requirements."
The October 2026 preview update also fixes a known issue preventing non-admin users from connecting to devices via Remote Desktop when the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled after installing the September 2026 Windows 11 non-security preview update (or Windows updates released since then).

articles.title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence - Microsoft Research
articles.text:
At a glance
- Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.
- To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings.
- The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss.
- Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material.
Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly.
Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence.
They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in.
We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform, which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars:
- Synthetic enterprise environments: simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data
- Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets
- Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation
Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data?
In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot.
Synthetic enterprise environments
Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve.
Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments: simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful.
Grounding in real world signals
To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources.
- O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates.
- Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions.
- SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization.
Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure.
Industry specific simulation
We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage:
- A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings
- A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews
- An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination
This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes.
Automated query generation
While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in.
The six-stage pipeline
We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios.
Validating synthetic quality
Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions:
- Structural fidelity: Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships?
- Contextual relevance: Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns?
- Behavioral realism: Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics?
- Content safety: Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals?
End-to-end automation
While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including:
- Reproducibility: Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases.
- Scale: The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand.
- Iteration speed: Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles.
- Cross-team consistency: Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels.
This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results.
PODCAST SERIES
Privacy and safety by design
Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline. Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk.
Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline.
This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible.
Results and impact
Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions.
On synthetic data quality, our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments.
On scale and efficiency, each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs.
On organizational adoption, our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure.
Conclusion
As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety.
Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next.
At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale.
Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets!

articles.title: Beyond AI: Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 to spotlight new technologies, markets and opportunities
articles.text:
Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026
View Brand Publisher
Beyond AI: Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 to spotlight new technologies, markets and opportunities
The 29th edition of Bengaluru Tech Summit will bring together global technology leaders, investors, and entrepreneurs to explore emerging sectors and business opportunities.
For technology entrepreneurs, staying ahead increasingly means looking beyond their immediate business environment. New technologies are emerging rapidly, industries are converging, and opportunities for partnerships, investment, and market expansion are often found at the intersection of different ecosystems.
This makes technology-focused platforms that bring together businesses, innovators, investors, researchers and global technology communities particularly valuable. Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026, taking place from November 17–19 at Bangalore International Exhibition Centre, is one such platform worth keeping on the radar.
The 29th edition of BTS will bring together tech companies, startups, investors, R&D institutions, and global technology ecosystems across a wide range of sectors. The participation of global technology giants, Indian conglomerates, unicorns, and soonicorns creates an environment where entrepreneurs can gain a broader understanding of where their industries are headed while identifying potential business connections.
The convergence of the global tech ecosystem
The international dimension is equally significant. Technology communities from 75+ countries, including Sweden, Italy, Australia, Poland, USA, Israel, Spain, Japan, China, Germany and South Korea, will participate across the expo, conference and special events.
This creates an opportunity to engage with ecosystems beyond India for businesses or startups looking to understand international markets, explore collaborations, or simply broaden their technology network.
The grand co-location of embedded world India, organised by Nuernberg Messe India, brings embedded technologies into sharper focus at BTS 2026. With embedded systems increasingly underpinning applications across electronics, automotive, industrial technology and connected devices, its presence adds another important dimension to the technology landscape represented at the summit.
AI and robotics will take centre stage at BTS 2026 with the AI & Robotics Pavilion, led by Bharat fi.AI, spotlighting emerging innovations and advancements shaping the future of these transformative technologies.
Future makers in focus
For startups and emerging businesses, BTS 2026 offers opportunities that go well beyond the exhibition ﬂoor. Through workshops, masterclasses, mentoring sessions, pitching opportunities and product launches, entrepreneurs can gain practical insights, showcase their innovations, connect with potential investors, and explore new business opportunities.
The Future Makers Conclave further brings together founders, investors, and industry leaders, creating a platform for meaningful conversations around innovation, funding, and scaling businesses. Together, these initiatives aim to help entrepreneurs expand their networks, gain visibility, and build connections that can accelerate their growth.
Focus areas at BTS 2026
The breadth of sectors represented is another reason the summit stands out. From IT & deeptech, frontier tech, fintech, health & biotech to electro-semicon, cybersecurity, data centers and Global Capability Centres (GCCs), the summit explores technologies transforming businesses and creating new avenues for growth. It also looks beyond conventional technology domains to emerging opportunities in electric mobility, circular economy, orange economy, and edtech, highlighting how innovation is reshaping industries, opening new markets, and creating possibilities for entrepreneurs.
