articles.title: Saffron Box dreams of one day turning Canada into the next saffron superpower | BetaKit
articles.text:
Vikash Sangwan spent too much time sitting behind a computer. Like so many young Indian expatriates, Sangwan came to Canada in the 2010s looking to advance his career. An engineer by trade, he entered through Canada’s Federal Express Entry program and later landed a nine-to-five at one of the Big Four consulting agencies. But after years of working a desk job, Sangwan was desperate for change.
Today, Sangwan’s working environment is split between the glassy towers of Calgary, where he continues to work as a consultant with KWA Analytics, and a rustic, retrofitted barn in the neighbouring foothills. It’s there that Sangwan tends to more than 40,000 saffron bulbs that make up the inventory for his startup, Saffron Box.
“We want early investors and ecosystem partners to see that our [technology is] thoroughly proven before deploying at commercial scale.”
Vikash Sangwan,
Saffron Box
Pound for pound, Saffron is the most expensive spice in the world. It routinely sells for as much as $18,000 USD ($25,000 CAD) per kilogram on the wholesale market. To contextualize that, cocaine retails wholesale in Canada for around $18,000 per kilogram.
While saffron’s not an illegal substance, its supply chain is similarly fraught. Global supply is heavily concentrated, with around 90 percent of saffron originating from Iran. Secondary markets—the largest among them India and Afghanistan—have in recent years declined amid climate-change-induced droughts, driving up prices even further.
Sangwan’s Saffron Box is hoping to capitalize on that market scarcity, while also changing it.
Canadian-grown saffron
Founded in February 2026, Saffron Box is using vertical farming techniques and climate controls to attempt to replicate the precision horticulture required to grow the infamously fickle plant. In doing so, Sangwan hopes to create a whole new market stream for saffron right here in Canada.
Saffron Box is still very much an early-stage company. A husband-and-wife team, the company has no commercial customers. Instead, Sangwan is focused on research and development.
“Three years ago I tried growing corms [the garlic-like bulbs from which the saffron flower grows] in a basement grow tent and completely failed. Last year, I upgraded to a custom walk-in cooler in my residential garage. Now, we’ve scaled up to the barn level specifically to prove out the commercial ROI and unit economics,” Sangwan told BetaKit.
Cultivated from the saffron crocus flower, saffron grows in an inverted lifecycle, blooming in the autumn, producing foliage throughout the winter, and going dormant in the summer. In order to harvest the stigmas—the waxy portion of a saffron flower’s female reproductive system—that constitute the spice, precise conditions need to be met. In nature, those conditions are only found along a narrow stretch of geography with Mediterranean-like weather.
“In nature, Saffron breaks its summer dormancy only when prompted by a specific sequence of autumnal climate shifts,” Sangwan told BetaKit in an email.
That actually makes growing the spice outside of its natural harvest season more difficult in hot places like Iran, where growers need to invest in expensive cooling systems to produce multiple harvests throughout the year.
Images courtesy Saffron Box
Inside his barn, Sangwan is leveraging the brisk Alberta weather to avoid those costs.
“By mid-October, Canadian ambient outdoor temperature naturally matches the thermal profile required for floral induction,” Sangwan said.
Sangwan has set up an industrial air-handling unit to circulate that October air into the barn, keeping the temperature at the eight to 10 degrees Celsius needed to trigger saffron flowering. He pairs that with a hydronic boiler system (a heating device using heated, closed-loop water) that can supply targeted heat to counteract cooler winter temperatures that would otherwise destabilize the microclimate.
Sangwan cultivates his saffron corms without soil, meaning they can be stacked by the tens of thousands along vertical farming shelves, where they’re helped along the growth cycle with specialized light arrays and moisture monitoring.
“Throughout the transition, sensor arrays continuously monitor ambient temperature and moisture to maintain relative humidity,” Sangwan said. “When the flowers emerge, we deploy spectrum-tuned LED [lights] with targeted ratios of blue-to-red light.”
Big dreams start small
Ultimately, Sangwan hopes to commercialize his saffron farm. The founder envisions a future where Saffron Box’s product is grown in insulated, trailer-pod vertical farms capable of producing multiple yields per year regardless of the season.
“By controlling the climate … and staggering dormant batches, we [could] achieve up to four harvests per year rather than a single seasonal bloom,” he said.
Sangwan sees a future where these farm pods could be franchised out to independent growers nationwide, serving as a foundation for Canada to transition from saffron importer to exporter.
RELATED: After 15 years, GoodLeaf proves there’s profit in vertical farming
“Deploying this modular fleet would not only satisfy North American [saffron] consumption, but it would position Canada as a premier exporter,” he said.
That dream is, admittedly, quite a way off. While Sangwan claims to have secured at least one of the 53-foot trailers he hopes to convert to a vertical farming facility, he has not yet physically retrofitted it nor validated its ability to match the precision climatics present in his barn model, nor the economic viability of franchising said pods. 
To do that, the 36-year-old entrepreneur would need some serious capital. He’s not there yet, but said the company is actively seeking pre-seed investment. “Physical fabrication is our immediate milestone, which our open pre-seed capital raise is structured to fund,” Sangwan said. 
A/B testing
Just because Saffron Box isn’t ready to begin franchising out vertical farms doesn’t mean the company isn’t making efforts to expand beyond its current footprint. Sangwan has secured an outdoor plot of land in British Columbia’s Fraser Valley—which he says is about as close to the ideal climate for saffron as one can find outdoors in Canada—where he’s propagating another 20,000 saffron plants using traditional methods. The plan, he says, is to execute a comparative study between the indoor and outdoor yields.
“Running both parts simultaneously allows us to gather … the data and compare indoor, climate-controlled corm reproduction rates, sizing, and mortality, against traditional cultivation,” Sangwan said.
Sangwan is also in the midst of validating his multi-harvest thesis, staggering crop cycles through the year until June of 2027 in an effort to de-risk his business model. He hopes that by proving his methods, he might better attract the investors who could take his lofty dreams closer to reality.
“We want early investors and ecosystem partners to see that our biological triggers and CapEx models are thoroughly proven before deploying at commercial scale,” he said.
Some might say Saffron Box’s vision of Canada as a global saffron supplier is unrealistic. But so is the idea of growing saffron on the Canadian prairie in the first place. And so far, Sangwan’s been able to do just that.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy of Saffron Box. Photo by Vikash Sangwan.

articles.title: Enzi’s Oji Udezue Says Africa Needs Cheaper AI
articles.text:
Africa’s ability to benefit from artificial intelligence will depend on bringing down the cost of using it, Oji Udezue, president of Enzi, told Moonshot by TechCabal in Lagos.
Udezue said reducing the cost of inference, the process through which AI models generate responses and perform tasks, was essential to making the technology affordable for businesses and individuals across the continent.
“Our goal is to make AI cheaper for Africa and America,” he said. “The future of AI really goes through inference.”
His argument shifts attention from the race to build more powerful models to the economics of putting them to work. For businesses using AI to answer customer enquiries or support employees, the expense recurs each time the system performs a task. Those costs can determine whether a promising application becomes viable for everyday use.
Udezue highlighted the gap between the cost of using AI and what many Africans earn, warning that access to a tool means little if people cannot afford to use it consistently.
The distinction matters as companies seek to integrate AI into their operations. A service affordable for occasional queries may prove too expensive when used throughout the working day or offered to thousands of customers. Lower inference costs could make those applications more commercially practical.
Affordability is one part of a wider infrastructure challenge. The World Bank’s Digital Progress and Trends Report 2025: Strengthening AI Foundations identifies connectivity, computing resources, locally relevant data and digital skills as foundations for AI adoption. Its findings underline the importance of the systems and capabilities needed to put the technology to use.
For African developers, that also means ensuring models can work in local languages and respond to the circumstances of the people using them. A cheaper service will have limited value if its answers are poorly suited to customers’ needs.
Udezue emphasised practical demonstrations as a way to show what developers could achieve. His focus was on turning improvements in the technology into tools people could afford to use.
The economic test, in his account, is whether AI becomes cheap enough to support routine work across a much wider market. More capable models may expand what the technology can do; the cost of running them will help determine who can benefit.

articles.title: Run AI Models for Edge Application Development with Just a Few Commands | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
AI is expanding beyond the data center as developers build a new generation of agents to act at the edge: monitoring driver attention and cabin conditions, helping robots understand their surroundings and plan tasks, and coordinating fleets of machines on production lines. These physical AI applications rely on models that perceive, reason, and act within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. But getting a model ready to run can involve substantial setup.
NVIDIA DGX Spark, now available in a 64GB configuration, gives embedded developers a platform to prototype, fine-tune, and test models and agents. NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM provides a lightweight C++ inference runtime designed for embedded workloads, bringing the same inference framework to development on Spark and deployment on platforms such as NVIDIA Jetson Thor, NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor, and NVIDIA IGX Thor.
You can get started in just a few commands with the trtedge command-line interface (CLI). It downloads your selected model and builds TensorRT engines optimized for inference on Spark.
In this tutorial, you’ll run NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning, a text-only model, on Spark using TensorRT Edge-LLM. You’ll test prompts in your terminal and serve the model through an API for application prototyping. You’ll also enable DSpark speculative decoding to accelerate generation.
Prerequisites: Set up your development environment
To get started, you’ll need a DGX Spark with a supported NVIDIA software stack, NVIDIA CUDA 13, TensorRT 10.16.1.11 or newer within the 10.x series, and Python 3.10 to 3.12. The examples below were tested with TensorRT Edge-LLM 0.11.1 and TensorRT 10.16.1.11.
Open a terminal on your DGX Spark, create and activate a virtual environment, and install TensorRT Edge-LLM:
python3 -m venv --system-site-packages .venv-edgellm
source .venv-edgellm/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install "tensorrt-edgellm[server]==0.11.1"
Note: The virtual environment keeps newly installed packages separate while allowing access to all system Python packages, including TensorRT.
Check the TensorRT version and confirm that the TensorRT Edge-LLM runtime loads:
python -c "import tensorrt as trt; v = tuple(map(int, trt.__version__.split('.'))); assert (10, 16, 1, 11) <= v < (11,), f'TensorRT >=10.16.1.11 and <11 required; found {trt.__version__}'; from tensorrt_edgellm import runtime; runtime.load()"
Note: If compatible system TensorRT bindings are unavailable, follow the NVIDIA TensorRT pip installation instructions to install a compatible TensorRT 10.x version in the activated environment, then rerun the verification command.
With the virtual environment still active, start a chat with Nemotron-3.5 Lightning:
trtedge chat nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4
On your first launch, wait for the model download (approximately 21GB) and engine build to finish. Files are stored in ~/.cache/tensorrt-edgellm by default, so allow space for both the model and engines. Later launches reuse matching cached engines.
Once the chat prompt appears, enter:
Convert 25°C to Fahrenheit. Answer in one sentence.
Example response:
25°C is equal to 77°F.
Continue the conversation with follow-up questions, or type /exit to end the session.
Serve your model
Serve your model through a local OpenAI-compatible API on Spark for application development and testing.
With your virtual environment active, start the server:
trtedge serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8000
The server builds or reuses an engine for this configuration. Once startup completes, open a second terminal on your DGX Spark and check that it is ready:
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/ready 
A response containing "status":"ready" confirms that the server is ready. Send your first prompt to the chat completions endpoint:
curl -fsS -N http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
  "model": "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Convert 25°C to Fahrenheit. Answer in one sentence."
    }
  ],
  "stream": true,
  "temperature": 0,
  "max_tokens": 128
}'
The response streams as JSON events. Keep the server running for more requests, or press Ctrl+C in the server terminal to stop it.
Optional: Enable speculative decoding
You can speed up generation with DSpark speculative decoding, which uses a draft model to propose several tokens for the main model to verify in a single pass. To enable it with three draft tokens, press Ctrl+C in the server terminal, then restart the server with DSpark enabled:
trtedge serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8000 \
  --speculative-config '{
    "method": "dspark",   
    "model": "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4-DSpark",
    "num_speculative_tokens": 3
  }'
Once the server is ready, send another prompt to the chat completions endpoint to try DSpark-enabled generation.
You can experiment with num_speculative_tokens and other settings to tune generation speed for your workload. See the speculative decoding documentation to learn more.
Performance on DGX Spark 64GB
TensorRT Edge-LLM delivers low response latency and fast token generation with NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning on DGX Spark 64GB.
The table below reports time to first token (TTFT) and generation speed with and without DSpark speculative decoding.
| Decoding | Workload | Median TTFT (ms) | Mean generation speed (tokens/s) | 
| DSpark OFF | SpeedBench 1K | 201.0 | 73.3 | 
| DSpark OFF | SpeedBench 2K | 329.5 | 72.8 | 
| DSpark OFF | HumanEval prompts | 98.1 | 73.4 | 
| DSpark ON | SpeedBench 1K | 203.0 | 108.5 | 
| DSpark ON | SpeedBench 2K | 331.6 | 105.3 | 
| DSpark ON | HumanEval prompts | 98.7 | 126.9 | 
Generation speed is the average token generation rate per request, excluding time to first token. DSpark uses three draft tokens. Peak total system memory use during inference with DSpark was 27.9GB, including the OS.
Measured on DGX Spark 64GB running DGX OS 7.6.0 (Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS), using NVFP4 with thinking enabled, batch size one, one concurrent streaming request, and a 128-token output limit. Average input lengths were 1,153 tokens for SpeedBench 1K, 2,247 for SpeedBench 2K, and 139 for HumanEval.
Next steps
Try another model from the supported models list and continue developing your application on Spark. Options include vision-language models that interpret images and video, as well as speech recognition and text-to-speech models.
Explore the TensorRT Edge-LLM documentation for model-specific workflows and requirements on your target embedded platform.
And visit the Nemotron developer page for resources to get started. Explore open Nemotron models and datasets on Hugging Face and Blueprints on build.nvidia.com.

articles.title: Cette appli utilise l’IA pour améliorer vos photos et vidéos sans les envoyer sur Internet !
articles.text:
Une vieille photo qui manque de détails ? Une vidéo floue sur grand écran ? QualityScaler utilise l’intelligence artificielle pour agrandir les images et les vidéos, réduire le bruit et atténuer certains défauts. Disponible gratuitement depuis son code source sur GitHub, le logiciel fonctionne directement sur le PC, sans connexion Internet une fois les composants nécessaires téléchargés.
L’upscale consiste à augmenter la résolution d’un fichier. Mais se contenter de multiplier les pixels ne suffit pas à restituer les détails correctement. QualityScaler s’appuie sur des modèles d’IA pour reconstruire une image mieux définie, avec une interface graphique qui évite de manipuler des scripts lors de son utilisation. Le projet est open source et distribué sous licence MIT, l'une des plus permissives. C'est sa version gratuite, accessible sur GitHub et à installer manuellement, qui nous intéresse ici.
Améliorer aussi bien les photos que les vidéos
QualityScaler prend en charge plusieurs formats d’images (JPG, PNG, WebP, HEIC…), mais également de vidéos (MP4, MKV, MOV…). L’utilisateur peut augmenter la résolution d’une photo pour mieux l’afficher ou l’imprimer, mais également traiter une vidéo pour améliorer son rendu sur un écran plus grand. La réduction du bruit s'applique notamment aux images dégradées ou compressées.
Le logiciel peut découper automatiquement une image en zones de traitement pour contourner les limites de mémoire vidéo. Pour les séquences les plus longues, il est également possible de suspendre l’opération et de la reprendre plus tard.
- Traitement des photos et vidéos
- Compatibilité GPU multimarque
- Traitement local des fichiers
Comment installer gratuitement QualityScaler sur Windows ?
QualityScaler peut être utilisé gratuitement en téléchargeant son code source depuis GitHub. Contrairement à une installation classique, cette méthode nécessite quelques manipulations pour configurer le logiciel et ses modèles d'intelligence artificielle.
- Installer les prérequis. Téléchargez et installez Python et Visual Studio Code sur votre ordinateur.
- Télécharger QualityScaler. Rendez-vous sur le GitHub officiel, cliquez sur le bouton vert « Code », puis sur « Download ZIP ». Décompressez ensuite l'archive dans le dossier de votre choix.
- Récupérer les modèles d'IA. Téléchargez les modèles fournis par le développeur, puis extrayez leurs fichiers dans le dossier "AI-onnx" de QualityScaler.
- Ajouter FFmpeg. Téléchargez l'archive ffmpeg-release-essentials.7z depuis le site de distribution de FFmpeg. Extrayez le fichier ffmpeg.exe situé dans le dossier bin et placez-le dans le dossier Assets de QualityScaler.
- Installer les dépendances. Ouvrez le dossier du logiciel dans Visual Studio Code, sélectionnez le fichier QualityScaler.py, puis ouvrez un terminal intégré et exécutez la commande suivante : pip install -r requirements.txt
- Lancer QualityScaler. Une fois les dépendances installées, fermez puis relancez Visual Studio Code. Ouvrez le fichier "QualityScaler.py" et cliquez sur le bouton de lancement en haut à droite. Si nécessaire, installez l'extension Python proposée par l'éditeur.
L'interface de QualityScaler devrait alors s'ouvrir. Vous pourrez importer vos images ou vidéos, choisir un modèle d'IA et lancer le traitement sans passer par un service en ligne. L'installation demande un peu de temps, mais permet de profiter gratuitement des fonctionnalités du logiciel.
Pas de cloud, mais une bonne carte graphique indispensable
QualityScaler effectue les traitements sur la machine et n'a pas besoin de connexion Internet pour travailler. Disponible sur Windows 10 et 11, il fonctionne avec les GPU compatibles DirectX 12, que ce soit NVIDIA, AMD ou Intel. Pour l'accélération graphique, la configuration minimale annoncée est de 8 Go de RAM et une carte graphique avec au moins 4 Go de mémoire vidéo.
Une carte graphique adaptée reste fortement recommandée, notamment pour les vidéos. Le logiciel peut toutefois utiliser le processeur lorsque l'accélération GPU n'est pas disponible, au prix de traitements nettement plus longs.
De plus, il faut garder à l'esprit que l’IA n'est pas une baguette magique : elle ne "récupère" pas les détails originaux perdus. Elle en reconstruit une approximation, qui peut parfois produire des textures artificielles.
QualityScaler convient aux utilisateurs qui veulent améliorer des médias en local, notamment pour traiter des vidéos ou des lots d’images. Sa version gratuite demande un peu plus d'efforts à l'installation, mais permet de profiter de ses fonctionnalités sans abonnement ni traitement dans le cloud. Pour une retouche ponctuelle sur un ordinateur peu puissant, un outil plus léger sera probablement plus adapté.

articles.title: Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US), providing access to OpenAI’s frontier models through two components. Work completes complex, multi-step tasks and delivers review-ready results, and Codex is a coding agent for developing, testing, and reviewing software.
This walkthrough is intended for organizations whose security architecture requires model inference to use AWS GovCloud (US) identities, endpoints, and Regional controls. It configures Codex to route model requests through Amazon Bedrock Mantle in us-gov-west-1, where access can be governed using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and existing AWS GovCloud (US) network controls.
Codex is the OpenAI coding agent for AI-powered software development. With GPT models powering inference, Codex introduces a new class of intelligence optimized for complex, long-horizon developer workflows. You can use the ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI, and IDE integrations with Visual Studio Code, JetBrains, and Xcode. Model inference is routed through the Responses API on Amazon Bedrock.
For customers with data residency requirements, processing stays within the Amazon Bedrock AWS Region that you select. You pay per token with no seat licenses and no per-developer commitments. Zero data retention (ZDR) is also supported. In this configurable mode, prompts and responses are processed without being written to durable storage by AWS or shared with model providers. This helps you protect sensitive information and meet stringent data-governance, privacy, and security requirements.
This post walks through a controlled local deployment of the ChatGPT desktop app that sends model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West). The configuration uses API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions. These restrictions allow access only to the approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint while disabling other external connections and network-enabled capabilities. The result is a deployment that an agency security team can test and document before approving broader use.
Using AWS GovCloud (US) and following this guide do not, by themselves, authorize your workload. Your organization remains responsible for reviewing the selected model, AWS services, Region, endpoint, workstation controls, repositories, credentials, and data flows against its system security plan and authorization process.
Solution overview
You can use the ChatGPT desktop app in two ways:
- Work for larger tasks that need planning, research, files, and a finished result.
- Codex for technical work such as editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests.
The ChatGPT desktop app runs on an organization-managed computer through the desktop app or CLI. It uses the configured AWS credentials to securely send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint in us-gov-west-1. Because this setup uses AWS directly, ChatGPT workspace rules and user roles don’t control it. The main security controls are the computer’s policies and the AWS identity and permissions being used.
Walkthrough
The configuration has three main steps: set up authentication, set up the ChatGPT desktop app configuration files, and then launch, initialize, and verify the deployment.
Prerequisites
Before setting up the ChatGPT desktop app with AWS GovCloud (US), make sure your version of the ChatGPT desktop app supports Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). You need an approved AWS GovCloud (US) account, an IAM identity and approved credentials, access to the approved model, AWS Region, and endpoint, and permission to use them. You also need to set up the requirements.toml and config.toml files.
Step 1: Set up authentication
Select the approved AWS GovCloud (US) account and IAM identity or role with access to the approved model in us-gov-west-1. Obtain credentials through your organization’s approved mechanism. This walkthrough uses the named profile codex-il5. Keep credentials, bearer tokens, session tokens, and other secrets out of TOML files.
Protect the profile configuration, credential source, SSO token cache, and any credential helper from ChatGPT desktop app task writes, while allowing approved authentication tools to maintain and refresh credentials.
The ChatGPT desktop app supports two Amazon Bedrock authentication pathways: an Amazon Bedrock API key or the AWS SDK credential chain. AWS SSO through AWS IAM Identity Center is supported within the credential-chain pathway.
The app first checks for AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK in its environment. For desktop use, this variable can be supplied through %USERPROFILE%\.codex\.env on Windows or ~/.codex/.env on Linux and macOS. When present, the bearer token takes precedence over profile-based authentication.
If no bearer token is available, the app falls back to the standard AWS SDK credential chain. The chain can read AWS credentials from ~/.aws/credentials and related profile settings from ~/.aws/config. On Windows, the corresponding default paths are %USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\config. The chain also supports SSO profiles. For SSO, it uses the profile settings in the AWS config file and the cached SSO session to obtain temporary role credentials. These credentials don’t need to be manually stored in the AWS credentials file. See OpenAI’s Bedrock authentication documentation and the AWS IAM Identity Center credential provider documentation.
Step 2: Set up ChatGPT desktop app configuration files
You must create two ChatGPT desktop app configuration files: config.toml and requirements.toml.
Important: the configuration files need to be set up before the application is launched. The following table shows the file locations.
| Operating system | User config.toml | Admin requirements.toml | 
| Windows | %USERPROFILE%\.codex\config.toml | %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml | 
| Linux | ~/.codex/config.toml | /etc/codex/requirements.toml | 
| macOS | ~/.codex/config.toml | /etc/codex/requirements.toml | 
Start from the requirements.toml file. requirements.toml is an administrator-controlled rules file. It sets security limits that users can’t override, for example, restricting which permission levels, tools, or settings the ChatGPT desktop app is allowed to use.
Use the following baseline for the supported AWS GovCloud (US) Amazon Bedrock deployment. The [windows] section applies only to Windows, and sandbox_private_desktop must be supported by the approved runtime.
Next, configure the config.toml file. config.toml tells the ChatGPT desktop app how to operate, including which model provider to use (amazon-bedrock), which model to select, and settings such as permissions or context limits.
Replace the model ID and named profile (for example, codex-il5) with approved values.
Step 3: Launch, initialize, and verify
Download the app from the ChatGPT site and install it. Leave the app closed after installation. If it opens automatically or if the app has been launched previously, fully exit ChatGPT and end any lingering ChatGPT or Codex processes.
Make sure requirements.toml and config.toml are in place before the first app launch.
Start the app to load the requirements.toml and config.toml settings. Make sure it shows amazon-bedrock as the model provider.
In the Codex CLI, you should see a /status tab that looks like this:
In the ChatGPT desktop app, you can also confirm amazon-bedrock as the model provider.
Troubleshooting
The application prompts for an OpenAI account. Verify that requirements.toml and config.toml use the exact locations and file names shown in the preceding table, terminate all ChatGPT and Codex processes, and relaunch. The files must precede app launch.
AWS GovCloud (US) endpoint is reported as unsupported. Confirm the exact desktop or app-server release, endpoint, and model with OpenAI. Changing the URL alone does not establish support.
The wrong AWS identity is used. Inspect the effective credential source and named profile. Check whether an Amazon Bedrock API key takes precedence over the profile.
Capability restrictions are missing. Inspect the full effective requirements after restart. The API-only sign-in setting doesn’t apply the capability policy.
Rollback and cleanup
If a validation check fails, stop the rollout. Return the affected devices to the previously approved policy and provider settings, then restart the ChatGPT desktop app. Revoke any temporary AWS credentials or API keys, and confirm that those devices can no longer connect to Amazon Bedrock. Keep a record of the test and clearly document what failed before trying again.
Conclusion
The ChatGPT desktop app on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) gives you a controlled way to use OpenAI frontier models and coding assistance. Inference stays in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. By validating the configuration, confirming the approved AWS identity and endpoint, and verifying security controls, you can confidently prepare the deployment for broader use. This approach supports innovation while aligning deployment decisions with each organization’s security, authorization, and data-handling requirements.
Ready to explore the ChatGPT desktop app with Codex on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)? Start with a controlled deployment, validate your security controls, and work with your security team to prepare for broader adoption.
Related resources
- Bedrock AWS GovCloud (US) configuration – ChatGPT desktop app device, provider, network, verification, and troubleshooting guidance.
- Responses API on Amazon Bedrock – AWS Regions, endpoint behavior, authentication, and permissions for the Responses API.
- AWS GovCloud (US) compliance – Compliance programs and customer authorization considerations.
- OpenAI’s Bedrock authentication documentation – Amazon Bedrock API key and AWS SDK credential-chain authentication, including SSO.
- AWS IAM Identity Center credential provider documentation – SSO profile configuration and temporary AWS credentials.

articles.title: London’s Easol secures €26.78 million Series A extension as it launches AI agents for experience businesses | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Easol, a London-based experience commerce platform, has closed a €26.78 million ($30 million) Series A extension round, bringing its total raised to date to €53.57 million ($60 million).
The round comprises €17.85 million ($20 million) in equity and an €8.92 million ($10 million) debt facility. The equity portion was led by Y Combinator, with participation from Tiger Global, Foundation Capital, FMZ Ventures, Notion Capital, and Eight Roads. The debt facility was provided by Viola Credit.
“We built Easol to give experience businesses control over their entire business and bring their technology in-house. AI is now allowing us to do so much more, with rising costs and tighter margins we can now support experience creators in scaling their business growing revenue in ways we couldn’t have imagined when we first launched the platform in 2021,” said Ben Simpson, co-founder and CEO of Easol.
Founded in 2021 by husband and wife duo Ben and Lisa Simpson, co-founders of Rise Festival, who previously managed live experiences drawing two million guests annually across locations from the French Alps to the Sahara Desert. While running Rise Festival, the Simpsons grew frustrated with managing experience businesses across too many disconnected tools that offered no real data ownership.
“The technology and software solutions that experience businesses must stitch together to be able to offer a variety of different booking, payment and activity options develops a working environment for creators that is complex, inflexible, and expensive,” they told EU-Startups.com in 2022.
To overcome this disconnected tools bottleneck, they set out to build a platform that gave experience creators genuine control of their operations. As an all-in-one platform, Easol brings bookings, payments, marketing, customer support and guest data under a single connected system, all hosted on the client’s own domain and kept entirely within the business’s ownership. The company says it has never sold its customers’ data to third parties.
Easol now has offices in London, New York, and Los Angeles, and has powered experiences booked by 2.8 million guests across more than 135 countries so far in 2026. Its client roster includes Coachella, Stagecoach, Defected, Afronation, Rapha, Swingers – The Home of Revelry, Boots in the Park, State of Play Hospitality, Bingo Loco, Snowboxx, The Cube, and Hijingo, among others.
The funding enabled Easol to develop and launch Teammates, its new agentic AI tools built natively inside the platform. Teammates helps experience businesses to create their own AI agents covering sales, support and operations. These agents rely on live business data to identify missed revenue, resolve guest queries, update bookings and surface actionable insights automatically.
Easol says many experience businesses run on lean central teams, leaving significant revenue on the table. In early deployments, one Teammates agent reportedly identified approximately $50,000 in upsell opportunities from guests with no add-ons attached to their bookings, and generated the outreach to pursue them while another client recovered $28,000 in outstanding payments in seconds.
Eve Szlendak, Head of Sales, State of Play Hospitality UK, said, ”I used to spend up to three days building reports to capture every possible scenario. Now, the dashboards give me the information I need instantly.”
Since its earliest days, Easol has argued that digitising the experience economy is not merely a convenience but a commercial necessity. With surging demand for live and in-person experiences, the company sees AI as a competitive advantage to operate, analyse, and take action across whole businesses.

articles.title: Doomformer: Diese KI wurde in Doom geschaffen – was sie leisten kann
articles.text:
Doomformer: Diese KI wurde in Doom geschaffen – was sie leisten kann
Egal, ob in der Google-Suche oder auf einem Satelliten der ESA: Doom wurde mittlerweile auf so vielen verschiedenen Plattformen spielbar gemacht, dass die meisten Gamer:innen wohl schon lange mit dem Zählen aufgehört haben. Etwas seltener sind die Versuche, etwas anderes als einen Ego-Shooter aus Doom zu machen. So versucht es derzeit der Entwickler, der sich auf GitHub den Nicknamen „mottopanikeiku“ gegeben hat.
Doom als KI? Wie das funktionieren soll
Sein Projekt trägt den Namen „Doomformer“ und ist eine Wortneuschöpfung aus Doom und einem Transformermodell. Im Grunde hat er den Ego-Shooter in ein neuronales Netzwerk umgewandelt, das in der Lage ist, Arithmetik durchzuführen. Um das zu realisieren, nutzt er sogenannte „Voodoo Dolls“ aus Doom. Das sind Klone der Spielfigur, die immer dann auftauchen, wenn das Spiel einen zusätzlichen Spielerstartpunkt im Level entdeckt.
Um das neuronale Netzwerk zu bauen, werden laut dem Entwickler 1.355 Voodoo-Puppen genutzt, die zusammen ein MNIST-Netzwerk auf der Map bilden. Die Puppen fahren auf Bahnen hin und her und überqueren dabei Linien, die als Gewichtungen fungieren. Kommt es zu einer Aktivierung der Puppen, wird eine bestimmte Anzahl über eine Treppe nach oben in die zweite Ebene befördert. Das passiert, weil das Überqueren jeder Linie das Licht und die Ebenenhöhe verändern kann. So können sie Elemente im Spiel verändern und etwa Zahlen anzeigen.
Um die Fertigkeiten des Netzwerks zu testen, hat der Entwickler auch die Spielfigur etwas modifiziert. Spieler:innen können auf einem vorgefertigten Bereich die linke Maustaste gedrückt halten, die eigentlich zum Schießen in Doom gedacht ist. In der modifizierten Version malt das Gedrückthalten auf den Boden. Wird die Spielfigur bewegt, malt sie also auf den Boden.
Kann sich die Doom-KI selbst spielen?
Das neuronale Netzwerk ist in der Lage, so gemalte Ziffern zu erkennen. Sobald die Puppen an ihrer Position angekommen sind, vergleicht ein Python-Skript die Werte miteinander. In einem Test mit 10.000 Versuchen konnte „Doomformer“ insgesamt 9.716 der Zahlen korrekt identifizieren. Doch damit sind die Fertigkeiten der Doom-KI nicht am Ende.
Der Entwickler experimentiert derzeit damit, dass die Doom-KI selbst Doom spielen kann. Dabei werden die Screenshots des Spiels an 1.345 Voodoo-Puppen geschickt, die zusammen eine Entscheidung treffen, was die Spielfigur als Nächstes tun soll. Noch ist das aber fernab von einem „spielbaren“ Zustand, wie der Entwickler schreibt. Eine Entscheidung benötigt etwa 22 Sekunden. Für die Tests wurden deshalb Dämonengegner eingefroren, solange die KI überlegt.

articles.title: Waymo usará autos de Toyota para sus robotaxis en Japón y el Reino Unido, con pruebas desde 2027
articles.text:
Toyota fabricará los autos eléctricos que Waymo usará como robotaxis en Japón y el Reino Unido. Las dos empresas anunciaron el 30 de octubre que las pruebas del modelo bZ4X comenzarán en el país asiático en 2027, con despliegue posterior en territorio británico y en otros mercados donde opera la filial de Alphabet.
Según el comunicado de la automotriz, los vehículos se construirán en la planta de Takaoka, en la ciudad de Toyota, prefectura de Aichi. Todo el proceso ocurrirá en el mismo lugar: desde el armado del auto base hasta la instalación del hardware de conducción autónoma de Waymo.
El modelo llevará puertas automáticas, portón trasero eléctrico, iluminación ambiental y más espacio para las piernas en el asiento trasero. Toyota presentó el proyecto como el primer servicio de transporte totalmente autónomo de Japón con vehículos fabricados en el país.
Los autos serán de nivel 4, es decir, el sistema conduce por sí solo en condiciones definidas y no requiere conductor. Waymo comenzará por los mercados donde se maneja por la derecha. “Empezaremos con los mercados de conducción por la derecha, Japón y el Reino Unido”, dijo el codirector ejecutivo, Dmitri Dolgov, recogió Reuters.
Dolgov afirmó que la alianza con Toyota permitirá llevar la tecnología de Waymo a una operación comercial a gran escala. La empresa nipona sostuvo en su comunicado que el objetivo es reducir los accidentes causados por errores humanos y facilitar la movilidad de quienes no pueden desplazarse con facilidad.
Sin cantidad de autos ni ciudad definida
Las empresas no informaron cuántos bZ4X desplegarán al inicio ni en qué zona de Japón operarán, indicó Reuters. Hiroki Nakajima, de Toyota, dijo que las primeras operaciones usarán pocos vehículos. Dolgov afirmó que no hay otros países ni plazos para compartir.
El diario japonés Asahi Shimbun informó que los detalles, como la empresa de taxis que operará el servicio, se definirán más adelante. El anuncio llega 18 meses después del acuerdo preliminar firmado en abril de 2025 para explorar una plataforma de vehículos autónomos. TechCrunch señaló que el pacto se parece más a un contrato convencional de proveedor de autos.
Waymo prueba hoy autos Jaguar I-Pace en Japón y mantiene un piloto con ellos en 2027, dijo Dolgov a Reuters. En Londres, TechCrunch informó que la empresa los prueba desde hace meses y lanzará el servicio cuando obtenga los permisos necesarios.
Más allá del robotaxi: autos particulares
Toyota y Waymo también seguirán estudiando cómo llevar la tecnología autónoma a autos Toyota de propiedad particular. Junto con Woven by Toyota, evaluarán otras iniciativas para reducir accidentes, con datos de la operación real de Waymo.
Nakajima dijo que la automotriz asiática seguirá explorando cómo la integración de los vehículos con la infraestructura vial puede hacer las calles aún más seguras. Toyota también fabrica versiones con volante a la izquierda del bZ4X, pero quiere ganar experiencia en Japón antes de buscar otras oportunidades.
El primer hito confirmado es el inicio de las pruebas y la validación de la flota de bZ4X autónomos en Japón en 2027.

articles.title: Can AI data centers be mass-produced like cars? This startup aims to find out | TechCrunch
articles.text:
AI infrastructure company Runware is making news again, just months after unveiling the Sonic Inference Pod, a modular data center built in a factory and shipped to customers ready to install. Now the company has bigger plans. It told TechCrunch it wants to build a factory that assembles these pods on a production line, as if they were cars.
The idea isn’t entirely new. Companies like Crusoe and Schneider Electric also sell prefabricated pods, but Runware says it can ship its pods faster.
Flaviu Radulescu, co-founder and CEO of Runware, told TechCrunch that the company plans to scale production at its Romania-based factory to 30 megawatts of data center capacity per day by 2028, or nearly 1 gigawatt per month. That’s a whole lot of capacity: At that pace, Runware would produce roughly as much in a year as the entire U.S. was expected to add in data center power this year, about 10 gigawatts. But it also reflects an industrywide push to deploy data centers faster and more efficiently.
Nvidia announced, for example, the Vera Rubin AI factories and the DSX POD earlier this year. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one.
Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year.
Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said.
The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they’re ordered, which works in Runware’s favor. “Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered,” he said. “For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly.”
Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion, which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December.
“Our cost structure is very different,” Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival’s fate. “We do have headcount and materials cost,” he continued. “But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI.” He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. “We’ve brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right.”
Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, “representing over 20 megawatts, which we’re now working to deliver,” Radulescu said.
Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company’s pods only need power and an internet connection. They’ll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don’t really need a water connection. “We’re working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts,” he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google.
The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn’t further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run “completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible,” he continued. “We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We’re aiming to have renewables as our main energy source.”
Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become “the standard for large AI deployment,” Radulescu said.
“Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years,” he added.

articles.title: Review: You Can See Everything blurs the view of Elizabeth Holmes' deceit
articles.text:
In 2015, biomedical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes was Silicon Valley’s golden girl, lauded as the youngest and richest self-made female billionaire thanks to the company she founded, Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion at the height of its success. Then it all came crashing down when accusations of fraud surfaced about the company’s signature blood-testing device, culminating in a sensational trial. Holmes was convicted on four counts and sentenced to 11 years in prison.
Holmes is back in the headlines thanks to a new film, You Can See Everything, which depicts the final days before Holmes, having exhausted her appeals, went to prison. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it’s a surreal, absurdist piece that has largely been received with gushing enthusiasm and no small amount of hype, with some declaring it the best film of the year. A few contrarian voices have emerged over the past week with much-needed reality checks, but there’s no denying the film is destined to be an awards-season darling.
Pardon me for joining the buzzkills, but I cannot in good conscience jump on the You Can See Everything bandwagon. Sure, it has its moments, and the second half is highly entertaining, but there’s nothing here to warrant all the breathless hyperbole. For all their much-touted access, Oppenheim and Fielder have produced a surprisingly shallow film that runs in circles, yielding very little fresh or novel insight—into Holmes, personally, or much else.
I get that manufacturing ambiguity is the much-ballyhooed point. I get that much of the film’s appeal lies in how much fun people have afterward vigorously debating their interpretations of key scenes. (Perhaps the film should have been titled You Can See Whatever You Want to See.) But there’s no real mystery here. Holmes is still spouting all the same talking points and self-justifications, still playing the victim, dodging accountability, and affixing blame on anyone except herself, just as she did all the way through her trial. The only mystery is why a convicted fraudster is still deemed worthy of our attention.
tl;dr: Elizabeth Holmes is back on her bulls—t, and some people are falling for the act all over again.
(Spoilers below the first gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
There is already an excellent HBO documentary about Holmes and Theranos by Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney: The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley, a companion piece to journalist John Carreyrou’s 2018 book, Bad Blood. (I reviewed Gibney’s latest, Musk, earlier this month.) Holmes was also the focus of the 2022 Hulu fictionalized miniseries (and associated podcast) The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried as Holmes. None showed Holmes how she clearly wished to be perceived, so she reached out to A24 about making a documentary to tell her side of the story.
You will be shocked to hear that Holmes believes she is innocent and thought all she needed to do was “speak her truth” in order to convince everyone else, too. It didn’t work on a jury of her peers—who deemed her the least credible witness of the entire trial—but apparently it worked on Fielder. At least he’s in good company: Holmes fooled a lot of smart, savvy people for years before a pair of whistleblowers (Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung) exposed her lies.
Fielder, for those unfamiliar with his work, is a comedian, best known for his Comedy Central series (currently streaming on HBO) Nathan for You. Fielder played a fictionalized version of himself as a recent business graduate who “consulted” for struggling local businesses in LA. The gimmick: Fielder’s advice, offered in his trademark deadpan style, was deliberately weird, such as suggesting an ice cream store offer a poop flavor to generate headlines and draw customers. In another episode, he faked a video, which actually went viral, of a pig rescuing a goat at the local petting zoo.
Fielder was also an executive producer on the (excellent) HBO series How To With John Wilson before creating the docu-comedy, The Rehearsal, in which another heightened reality version of Fielder helps people prepare for difficult conversations by re-creating the conditions and environments in which those conversations will take place, frequently building extravagant sets to do so. If cringe humor is your thing (think Sasha Baron Cohen, with whom Fielder has also worked), then you’ll likely find Fielder’s schtick appealing—and you’ll be far more likely to love You Can See Everything.
Still, at first glance, he was a puzzling choice to co-direct this film, as was Oppenheim, who calls himself a “docu-fantasist.” The two men met at some point, became friends, and wanted to work on a project together; Holmes and current partner Billy Evans were Fielder fans. Thus, You Can See Everythingwas born.
Who’s playing who?
WARNING: Spoilers begin here.
Fielder and Holmes engage in a stare-down contest
A24
Fielder and Holmes engage in a stare-down contest
A24
Holmes reacts to watching the fictionalized version of her rise and fall: the Hulu series The Dropout.
A24

A24
Fielder and Holmes engage in a stare-down contest
A24
Holmes reacts to watching the fictionalized version of her rise and fall: the Hulu series The Dropout.
A24
Fielder and Oppenheim don’t spend much time rehashing the Theranos debacle and Holmes’ subsequent trial and conviction, which is fine; that has been covered exhaustively elsewhere, including the Gibney documentary, and it’s not what they were interested in capturing. They’re more keen on the vibes than the facts. Holmes and Evans invited Fielder and the film crew to stay with them for the 34 days before her imprisonment, and given the strangeness of their initial interactions, Fielder became a major on-camera presence in the film.
The first half of the film is on the dull side, featuring lots of footage of Fielder and Holmes staring at each other, unblinking, in an attempt to convince each other of their sincerity. (Jimmy Fallon and Jamie Lee Curtis hilariously spoofed this dynamic in a cold open for The Tonight Show.) There is a tiresome segment quibbling over the relative meanings of the words “can” and “could.” Another segment dissects whether or not Holmes is capable of understanding the humor behind the classic “Who’s on First” sketch.
Fielder’s deadpan comedic style is used to good effect. Any laughs in that first half come from his reaction shots, such as his expression when Holmes insists, blue eyes extra wide, that she has never once lied in her entire life. And it’s just innately funny seeing him pop up again and again at the edges of the frame, like an awkwardly diffident stalker.
Much has been made of the scene where Evans insists Fielder film him working out at the gym—including a post-workout shower scene with Evans faux-nonchalantly displaying side-frontal nudity. It’s nothing we haven’t seen before; HBO flashes its viewers all the time. Still, I can never unsee Evans’ flaccid junk, so thanks for that image being burned into my retinas, guys. But it fits the sleight-of-hand theme Fielder and Oppenheimer develop throughout the film. On the one hand, we are literally seeing everything. On the other, it is only the illusion of transparency, because Evans is so relentlessly squirrely and evasive—when not outright combative—about answering Fielder’s questions.
Frankly, Holmes and Evans just aren’t sufficiently interesting to carry a three-hour film, which is why Amanda Seyfried is such a breath of fresh air when she turns up for the second half to help Fielder and Oppenheim work around the physical absence of their primary subject. Seyfried plays Holmes in several carefully staged re-enactments—a fascinating window into the actor’s process—but she also becomes Fielder’s sounding board and (at times) co-conspirator. The film comes to life when she appears, akin to tossing a firecracker into a lackluster dinner party.
Seyfried, for instance, goads Evans into revealing that he has power of attorney and manages most activity on Holmes’ X account. She challenges Fielder about being reluctant to include footage that might show Holmes in a negative light because he’s come to care about her. And the film doesn’t let Seyfried off the hook either, forcing her to confront how her portrayal in The Dropout might have been painful for Holmes, despite clearly being fictionalized to allow for taking a few liberties with the facts.
An “absurdist reality show”?
Holmes mid-body scan so an AI avatar can be used while she’s incarcerated
A24
Holmes mid-body scan so an AI avatar can be used while she’s incarcerated
A24
Holmes en route to federal prison to serve her sentence.
A24
Holmes en route to federal prison to serve her sentence.
A24
Holmes mid-body scan so an AI avatar can be used while she’s incarcerated
A24
Holmes en route to federal prison to serve her sentence.
A24
Ars Technica senior editor Sam Axon, who loved the film, describes it as “an absurdist reality show” or a “post-postmodern comedy rather than an interesting documentary” that is “more for fans of Nathan Fielder than for people interested in Theranos.” Fair enough. But it has been marketed as a documentary. That label carries certain expectations. Yes, Fielder and Oppenheim are deliberately (and skillfully) thwarting those expectations, but to what end? Savvy consumers already know that documentaries frame their subjects in specific ways. Gibney, for one, unapologetically makes documentaries that espouse his personal point of view, rejecting the so-called “view from nowhere”—i.e., the illusion of objectivity. And reality TV has been around for decades. We know it’s innately performative, and that cameras subtly alter human behavior, blurring the boundary between truth and fiction. This is not a novel insight.
Fielder makes a show of approaching his subject with an open mind in order to be more “objective,” but there are plenty of details that Fielder omits to better shape his preferred narrative. For instance, Evans claimed they took a private jet to the Texas federal prison, whereas the film shows them driving there. More significantly, it’s clear Fielder deeply dislikes Evans (by the end of filming, the feeling was mutual), which is why he deliberately features moments that portray Evans as a controlling, manipulative, and almost comically vain Silicon Valley bro.
Evans may be all of that and more, but Holmes is treated with kid gloves by comparison. This is not the smart, savvy, high-powered businesswoman who graced magazine covers and wowed tech reporters with her rosy vision of a diagnostic future free of anxiety-inducing blood draws. Even whistleblower Tyler Shultz has said this version of Holmes seems “broken.” But she’s still a very good liar.
Shultz points out in an article for STAT News that Holmes and Evans were living in the $125 million Green Gables estate just prior to filming. They moved to a smaller, average-looking rented condo on the beach for the duration of the shoot (which still rents for around $28,000 a month)—a strategy Holmes employed before when being profiled by journalists. And the disassembled Theranos blood testing device Holmes displays for the cameras—in the scene that triggered the “can” vs. “could” discussion—is not the correct device, per Shultz:
That was not the device I worked with 12 hours a day, not the device we hid from regulators, not the device that constantly failed quality controls, not the device we used to knowingly give patients inaccurate medical results. The device she showed Fielder on the kitchen table was not the reason she went to prison. Elizabeth showed him a future version of the Theranos product that was never completed and never used in order to lead Fielder down this BS semantic rabbit hole and to trick him into litigating the entirely wrong thing.
Did Fielder catch the misdirection? Was he taken in by the subterfuge, like so many before him? Or is he willfully ignoring those aspects because they don’t suit his purposes? I’ll take Gibney’s transparent subjectivity any day over Fielder’s ambiguous gamesmanship.
You Can See Everything is obsessed with whether Holmes is lying, believes her own lies, or even understands what lying entails. Perhaps it’s not that black and white. I’m willing to grant that Holmes’ tears at having to leave her newborn child to serve her sentence are genuine; any mother would be heartbroken. But it also serves her broader purpose of crafting a more sympathetic narrative. The portrait that emerges is one of Holmes as the victim of yet another controlling, abusive man. It’s her entire legal defense during her trial, re-created here for Fielder’s (and our) benefit, with Evans taking on the scapegoat role of Holmes’ former business and romantic partner, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, currently serving a 12-year sentence for his part in the Theranos debacle.
Fielder has built his entire brand around the unreliable narrator trope, while Oppenheim has been accused of misleading his subjects while making a 2017 short for The New York Times, so it’s fair to say both men might have a complicated relationship with the truth. Perhaps Holmes got the “documentarians” she deserved, and this is a match made in heaven. One can’t rule out the possibility that she and Evans were in on the game from the start. The entire film is an elaborate performance piece, manufactured for our post-truth consumption: ‘Haha, look at these people trying to out-manipulate each other for the cameras, like contestants on the latest reality show.’ Are you not entertained?
The cynical nihilism of it all is exhausting, and ultimately the joke is on us. Facts matter. Accountability matters. Even in a world awash in deep fakes and misinformation, there are still some truths that can be known, no matter how doggedly Fielder and Oppenheim try to muddy the waters. They want us to believe that Elizabeth Holmes is “unknowable and everything is ambiguous,” as Carreyrou—who, unlike me, loved the film and thinks it should win the Oscar for best picture—recently wrote on X. “She went after Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung with everything she had. I was threatened with litigation on a daily basis for months on end. It was a ruthless cover-up of a breathtaking fraud, and she was at the controls. Just a little context for those who have forgotten or didn’t follow the original story.”
In the grand scheme of things, nobody cares what the science-and-culture writer at Ars Technica thinks about this film. I am firmly in the minority with my assessment, and I’m good with that. Oppenheim and Fielder will rake in box-office millions and collect a bunch of prestigious awards, including a possible Oscar. Holmes will serve her time—in fact, she’ll be eligible for a halfway house next year—and Evans is already hard at work raising capital for a new biomedical startup. Holmes will once again try to rehabilitate her image by spinning some new variation on how she did nothing wrong, the device really does work, and she is the victim here. It’s the only story she knows how to tell.
But we don’t have to keep falling for it.
You Can See Everything is now playing in theaters.
Jennifer is a senior writer at Ars Technica with a particular focus on where science meets culture, covering everything from physics and related interdisciplinary topics to her favorite films and TV series. Jennifer lives in Baltimore with her spouse, physicist Sean M. Carroll, and their two cats, Ariel and Caliban.

articles.title: Resumo da semana: Lula é reeleito, IA avança e big techs têm perdas bilionárias
articles.text:
A última semana de outubro foi marcada pela reeleição de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), por movimentações importantes no setor de inteligência artificial e por resultados financeiros que aumentaram as dúvidas sobre o ritmo dos investimentos das grandes empresas de tecnologia. Também acompanhamos um ataque bilionário à Binance, novidades na exploração espacial e mudanças na indústria automotiva brasileira.
Lula é reeleito e terá desafios na agenda de ciência e tecnologia
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) foi reeleito presidente do Brasil no domingo (25), com 51,79% dos votos válidos. O novo mandato terá desafios importantes em áreas como inteligência artificial, proteção de dados, data centers, terras raras e transição energética.
A agenda do governo eleito inclui propostas para ampliar a capacidade tecnológica nacional e atrair investimentos em infraestrutura. O Olhar Digital analisou os planos para essas áreas e ouviu especialistas sobre os impactos econômicos, os desafios geopolíticos e as dificuldades para transformar as propostas em políticas públicas.
Gastos com inteligência artificial derrubam ações de big techs e acendem alerta sobre bolha
Os balanços das grandes empresas mostraram o peso desse mercado. A Microsoft registrou lucro líquido de US$ 36,6 bilhões no trimestre, enquanto a Alphabet ficou abaixo das expectativas de receita e lucro por ação. A Samsung teve alta de 783,1% no lucro operacional, impulsionada pela demanda por chips de memória usados em sistemas de IA. Já a Amazon apresentou resultados abaixo das projeções de Wall Street e manteve a previsão de investir US$ 220 bilhões em 2026. Apesar do crescimento de 39% da AWS, o fluxo de caixa livre da companhia ficou negativo em US$ 42,4 bilhões nos últimos 12 meses, reflexo do aumento dos gastos com infraestrutura.
A reação dos investidores evidenciou a preocupação com o tamanho desses gastos. Na sexta-feira (30), as maiores empresas de tecnologia perderam quase US$ 900 bilhões (R$ 4,88 trilhões) em valor de mercado. Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft mantiveram os planos de ampliar investimentos em chips e data centers, mas o mercado passou a cobrar sinais mais concretos de que a aposta em IA será convertida em receitas.
Hackers roubam US$ 6,3 bilhões da Binance
A Binance foi alvo de um ataque que resultou no roubo de US$ 6,3 bilhões, no maior caso do tipo já registrado no setor de criptomoedas. O episódio chamou atenção pelo volume envolvido e pelos riscos associados à segurança de plataformas que movimentam grandes quantias em ativos digitais.
O caso também levantou dúvidas sobre os mecanismos de proteção adotados por empresas do setor. A Binance afirmou que os brasileiros não foram afetados pelo ataque e garantiu a segurança dos recursos dos clientes no país.
OpenAI quer comprar chips de inteligência artificial do Google
A OpenAI planeja comprar chips de inteligência artificial do Google, em uma possível parceria comercial entre duas empresas que competem diretamente no desenvolvimento de modelos e serviços de IA. O movimento pode ampliar as alternativas da companhia à Nvidia, que domina o mercado de processadores usados no treinamento e na operação desses sistemas.
A negociação também mostra como a demanda por capacidade computacional tem aproximado empresas que disputam espaço no mercado de inteligência artificial. Os chips do Google são uma alternativa aos processadores da Nvidia, utilizados por boa parte das principais empresas do setor.
Anthropic prepara abertura de capital, mas registra prejuízos bilionários
A Anthropic formalizou os planos para abrir capital nos Estados Unidos. A operação pode movimentar mais de US$ 100 bilhões e avaliar a empresa em até US$ 2 trilhões, em uma das maiores ofertas públicas iniciais já planejadas para o setor de tecnologia.
Os documentos apresentados também revelam prejuízos bilionários e riscos associados ao desenvolvimento e à utilização de sistemas de inteligência artificial. A abertura de capital deve colocar as contas da empresa sob maior escrutínio de investidores.
Justiça manda Meta remover posts que incentivam demissão por voto
A Justiça do Trabalho determinou que a Meta retire do Instagram publicações que incentivam empregadores a vigiar, expor e demitir funcionários por suas escolhas políticas. A decisão também exige avisos contra discriminação política e assédio eleitoral no Instagram, Threads e Facebook.
O Ministério Público do Trabalho registrou 3.396 denúncias de assédio eleitoral nas eleições de 2026 e pede R$ 50 milhões em indenização por danos morais coletivos. A decisão determina que a empresa preserve as publicações removidas e seus dados técnicos durante o processo.
NASA quer testar supercomputador com IA na Lua
A NASA pretende levar um supercomputador equipado com inteligência artificial à superfície lunar para testar recursos de navegação autônoma. O equipamento deverá analisar imagens, processar mapas e ajudar um veículo robótico a evitar crateras sem depender de GPS.
A iniciativa busca avaliar como sistemas de computação e inteligência artificial podem apoiar futuras operações na Lua. O processamento local também pode reduzir a dependência de comunicação constante com a Terra durante a exploração da superfície lunar.
MacBook Pro ganha tela sensível ao toque pela primeira vez
A Apple apresentou uma nova geração do MacBook Pro com tela sensível ao toque, recurso inédito na linha. O notebook também traz os chips M5 Pro e M5 Max, tecnologia de tela PROLED XDR e integração da Dynamic Island ao macOS.
No Brasil, os preços começam em R$ 34.999 e chegam a R$ 57.999. A novidade representa uma mudança na interação com os notebooks profissionais da empresa, que até então priorizavam o uso do teclado, do trackpad e de outros dispositivos de entrada.
BYD avança na Bahia e quer comprar antigo porto da Ford
Um ano após inaugurar sua fábrica em Camaçari, na Bahia, a BYD prevê iniciar até dezembro a produção de carros com etapas industriais realizadas integralmente no Brasil. A montadora também demonstrou interesse em comprar o antigo porto da Ford, em Candeias.
A aquisição poderia ampliar a capacidade de exportação da empresa, que vem expandindo sua operação no país. O movimento faz parte dos planos da fabricante chinesa para fortalecer sua presença na indústria automotiva brasileira.
Gases de efeito estufa atingem níveis recordes na atmosfera
A concentração de gases de efeito estufa na atmosfera chegou a níveis recordes em 2025, segundo relatório da Organização Meteorológica Mundial (OMM). O dióxido de carbono atingiu 426,8 partes por milhão, o equivalente a 153% dos níveis registrados na era pré-industrial.
Metano e óxido nitroso também alcançaram máximas históricas. O relatório aponta que o acúmulo desses gases na atmosfera continua contribuindo para o aquecimento global e para as mudanças no clima.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth
articles.text:
Google’s AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku about being in space:
Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth
The Project Suncatcher satellite generated a haiku about being in space.
Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core. ✨
Google says it tried out other space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts as well. The test is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, an experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google launched the satellite into orbit earlier this month.
“Next, we will continue with a series of tests to evaluate how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit,” Google says. “Verifying our TPUs can reliably execute workloads in space paves the way for our next milestone of twin interconnected satellites in 2027.”

articles.title: Drupal warns of critical Commerce Core flaw exploited in attacks
articles.text:
Drupal warned admins to patch a critical access bypass vulnerability in the Commerce Core module that attackers are exploiting in the wild.
Tracked as CVE-2026-118539, this flaw stems from a missing authorization weakness that can be abused by unauthenticated attackers and affects Commerce Core versions 0.0.0 through 2.41 and 3.0.0 through 3.3.13.
The Drupal security team asked admins on the 3.x branch to upgrade immediately to Commerce Core 3.3.13 (or Commerce Core 8.x-2.41 for earlier versions) and audit orders for inconsistencies, since threat actors are exploiting this vulnerability in attacks.
"This module enables you to sell goods and services to customers through an included shopping cart and checkout form or through decoupled applications via APIs," Drupal said in a Wednesday advisory tagged as highly critical.
"The module doesn't sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields, leading to an access bypass that may financially impact the vendor. This vulnerability is being actively exploited in the wild."
Commerce Core is a community-developed Drupal module used by more than 42,000 websites, including many high-profile organizations such as Fortune 500 companies and research universities.
The module provides a software framework for building and running e-commerce sites and shopping apps on top of the Drupal Content Management System (CMS).
In May, Drupal also warned that attackers were exploiting an SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-9082) in the database abstraction API that could lead to privilege escalation, information disclosure, and remote code execution.
Days later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog and ordered federal agencies to patch their systems within three days.
Two weeks ago, Drupal patched two more remote code execution security issues (CVE-2026-108097 and CVE-2026-108099) that could allow threat actors to execute code remotely, and urged admins to apply updates as soon as possible because attackers could develop exploits "within hours or days."
Over the last several years, CISA has flagged 5 Drupal vulnerabilities exploited in the wild, two of which have also been abused by ransomware gangs.
