articles.title: Bloomsco raises $1 million pre-seed from BDC, Telegraph for military training platform | BetaKit
articles.text:
As defence spending grows in Canada, a Montréal AI startup is hoping to serve the education and training gap between contractors and the military.
The news: Bloomsco, which is developing a software platform that defence contractors can use to create training materials for the military, announced on Thursday a $1-million pre-seed equity round from BDC Capital’s Seed Venture Fund and Montréal-based Telegraph Ventures.
The company said it will use the funding to grow its engineering team and refine its tech for use in classified and air-gapped environments (meaning it’s isolated from the internet).
From the source: “The whole focus of a military is training people well to do the work they need to do,” Bloomsco co-founder and CEO Hugh McGuire said in an interview with BetaKit. “With more complex technologies that are changing fast, how do we build a training system that is able to adapt?”
The context: Bloomsco uses AI to turn technical manuals, data, and product specs into training plans, learning materials, and simulation scenarios that the end customer can adapt as they see fit. It has already secured a contract with the Department of National Defence (DND) to create a qualification standard and training plan for an officer role.
McGuire founded Bloomsco alongside CTO Hadrien David, who was a founding engineer at healthtech company Dialogue. Though neither has a background in defence, they found validation in their idea through retired Vice-Admiral Ron Lloyd, a former commander of the Royal Canadian Navy and a former chief data officer at the Department of National Defence (DND), who is now a Bloomsco adviser.
Final thought: With new military spending, the Canadian Armed Forces is set to buy a flood of new equipment and technology. For example, Canada started a new defence drone procurement initiative to fast-track buying uncrewed drone and counter-drone systems. Bloomsco is betting that there’s enough demand for learning how to use this technology that it will create more contracts.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: London’s Ares Intelligence raises €2.9 million to turn employee insights into AI adoption plans | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Ares Intelligence, a London-based startup building what it describes as an evidence-based platform for AI transformation, has secured €2.9 million (£2.48 million) in funding.
The round was backed by Creandum and Lakestar, with participation from angels connected to Google DeepMind.
“Enterprise AI today is mostly coding, and that’s only the start. The opportunity across the rest of the business is far bigger and still largely untapped, and we’re at the very beginning of enterprise adoption,” said Richard Keuntje, Vice President, Creandum.
Founded in 2026 by Matt Falconer and 21-year-old Alfie Ranstead, Ares Intelligence was built to solve a problem the founders encountered first-hand while running Instruct, their previous automation company. It says customers ran into the same problem: they wanted to automate parts of their business but had no reliable way of knowing where to begin. Ares Intelligence was to fix this knowledge gap.
The platform deploys an AI interviewer that holds confidential, voice-based conversations with every employee in an organisation, in more than 70 languages. Within weeks, leadership receives a prioritised, evidence-led roadmap identifying where AI can save time and money.
Ares’ platform is GDPR- and SOC 2-compliant, with anonymisation controls that let businesses mask names, redact voices, or strip role metadata before reports reach leadership. Customers can deploy it on their own cloud or use Ares’ infrastructure, in the EU or the US, with data retention windows set by the business.
The founders say the entire process, from training employees on what AI can do to conducting individual interviews, collecting insights and drafting recommendations, takes weeks rather than the months usually taken by a consulting firm.
Ares Intelligence’s approach also flips the script on top-down AI strategy by not relying only on a handful of senior managers to identify AI transformation opportunities. The company’s AI interviewer captures the knowledge of the people closest to the day-to-day work, identifies gaps such as manual workarounds, broken handoffs, and use of unapproved AI tools.
“Businesses across Europe know they need to adopt AI, but many still don’t know where to start. It’s vital that companies begin their AI transformations now to avoid falling behind,” said Falconer, co-founder and CEO, Ares Intelligence.
He added, “The people doing the work every day have a huge amount of knowledge about where AI could make a difference, but they’re rarely asked. Ares gives them a voice across departments, countries and languages, and turns what they share into a practical plan. This funding helps us expand and bring that approach to more businesses.”
Since launch, Ares Intelligence has signed enterprise customers across Europe and the United States in approximately seven months. Tremonia, a Mercedes-Benz spin-out, uncovered more than 400 hours of avoidable manual work per month within four weeks of Ares’ AI interviewer interviewing everyone from senior leadership to the paint shop floor.
“The gap between AI ambition and real-world evidence is the right challenge to back. I’m building a business with AI myself, and there’s a significant difference between an impressive demo and something you can rely on in your actual work. What appeals to me about Ares Intelligence is getting the insight from the people closest to the work,” said Enrico Mellis, Venture Partner, Lakestar.
Ares Intelligence says the fresh capital will help the company expand operations and bring its AI-driven workforce intelligence to more businesses.

articles.title: Binance links $6.3 billion crypto theft to compromised DevOps laptop
articles.text:
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has linked the theft of about $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency to a DevOps engineer's compromised laptop.
The crypto exchange said the access let attackers submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions after they accessed a service container, and it hasn't yet found evidence of a leaked wallet private key.
"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual," Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said.
Binance also said it "uncovered additional points of breach" but was "still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."
The company confirmed the breach in a statement shared with BleepingComputer on Thursday and reassured customers that their funds were safe.
"Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and the company's funds. User funds are safe. We will also publish an updated Proof of Reserves once the remediation is complete," it said.
Since the attack, Binance has suspended deposits and withdrawals while it conducts security checks, revoked authorizations for the affected address, and is working with blockchain intelligence partners and law enforcement to trace and recover the stolen funds.
Crypto theft linked to North Korean hackers
Although the company didn't link the incident to a hacking group or threat actor, blockchain analysis firm TRM attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking unit also tracked as Lazarus Group and APT38.
"On October 29, 2026, an attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes starting at 20:05 UTC. That makes this the largest crypto theft on record, about four times the USD 1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025," TRM said.
Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis confirmed TRM Labs' findings, stating with "a high degree of confidence" that TraderTraitor is responsible for the Binance $6.4 billion hack.
While stablecoin issuers Tether, Circle, Ripple, and others have frozen roughly $2.7 billion since the incident, the attackers still have control of about $2.4 billion that can't be frozen.
"Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze about USD 2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum's Security Council froze 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB on its network, for a total of roughly USD 2.7 billion," TRM added.
"The attacker raced the freezes by selling USDT to market makers and borrowing ETH against USDT on Aave. It now holds more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, about USD 2.4 billion in assets beyond any issuer's reach."
The TraderTraitor hackers were previously linked to many other major crypto theft incidents, including the theft of $1.5 billion in the February 2025 Bybit hack. At $6.36 billion, the Binance attack is now the largest recorded crypto heist.

articles.title: Del cobre a la luz: cómo la fotónica podría reducir el consumo energético de la inteligencia artificial
articles.text:
La expansión de la inteligencia artificial aumenta la capacidad de cálculo requerida por los centros de datos y, con ella, la demanda de electricidad, agua y cobre. Ante ese panorama, empresas tecnológicas y laboratorios desarrollan sistemas que usan luz para transmitir información y reducir el calor de los equipos, una alternativa que podría disminuir la energía destinada a enfriarlos.
La tecnología se llama fotónica. En lugar de mover la información mediante señales eléctricas a través de cables de cobre, la transporta con luz por fibra óptica. La fibra ya se utiliza en las comunicaciones de larga distancia, pero ahora la industria busca incorporarla a las conexiones internas de estas instalaciones, entre servidores, procesadores y equipos de red.
“Creo que estamos llegando al final de la era del cobre”, afirmó Chris Sharp, director de Tecnología de Digital Realty, en declaraciones recogidas por la BBC. Con esa frase no sugirió que el metal dejará de utilizarse, sino que su peso en las conexiones internas podría disminuir.
Una instalación de 100 megavatios puede requerir unas 400 toneladas de cobre, según el medio británico. La mayor parte se destina a la red eléctrica y a los equipos de refrigeración; del total, unas 70 toneladas se usan en los servidores y cerca de 20, en el cableado que los conecta.
La transmisión de datos con luz genera menos calor
El cobre conduce las señales eléctricas con eficacia, aunque ese proceso produce calor. El efecto cobra importancia en edificios que reúnen miles de procesadores, incluidos los que se utilizan para entrenar y operar herramientas de inteligencia artificial. A mayor temperatura, mayor es la energía que debe destinarse a mantener los equipos dentro de un rango seguro.
La fotónica busca reducir esa carga térmica. Para aplicarla, los fabricantes deben unir componentes ópticos, que trabajan con luz, y circuitos electrónicos, que funcionan con electricidad. En algunos casos, esa integración se realiza en los propios procesadores.
“Se puede ahorrar muchísima energía”, dijo Callum Littlejohns, subdirector de Cornerstone Labs, una fábrica de componentes de fotónica de silicio, según la BBC. La diferencia reside en que la luz no genera el mismo calentamiento que la corriente eléctrica cuando transmite datos.
Menos calor puede traducirse en una menor necesidad de electricidad para refrigerar los servidores. Cuando las instalaciones emplean agua para ese fin, esa reducción también podría aliviar su demanda hídrica. El impacto, de todos modos, depende del sistema de enfriamiento y del diseño particular de cada centro de datos.
La fibra óptica ofrece otra ventaja: permite enviar varios flujos de información por un mismo canal. De ese modo, se puede ampliar la cantidad de datos que circula por la red sin multiplicar el cableado al mismo ritmo, una posibilidad relevante para instalaciones que conectan cada vez más servidores.
La producción a gran escala todavía presenta obstáculos
El uso de luz para transmitir datos existe desde hace décadas, pero fabricar componentes fotónicos integrados en grandes volúmenes resultó complejo. Por su parte, Peter O’Brien, responsable de investigación sobre integración de sistemas fotónicos en el Instituto de Investigación Tyndall de Irlanda, explicó que investigadores y empresas llevan años trabajando en este campo, aunque las dificultades de fabricación demoraron su adopción.
“Lo que está ocurriendo ahora con la óptica y la fotónica es que se está produciendo una especie de reinicio”, señaló O’Brien ante la BBC. El respaldo de compañías de procesadores, entre ellas Nvidia, impulsó el interés por una tecnología que busca salir de aplicaciones limitadas y alcanzar un uso más extendido.
El reemplazo de conexiones de cobre por fibra no será inmediato. Andrew Wheeler, vicepresidente sénior de Hewlett Packard Labs, recordó que la industria eléctrica lleva años perfeccionando el diseño, la producción, las pruebas y la instalación de sus componentes. La fotónica aún necesita reducir costos y consolidar procesos de fabricación confiables.
La temperatura y el tendido de fibra exigen nuevos cuidados
Los dispositivos ópticos generan menos calor que sus equivalentes eléctricos, pero no eliminan el problema térmico. Otros equipos del centro de datos continúan elevando la temperatura ambiente y los componentes que trabajan con luz son sensibles a esas variaciones.
Wheeler advirtió que la fiabilidad de estos sistemas depende de que fabricantes y operadores mantengan controles estrictos sobre la temperatura. Por eso, la adopción de la fotónica requerirá cambios en el diseño de las instalaciones y nuevas rutinas de mantenimiento.
El tendido de fibra también demanda capacitación específica. Sharp explicó que estos cables no toleran curvas muy cerradas, una diferencia frente al cableado de cobre. Los responsables del diseño de redes, los técnicos de soporte y los instaladores deberán considerar esas condiciones para evitar pérdidas de señal y fallas de conexión.
Para Ofer Shapiro, director ejecutivo de Resolight.ai, el ahorro podría ser mayor si la luz se utilizara tanto para transportar datos como para procesarlos. La empresa propone reemplazar los equipos electrónicos que dirigen el tráfico entre servidores por otros que funcionen de forma íntegramente óptica, con el fin de evitar conversiones constantes entre señales de luz y eléctricas.
Esa posibilidad todavía se encuentra en una fase posterior. Por ahora, el desafío principal consiste en aumentar la fabricación de estos componentes y abaratarla. Littlejohns indicó que algunas de estas piezas son más grandes que las de los procesadores convencionales, por lo que pueden producirse con equipos de generaciones anteriores de la industria electrónica.

articles.title: $2 Million+ Drained From Polymarket Traders in New Supply Chain Attack
articles.text:
Polymarket halted trading on its international platform on October 29 after users reported unauthorized withdrawals.
According to the prediction market’s status page, the exchange was first switched to cancel-only mode, with relayer actions suspended.
“We’ve identified & fixed an issue impacting our international platform, Polymarket.com. One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement. Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole,” the company said.
Trading resumed about an hour later, and Polymarket pledged to reimburse all affected traders. It has not named the vendor or disclosed losses.
Researchers have linked the theft to malicious code served from DebugBear, a UK-based website performance monitoring firm. Polymarket’s US platform was reportedly unaffected.
DebugBear confirmed being “impacted by an ongoing security incident” and urged users of its real user monitoring (RUM) product to pull its snippet from their websites. It also said it brought in specialist incident responders.
Hudson Rock obtained a copy of the malicious JavaScript from a DebugBear address used by Polymarket. The code hunted for a logged-in user’s trading tools and portfolio. Depending on the account type, it then tried either to sell positions and move the proceeds, or to send position tokens straight to an attacker-set address.
“The sample reads credential-related material, but our review did not identify a routine that sends the credential map, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to its reporting endpoint. Its central approach is to reuse authority already available in the authenticated application,” Hudson Rock said.
The firm also spotted a Polymarket production build, timestamped 17:59 UTC, with a change note about removing the DebugBear script.
Loss figures vary. A screenshot reviewed by Hudson Rock showed about $2.19 million at the script’s hard-coded fallback address, though the firm said this is not a verified tally.
Blockchain security firm GoPlus, which also attributed the attack to a supply chain compromise of DebugBear’s RUM script, puts losses at roughly $2.71 million. According to its on-chain analysis, the main attack path ran through 710 deposit wallets and 731 addresses, though the address count does not equal the number of victims.
Arkham data showed a suspected attacker wallet holding approximately $2.65 million. That is the same address hardcoded in the script as its fallback recipient.
Hudson Rock has not determined how the script was tampered with or how many users were hit. Its findings do not indicate that other DebugBear customers were targeted.
The attack came the same day Binance was hit by a roughly $6 billion hack that blockchain intelligence firms have attributed to North Korea. In June, Polymarket disclosed another third-party compromise that injected a malicious script into its frontend, with losses reported at around $3 million.

articles.title: 267 ventes par mois : le nouveau SUV électrique chinois de Volkswagen vire au fiasco total
articles.text:
Pour tenir le rythme, Volkswagen développe continuellement une gamme dédiée au marché chinois. Mieux encore, la marque allemande s’est carrément alliée à Xpeng pour cerner au mieux les attentes locales. Elle pensait alors avoir trouvé la recette magique pour renouer avec le succès. Hélas, la mayonnaise a bien du mal à prendre puisque le premier modèle de cette collaboration s’avère être un échec.
Les chiffres de ThinkerCar sont sans appel : avec 267 exemplaires vendus chaque mois, l’ID. Unyx 08 est complètement à la traîne. Par rapport aux objectifs de Volkswagen qui étaient fixés à 3 622 modèles par mois, c’est la douche froide. Le constructeur allemand, qui a vu ses ventes fortement chuter en Chine, comptait pourtant beaucoup sur cette nouvelle génération de modèles pour remonter la pente.
L’alliance avec Xpeng : l’espoir déchu de Volkswagen
Cela semble malgré tout très insuffisant pour contrer la concurrence locale qui bataille à feu et à sang à coup de prix ultra agressifs. De fait, les performances commerciales de Volkswagen sont passées de 4,2 millions de voitures en 2019 à seulement 2,69 millions l’année passée. Les affaires ne risquent donc pas de s’améliorer. L’ID. Unyx 08 avait pourtant réuni tous les ingrédients pour réussir.
Basé sur l’imposant Xpeng G9, le SUV allemand en reprend les technologies pour se positionner ouvertement sur le segment premium. Son prix est par ailleurs bien placé avec un ticket d’entrée fixé à environ 32 000 €. Attrayant, mais pas encore assez pour espérer tailler des croupières aux stars du marché : les Xiaomi YU7 et Zeekr 7X demeurent moins chers et plus largement distribués en Chine.
Des tarifs attractifs, mais déjà dépassés par la réalité du marché
Alors que l’ID. Unyx 08 est uniquement vendu chez les concessionnaires Volkswagen, le Xiaomi YU7 peut se trouver chez des revendeurs multimarques plus facilement accessibles. Pour les clients cherchant à se procurer le plus rapidement possible une nouvelle voiture, ça peut énormément jouer. On pensait l’accord avec Xpeng une opportunité rêvée pour se mettre au niveau des modèles chinois. Mais l’allemand est en réalité déjà dépassé.
Le Xiaomi YU7 profite par exemple d’un ensemble de capteurs bien plus avancés au service de la conduite autonome. Le Zeekr 7X, lui, fait valoir sa recharge rapide ultra efficace réduisant les temps d’attente. Puisque les concurrents en offrent plus pour moins cher, les clients ne voient aucun intérêt à aller vers l’ID. Unyx 08. Cela aurait possiblement fonctionné il y a vingt ans de cela. Malheureusement pour Volkswagen, le monde a changé…

articles.title: Why Trust Is Becoming Essential for Agentic Commerce | BetaKit
articles.text:
When tickets for your favourite artist go on sale in the middle of a critical meeting, the idea of dispatching an AI agent to buy them for you sounds pretty appealing. But how do you know it will buy the right tickets, stick to your budget, and keep your payment information safe?
“Trust is foundational to agentic commerce being able to truly scale.”
Answers to those questions are becoming more important as agentic commerce scales in Canada and AI agents move from recommending purchases to making them. A Mastercard report predicts that by 2030, more than one in 10 online shoppers will routinely use agents to shop and pay.
Making those purchases secure takes a lot of work behind the scenes, and trust built into every side of the transaction. As the buyer, you need to trust the agent to follow your instructions. The seller has to know it’s legitimately acting on your behalf, while the financial institution needs to verify that the purchase matches what you authorized before approving the payment. All of this must happen in real time, with safeguards against fraud and attempts to manipulate the agent.
Canada is already putting the technology to the test. This fall, Mastercard worked with AI company Flybits and credit card issuer Rogers Bank to complete its first Canadian transaction through Agent Pay, its agentic commerce service. The transaction went beyond showing that an agent could make a purchase. The participants were able to verify that the agent was legitimate, had permission to act, and that the transaction amount matched the consumer’s authorized intent, said Amisha Parikh, vice-president, security solutions at Mastercard, Canada, in an interview with Betakit. “I think the real learning here was that it works,” she said.
“Human-led, agent-executed” transactions
For Canadian startups building AI tools, selling online or developing payment technology, that first purchase by an AI agent offers an early look at what it takes to make these transactions secure.
Parikh described the arrangement as “human-led, but agent-executed,” with the customer deciding what to buy and how much to spend.
In her concert-ticket example, you could specify two seats for a Toronto show, the dates you are available, your preferred sections, and a $500 budget. The agent has room to find tickets that fit. It should not decide that a more expensive show in another city is close enough.
“The agent is executing, but the human has set those guardrails,” she said.
Businesses already use tools such as multifactor authentication and biometrics to check that you, as the buyer, are who you say you are. When an agent shops on your behalf, they also need to confirm that it genuinely represents you and has permission to make the purchase.
Parikh said by using Agent Pay, the agent used is legitimate and has the customer’s permission to make a purchase on their behalf. “Verifiable intent becomes very important,” she said.
What if someone interferes?
Even an authorized agent can still become a target for attack. Just as someone could take over a customer’s account, they could potentially try to redirect an agent by giving it different instructions—an attack known as a “prompt injection.”
The risks also extend to where it shops. A fraudulent merchant could appear to offer exactly what the agent has been asked to find and draw it into a scam.
As merchants introduce agents of their own, software could interact on both sides of a purchase. Parikh says it becomes important to establish which person or business each agent represents and whether it is following their instructions.
Existing fraud controls also need to evolve to distinguish legitimate AI agents from malicious bots and recognize when an agent is acting with a customer’s authorization, she said.
This is where Mastercard’s Agent Pay Trust Framework helps address the need to recognize legitimate agents and assess the risks around their purchases. That means understanding who an agent represents, what it has permission to do, and whether the merchant can be trusted.
Mastercard brings together insights about identity, customer intent, behavioural patterns, and fraud risk to help banks and merchants better understand agent-led purchases. Parikh said the challenge is turning those signals into timely, actionable intelligence: helping to distinguish legitimate activity from potential threats, identify when additional checks are needed, and reduce unnecessary friction for customers.
Canada and the future of commerce
Parikh said advancing agentic commerce in Canada will require cooperation among financial institutions, retailers, government, academia, and payment networks.
She pointed to Mastercard’s Global Intelligence and Cyber Centre of Excellence in Vancouver as an example of how talent, research and partnerships contribute to advancing work on digital trust and intelligence.
“As AI capabilities evolve, she said, the safeguards around them must evolve, too. For agentic commerce, that means maintaining confidence that agents are acting with permission, within agreed limits, and with clear accountability.”
“Trust is foundational to agentic commerce being able to truly scale,” she said.

articles.text:
Good morning, and cheers to an unforgettable Moonshot! ☀️
Moonshot 2026 is over, and what an eventful, blockbuster two days it has been. Thousands of founders, investors, operators, policymakers, and builders packed the National Theatre in Lagos, Nigeria, for conversations that stretched from AI and fintech to capital markets, commerce, cybersecurity, and the future of African technology. Packed stages, hurried hallway conversations, familiar faces, new connections, and ideas kept us talking long after the lights went out. If you were there, thank you for being part of it. If you missed it, we’ve got plenty of stories, interviews, and takeaways coming your way.
Thank you, Lagos!
—Emmanuel
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Moonshot
Acecore wins $10,000 at Moonshot 2026’s TC Battlefield
If you thought African startups were running out of problems to solve, you only needed to spend some time at Moonshot 2026’s Startup stage in Lagos to reconsider.
Fertitude, a healthtech startup, pitched its digital platform that combines reproductive health tracking, AI-powered guidance, and access to healthcare specialists. Lena, an edtech startup, showed how it uses AI-powered games to help children learn subjects such as mathematics and science. Qiqi Farms pitched its technology-driven food distribution business, which connects farmers to markets and uses cold-chain infrastructure to deliver fresh produce.
These startups, alongside seven others, made the final ten of TC Battlefield 2026, TechCabal’s annual startup pitching competition, sponsored this year by Yango Group, the Dubai-based technology company. The competition allowed founders to pitch their businesses to investors and compete for $17,500 in equity-free funding.
After the pitches, Acecore won, taking home the $10,000 grand prize. The Nigerian climate-tech startup is building locally manufactured, AI-powered solar battery systems through its Powercell product. Paired with its Powercore app, the system allows users to monitor energy performance and manage their power supply, offering an alternative to unreliable electricity.
Supplya, a Nigerian startup that helps small retailers source inventory from manufacturers and access interest-free buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) financing, was first runner-up, winning $5,000. Navidyn Limited finished third, taking home $2,500.
TC Battlefield is an annual startup pitching competition, held as part of the Moonshot conference. It gives early-stage African startups a platform to showcase their products and compete for equity-free funding and other growth opportunities. The competition has become a recurring feature of Moonshot, with Ulé Homes, a Nigerian proptech startup that helps people finance rent payments, winning last year’s edition.
Founders who missed out this year have an opportunity for redemption. TC Battlefield will return at next year’s Moonshot.

Moonshot Day 2 recap from Muktar’s POV
It’s a wrap. Moonshot 2026, the biggest gathering in African tech, ended after two packed days at the National Theatre. You got it all. Next year, Moonshot returns for three days, and you can safely guess it will be bigger. If, like me, you couldn’t be in two places at once and missed a few sessions, catch up on the best of them on our website.

Telecoms
Herotel must open its fibre network to rivals
Herotel built its fibre business like a private road. If you wanted to use the road, you also had to buy Internet from Herotel. South Africa’s competition regulator is now making it open the gates to rivals.
What happened? Herotel, South Africa’s third-largest fibre network operator, will begin selling wholesale access to its network to other Internet service providers (ISPs). The change was imposed as a condition of Vumatel’s takeover, completed in June. Vumatel now indirectly owns 99.9% of Herotel.
Third-party ISPs must also receive the same pricing, service quality, and delivery terms offered to companies inside Vumatel’s parent group.
Explain like I’m new here: Herotel started by connecting smaller towns and underserved communities using fixed wireless Internet, before expanding aggressively into fibre in 2019. Unlike most large South African fibre operators, it kept the entire customer relationship to itself. Herotel built and owned the fibre, then sold Internet directly over it.
Vumatel works differently. It builds fibre networks and lets dozens of ISPs compete to sell internet over those lines.
Between the lines: Open access changes Herotel’s economics. It no longer gets every retail customer connected to its infrastructure, because another ISP can now win that customer. But every rival that sells a package over Herotel fibre also becomes a wholesale customer.
That trade-off becomes more important as Herotel expands. It wants to reach another 800,000 homes, taking its footprint beyond 1.4 million, largely in places bigger fibre operators have historically overlooked.
Why it matters: Fibre is expensive to build and cheap to leave idle. Opening Herotel’s network gives more ISPs an incentive to sell connections over existing infrastructure, potentially increasing how many homes actually take up fibre.
Herotel is losing exclusivity over its roads. The bet is that more traffic can make up for it.
Capital markets
Banque du Caire’s IPO is 27x oversubscribed
For weeks, we’ve been talking about Banque du Caire’s imminent initial public offering (IPO), and the listing is now gaining momentum. Apparently, Egypt’s sixth-largest bank is popular with retail investors. The lender hasn’t gone public yet, but investors are asking for more shares than it has to give—a lot more.
What happened? Retail investors ordered about 9.29 billion shares in the Egyptian state-owned bank, even though only 343.1 million shares were available to them. That made the retail portion of the IPO about 27 times oversubscribed.
At the final price of EGP 5.30 ($0.10) per share, roughly EGP 49.2 billion ($921 million) was chasing just EGP 1.8 billion ($34 million) worth of stock. Investors will receive about 3.7% of the shares they requested.
Explain like I’m new here: The IPO was due to “execute” on October 29, while normal trading begins on November 2. Those are two different things.
Execution does not mean investors are already trading Banque du Caire shares with one another. It is the step where the IPO orders are finalised, shares are allocated to successful investors, and Banque Misr, Banque du Caire’s owner, completes the sale. Once those shares sit in investors’ accounts, regular trading can begin on the Egyptian Exchange (EGX).
Think of it as buying a concert ticket before the doors open. You already own your ticket, but the event has not started.
Between the lines: Retail demand looks huge, but oversubscription only tells us investors wanted the shares at EGP 5.30 ($0.095). The bigger test begins when trading opens, and buyers and sellers can set the market price.
Retail investors also have some protection. During the first 30 days of trading, they can submit shares for sale at the IPO price under a stabilisation arrangement.
If Banque du Caire trades comfortably above EGP 5.30 ($0.095), Egypt will have something more useful than a heavily oversubscribed IPO: evidence that demand survived the jump from the order book to the open market.

articles.title: Philadelphia’s Academy of Natural Sciences just closed – a blow for budding young scientists like me
articles.text:
When I was a freshman in college at Villanova University outside Philadelphia, I visited the Academy of Natural Sciences for the first time.
My friends who were Philly natives were my tour guides, and I was inspired by their passion for the exhibits. I listened not only to the facts they shared about the museum, but also their childhood stories surrounding it.
As a kid, I remember going to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City and looking up at the massive dinosaur displays. I wondered how creatures as big as those used to walk the same ground as me. My favorite exhibit was the Hall of Ocean Life, where behind the staircase you see a dark, unlit diorama of a giant squid attached to a sperm whale.
The museum gave my curiosity a place to grow.
Now, as a Ph.D. student in physics, I research black holes, with the goal of one day becoming a professor and mentoring students. I was shocked when I heard the news that the Academy of Natural Sciences would be closing.
Over 200 years of hands-on science
Founded in 1812, the Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia is the country’s oldest natural science museum. For two centuries, it has played a vital role in scientific research, education and public engagement. The academy’s research centered heavily on biodiversity, evolution, paleontology and environmental science. In 2011, Drexel University acquired the academy and manages its endowment.
The academy had offered a range of experiences, from the Dinosaur Hall to its butterfly garden, and provided generations of visitors with opportunities to explore science beyond classrooms and textbooks.
On Sept. 1, 2026, however, Drexel University abruptly announced that the museum would close by the end of the month, citing financial difficulties and declining attendance. The last day it was open to visitors was Sept. 27, 2026.
Critics of the decision to close are rallying to “Save the Academy” and reopen it. Even members of the Philadelphia City Council expressed surprise that they had not been approached for support before the closing was announced.
The William Penn Foundation offered to cover operating subsidies for at least another year, potentially giving the academy time to explore a sustainable future. However, the museum remains closed for now, and Drexel maintains it needs a long-term financial solution. At a hearing on Oct. 26 that lasted nearly four hours, Philadelphia City Council members tried to understand why the museum closed and what Drexel would need to reopen it. The hearing is scheduled to resume on Nov. 16.
Cultivating future scientists
While museums may be viewed simply as sites for school field trips or family outings, their impact extends far beyond entertainment.
Natural science museums preserve scientific history through linking the past to future generations, supporting research and introducing young people to subjects they might otherwise never encounter. Philly kids who visited the academy could experience different ecosystems, from the snowy lands of the bobcat to rainforests home to giant monkeys. These dioramas are a snapshot in time that allow children to cultivate their own imagination and passions.
Not everyone has the opportunity to attend college or pursue a career in STEM. Museums help close that gap, giving families, students and children a chance to experience science firsthand – something that textbooks, social media and even classrooms sometimes cannot do.
Thinking back to my own childhood, I can pinpoint how my academic interests were fostered through museums, whether gazing up at galaxies at the Hayden Planetarium or sleeping under the belly of the blue whale in the Hall of Ocean Life. I was able to talk to real scientists in careers I dreamed to achieve, and I was told it was possible for me.
These experiences were integral to my becoming a first-generation college student and pursuing a career in academia. They made a career in science feel tangible rather than mystical or intimidating.

articles.title: « Cette décision n'a vraiment pas été facile à prendre » : Volkswagen suspend l'ID. Golf
articles.text:
Dans le plan produit de Volkswagen, la Golf n’est pas un modèle comme les autres. Et si l’ID.3 Neo n’a pas été nommée ID. Golf lors de son lancement cette année, ce n’est pas pour rien. La Golf, c’est une icône cinquantenaire, un repère pour des millions d’automobilistes. Pourtant, même ce monument n’échappe plus à l’austérité budgétaire.
Thomas Schäfer, CEO de la marque Volkswagen, a annoncé ce vendredi 30 octobre 2026 que les travaux préparatoires sur l’ID. Golf étaient suspendus. Il l’a fait dans un message interne aux salariés consulté par l’agence Reuters. « Je sais ce que la Golf représente pour Volkswagen et pour Wolfsburg. C’est pourquoi cette décision n’a vraiment pas été facile à prendre pour nous », écrit le dirigeant, avant d’ajouter : « Nous n’avons tout simplement pas les moyens de financer ces travaux actuellement. »
Wolfsburg sous pression budgétaire
Pour justifier la pause, Thomas Schäfer met en avant les comptes de l’usine historique. Wolfsburg n’atteint pas ses objectifs de baisse des coûts de production, et il lui manque environ 300 millions d’euros sur l’exercice en cours. « La situation est grave », écrit-il.
En revanche, les usines d’Emden et de Zwickau sont sur la bonne voie. Pourtant, elles font partie des quatre sites allemands menacés de fermeture par la restructuration, alors que Wolfsburg n’est pas sur la liste. Le dirigeant veut relancer l’ID. Golf le plus vite possible, à condition que les économies continuent.
Le gel des dépenses sur l’ID. Golf est donc une mesure d’urgence pour limiter les sorties de liquidités à court terme. Le comité d’entreprise, lui, tente de rassurer. Les représentants du personnel affirment que ce coup d’arrêt ne retardera pas le lancement de la voiture et s’engagent à combler le retard dès la reprise des investissements, tout en reconnaissant que ce gel constitue un « signe supplémentaire de la situation financière tendue du groupe ».
La plateforme SSP au cœur des interrogations
L’ID. Golf doit être le premier modèle de la marque Volkswagen à adopter la nouvelle architecture logicielle et technique du groupe, la plateforme SSP (Scalable Systems Platform). Conçue pour remplacer à terme la base MEB, standardiser les composants électroniques et réduire fortement les coûts de production, cette plateforme a déjà subi plusieurs décalages par rapport à sa feuille de route initiale.
Lors d’une table ronde organisée pendant le Mondial de Paris, Numerama a pu échanger avec Thomas Schäfer et la question de la plateforme SSP a été abordée. Les équipes de Volkswagen se voulaient rassurantes à ce sujet, précisant qu’elles souhaitaient faire les bons choix technologiques pour cette plateforme cruciale pour le groupe. Thomas Schäfer présente même ces retards comme une chance de revoir les choix techniques pour mieux coller aux attentes des clients.
« Pour être honnête, je suis en fait content que ça se soit passé ainsi », nous a-t-il confié, avant d’ajouter : « Dans le contexte concurrentiel de cette période, nous l’aurions probablement mal configuré. Nous avons donc revu la plupart de nos objectifs en matière de coûts de matériel et de performances des véhicules. »
Si l’on suit le raisonnement de Thomas Schäfer, cette nouvelle pause pourrait aussi déboucher sur une ID. Golf mieux conçue dans quelques années. Volkswagen met l’ID. Golf en veille faute d’argent, sans abandonner le projet. Mais voir le symbole même du renouveau de la gamme mis sur pause montre à quel point les marges de manœuvre du géant allemand sont devenues étroites.

articles.title: Le scénario catastrophe d'une IA qui pirate un pays entier : "Techniquement, rien ne l'empêche", alerte le monde cyber
articles.text:
Une intelligence artificielle peut-elle mener seule une cyberattaque ? Depuis l'intrusion d'agents d'OpenAI chez Hugging Face, la question n'a plus rien de théorique. Six experts ont mesuré jusqu'où un agent IA peut déjà aller.
À force de prendre connaissance d'actualités toujours plus inquiétantes sur l'essor et les dérives de l'intelligence artificielle, beaucoup se demandent si une IA pourrait pirater seule une entreprise, voire faire tomber un pays entier ? D'autres, amateurs de Terminator, feront le parallèle avec Skynet. Nous avons profité de notre couverture des Assises de la cybersécurité de Monaco pour interroger directement ou recueillir le témoignage de responsables de Sekoia, Check Point, Illumio, KnowBe4, DataDome et SNCF Connect & Tech, à ce sujet. Le constat est plutôt partagé. Oui, l'IA a fait entrer les cyberattaques dans une autre dimension de vitesse, mais derrière les machines, on trouve encore le plus souvent un humain, toujours le facteur X.
L'intelligence artificielle fait passer les cyberattaques en accéléré
Il y a quelques années encore, les entreprises avaient le temps de voir venir. En 2018, rappelle Adrien Merveille, directeur technique France de Check Point, il s'écoulait en moyenne un peu plus de deux ans entre la découverte d'une faille et les premières traces de son exploitation par des pirates. Aujourd'hui, l'attaque devance parfois la publication même de la faille. « On est en négatif dans le temps », résume-t-il assez justement. Selon lui, l'agence américaine de cybersécurité, la CISA, aurait même renoncé à référencer les failles les moins graves, faute de pouvoir suivre le rythme. Ce que l'IA a « fondamentalement changé », c'est donc « la vitesse d'exploitation des vulnérabilités ». La veille de notre entretien, le hacker éthique Clément Domingo en a fait la démonstration en direct. En vingt minutes, sans connaissances poussées en cyber ou en réseau pour son expérience, il a obtenu grâce à l'IA un chemin d'attaque qui fonctionne.
Même constat chez Francis Bergey, le RSSI de SNCF Connect & Tech. Lors d'une conférence donnée avec AWS, à laquelle nous avons pu assister, il a cité des piratages qui prenaient « avant trois semaines avec des équipes de Red Team », ces spécialistes chargés d'attaquer une entreprise pour éprouver ses défenses, et qui « peuvent se faire en une trentaine d'heures avec des agents IA », comme YesWeHack le montre régulièrement ces derniers temps. La machine, elle, ne sera jamais fatiguée. « Une IA va être extrêmement déterminée. On a besoin de fermer toutes les portes, toutes les fenêtres. » Le RSSI voit ici un défi pour la détection. Si l'intrusion n'est repérée qu'au bout de trois semaines, qu'elle ait duré trois semaines ou 30 heures, « ça ne va pas changer grand-chose ».
En plus, et c'est un peu l'extension du problème, l'intelligence artificielle ne se contente pas d'aller plus vite, elle orchestre. Le phishing artisanal, truffé de fautes d'orthographe et de logos approximatifs, c'est presque de l'histoire ancienne. Le directeur Europe du Sud de KnowBe4, Florian Malecki, décrit des attaques préparées à partir de tout ce que la cible a laissé traîner sur le web et les réseaux sociaux, puis menées sur plusieurs fronts, admettons un e-mail impeccable, un message WhatsApp, un appel vocal piégé, voire une vidéo truquée du PDG, le tout synchronisé pour mettre la victime sous pression. L'IA, prévient-il, « automatisera la constitution des attaques, et puis les attaques elles-mêmes ». Anthony Hervé, ingénieur avant-vente chez Illumio, voit surtout s'effondrer la barrière d'entrée. Il fallait autrefois « un groupe chevronné » pour exploiter une faille et s'introduire dans un réseau. Désormais, « il suffit d'une personne vraiment motivée », qui sait bien prompter, parler à l'IA.
Une IA sortie de son bac à sable, et tout bascule
Une IA peut-elle déjà frapper seule ? François Deruty, directeur des opérations de Sekoia et ancienne pointure de l'ANSSI, cite le cas Hugging Face, qui a secoué le secteur cet été. Si vous avez bonne mémoire, vous vous souvenez peut-être qu'en juillet, des modèles d'OpenAI soumis à un exercice de cybersécurité offensive ont quitté leur environnement de test pour s'introduire dans les serveurs de la plateforme. « Elle l'a menée seule », dit-t-il à propos de l'attaque, « non pilotée, non commanditée ». Selon lui, l'agent a enchaîné 17 500 actions en quatre jours, un rythme fou, qui ne laisse aucun répit aux défenseurs. Longtemps, l'IA a surtout servi aux pirates à produire en masse des contenus bien ficelés. Il estime qu'on n'est plus très loin d'une IA capable de monter elle-même l'infrastructure d'une attaque, qu'il s'agisse de la recherche de failles ou du déploiement des machines. Le donneur d'ordre n'aurait alors plus qu'une consigne à donner : « Je dis à l'IA, voilà ma cible, tu te "démerdes" », et la machine infernale serait inarrêtable.
Ce qui rend ces agents redoutables, c'est leur obstination. « Ce qui compte, ce ne sont pas les règles, ce sont l'objectif qu'on lui donne », note Anthony Hervé à propos du même cas, où l'agent a selon lui contourné toutes les règles pour atteindre son but. Florian Malecki a sa métaphore. Demandez à une IA d'aller de Paris à Marseille, et si elle juge qu'il faut passer par Lyon et « creuser un tunnel », « elle va effectivement le faire ». Ces détours, prévient-il, peuvent déboucher sur des cyberattaques. C'est précisément ce qui s'est produit chez OpenAI, sans qu'aucun pirate ne s'en mêle. L'agent s'est échappé de son bac à sable, l'espace isolé où on le testait, car il s'est dit que « la solution est à l'extérieur de la sandbox », résume François Deruty. Un agent d'OpenAI s'en est aussi pris à un portail de santé du gouvernement australien, ce que l'entreprise a reconnu en septembre.
Heureusement, tous ne vont pas aussi loin. Gilles Walbrou, directeur technique de DataDome, reconnaît que ces IA savent déjà trouver facilement des failles, et qu'elles pourraient en théorie infecter des appareils dans le monde entier pour lancer une attaque de grande ampleur. Mais il ne voit pas encore « une IA faire ça de soi-même ». « Il faudra qu'on le lui demande, qu'on la pilote », estime-t-il,, en rappelant qu'OpenAI et Anthropic ont documenté des acteurs malveillants qui se servent de leurs modèles pour orchestrer des attaques. François Deruty le rejoint en partie. Côté défense, on est passé du human in the loop, où un humain contrôle régulièrement le travail de l'IA, au human on the loop, où il en garde seulement la supervision. Les pirates qui visent une rançon ou un sabotage devront eux aussi superviser leurs machines. Et l'IA a déjà rejoint leur arsenal. Le spécialiste nous cite LameHug, un logiciel malveillant du groupe russe APT28 qui, une fois dans le réseau d'une victime, interroge une IA en ligne pour se transformer en temps réel et passer sous les radars.
Faire tomber un pays, un scénario que personne n'exclut
Et à l'échelle d'un pays alors ? « Techniquement, rien ne l'empêche », répond François Deruty, surtout si l'on atteint un jour l'AGI, cette IA générale censée égaler l'humain. Ce n'est pas pour tout de suite, juge-t-il, mais il faut se méfier, car ces échéances arrivent souvent plus vite que prévu. Il distingue toutefois l'IA qui agirait d'elle-même, de l'humain qui lui ordonnerait d'éteindre un pays, ce qui poserait, en cas de conflit, de sérieuses questions de belligérance. Pour mesurer le danger, il nous rappelle la jurisprudence NotPetya. En 2017, ce logiciel malveillant caché dans une mise à jour du logiciel comptable ukrainien M.E.Doc avait échappé à tout contrôle et paralysé des géants comme Saint-Gobain ou Maersk. « Qu'est-ce qui empêcherait une IA de faire un autre NotPetya aujourd'hui ? Elle peut faire beaucoup mieux, bien pire », s'inquiète l'expert.
« Je pense que tout est possible », abonde Gilles Walbrou, pour qui l'origine d'un tel scénario resterait « toujours une erreur humaine ». Si une IA venait à perturber la production d'énergie d'un pays, ce serait « parce qu'on lui en a donné la possibilité ». Reste à savoir qui en porterait la responsabilité, la plateforme qui fournit l'IA, comme OpenAI, ou celui qui a lancé l'agent. Hors de ces plateformes, il faut en outre sa propre puissance de calcul pour faire tourner des agents. « Un gouvernement, un État pourrait le faire aujourd'hui, mais ça devient une arme, c'est clairement une arme. » Les armées l'ont bien compris : en Ukraine comme en Israël, « dans les doctrines des armées, il y a l'idée de détruire le système de tel pays », relève Francis Bergey.
Faut-il pour autant baisser les bras ? Pas vraiment. « C'est une arme qui est dans la main des attaquants, mais c'est aussi un moyen de défense qui est disponible pour les entreprises », rappelle Adrien Merveille. Francis Bergey évoque la détection. Les IA offensives sondent tout le réseau et multiplient les essais, alors « profitons du fait qu'elles soient assez bruyantes pour détecter ces signaux-là », en semant par exemple des leurres, les honeypots. Son entreprise, donc la SNCF, s'est aussi préparée au pire, un scénario où tout son environnement AWS serait effacé. Grâce à l'infrastructure as code, qui consigne toute l'architecture informatique sous forme de code, elle sait désormais tout remonter en quelques semaines, quand des sociétés mal préparées, frappées par un rançongiciel, ne sont toujours pas revenues à la normale au bout d'un an. Encore faut-il ne pas traîner. « Il faut vraiment mettre le turbo parce que l'IA, elle, n'attend pas », conclut Florian Malecki. Nous n'aurons pas mieux pour le mot de la fin.

articles.title: Chinese hackers build PHP2SHELL exploit, use it to root 25 servers, breach US government-affiliated firewalls
articles.text:
Chinese hackers build PHP2SHELL exploit, use it to root 25 servers, breach US government-affiliated firewalls
Palo Alto Networks firewalls running outdated OS seem to be the target
- Researchers report the first confirmed PHP2Shell compromises, targeting organizations linked to the US government
- Attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux privilege-escalation flaw to gain root access and persistence
- Breaches progressed from initial compromise to Active Directory attacks within minutes, underscoring patching urgency
We now have confirmation of the first successful exploits of the infamous PHP2Shell vulnerability discovered earlier this month.
The news comes courtesy of cybersecurity outfit Dream, who claim to have seen attackers breach organizations affiliated with the US government.
PHP2Shell is a name given to two critical-severity vulnerabilities found in PHP. When they were first disclosed, most of the cybersecurity community went full panic mode, given that PHP powers roughly 70% of all websites and web apps on the internet, and there was no patch at the time. The flaws allegedly enabled complete website takeover, and some government and education organizations in Europe even preemptively shut down their websites, in anticipation of mass exploitation attempts.
But after the dust settled, a strange thing happened - there were no successful attacks. Researchers were seeing attempts and probes, but no successful breaches. Amazon said it observed first attacks four days before the patch, and Cloudflare later tracked “thousands” of attempts in the 10 hours before the patch was announced. This grew to tens of thousands within an hour of disclosure, and hundreds of thousands within two hours. Now, it’s gone into the millions.
Some said exploiting the bugs was easier said than done, and that threat actors were hitting different roadblocks, including Address Space Layout Randomization, a security feature that randomly changes where a program’s code and data are stored in memory every time it runs. Still, they warned that all of that might be temporary, and that a successful hit was a question of “when”, not “if”.
Targeting firewalls
Now it seems the claims were on point, as Dream says Chinese threat actors successfully chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation flaw against Palo Alto Networks firewalls, breaching 25 servers, some allegedly belonging to US government-affiliated organizations.
The attacks started on October 23 2026, probing firms in the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and soon focused on Palo Alto Networks’ PAN-OS-powered devices, running an older, vulnerable version of the OS.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
According to Dream, the crooks chained PHP2Shell with Fragnesia, a local privilege escalation flaw that allows unprivileged users to obtain root access. It was disclosed in mid-May this year and is tracked as CVE-2026-46300.
After breaking into the devices, the attackers ran some 40 custom post-exploitation scripts, Dream added.
“Within hours of compromising a US government-affiliated firewall, they had tunneled into the internal network, compromised a third server using the same PHP2Shell exploit, and launched a full Active Directory attack campaign - all through a chain that started with a single unauthenticated HTTPS request to a management interface that should never have been exposed to the internet,” the company’s report reads.
Not automated
To make matters worse, the researchers believe the attackers still have unabated access.
“The total chain - from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell - completes in under 15 minutes,” Dream said. The researchers could not say what the endgame was here because that information was not found in the artifacts they retrieved. Besides the obvious, which seems to be persistent access and credential theft, the threat actors could do anything from dropping backdoors to exfiltrating sensitive information.
In the context of “Black October”, and the fact we’re seeing a significant increase in automated attacks, it is also worth mentioning that this incident was likely not AI-powered.
Dream did find evidence of AI usage but believes it was not fully automated. Claude Code was installed, as was an offensive security platform called AIscan, which was configured with Chinese AI models DeepSeek and Kimi. Furthermore, they found API keys for FOFA, a Chinese counterpart to the Shodan search engine.
With the help of FOFA, the attackers allegedly identified around 19,000 internet-connected Palo Alto Networks firewalls, which they used as a starting point for their attacks.
Via The Register

articles.title: Omio founder’s advice to entrepreneurs: Find a problem worth solving and stick with it
articles.text:
Omio founder’s advice to entrepreneurs: Find a problem worth solving and stick with it
At TechSparks 2026, Naren Shaam, Founder and CEO of Omio Group, advised entrepreneurs to think globally from day one, tackle difficult problems, and stay committed for the long term.
AI has made it easier to build products, but entrepreneurs still need to decide what to build and whether they can stay committed long enough to turn an idea into a sustainable business.
For Naren Shaam, Founder and CEO of Omio Group, the answer is to solve difficult problems, stay focused, and avoid chasing the next big thing.
Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Shaam spoke about building Omio, which operates across 56 countries, and why Indian entrepreneurs should think globally from the beginning.
“If I were to rebuild Omio today, I would start here because there is so much growth and opportunity in India today. But the principles remain the same. You need to go after really hard problems and focus on solving them for a very long time,” he told YourStory.
Shaam founded Omio after identifying a problem in global transportation: operators had separate systems for trains, buses, and ferries. After moving to Germany, he spent two and a half years working on the supply side before launching the company's first product.
“Building a billion-dollar business is really hard. The stories of companies going from zero to a billion dollars very quickly are rare. Don’t get inspired by the exceptions as for most, it is a daily grind,” he said.
Think global from day one
Shaam believes entrepreneurs need not wait until they have succeeded in India before expanding overseas. While some businesses cater to local needs, sectors such as education, healthcare, and deeptech offer opportunities across markets.
“If your problem statement is already global, you should start early. We entered 30 countries in our first three or four years, even though people told us to win Germany first. That bet, despite the capital required and the mistakes we had to correct, probably helped make us become the company we are today,” he said.
AI has also made international expansion easier. Shaam recalled that when Omio expanded in Germany, it employed around 30 people to handle translations. That work is now done by AI.
However, lower barriers to entry also make it easier for competitors to copy products. Shaam believes entrepreneurs must therefore be more careful about where they invest their time and resources.
“The onus moves from bias to action to judgement: what should I focus on? Which industry has a bigger moat? What will that moat look like 10 years from now? Starting is easy now but choosing what to pursue and committing to it is the hard part,” he said.
AI may change distribution, but trust remains important
Shaam said AI agents could change digital commerce, including how people book travel. However, widespread adoption will depend on bringing down costs and finding sustainable business models.
“Consumers need these agents to be very cheap before they penetrate the market. There is a cost barrier and a business-model problem to solve. I see this as a major transformation and not an overnight event,” he explained.
Even as more transactions move to AI agents, Shaam believes businesses will still need to deliver reliable services in the physical world.
“Real life happens outside the internet. If an agent buys something or orders food, people need to trust that it will arrive every single time. Businesses that can solve these operational problems at scale will have something valuable to build on,” he said.
For aspiring founders, his advice was to focus on solving a problem rather than on the appeal of becoming an entrepreneur.
“Find a great problem. Don’t become an entrepreneur simply because you want to be one. This is a journey with long periods of darkness, and you need to be passionate enough about what you’re solving to keep going,” Shaam concluded.

articles.title: Intel Q3 2026 Earnings Data Center Soars While PC Faces Memory Pressure
articles.text:
Intel reported third-quarter 2026 earnings with revenue of $16.5 billion, up 21% year-over-year. Non-GAAP gross margin reached 44.1%, and non-GAAP EPS came in at $0.52. Data center demand is surging while the client PC business is struggling (mightily) under memory market conditions. We do not always cover these, but Patrick asked me to do this one because it shows a trend we have seen recently at STH.
Intel Q3 2026 Results Show Contrasting Segments
First off, at an overall level, Intel’s headline numbers are relatively positive. Up almost 21% Y/Y is good, but last year was not great for Intel.
The Data Center and AI (DCAI) group delivered $7.3 billion in revenue, up 78% year-over-year. David Zinsner, Intel’s CFO, called it Intel’s strongest data center revenue growth in 15 years. Segment operating income reached $3.0 billion with a 41.5% margin. One of the interesting bits on why we were covering this announcement is that the demand in the market has shifted towards AMD’s 192-core Turin parts, which Intel does not have a direct competitor for (maybe Clearwater?), but partners tell us that Xeon 6 is selling because basically everything is selling.
Demand is strong across hyperscale, enterprise, and neo cloud customers, with “Purpose Built Silicon” revenue more than doubling year-over-year. Lip-Bu Tan, Intel’s CEO, said Intel’s immediate priority is unlocking additional supply to meet extraordinary demand for the Xeon family. On the call, he said that substrate availability is limiting output and it would take some time to ease.
The client side looks very different. Client Computing and Physical AI Group (CCPG) revenue fell 5% year over year to $8.1 billion. Overall inflation is well north of zero depending on the index you use, so revenue falling is not good. On the call Intel cited industry-wide memory shortages impacting the total addressable market. Higher DRAM and NAND prices are pushing system costs up and hurting demand. On the call, it sounded like Intel was looking for 18A supply to be used on the data center side pending substrate availability.
Intel expects the PC slowdown to continue at least through the first half of next year. Memory and NAND pricing pressure is expected to persist into 2027, which means client system costs are likely to stay elevated for a while longer. For those who see today’s memory prices and think they are shocking, the earnings call commentary did nothing to make me think Q1 would see a decline in memory pricing.
Intel Foundry posted $6.7 billion in revenue, up 58% Y/Y, though that figure includes intersegment transactions rather than external customer sales alone. The segment still recorded an operating loss of $1.9 billion with a negative 27.7% margin, but that is narrower than the $2.3 billion loss a year ago.
Improved yields and cycle times are reducing wafer costs. Intel released the Intel 14A 0.9 process design kit in October as committed, and expansion continues across sites including Ohio.
Final Words
We do not cover all earnings calls, but Patrick’s thought was that this was an important one since it also tells a story of STH. Folks wonder why we have been doing a lot of AI desktop and server/ networking coverage, and fewer mini PCs. Intel’s Panther Lake is a cool product, but it is not running larger local models. Right now, DRAM and NAND are being priced for the value they bring attached to AI nodes. Likewise, the NVIDIA-Intel investment and the many NVIDIA GPU-based systems with Intel Xeon CPUs are helping drive Xeon 6 sales and push pricing up. As a result, we are seeing the market demand for non-local AI PCs drop due to higher prices, while the AI-related markets are cooking. We know folks want more mini PC reviews, but this is a fundamental industry challenge. A smaller client-side market also means fewer small companies trying to innovate on form factors, while the data center market is the exact opposite. This came out very clearly in Intel’s earnings.

articles.title: Son sous-marin de 4 tonnes disparaît, il le retrouve en vente sur Leboncoin pour une centaine d'euros
articles.text:
Sous-marin volé : son propriétaire le retrouve en vente sur Leboncoin pour une centaine d’euros
Une affaire vite remontée à la surface
Quatre tonnes, une coque orange et une annonce bradée sur le site de petites annonces le plus consulté de France. Volé début octobre dans l'Ain, un sous-marin a refait surface sur Leboncoin dans le Doubs, et son propriétaire n'a eu qu'à faire défiler son écran pour le retrouver. La police de Besançon a fait le reste.
Il trônait comme objet de décoration dans un commerce de matériel de plongée de Ferney-Voltaire, dans l'Ain, à deux pas de la frontière suisse. Entre le 1er et le 21 octobre 2026, ce sous-marin jaune de quatre tonnes a disparu. Le propriétaire porte plainte, puis surveille les petites annonces. Quelques jours plus tard, il tombe sur son engin, proposé à la vente sur Leboncoin dans le secteur de Besançon.
Une annonce Leboncoin à une centaine d'euros pour un engin de quatre tonnes
D'après Le Progrès, cité par Radio Scoop, l'annonce affichait une centaine d'euros. L'engin vaut plusieurs milliers d'euros.
Le propriétaire a joué la prudence : il a prévenu les gendarmes d'Ornex au lieu de contacter lui-même le vendeur. Le dossier a ensuite été confié à la brigade des atteintes aux biens du commissariat de Besançon, rapporte ICI Besançon. Les enquêteurs ont épluché le profil du vendeur, puis une surveillance discrète a confirmé l'emplacement du submersible.
Un sous-marin en vente près de Besançon?
En octobre, un sous-marin a été volé dans l'Ain, puis repéré en vente sur Leboncoin à Besançon.
Nos policiers 👮♀️👮ont plongé dans l'affaire
➡️ engin récupéré et deux suspects convoqués devant la justice.
Une enquête menée à bon port! 🌊🔍 pic.twitter.com/DdXboA2ik6
— Police Nationale 25 (@PoliceNat25) October 29, 2026
Le 26 octobre, une opération réunissant plusieurs unités a conduit à l'interpellation d'un Bisontin de 27 ans. Selon BFMTV, le sous-marin était entreposé chez lui, et c'est lui qui aurait publié l'annonce.
Un second homme, âgé de 47 ans, a été entendu. Les policiers le soupçonnent d'avoir aidé à transporter l'engin, ce qui demande un sérieux matériel de levage. La photo diffusée par la police montre d'ailleurs une grue en train de soulever le sous-marin depuis un camion.
Vol en réunion et recel : ce qui attend les deux suspects
Les deux hommes seront convoqués devant le délégué du procureur de la République de Besançon, pour "vol en réunion" et "recel de vol". En attendant, le submersible a été mis à l'abri et retrouvera bientôt son propriétaire.
L'histoire rappelle une règle simple : quand on repère un bien volé en vente sur Leboncoin, on garde une capture de l'annonce et on prévient les forces de l'ordre avant tout rendez-vous avec le vendeur. Ici, les enquêteurs n'ont eu qu'à suivre l'annonce jusqu'à l'engin, qui n'avait rien de discret.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

articles.title: Samsung vende la memoria más cara que nunca. Uno de sus clientes más perjudicados es Samsung
articles.text:
Samsung ha cerrado el trimestre más rentable de la historia de una tecnológica: 107,4 billones de wones de beneficio operativo, unos 80.000 millones de dólares. Casi todo sale de vender memoria para IA. Y casi todo lo que pierde, también.
Por qué es importante. La memoria está tan cara que Samsung gana una fortuna fabricándola y pierde dinero metiéndola en sus propios productos. Móviles, televisores y electrodomésticos han perdido 600 millones de dólares este trimestre. Hace un año, esa misma división ganaba unos 2.600 millones.
No es, en cualquier caso, un "lo que la IA te da, la IA te quita". El beneficio conseguido es bestial y compensa con creces. Pero la unidad de negocio de dispositivos, Device eXperience (DX) sale perdiendo.
El contraste:
- Chips: unos 79.400 millones de dólares de beneficio operativo, el 99% del total.
- Memoria: unos 104.900 millones de dólares en ventas, cinco veces más que hace un año.
- Todo lo demás: en rojo. Móviles y redes pierden unos 450 millones de dólares. Televisores y electrodomésticos, unos 150 millones.
Entre líneas. Lo que cuenta la propia Samsung en su nota de resultados: la demanda de los servidores ha subido el precio de la memoria en todo tipo de productos, incluidos los smartphones. La división móvil ha vendido más gracias a los nuevos plegables, pero ha ganado menos que hace un año por los costes.
Y luego está el plan para 2027. El objetivo que Samsung se marca para los Galaxy es minimizar la caída de beneficios. Ni una palabra sobre crecer. Solo amortiguar.
Sí, pero. Al accionista eso le debe preocupar bastante poco. La acción ha caído un 4,13%, pero por otros motivos:
- Esperaba recompras, y Samsung las ha aplazado a finales de enero.
- Esperaba un horizonte como el de SK Hynix, que ve escasez hasta 2030. Samsung habla de 2028.
Hoy, Samsung es un fabricante de memorias con un negocio poco relevante (en cifras puras) pegado como es el de los móviles.
Y ahora qué. La escasez va para largo. Samsung calcula que en 2027 la demanda de IA superará a la oferta todavía más que este año, y su HBM del año que viene ya está vendida.
Mientras dure, la división de chips seguirá cobrando caro y la de móviles seguirá pagando. Es la misma empresa a los dos lados del mostrador.
