articles.title: Lua hoje: confira a fase da Lua deste sábado 31/10/2026
articles.text:
Hoje, 31 de outubro de 2026, a Lua está na fase cheia e 67% visível. Confira o calendário completo de fases da Lua deste mês, de acordo com o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet).
Confira as próximas fases
As fases da Lua no mês de outubro de 2026 começam no dia 3 com a chegada da Lua Minguante, às 10h26 (horário de Brasília). Depois disso, no dia 10, foi a vez da Lua Nova, que chegou às 12h50. A Lua Crescente surgiu às 13h13 do dia 18. Por fim, veio a Lua Cheia, dia 26, à 1h13.
Leia mais:
- Entenda o que é a Lua, como e quando ela se formou
- Saiba como tirar a melhor foto possível com uma câmera de celular
- 7 dicas para fotografar a lua com seu celular
Calendário das fases da Lua em outubro de 2026
- Lua Minguante: dia 3, às 10h26
- Lua Nova: dia 10, às 12h50
- Lua Crescente: dia 18, às 13h13
- Lua Cheia: dia 26, à 1h13
O que é o ciclo lunar?
Uma lunação ou ciclo lunar, como é chamado o intervalo de tempo entre luas novas, é sutilmente variável, com média de duração de 29,5 dias. Durante esse período, ela passa pelas quatro fases principais (nova, crescente, cheia e minguante), e cada uma se prolonga por aproximadamente sete dias.
Também existem as “interfases”: quarto crescente e crescente gibosa (entre as fases nova e cheia) e minguante gibosa e quarto minguante (entre a cheia e a minguante).
Entenda cada fase da Lua
Lua Nova
Na Lua Nova, o satélite se posiciona entre a Terra e o Sol. Isso faz com que o lado iluminado da Lua fique voltado para o Sol, enquanto o lado escuro fica voltado para nós. Por esse motivo, a Lua não é visível no céu noturno. Essa fase marca o início de um novo ciclo lunar e está relacionada ao recomeço e a novas possibilidades.
Lua Crescente
Depois da Lua Nova, surge a fase Crescente. Aos poucos, uma pequena faixa iluminada começa a aparecer no céu, aumentando noite após noite. No início, vemos apenas um fino arco de luz, mas com o passar dos dias a parte iluminada cresce até que metade da Lua esteja visível, momento chamado de Quarto Crescente. Essa fase simboliza crescimento, desenvolvimento e a construção de novos caminhos.
Lua Cheia
Na Lua Cheia, a Terra se encontra entre o Sol e a Lua. Isso permite que o lado lunar voltado para nós receba luz por completo, tornando-se totalmente visível e brilhante no céu. É o período de maior intensidade luminosa, quando a Lua nasce no horizonte exatamente no momento em que o Sol se põe. A Lua Cheia é associada à plenitude, ao auge de processos e à energia em seu ponto máximo.
Lua Minguante
Após a Lua Cheia, a luz da Lua começa a diminuir gradualmente. A cada noite, vemos menos da sua superfície iluminada. Quando apenas metade dela está visível, ocorre o Quarto Minguante, fase oposta ao Quarto Crescente. A Lua continua a perder luminosidade até chegar novamente à Lua Nova, reiniciando o ciclo. A fase Minguante simboliza reflexão, encerramento e preparação para novos começos.
Qual a fase da Lua hoje?
Hoje a Lua está na fase Cheia.
Flávia Correia é jornalista do Olhar Digital, cobrindo Ciência e Espaço.

articles.title: Build Specialized Agents on a Stack You Control with NVIDIA NemoClaw | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Building an autonomous agent requires a model, a harness, and domain-specific tools. To deploy an agent more securely, developers need a runtime that enforces policies, along with optimization and observability tools for reliable execution.
For production agents, the challenge lies in making these agents capable and safe to operate with access to real enterprise systems and data.
This post explains how these components work together, with a focus on how NVIDIA NemoClaw open blueprints enable developers to build specialized agents on a stack they can own, customize, and run. This post provides criteria to help developers integrate NemoClaw with a harness they already use: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, or LangChain Deep Agents.
What an agent harness provides
An agent requires four things:
- A model that reasons.
- A harness that defines how the agent operates.
- Tools and skills that extend its capabilities.
- A runtime that governs what the agent can access and do in production.
NemoClaw works with agent harnesses
NemoClaw open blueprints currently support three harnesses:
- OpenClaw can access files and applications, write code, spawn sub-agents, and maintain context across sessions. It runs on your own machine or server and supports long-running sessions, memory, and scheduled tasks.
- Hermes Agent, from Nous Research, is designed to get better with use. As teams correct the agents’ approach and repeat workflows, Hermes captures those patterns as durable skills that can be reused in future work.
- LangChain Deep Agents provides a customizable harness for complex, multistep tasks. It combines planning, file-based context management, memory, and delegation to specialized subagents.
Each harness gives an agent skills, tools, orchestration, and memory.
Using NemoClaw for full-stack production agents
NemoClaw is not a competing harness, and it is not a runtime. It is a collection of blueprints that assembles an open agent stack on top of the harness selected by the developer. The stack combines model and harness optimization with runtime governance.
Each NemoClaw blueprint brings together four components:
- A tuned open harness, such as Hermes Agent, LangChain Deep Agents, or OpenClaw, optimized to work with NVIDIA Nemotron.
- Nemotron open models.
- NVIDIA NeMo tools for optimization, including NVIDIA NeMo Relay for observing and improving agent execution, plus routing capabilities that can help improve throughput, cost, and reliability.
- NVIDIA OpenShell is the secure runtime that governs agent access to files, networks, credentials, and tools.
If you are already building with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, or LangChain Deep Agents, a NemoClaw blueprint can assemble the surrounding stack without requiring you to rewrite the agent.
Why co-optimizing the model and harness matters
An agent combines a model and a harness. The model thinks, while the harness provides the environment in which it operates. When the two are matched, the model can focus on the task. When they aren’t, it may ask for context again, stop early, or loop without progress.
For example, LangChain tuned its Deep Agents harness for Nemotron 3 Ultra by adjusting prompts, tools, and middleware without retraining the model. Starting from an already strong baseline, the harness tuning brought Nemotron 3 Ultra to near-frontier performance at approximately 10x lower cost per run compared with leading closed models.
The NemoClaw blueprint for LangChain Deep Agents packages these optimizations directly. Every developer using LangChain Deep Agents with Nemotron 3 Ultra can access these optimizations without reproducing the tuning work. The tuned Nemotron 3 Ultra model profile is available through LangChain on GitHub.
When to use each
Use a harness such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, or LangChain Deep Agents to build and experiment with the agent’s skills, tools, memory, and orchestration logic.
Use a NemoClaw blueprint to assemble and run a specialized agent on an open stack that combines a tuned harness, models, optimization, telemetry, and OpenShell runtime controls.
| Question | Agent harness | NemoClaw blueprint | 
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Software that manages how an agent uses tools, maintains context, and carries out tasks | A reference stack that combines a supported harness with models, optimization tools, and a runtime | 
| What it provides | Tools, skills, memory, and orchestration | A tuned harness, models, optimization tools, and OpenShell runtime controls | 
| How they work together | Provides the agent’s execution logic within the stack | Combines the harness with the other stack components | 
| When to use it | To build and customize an agent’s behavior | To assemble and run an agent with model and harness optimization and runtime controls | 
A harness helps you build a capable agent. A NemoClaw blueprint helps you run that agent on an open stack with model and harness optimization, telemetry, and runtime governance.
Example: A memory-driven Chief of Staff, built on Hermes
The NemoClaw community repository includes a memory-driven Chief of Staff recipe. The agent maintains a persistent, human-readable model of the people, projects, priorities, and working patterns it encounters, so it doesn’t have to reconstruct context from scratch on every task. It is built as a deployable Hermes profile for NemoClaw, as outlined in the technical design walkthrough.
The recipe shows the stack working together rather than in isolation. OpenShell governs the agent’s file system, process, and network access, and keeps credentials for managed inference and Model Context Protocol (MCP) connections outside the sandbox. This helps keep the agent bound by policy even when its memory or retrieved context leads it toward an unintended action. NeMo Relay is integrated natively into the Hermes session. It closes trace spans at real session boundaries, including a new session, reset, or expiry, and exports the resulting trajectories for audit and further optimization.
Importance of agent governance
Every NemoClaw reference includes OpenShell, the runtime that adds security and policy enforcement around the agent harness and tools, governing the actions a model can take. The OpenShell tutorial covers how to create your first policy to prevent data exfiltration to GitHub. NemoClaw references include more sophisticated OpenShell policies that govern agent connections across many different internal tools, sites, and communication channels.
Deploy across cloud, data center, and local systems
NemoClaw agents can run in the cloud, in data centers, on NVIDIA DGX Spark, and on NVIDIA RTX PCs and workstations. A NemoClaw clinical agent for a hospital and a NemoClaw simulation agent for electronic design automation can run on the same stack while using entirely different tools and skills.
NemoClaw agents can also work alongside frontier agents. Claude, Codex, or Cursor agents can delegate domain-specific subtasks to NemoClaw-powered specialists running on open models and owned infrastructure.
Get started
Choose a NemoClaw blueprint for your harness, then customize its tools, models, and runtime policies for your workflow.
- Take the Deploy Secure Agents with NemoClaw DLI course—a 101-level introduction to the stack.
- Follow the NemoClaw quickstart to deploy an agent through a NemoClaw blueprint.
- Explore the NemoClaw GitHub repository for the full example and additional blueprints.
- Learn how to deploy self-evolving agents for faster, more secure research with Hermes Agent and NemoClaw.
Stay up to date on NVIDIA AI by subscribing to NVIDIA news and following NVIDIA AI on LinkedIn, X, Discord, and YouTube. Visit the developer page for resources to get started. Explore open Nemotron models and datasets on Hugging Face and NVIDIA Blueprints on build.nvidia.com. And engage with Nemotron livestreams, tutorials, and the developer community on NVIDIA forums and Discord.

articles.title: Coveo buys Y Combinator alum to bolster AI commerce search | BetaKit
articles.text:
Coveo has acquired a Y Combinator alum as it looks to improve its search and recommendation platform in the age of AI assistants.
The news: Montréal-based Coveo acquired Silicon Valley-based Anglera for an undisclosed amount, the company announced on Thursday alongside its second-quarter earnings report. Coveo CFO Karine Hamel said on the company’s earnings call that the acquisition was funded with cash on hand, and that the deal was a “modest upfront investment,” with another potential payment coming in early 2028 based on commercial performance.
Anglera’s platform extracts and manages hundreds of technical attributes from products, such as dimensions, materials, and compatibility. Coveo hopes to make those detailed product specifications more accessible through its intelligent search and recommendation platform, making it easier for AI assistants to find and compare products on behalf of consumers.
From the source: On Coveo’s earnings call, co-founder and CEO Laurent Simoneau said Anglera automates data enrichment that a lot of its customers are struggling to do manually.
“Ultimately, it creates a lot of value in the form of additional conversion, revenue per visit, margin, et cetera,” Simoneau said. “The ability to surface content to those external AI assistants in the context of commerce is a growing priority for customers in retail, especially, and we believe that this acquisition will provide a lot of value here.”
The context: Coveo’s stock trades on the Toronto Stock Exchange under the symbol $CVO. Its Q2 earnings report showed an eight-percent revenue jump compared to Q2 last year, with the company earning $40.4 million USD ($56.4 million CAD) in the fiscal period. The company also improved its net loss to $3.1 million USD, up from $4.4 million USD in the same period last year.
Coveo’s stock saw a 1.5-percent bump the morning after its earnings report, trading at $4.84 per share; still a far cry from the $8 per share it was trading at during the same time last year.
Final thought: As more consumers turn to AI assistants to help with their shopping, more companies like Coveo see value in bolstering their generative engine optimization capabilities. Coveo claims that a 30-day Anglera A/B test with an apparel retailer saw a 120-percent jump in organic landing-page traffic to product pages equipped with its extracted data, as well as a 270-percent increase in AI-referred visits, compared to a control group.
Feature image courtesy Coveo.

articles.title: Desarrollan un robot inspirado en insectos que promete revolucionar la exploración en entornos extremos
articles.text:
Un equipo de la Universidad de California, Los Ángeles, (UCLA) y la Universidad de California en Davis (UC Davis) desarrolló un diminuto robot volador inspirado en insectos que puede recuperar el vuelo después de colisiones y soportar compresiones extremas. El dispositivo, presentado en la revista Science Robotics, busca operar en espacios estrechos o zonas inaccesibles para otros robots y para las personas, según TechXplore, el portal especializado en ciencia y tecnología.
El prototipo genera una fuerza ascendente equivalente a tres veces su propio peso, despega sin asistencia y asciende a una velocidad promedio de 40 centímetro por segundo. También pudo volver a volar después de recibir un golpe con un matamoscas o de ser aplastado por cargas de unas 11.000 veces su peso.
Diseño íntegramente hecho con polímeros
El robot pesa apenas 185 miligramos —menos de un quinto de gramo— y está construido por completo con polímeros, materiales formados por largas cadenas de moléculas enlazadas. Combina un músculo blando activado por electricidad con alas flexibles de forma cónica.
Qibing Pei, profesor de los departamentos de Ciencia e Ingeniería de Materiales e Ingeniería Mecánica y Aeroespacial de la UCLA y autor principal del estudio, explicó que su laboratorio trabaja desde hace años en robótica blanda y tomó como referencia la forma en que los insectos sobreviven a choques y otras perturbaciones físicas. “Muchos robots del tamaño de un insecto dependen de componentes frágiles, lo que dificulta su funcionamiento fuera del laboratorio. Vimos la oportunidad de utilizar materiales poliméricos sensibles a la electricidad para crear un diseño más simple y resistente”.
Yuan Zhu, investigador posdoctoral del departamento de Ciencia e Ingeniería de Materiales, también de la UCLA, y primer autor del trabajo, detalló que el músculo de las alas es una película delgada de un polímero ferroeléctrico relajador, un material plástico que reacciona y se deforma al recibir una carga eléctrica. “La expansión del material inducida por el campo eléctrico, conocida técnicamente como electrostricción, es enorme y reversible. Podemos aprovechar el movimiento de la película para generar potentes aleteos con una respuesta muy rápida”.
El polímero se dobla con rapidez y mueve las alas directamente, sin requerir un sistema mecánico de transmisión independiente. Hanxiang Wu, investigador posdoctoral de UCLA y el también primer autor, señaló que esa solución simplifica la estructura del vehículo aéreo.
La geometría aerodinámicamente asimétrica y las deformaciones parciales durante cada aleteo permiten generar sustentación. Al mismo tiempo, la flexibilidad de las alas hace que se deformen al entrar en contacto con una superficie sin doblarse de manera permanente, una propiedad que las protege frente a los impactos.
Tecnología y aplicaciones más allá del laboratorio
Los investigadores conectaron el primer prototipo a una fuente eléctrica externa mediante cables. Luego evaluaron su capacidad para despegar, resistir compresiones con cargas pesadas, reiniciar el vuelo tras colisiones y mantener una velocidad media de ascenso.
Wenzhong Yan, investigador del departamento de Ingeniería Mecánica y Aeroespacial de la UC Davis, resumió: “Nuestro robot generó una sustentación de hasta tres veces su propio peso y pudo volver a volar después de ser golpeado o aplastado”.
Para Yan, el comportamiento del aparato expresa una forma de “inteligencia mecánica”: “Respuestas útiles incorporadas en los materiales y la estructura, como adaptar pasivamente la morfología de las alas para generar sustentación y deformarse durante el contacto para luego recuperarse. Ese enfoque podría ayudar a los diminutos robots voladores a resistir las interacciones impredecibles que encontrarían fuera del laboratorio”.
Para funcionar de forma autónoma, una versión futura del robot deberá incorporar una fuente de energía propia, componentes de control de vuelo y sensores. El equipo también planea mejorar los giros y aterrizajes, y aumentar la capacidad de carga, con miras a probar el robot en aplicaciones concretas como el monitoreo ambiental, la polinización agrícola y las operaciones de búsqueda y rescate en zonas de difícil acceso.

articles.title: Max-Severity GitLab Vulnerability Exploited Against Alpine Linux
articles.text:
A recent code execution vulnerability in GitLab was exploited one week after disclosure in a failed attack against Alpine Linux’s instance.
Tracked as CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS score of 10/10), the flaw stems from insufficient regular expression validation in Onigmo, Ruby’s regular expression engine.
The bug “could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration,” GitLab noted in an October 12 advisory.
According to Alpine Linux, a threat actor targeted its GitLab instance with a CVE-2026-97229 exploit on October 20 and 21. The attack failed, but the Linux distribution rebuilt the instance from scratch.
“Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with,” Alpine Linux notes.
It is still testing the GitLab instance before public release, and has reset all passwords, warning of observed automated login attempts using passwords compromised in other leaks.
As part of the October 20-21 attack, the hackers used a newly registered account to send crafted CI configurations to Alpine Linux’s GitLab instance, crashing the worker process.
“In 4 of those crashes, the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build. We have found no evidence that the attacker ran code on the server, but we cannot rule it out,” Alpine Linux says.
Because the underlying vulnerability resides in Ruby, not in GitLab, and the Linux distribution’s image runs standard Ruby, the vulnerability was not patched after updating to GitLab 19.3.6.
“If you run GitLab with your own Ruby (from source or in your own container image) rather than GitLab’s packages, upgrading GitLab is not enough: you also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later,” Alpine Linux notes.
On Thursday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA added CVE-2026-97229 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, urging federal agencies to patch it within three days, as mandated by BOD 26-04.

articles.title: Rocket Report: Winter is coming for Themis; Cowboy Space adds iron to the fire
articles.text:
Baiju Bhatt, founder and CEO of Cowboy Space Corporation, attends an event in Palo Alto, California, to reveal the company's architecture for a new medium-lift rocket and data centers in space.
Credit:
Thos Robinson/Getty Images for Cowboy Space Corporation
Baiju Bhatt, founder and CEO of Cowboy Space Corporation, attends an event in Palo Alto, California, to reveal the company's architecture for a new medium-lift rocket and data centers in space.
Credit:
Thos Robinson/Getty Images for Cowboy Space Corporation
Welcome to Edition 9.17 of the Rocket Report! It’s been a while since an American company announced plans for a medium-lift new launch vehicle, but that’s what happened this week when a startup named Cowboy Space revealed specs for its Big Iron rocket, named for the classic country-western song by Marty Robbins. I’m a huge fan of the name. Maybe Cowboy Space is striking while the iron is hot as the space industry frets over demand for launch outpacing supply. However, Cowboy Space lags far behind so many other launch providers nearing the launch pad with their medium-class rockets, and the company didn’t have much hardware to show at this week’s big reveal. In other words, don’t mistake style for substance. But we’re rocket fans at Ars, and we wish them luck.
As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Virgin’s new rocket plane reaches home port. The first of Virgin Galactic’s new Delta-class rocket planes left its Arizona factory Wednesday for a trip to Spaceport America in neighboring New Mexico, where it will undergo preparations for a test campaign culminating in suborbital flights to the edge of space, Ars reports. Virgin Galactic expects the craft’s first commercial spaceflight to take place “early” in the second quarter of 2027, but like every other projected date in aerospace, this should be taken with a grain of salt. Virgin Galactic halted commercial flights of its previous vehicle, VSS Unity, in 2024.
More to do … The company also revealed the rocket plane’s name: Apeiron. Engineers and technicians at Spaceport America will complete work on the vehicle’s avionics equipment and flight software. Following additional ground tests, Apeiron will be mated again to its carrier aircraft for captive carry tests, followed by a drop test and ultimately a powered test flight above 80 km. With Blue Origin’s retreat from the suborbital spaceflight market and SpaceX’s planned retirement of the orbital-class Dragon spacecraft, Virgin Galactic is the only company with a realistic chance of flying paying commercial passengers to space anytime soon.
ESA’s reusable rocket testbed seems cursed. The European Space Agency’s Director of Space Transportation, Géraldine Naja, said on October 22 that she was uncertain whether the agency would be able to complete the first flight of its Themis reusable rocket demonstrator before the end of the year, European Spaceflight reports. The single-stage rocket hopper has completed two countdown rehearsals at Esrange Space Center in Sweden, but the harsh Scandinavian winter may prevent Themis from taking flight this year.
Missed schedules … ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher said in January that the Themis rocket’s first hop test would happen in the first quarter of 2026. Delays are nothing new for Themis. Officials originally expected the rocket’s first low-altitude hop test to occur in 2022. The rocket is powered by a reusable methane-fueled Prometheus engine. ArianeGroup, the company behind Europe’s Ariane rocket family, is the main contractor on Themis, which is supposed to test technologies for an eventual reusable replacement for the expendable Ariane 6.
Rocket Report
Keep up with the latest in space exploration and rocket launches.
Cowboy Space unveils new rocket. Cowboy Space on Monday released the first details about the launcher that it plans to loft before the end of 2028, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports. The rocket, named Big Iron, will be 282 feet (86 meters) tall and about 15 feet (4.7 meters) in diameter. Cowboy Space is developing a methane-fueled engine named Clydesdale. Nine of them will power the first stage, and the second stage will fly a single Clydesdale. Big Iron’s payload capacity will be up to 18 metric tons (39,700 pounds) to low-Earth orbit.
Let the horses run … Baiju Bhatt, the billionaire co-founder of Robinhood, started his space company, originally named Aetherflux, in 2024. He rebranded the company as Cowboy Space earlier this year. Bhatt is chasing the market for space-based AI led by SpaceX. After launching into orbit, the upper stage of the Big Iron rocket will form the core of Cowboy Space’s data center spacecraft, with five racks of GPUs, six inter-satellite laser links, and solar arrays stretching the length of one-and-a-half football fields.
More good news for Stoke Space. The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital announced Monday a conditional commitment to provide a $150 million loan to Stoke Space for construction of a second launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, GeekWire reports. Stoke Space is well along in construction of its first launch pad at Cape Canaveral for its reusable medium-lift Nova rocket. The second pad would accommodate an upgraded Nova Block 2 vehicle for heavier payloads.
Swimming in cash … The $150 million government loan is subject to financial, legal, technical, and due diligence requirements. It follows Stoke Space’s $1 billion Series E fundraising round in September, bringing the company’s total amount of capital raised to $2.3 billion. Stoke aims to launch its Nova Pathfinder rocket next year, followed by Block 2 in 2029. The company’s reusable upper stage, the most innovative segment of the rocket, is now undergoing qualification testing at Moses Lake, Washington.
Industry execs forecast launch crunch. The US government may have moved too quickly to conclude that the commercial launch market could support its growing military needs, industry executives warned at a conference this week, Space News reports. The Space Force’s launch strategy, which is designed to broaden competition by tapping commercially developed rockets, has expanded the number of companies eligible to compete for military launches. But executives speaking at the 2026 Silicon Valley Space Week conference questioned whether enough capacity will be available as national security demand rises and SpaceX begins a long-planned transition from its workhorse Falcon 9 to its next-generation Starship rocket.
Pertinent quotes … An executive at Stoke Space, one of the companies seeking to break into the military launch business, said it “may have been a strategic error” for the government to assume the launch problem had been solved. Devin Papandrew, Stoke’s vice president of business development, said the government should consider additional funding, along with relief from regulatory and infrastructure constraints. The head of government relations at United Launch Alliance, the military’s leading launch provider after SpaceX, said the launch supply crunch should ease as new rockets enter service. When might that happen? “2030-ish is the best I would hope for right now,” Hunt said.
SpaceX no longer needs NASA. In a comprehensive feature story this week, Ars reports on the fraying relationship between SpaceX and NASA. For the last decade and a half, NASA has relied upon Elon Musk’s space company to resupply the International Space Station, end US reliance on Russia for crew transport, and develop a critical piece of the puzzle for beating China back to the Moon. But Musk is now all-in on AI, and SpaceX’s clear priority today is focusing on how to rapidly deploy compute on Earth and in space.
The signs are there … SpaceX continues to work on a human-rated lander for NASA’s Artemis Moon program, but there are signs of a partial breakup looming. SpaceX wants to end flights of the Crew Dragon spacecraft by 2030, and is already winding down its remarkably successful Falcon 9 rocket in favor of the company’s much larger but relatively unproven Starship. And Starship’s launch capacity will be filled by SpaceX’s internal demand for Starlink and Starmind, the company’s orbital data center constellation. SpaceX now seems increasingly disinterested in the US government for most contracts outside of data services, such as Starshield for military communications and observations.
ULA to develop upgraded Centaur for SLS. During a lengthy news conference on October 23, NASA provided a detailed overview of how it plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface as soon as 2028 as part of its Artemis program, Ars reports. The changes include revised architectures for getting astronauts to the lunar surface on landers provided by SpaceX and Blue Origin. On the launch front, NASA confirmed it will contract with United Launch Alliance to develop an upgraded version of its Centaur V upper stage to fly on the Space Launch System rocket.
LLO or bust … The “extended” Centaur V is a larger version of the upper stage that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Incorporating the extended Centaur onto the SLS rocket will allow the Orion spacecraft to reach low-lunar orbit, a capability it does not have with the current SLS upper stage. In fact, NASA officials said the extended Centaur will be higher-performing than the costly Exploration Upper Stage the agency originally planned to develop as an SLS enhancement. “Getting Orion to low-lunar orbit means solving propulsion and spacecraft integration problems that were left unaddressed for far too long,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said.
Vulcan’s return-to-flight mission has a launch date. United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company’s 2026 launch schedule into oblivion, Ars reports. The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval.
An important mission … The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA’s primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan. It’s also important for the Space Force and Amazon, which have staked much of their future satellite fleets on the success of the Vulcan rocket.
Space Force says America needs a new spaceport. US Space Force leaders want a new spaceport up and running by 2030, adding a third heavy-lift launch site to relieve pressure on bases in Florida and California that have launched rockets into orbit for nearly 70 years, Ars reports. The obvious problem with that ambition is that 2030 is four years away, and Pentagon officials have not determined where the new spaceport should go or how to acquire land for it.
All options on the table … “We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist,” said Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, head of Space Systems Command. “That is not an inconsequential demand to build a spaceport when you factor in orbital regimes, safety, access to commodities, the Americans that live near it. In many ways, it’s much like an airport, but even louder. So there’s a lot of consideration.” Officials haven’t decided where to put a new spaceport. Garrant later said all options are on the table: a public-private partnership, a new military base, state land, or commercial land.
Next three launches
October 30: GSLV Mk.II | NVS-03 | Satish Dhawan Space Center, India | 18:21 UTC
October 31: Falcon 9 | Starlink 15-18 | Vandenberg Space Force Base, California | 03:48 UTC
November 2: Electron | QPS-SAR-20 | Māhia Peninsula, New Zealand | 08:45 UTC
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

articles.title: Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru
articles.text:
Starbucks could eventually show you a personalized digital menu when you pull up to the drive-thru. During an earnings call on Thursday, Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol said the company is going to explore “experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless,” as spotted earlier by More Perfect Union.
Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru
The coffee chain aims to ‘recognize’ customers as they arrive.
It sounds similar to the technology that Taco Bell is experimenting with, which could change the layout, content, and visuals on a digital menu board “on a car-by-car basis.” McDonald’s also recently showed off an AI-powered feature it’s piloting at a handful of drive-thrus, allowing its “ArchIQ” chatbot to identify repeat customers and let them order their “usual.”
Starting in 2027, Starbucks will also begin testing background AI models at the drive-thru to help baristas “input orders more accurately and efficiently,” according to Niccol. The company also plans to integrate AI into the Starbucks app’s search and discovery features, and may allow “conversational and agentic” ordering in the future.
Starbucks has already started allowing customers to place orders through ChatGPT, and also rolled out an AI-powered Green Dot Assist that employees can use to ask questions about things like recipes and service standards.
It’s still not clear how soon we can expect to see personalized digital menu boards at Starbucks, but Niccol says it’s still “early,” adding that “we’ll test, learn, and scale what works.”

articles.title: Float’s Rob Khazzam on how Canadian companies should rethink AI spending | BetaKit
articles.text:
Rob Khazzam has a funny story about keeping business AI costs under control. A few months ago, he discovered his own usage was costing $2,364 a day. He’d selected an expensive model without realizing it would remain the default for new conversations, so even routine prompts were running up the bill.
For the co-founder and CEO of Float, the Toronto-based startup building Canada’s intelligent financial operating system, it was a lesson in a challenge facing many of its nearly 10,000 customers.
“We’re seeing an explosion of spending, an explosion of adoption.”
Rob Khazzam
Float CEO
When looking at the data across Canadian businesses using Float, “We’re seeing an explosion of spending, an explosion of adoption,” Khazzam told BetaKit in a recent interview.
AI spending on Float grew twelve-fold over two years and more than four-fold in the past year alone, he said. In the past year, seventy percent of customers had experienced a month when their AI bill jumped 50 percent.
But bringing those bills down isn’t always the right response. Khazzam says that leaders need to understand how AI spending helps their teams accomplish more, while being able to catch costly habits like his own.
Drawing on Float’s experiments and expensive lessons, Khazzam shared what’s changing his thinking about spending, hiring, and helping employees get more out of AI. Here are five of his hottest takes.
1. Treat AI spending as an investment in your team
A rising AI bill doesn’t necessarily mean the company is becoming more expensive to run. If the tools help employees accomplish more without adding as many new hires, that spending could support a more productive business.
It’s why Khazzam has moved away from treating AI as a software expense to cut whenever it climbs too high. Instead, he said, “The right frame to me is to look at your payroll and your token spend together, and look at that combined number as your human capital investment.”
At Float, token spend rose from the equivalent of 0.1 percent of payroll a year earlier to about five to six percent in October. Khazzam now looks at the two costs together as a percentage of revenue, with the understanding that the business will grow alongside the combined expense.
The test extends beyond efficiency: “Do you solve customer problems faster? Do you build better product experiences faster? Does your organization learn faster?”
2. As part of the hiring process, consider what role AI can play
Before adding someone new to a team, Khazzam asks managers to consider how AI could help existing employees handle the work.
“Anytime someone wants to post a role, send us an email and explain why you need to fill this role and how AI can support the work,” he said, describing Float’s approach.
Hiring may still go ahead; Float is hiring now more than ever, but the exercise is designed to create a pause to help managers reconsider the responsibilities and resources required and how their team builds with AI first.
AI can also change what a company needs from a role. Float’s designers now build working prototypes using an internal tool called Surf. Khazzam said that’s changed what he looks for in a design team compared with a year earlier.
3. Match the model to the work
More powerful AI models can cost more to use, but their additional capabilities are not necessary for every job. Editing an email, for example, doesn’t need the same resources as solving a difficult data science problem.
“In most use cases, the marginal benefit of a frontier model is not needed,” he said.
Managing that difference requires more than instructions telling employees which model to select. Khazzam favours permissions that give people tackling complex technical problems, such as data scientists and principal engineers, more discretion over access.
Companies also need to catch spending increases as they happen. He recommended setting thresholds and assigning someone responsibility for flagging when usage crosses them, investigating the causes, and recommending adjustments.
4. Let employees explore, then choose shared tools
Letting employees try different AI tools has helped Float discover useful applications. But as adoption grew, people were sometimes solving the same problem with different products, making collaboration harder.
“We had, for example, 20 people trying to solve the same problem using five different tools,” said Khazzam.
Monthly adoption reports showed who was using which products and consuming the most tokens. Float eventually consolidated its tools. Khazzam noted that standardizing made it easier for Float to manage permissions, protect sensitive information, and give employees access to shared business context.
“Because the power of AI is not just editing an email. It’s being able to have it understand your business, the problem you’re trying to solve, and perpetually get smarter.”
5. Give learning time to pay off
A higher AI bill may arrive before the benefits show up in financial results. Khazzam cautioned against concluding an investment has failed simply because revenue per employee has not immediately risen in proportion to spending.
“It takes time,” he said.
At Float, company-wide hackathons have provided a useful way to assess progress. Watching employees build and ship something useful in a day or two gave leadership the confidence to keep supporting experimentation.
The events extend beyond engineering and product to include marketing, sales, and other non-technical teams who take part to ship new workflows and customer solutions both in and out of the product. Employees then show colleagues what they’ve built, helping practical knowledge spread across the business.
Khazzam sees that kind of learning as an investment that can compound: employees using AI now have more time to develop their capabilities than those who wait.
“I’m completely fine overspending for the next six to nine months, and culling it back if it means that the sum total of hours our team has spent learning is as high as humanly possible.”
PRESENTED BY

articles.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
articles.text:
HBM shortages threaten AI expansion; TSMC weighs price hikes; advanced packaging ramps; domain-specialized AI models; Infineon and UMC boost fab investments; Intel’s quantum move; Lam and imec advance 3D integration; Google expands TPUs; AI-driven earnings; CPU benchmarking methodology for agentic AI.
SK hynix expects memory supply constraints to persist through 2030, with DRAM and HBM volumes effectively sold out through 2029. Samsung expects tight memory supply through 2028, citing lengthy fab construction and equipment lead times, larger dies, and greater process complexity in next-gen HBM, as well as a shift of DRAM capacity toward HBM. Samsung said its 2027 HBM supply is already sold out.
Solidigm, SK hynix’s U.S. subsidiary, reportedly is discussing a proposed $45B NAND flash fab with the U.S. Commerce Department.
China’s CXMT plans to soon begin limited production of HBM3E memory, despite manufacturing yields of just 20% to 30%, per Reuters.
TSMC reportedly is considering a 20% price increase for CoWoS as AI demand continues to strain advanced-packaging capacity.
Applied Materials plans to increase its stake in Besi to ~20%, deepening a strategic partnership that is expanding beyond hybrid bonding into new interconnect architectures and advanced packaging technologies for AI.
Manufacturing
Intel Foundry reported improving manufacturing execution in Q3, citing better yields and cycle times on 18A. The company also released its 14A 0.9 PDK in October and said it continues to engage prospective external customers around 18A-P and 14A, while advancing its EMIB-T advanced-packaging technology.
Infineon plans to invest €1.1B through 2034 at its Villach, Austria facility to establish Europe’s first high-volume manufacturing facility for next-gen GaN power semiconductors on 300mm wafers.
UMC approved an additional $3.2B in capital spending to accelerate its capacity expansion in Singapore and Tainan as demand grows for advanced packaging and silicon photonics.
Lam Research and imec expanded their collaboration on advanced 3D integration, next-gen memory, and high-NA EUV patterning. The work includes deposition, etch, and plasma dicing processes for advanced packaging, along with Lam’s Aether dry resist technology.
AI tools and accelerators
Cadence introduced a portfolio of domain-specialized AI models for agentic chip and system design. Integrated with Cadence’s EDA tools, the portfolio spans multiple model sizes and architectures, combining post-trained LLMs, decision models, and self-improving agent skills.
Arm introduced a new CPU benchmarking methodology for agentic AI. The framework evaluates CPU performance across agentic workloads, including tool execution, orchestration, and reasoning, using repeatable measurements and end-to-end task outcomes.
Google is expanding the reach of its custom AI accelerators, with OpenAI reportedly planning to purchase its TPUs, reports The Information. Separately, Oracle will offer Google’s TPUs through its cloud infrastructure beginning in 2027 and plans to add Arm’s AGI CPUs in fall 2027.
Broadcom‘s XPUs and networking equipment will support Anthropic‘s AI infrastructure expansion, beginning in 2027, under a $63B financing arrangement.
Meta is expanding deployments of Nvidia and AMD AI infrastructure across its data centers, with both chipmakers also taking stakes in the company.
Deals and funding
Intel plans to acquireClassiq, a developer of automated quantum algorithm synthesis software. Intel says the acquisition will give it a full stack of quantum offerings, adding to its silicon spin-qubit technology and manufacturing.
Unconfirmed: Marvell is reportedly in advanced talks to acquire optical components makerLumentum, per Bloomberg. Onsemi reportedly is in talks to acquireFerric, a startup developing integrated voltage regulators for AI processors, for nearly $1B, according to The Information.
Earnings
Quarterly revenue and % growth versus the same quarter in the prior year, unless otherwise indicated:
Advantest: ¥477.7B, up 82%, with robust tester demand for AI.
Workforce | Education— AI in engineering education, VR-based fab training, and expanding university semiconductor workforce programs.
Events and Webinars— Micro 2026, PIC Summit, full-chip curvilinear patterning, and functional verification study.
Global
Asia
Vietnam‘s first semiconductor fab may miss its 2027 trial-production target, according to Reuters. The estimated US$1.3B Viettel project reportedly has yet to begin construction, while negotiations for ASML lithography equipment remain unresolved. Viettel maintains the project is on schedule.
ITIF says the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative has grown to 26 countries, coordinating on semiconductors, critical minerals, energy, advanced manufacturing, and AI infrastructure to reduce dependence on vulnerable supply chains.
Imec and Indiana University formed a semiconductor research partnership focused on advanced electronics, photonics, and workforce development. Initial research will test imec-developed electronic and photonic components in extreme environments, including space.
Cadence will provide U.S. Department of Energy National Laboratories with access to EDA, SDA, multiphysics simulation, digital twins, advanced packaging, and 3D-IC workflows, along with technical expertise.
ChipAgents is expanding its agentic AI platform across digital and analog chip design with a neural engine that combines persistent design knowledge, advanced reasoning and orchestration, dynamic model routing, and physics-aware models. It will also work with Nvidia to fine-tune Nemotron models.
Axiomise and Agnisys teamed up to verify NoCs using formal technologies.
AI power delivery
Infineon introduced new AI power-delivery technologies, including a ±400 V/800 V rack power-distribution reference board, a 5.6 kW M-CRPS reference design, and 900 V monolithic bidirectional GaN switches for solid-state transformers in AI data centers.
Compute, memory and photonics
PsiQuantum demonstrated an 8×8 optical circuit switch built on silicon photonics for AI infrastructure.
TetraMem taped out a 12nm analog in-memory computing SoC based on multi-level RRAM and developed using Synopsys‘ cloud EDA tools.
Fraunhofer IIS integrated permanent micromagnets directly into the silicon substrate of a magnetic sensor chip at wafer level.
Automotive
Infineon introduced a chip-embedding platform for high-voltage power electronics, LinearFET technology for solid-state power distribution in EVs and SDVs, new MOSFETs for 12 V and 48 V vehicle systems, and a high-voltage BMS reference design.
STMicro released an automotive safety sensor platform that combines accelerometers and gyroscopes for ADAS and vehicle-safety applications.
Bosch debuted a new MEMS inertial sensor platform, combining ADAS and vehicle-safety functions up to ASIL D.
Research
TU Munich researchers developed neural-network-based transistor models for 3nm nanosheet devices, accelerating standard-cell library characterization by up to 8× compared with a conventional compact model. The models kept delay-estimation errors below 0.11%.
A Brown University-led team demonstrated ultrathin multiferroic films that retain ferroelectric and magnetic properties at thicknesses of just a few angstroms, overcoming the dead-layer effect in bismuth ferrite. The films also exhibited altermagnetic properties, potentially enabling low-power memory and logic devices.
Chinese Academy of Sciences-led researchers developed a III-nitride-based in-sensor computing device that uses interfacial polarization to separate photogenerated carriers and reduce recombination losses. The sensor-memristor achieved responsivity on the order of 10⁶ A/W, an on/off ratio of 10⁵, and maintained high performance at temperatures up to 300°C.
University of Oxford-led researchers identified a pseudo-direct semiconductor in bismuth sulfide that combines strong light absorption with slower electron–hole recombination. Its unusual electronic structure was estimated to reduce recombination rates by about 75% at room temperature compared with conventional semiconductors with similarly strong absorption, potentially improving solar-cell efficiency.
Security
MITRE’s CWE Program released CWE 5.0, adding new weaknesses, including Hardware Simulation/Synthesis Mismatch. The new hardware weakness covers security-relevant cases where RTL behaves differently after synthesis, potentially exposing data, altering protected state, or bypassing security controls in the resulting hardware.
Alerts and hacks
TianoCore disclosed a critical vulnerability in its widely used EDK II UEFI firmware. The memory-corruption flaw could allow an unauthenticated network attacker to execute code during PXE boot, before the OS loads and before Secure Boot or measured boot can verify any OS component.
Supermicro disclosed nine BMC firmware vulnerabilities across two Oct. 26 advisories, including a critical flaw that could let an unauthenticated network attacker execute arbitrary IPMI commands on an active session. The disclosures also cover privilege-escalation, key-exposure, memory-access, and command-injection flaws.
Keystone said a breach exposed a key used to authenticate its hardware wallets, potentially allowing counterfeit devices to pass authenticity checks. The company is destroying 18,835 unsold devices containing the compromised key.
Government security news
NIST finalized its road map for transitioning to PQC, identifying the quantum-vulnerable standards that federal systems and technology providers will need to replace with quantum-resistant algorithms.
Eclypsium and Nvidia demonstrated how a compromised privileged component in AI compute infrastructure could alter model weights and outputs during live inference without modifying the stored model.
Rowhammer attack on Fil-C’s software capabilities (Independent researcher and U. Sussex)
Trending Video
Why Proof Convergence Matters: Leveraging patterns in formal verification to reach sign-off faster. Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise, talks about the impact of functional interactions involving safety and security, where to look for common patterns to prevent bugs from creeping into these designs, and how this all can be used to reduce time to sign-off with higher coverage.
NVision Quantum demonstrated a single-molecule spin-photon interface and partnered with HyperLight to integrate molecular qubits onto photonic chips using established semiconductor fabrication processes.
FZ Jülich-led researchers demonstrated 6.8-nanosecond single-qubit gates on a superconducting transmon, achieving 99.981% and 99.989% fidelity. Precision pulse shaping suppressed unwanted transitions, keeping leakage below 0.002% per operation.
A Technical University of Denmark team demonstrated integrated quantum light sources using 2D materials, coupling WSe₂ single-photon emitters to WS₂ waveguides on a chip, with an estimated minimum waveguide-coupled rate of 1.68 million photons per second.
Workforce, Education
In a new special report, Semiconductor Engineering examines how AI is changing the skills tomorrow’s engineers will need, with universities placing greater emphasis on strong math and physics fundamentals, critical thinking, and the ability to validate AI-generated results. Semiconductor employers say graduates will need both AI fluency and enough technical depth to recognize when AI gets things wrong.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.

articles.title: En 1965, París empezó a excavar un aparcamiento frente a Notre-Dame. Se encontró con una ciudad romana entera bajo sus pies
articles.text:
Hace más de 60 años, la ciudad de París ideó un plan para excavar un aparcamiento junto a su catedral más famosa. La excavación se alargó más de lo previsto, ya que sacó a la luz unos dos mil años de historia de la ciudad, apilados capa sobre capa. De hecho los restos siguen ahí, bajo el pavimento, y millones de visitantes cruzan la plaza frente a Notre-Dame cada año sin saber qué hay debajo.
Lo que hay es la Cripta Arqueológica de la Île de la Cité, un museo construido en torno a los restos que afloraron cuando París se preparaba para construir el aparcamiento a principios de la década de los 60.
Qué pasó. La excavación comenzó en 1965, justo antes de la construcción del aparcamiento subterráneo bajo la plaza, según el Ministerio de Cultura francés. Y duró hasta principios de los 70.
En los trabajos se encontraron una barbaridad de estructuras y elementos que datan de la época romana. El propio ministerio enumera un sistema de muelles galorromanos, casas con hipocaustos (calefacción bajo el suelo) y una sección de muralla de la época romana tardía.
París Musées cuenta además que se encontraron baños públicos y por encima de esas capas se encuentran niveles medievales con pozos, sótanos de casas y hasta los cimientos del Hospice des Enfants-Trouvés del siglo XVIII (la institución central donde acogían a recién nacidos y niños abandonados en la Francia del Antiguo Régimen). Además, también se descubrió la antigua calle Rue Neuve Notre-Dame, una calle medieval que pasaba frente a la catedral, según cuenta el estudio de AFAV.
Quién lo salvó. La cripta fue iniciada por Michel Fleury, vicepresidente de la Comisión del Viejo París y director de antigüedades históricas de la región de Île-de-France, según el Ministerio de Cultura. La revista Archaeology cuenta que, cuando se propuso el aparcamiento a principios de la década de 1960, Fleury hizo modificar los planos para dejar espacio a una exposición arqueológica subterránea.
La cripta se acabó acondicionando en 1974 y se abrió al público en 1980. El aparcamiento también se construyó, y sigue ahí.
Una catedral encima de una muralla. Según el Ministerio de Cultura, el obispo Maurice de Sully colocó la primera piedra de Notre-Dame en 1163. La muralla es muchísimo más antigua, pues data de principios del año 300, por lo que se mantuvo en pie aproximadamente 850 años antes de que se empezara a construir la catedral.
Fuego. El incendio de Notre-Dame en abril de 2019 cerró la cripta, pero acabó reabriendo año y medio después, el 9 de septiembre de 2020, con una exposición homenaje sobre la historia de la catedral. Es fácil pasar por alto la puerta, pues es bastante discreta y las escaleras tampoco ayudan.
Qué viene a continuación. La plaza de Notre-Dame está siendo remodelada y se espera que finalice para 2028. Ahora el antiguo aparcamiento se va a convertir en una zona de recepción de visitantes con un nuevo acceso a la cripta, y ya han comenzado las excavaciones. Las autoridades ordenaron una excavación preventiva, de 30 metros de largo y 4 metros de profundidad y se espera que dure unos ocho meses.

articles.title: TeamViewer Flaw Could Let Malicious Hosts Take Over Support Technicians’ Machines
articles.text:
A high-severity vulnerability in the popular remote-access tool TeamViewer could be exploited to take over a viewer’s (an IT support technician’s) system, cybersecurity firm Remedio warns.
Tracked as CVE-2026-111585 (CVSS score of 8.8), the flaw is described as an integer overflow affecting the remote-control screen processing component of TeamViewer clients across Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android.
Successful exploitation of the security defect could allow attackers to crash the viewer’s TeamViewer or execute arbitrary code on their system.
“Exploitation requires a user to establish a remote-control session to an attacker-controlled or compromised host,” TeamViewer notes in its advisory.
The issue, Remedio says, is rooted in how the host’s screen dimension is transmitted and used in the viewer: the host announces the geometry of the screen and the viewer uses the received dimensions to allocate an in-memory pixel buffer it then uses to decompress incoming screen updates.
This decode surface is only used if a hardware video decoder is not available for the session, but the host may refuse to negotiate the video codecs, thus forcing the viewer to that path.
A host can request a surface larger than what a screen can reach, and the path accepts it. An example would be 32768 by 32768 pixels at 32 bits per pixel, which overflows 32 bits, with every row past 31 being written out of bounds.
“The screen dimensions a host announces are used to size the drawing surface as-is, with no upper bound enforced on what arrives over the network,” Remedio explains.
The attacker-controlled host controls both the declared surface and the screen updates that can overflow the buffer, causing the viewer’s application to repeatedly crash.
“That means a malicious or compromised host can trigger the bug from inside an ordinary, established session, using only messages the protocol already supports,” Remedio explains.
In addition to triggering the denial-of-service (DoS) condition over a normal TeamViewer session, Remedio discovered that it could use CVE-2026-111585 to execute arbitrary code on the viewer’s system.
“The corrupted surface is a live object the viewer later calls through a pointer in its own first field, so overwriting that pointer redirects the call,” Remedio notes, explaining that it bypassed existing protections to route the call to WinExec and run the code in the viewer.
“The surface is reachable in the default configuration. An accepted session is all it takes, and that is the product’s normal mode of operation,” the company says.
Version 15.83 of TeamViewer’s clients (including Full Client, Host, Portable, and Remote Control App for Android) contains the necessary patches. TeamViewer also released security updates for multiple legacy versions.
The macOS and Linux updates also resolve CVE-2026-92372, an out-of-bounds write with similar consequences: an attacker could supply crafted screen-image data or convince a user to open a specially crafted TeamViewer session recording (.tvs) to execute arbitrary code.
“Missing destination bounds checking in the decoder allows crafted screen-image data to cause an out-of-bounds write to the image buffer. Exploitation requires user interaction,” TeamViewer notes.
On macOS, the updates also resolve CVE-2026-92374, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition with improper symbolic link handling flaw that could allow a low-privileged local attacker to install a malicious package and gain root privileges.
Additionally, TeamViewer patched six high-severity local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the TeamViewer Remote Management add-ons, urging users to update both the clients and the components to the latest versions.
TeamViewer says it is not aware of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.

articles.title: Waymo taps Toyota to supply robotaxis for Japan and the UK | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Waymo will begin testing autonomous Toyota bZ4X vehicles in Japan next year as part of a broader partnership with the automaker to provide electric vehicles for robotaxi operations in international markets, including the U.K.
Under the partnership announced Friday, Toyota will manufacture the 2027 bZ4X vehicles and integrate Waymo’s self-driving system at its Takaoka factory in Japan. (The electric vehicle is now known as the bZ in the North American market.)
The autonomous bZ4X vehicles will initially be tested in Japan, where Waymo intends to eventually operate a robotaxi service. But the intent is to deploy these vehicles in other right-hand driving countries such as the U.K. Waymo has been testing its autonomous Jaguar I-Pace vehicles in London for months and plans to launch a robotaxi service there once it receives the necessary permits.
The announcement comes 18 months after Toyota and Waymo signed a preliminary agreement to explore the development and deployment of an autonomous vehicle platform. At the time, the agreement fell into the “let’s see what happens” category, with language vague enough to leave plenty of room for interpretation.
For now, the partnership looks more like a conventional vehicle supplier deal that helps Waymo fill specific regional needs while adding a new model to its robotaxi portfolio.
But the partnership could go beyond robotaxis. The companies said they will continue to look at bringing Waymo’s autonomous technology to personally owned Toyota vehicles.
Toyota and Waymo also announced plans to look at other future “initiatives” that would use “insights from Waymo’s real-world operations” to improve safety for other road users. What that might mean is unclear, although Hiroki Nakajima, executive vice president of Toyota and a board member, provided some clues.
“This collaboration will help scale that technology and bring it to customers in Japan and beyond through Waymo’s ride-hailing service, and in parallel, Toyota will continue to explore how integrating vehicles with traffic infrastructure can make those roads safer still,” he said in a statement.

articles.title: Halloween: confira imagens astronômicas dignas de filme de terror
articles.text:
Neste sábado (31), é comemorado o Halloween, festividade típica dos países anglo-saxônicos, em especial os EUA, Canadá, Irlanda e Reino Unido.
Enquanto a celebração inspira decorações temáticas na Terra, registros revelam imagens sombrias do Universo capturadas ao longo de décadas, que mostram que a realidade cósmica muitas vezes pode ser mais assustadora que a ficção.
Em referência à data, reunimos imagens incríveis, que vão desde uma monstruosa mão zumbi esculpida nos ventos de uma estrela morta até um asteroide com formato de caveira que visitou a vizinhança da Terra. Prepare-se para uma viagem visual por nebulosas fantasmagóricas e estruturas cósmicas dignas de uma autêntica noite de terror.
Mão Fantasmagórica
Embora seja apelidada de “Mão de Deus”, a região vista nesta imagem de raio-X parece assustadora demais para ser chamada assim. Lembra mais uma monstruosa mão zumbi prestes a agarrar uma presa no espaço.
No entanto, trata-se, na verdade, de uma nebulosa de vento pulsar, produzida pelo denso remanescente de uma supernova. O que não deixa de ser fúnebre, afinal, supernova é um evento astronômico transitório que ocorre durante os últimos estágios evolutivos de uma estrela massiva ou quando uma anã branca inicia uma fusão nuclear descontrolada. Ou seja: significa a morte da estrela.
O grito da morte
O que dizer deste rosto horripilante que parece estar gritando enquanto sofre com uma morte miserável e ardente? Um cenário bem a cara do Halloween. Apesar de pavorosa, a cena, na verdade, não envolve nenhum crânio real. Trata-se de uma imagem de raios-X de um conjunto de galáxias conhecido como Aglomerado de Perseu, capturada pelo Observatório Chandra, da NASA.
Espíritos malignos em fuga
Esta captura feita pelo Observatório Nacional de Kitt Peak, que fica no estado norte-americano do Arizona, poderia ser uma cena de filme de terror, na qual espíritos malignos tentam fugir do calvário das trevas.
No entanto, o que ela realmente mostra é uma nuvem de gás e poeira interestelar chamada SH2-136, localizada a cerca de 1.200 anos-luz da Terra, na constelação de Cepheus.
Cabeça de bruxa
Uma bruxa verde está olhando para o espaço nesta imagem sinistra obtida pelo Explorador de Pesquisa em Infravermelho de Campo Amplo da NASA (WISE). O registro, na verdade, mostra a nebulosa IC 2118, que, em razão da aparência, recebeu o apelido de Cabeça de Bruxa.
O Olho de Sauron está observando você
Fomalhaut é a estrela mais brilhante da constelação de Peixe Austral. Localizada a cerca de 25 anos-luz da Terra, ela tem cerca de 440 milhões de anos, durante os quais acumulou um cinturão de poeira ao seu redor.
Nesta imagem, o sistema estelar Fomalhaut apresenta uma estranha semelhança com o temível Olho de Sauron da saga “O Senhor dos Anéis”. J. R. R. Tolkien descreveu o olho como sendo “bordado de fogo vigilante e intencionado, e a fenda negra de sua pupila se abriu em um poço, uma janela para nada”.
Caveira cinzenta
Há oito anos, um asteroide em formato de crânio humano fez uma passagem próxima da Terra. Durante sua aproximação máxima, a rocha espacial estava a cerca de 480 mil km do planeta, ou 1,3 vezes a distância média daqui até a Lua, o que não representava uma ameaça ao nosso planeta.
Por volta de três semanas antes de chegar a essa distância da Terra, o asteroide foi descoberto por astrônomos do observatório Pan-STARRS, localizado no Havaí, que lhe conferiram a designação oficial de “2015 TB145”.
Em 30 de outubro de 2015, o objeto de 400 m de largura foi fotografado pelo Observatório Arecibo, em Porto Rico, e, para surpresa de todos, ele parecia o rosto de uma caveira, ganhando o apelido de “Asteroide do Halloween”.
Flávia Correia é jornalista do Olhar Digital, cobrindo Ciência e Espaço.

articles.title: Wie Solid-State-Transformatoren den Strombedarf von KI-Rechenzentren stemmen könnten
articles.text:
Stromnetz am Limit: Wie Solid-State-Transformatoren jetzt Abhilfe schaffen könnten
Transformatoren sind ein zentraler, aber fast unsichtbarer Bestandteil unseres Stromnetzes: Die Großgeräte tragen dazu bei, Strom effizient über lange Entfernungen zu transportieren. Die Technik ist komplex und schwer zu bauen – immer noch. Da sich ihr grundlegendes Design seit etwa einem Jahrhundert kaum verändert hat, wären sie eigentlich reif für eine Modernisierung, doch die schien lange nicht zu passieren. Das ändert sich jetzt: Während die Welt darum kämpft, den steigenden Strombedarf von Elektrofahrzeugen, Rechenzentren und anderen Bereichen zu decken, suchen Forscher und Unternehmen nach Möglichkeiten, Transformatoren umzukrempeln. Und es gibt erste Erfolge: Neue Halbleiter-gestützte Varianten der Technik könnten dazu beitragen, Versorgungsengpässe teilweise zu lindern und sicherzustellen, dass das Stromnetz dem wachsenden Nachfragedruck standhalten kann.
