articles.title: When Electric Cars Were the Clean, Quiet Choice for Women
articles.text:
At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.
For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.
Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.
Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.
In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science
A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.
Who Invented the Mercury-Arc Rectifier?
Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images
Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.
The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.
A Carriage Maker Pivots to Electric Cars
I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.
This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens
According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.
Thomas Edison Designed a Bad Battery
Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.
While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).
Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens
Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.
When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.
Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science
Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)
Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.
Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.
Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.
An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.
References
For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.
Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)
- We’re Charging Our Cars Wrong ›
- False Starts: The Story of Vehicle-to-Grid Power ›
- This Power Grid Pioneer’s EV Prediction Came 100 Years Too Soon ›
Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

articles.title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
articles.text:
4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.
The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems.
Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, and TrustWave), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept.
eMudhra announced they’re exiting the public CA business and have claimed a mistake in a key generation script, but have not yet shared the script. They signed a certificate revocation list (CRL) with what might’ve been a correctly generated key, and subsequently corrected it to be signed with the weak key.
How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure.
Patching Cloudflare
Our primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets is being worked on.
We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using Pingora, responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week.
Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network?
To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21.
At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (which we mentioned in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched.
About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other organizations’ domains, unrelated to the Server Name Indication (SNI) requested in the handshake. Some of those names were domains related to consumer IoT devices. We noticed as well that those forged certificates were made after the keys leaked and some were valid for over two years, longer than any public CA may issue. However, these certificates looked like the servers' own default certificates rather than part of an attempt to intercept our connections. They named domains other than the ones being connected to, so they would have failed hostname verification anyway. And in several cases, a server presented the same certificate to connections from many of our locations, which means it came from the server itself rather than from something on a single network path.
Thus while there is no evidence of the weak keys being used to intercept Cloudflare's connections so far, these keys appear to have been used to forge certificates within hours of the weakness becoming public: one of the forged certificates we saw was dated October 20 at 18:19 UTC, less than an hour after Mozilla's bug report was made public. This does not exclude carefully targeted interception. For that we have to rely on the usual indirect signals of system compromise — and so far, we have not seen any such signals.
How many visitors are still vulnerable?
So much about patching Cloudflare, but what about our visitors? We cannot directly test whether a visitor still trusts the weak keys without breaking connections, so we have to do something more indirect. For that we used our challenge pages:
We rolled out an update to send out two probe connections on a fraction of challenge pages: one probe to ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and one to ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com. Initially we installed an eMudhra signed certificate on ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and a regularly signed certificate on ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com as control. Then we record whether these probes succeeded. This allows us to see if visitors that are served a challenge page still trust the weak eMudhra keys.
What did we find? With 50 million probes over the last week, we see this:
Big caveat upfront: by design the traffic to these challenge pages is highly skewed. There are many (unconfirmed) bots in there. Also, only clients that execute JavaScript (like browsers) will send probes.
The jump in the data is due to the following changes—all times are UTC:
- October 23 15:30, we changed our control endpoint to also serve an eMudhra certificate, but this time without signed certificate timestamps (SCTs). There were some differences in acceptance, but not large. We could’ve added a new endpoint, but that would’ve required a slow release of our challenge platform. Changing the endpoint was easier.
- October 23 16:30, our challenge platform rolled back to a previous version because of an unrelated issue. The probes returned October 27 at 10:00.
- October 27 16:37, we noticed we did not send the G3 cross-sign, which not all clients knew about, and added it to both endpoints. We removed SCTs from both.
- October 27 16:49, we switched ca2 to chain up to the AAA Certificate Services root.
- October 27 18:18, we ramped up probes to be included from 1% to 10% of all challenge pages served on non-paying customer zones.
With those caveats out of the way: what do we notice? Up-to-date modern browsers are mostly patched, but bots and old browsers are not. Also embedded browsers, like Android WebView, lag behind patching with 30–40% still accepting. Over the first weekend (with the monitoring gap), we see clear evidence of patching, but afterwards we see little movement.
On October 29 around 18:00 UTC, we released a detection that caught a large influx of bot traffic identifying as Chrome 150-154 on macOS. This can look like patching in the top graph, but it is actually a change in traffic classification: the same user agents show a corresponding increase in acceptance among traffic with bot signals detected in the bottom graph.
Chrome 150-154 on Linux is the notable exception: its acceptance continues to decline, consistent with further patching in that cohort. Given the bot-heavy and changing traffic mix, that evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Otherwise, we still see little movement.
Breaking down by network (ASN) we see:
Across the large networks, more than half of probes still accept the compromised chain, both among traffic with no bot signals detected (top graph) and traffic with bot signals detected (bottom graph). Over the weekend we saw some patching, but afterwards the trend has been flat.
The big caveat still holds: traffic is skewed by (unconfirmed) bots. But bots are also just software that need security updates. And if they’re in any way representative of overall software updates, then the picture is quite dire indeed.
What can you do?
Patch! Dennis Jackson has a great crowdsourced website with instructions. Especially if you’re a developer on macOS, you want to follow these instructions. If you’re a Cloudflare customer, check out last week’s blog post on what needs to be done on your end when using certain products like WARP or Tunnel.
Looking ahead
At Cloudflare, we have a quick-revocation mechanism in place in some products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys. As vulnerabilities are discovered at a faster pace than ever, it is vital that they can be addressed quickly and effectively.

articles.title: The delightfully messy state of Apple gadgets
articles.text:
The iPhone has more screens! The MacBook has a touchscreen! The HomeView does CarPlay apps! For the first time in a long time, Apple is in a period of unabashed gadget experimentation, and while the final results aren’t always perfect, it’s fun to watch the most successful product maker try some new things again. Even when, in this case, “trying” amounts to just slapping a touch panel on a lovely new MacBook Pro — just to see if you might use it.
The delightfully messy state of Apple gadgets
On The Vergecast: MacBooks, Duos, Instagram’s AI problem, and Brendan Carr’s war on the weather.
On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate the merits of a touchscreen laptop, Nilay explains why he is absolutely positively going to buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and David asks, as always, could this have been an iPad?
After that, the hosts discuss Instagram’s foray into long-form content, and Adam Mosseri’s increasingly complicated relationship with AI content. Instagram is at once extraordinarily powerful and under serious threat, and Mosseri’s going to have a hard time making it all work. Finally, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, news about Anthropic’s IPO and Anduril’s laptops, and much more.

articles.title: How to Check and Configure NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage for Your Platform | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage (GDS) accelerates GPU storage access in on-premises and cloud environments. It provides a robust, portable, and efficient data path between NVIDIA GPUs and storage targets to increase bandwidth, minimize latency, and reduce CPU and memory utilization across a broad range of platforms, application frameworks, and workload patterns.
Configuring NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage starts with understanding your environment. Which settings and storage paths are appropriate for your platform and workload? Extensive documentation describes how to configure and troubleshoot supported architectures and storage solutions, but you must navigate this information and optimize your deployment.
The gds-diag tool was developed by the GPUDirect Storage team to simplify optimization and configuration of GPUDirect Storage. gds-diag is a simple, open-source command-line utility that assesses environments, identifies problems, and suggests improvements to help you make the most of your GDS deployment.
It is also bundled with an optional agent skill that adds a natural-language interface and orchestration layer. The skill interprets your intent, selects and invokes the appropriate subcommands, and coordinates multi-step diagnostic workflows. Beyond command selection and routing, the skill extends gds-diag with model-guided reasoning. It can interpret diagnostic results, apply relevant system context, and propose or carry out appropriate remediation.
This post shows you how to get started with gds-diag using either the command-line interface or the agent skill.
Download and installation
To use gds-diag, you need a Linux system with Python 3.8 or newer. GPUDirect Storage requires an NVIDIA datacenter-class GPU and NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit 12.2 or newer, but these are not dependencies of gds-diag itself.
gds-diag is distributed as part of the NVIDIA Magnum IO GitHub repository with no other dependencies to install. Clone the repository on the machine where you plan to run it with git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/MagnumIO.git and select one of the following usage models:
- Command-line tool: This provides a deterministic, minimal-dependency path to diagnose GDS deployments. Go to the gds-diag directory, run gds-diag.py --help, and follow the Command-line usage guidance.
- AI agent: This provides the most intuitive, flexible, interactive, natural-language mechanism to diagnose GDS deployments while still retaining the reliable determinism of the underlying command-line tool. Open the gds-diag directory in your preferred AI coding assistant and follow the Agent skill usage guidance.
| Quick tip: The AI agent mode is recommended if this option is available in your environment. gds-diag is validated with both Claude and Codex, though it may work with other tools as well. | 
|---|
Command-line usage
The gds-diag command-line tool is a single Python script with multiple subcommands to focus on different diagnostic tasks. You can browse available subcommands by running ./gds-diag.py --help.
For more information about a specific subcommand, run ./gds-diag.py <subcommand> --help.
| Quick tip: Not sure where to start? Just run ./gds-diag.py all /path/to/check, and gds-diag will automatically run a complete sequence of diagnostics for that path. This works in bare-metal, virtual machine, and container environments. | 
|---|
Figure 2 groups the available subcommands into four categories.
Choose a diagnostic category based on your stage of deployment or the problem you need to investigate.
- End-to-end checks: Use all to automatically select appropriate diagnostics for your environment and run them in sequence.
- Preparing for installation: Use pre-install to check GPU support and CUDA Toolkit installation. Use support-matrix to view supported storage targets and plan your deployment.
- Validating an installation: Use post-install to check whether GDS is installed correctly and identify blockers. Use config-audit to review configuration files and environment variables that influence GDS behavior.
- Deep diagnostics: Use container-check to assess GDS support in container environments, including containerd, Docker, Enroot, and Kubernetes. Use mount-check to diagnose a specific mount point or directory.
The anatomy of a gds-diag finding
The output of most gds-diag subcommands is presented as a set of findings grouped into sections, as Figure 3 shows.
Each finding and each section has a status badge.
- “FAIL” indicates a hard blocker.
- “WARN” indicates a potential blocker.
- “INFO” communicates notable information.
- “PASS” indicates a nominal finding and is shown only when you use the --verbose option.
Each finding includes an explanation followed by a mitigation plan. gds-diag will not implement the mitigation plan or otherwise modify the system on its own. Its role is to identify problems and optimization opportunities and help you or your administrator make improvements. Multiple sections (and findings within those sections) may be shown.
| Quick tip: You can also emit all diagnostic reports as structured JSON data with the --json command-line option. This could be useful if you plan to ingest findings into another tool or archive them for future reference. | 
|---|
Most subcommands follow the same structure. The gds-diag.py support-matrix command is a notable exception: it emits output in the form of a table with footnotes. This subcommand shows which platform combinations GDS supports.
Use the --static option to present general data (shown in Figure 4) or the --live option to incorporate information from the system as presently configured.
Items marked in green are fully supported, items marked in yellow are supported depending on architectural or configuration caveats, and items marked in red are not supported.
| Quick tip: Most distributed storage vendors elect to present their file systems as nfs or nfs4 at the Linux operating system level, so this row of the support matrix corresponds to a broad range of product support. | 
|---|
Command-line demo
To demonstrate, consider preparing a new or modified GDS configuration file for production deployment. The config-audit subcommand is an ideal choice for this scenario. If called with no arguments, it will audit the current effective configuration, including both static configuration files and dynamic environment variable modifiers. The following example uses the --config option to specify a candidate configuration to review.
The configuration audit reveals a misspelled entry in the configuration file. After you correct the error, config-audit confirms that the configuration is valid and provides additional informational hints.
Agent skill usage
The gds-diag agent skill activates automatically when you open the gds-diag repository using a coding assistant such as Claude or Codex.
| Quick tip: You can explicitly activate gds-diag using the /gds-diag keyword in your coding assistant, but this isn’t strictly necessary. It will automatically choose it as the appropriate skill to use if you ask natural language questions about GDS. | 
|---|
The skill does not attempt to duplicate deterministic checks that are already provided by the gds-diag command-line tool. Instead, its primary role is to aid in routing between gds-diag subcommands and interpreting their output. The following are a few examples of queries you could pose using the skill:
- Is this system eligible to use GDS?
- Is it available for /mnt/data?
- How do I configure GDS optimally to access /mnt/data?
- What configuration files are being used by GDS?
- Do any configuration parameters need to be updated?
- Which NVMe device has the best locality to GPU3?
Agents are a capability multiplier for gds-diag; you can ask follow-up questions or even ask the agent to implement mitigations on your behalf.
Agent skill demo
Figure 6 shows how to combine the gds-diag agent skill with a model’s inherent reasoning to diagnose a container configuration problem. This example uses Anthropic Claude Code CLI.
In this case, the agent inspects the shell script used to launch the container and determines the best gds-diag tool to use to investigate the problem. It then offers the option to modify the script in response to its findings and confirms the solution. Note that the coding assistant will honor your local settings and site policies to determine which actions require confirmation.
Get started
Use gds-diag as your first diagnostic tool when investigating GPUDirect Storage configuration and optimization. Its modular design provides a foundation for additional diagnostics, such as checks for network transports, object storage systems, and application frameworks.
Have a diagnostic check or file system you would like to contribute? Community contributions are welcome and strongly encouraged. Both the source code and the agent skill are published under open-source licenses (Apache 2.0 and Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International). See the contributor guidelines to get started.

articles.title: Des moddeurs transforment le Lego PlayStation en véritable console capable de faire tourner les jeux PS1
articles.text:
Le très beau set Lego PlayStation permet de construire la première console de Sony en pas moins de 1 911 pièces (pour pas moins de 159,99 €). Cette réplique destinée avant tout aux collectionneurs reprend le design de la PS1 originale et s’accompagne de deux petits dioramas cachés qui rendent hommage à Gran Turismo et Ape Escape.
Malgré son réalisme et tout l’amour que l’on porte à la première console de Sony, le set reste un objet décoratif qui prend la poussière. Substance Labs veut changer ça avec le projet BrickStation. Cette équipe suisse est déjà derrière BrickBoy, un kit non officiel qui rend la Game Boy Lego jouable et qui a récolté plus d’un million d’euros sur Kickstarter fin 2025. Cette fois, les créateurs s’attaquent à la console de salon de Sony avec la même idée : intégrer l’électronique nécessaire dans le Lego, sans le dénaturer.
Thomas Bertani, inventeur et responsable technique de l’équipe, en a détaillé le fonctionnement ce vendredi 30 octobre 2026 auprès du site spécialisé Time Extension. L’équipe a commencé à travailler à partir des fuites sur le set, avant même sa sortie.
La BrickStation prend la place du petit module latéral consacré à Ape Escape dans le Lego original. Ce boîtier fait tourner les jeux PS1 par émulation, c’est-à-dire en imitant la console par logiciel. La console en briques peut alors se brancher à un téléviseur via HDMI, tandis que les jeux sont chargés depuis une carte microSD. Les manettes USB et Bluetooth sont prises en charge, tout comme les cartes mémoire originales de la PlayStation 1. Il devient ainsi possible de lancer un jeu PS1 et de retrouver ses anciennes sauvegardes.
Le Lego PlayStation est maintenant capable de lancer des jeux PS1
Les concepteurs ont également poussé le souci du détail assez loin. Le bouton Power du Lego permet réellement d’allumer la console en briques, tandis qu’un petit haut-parleur et un moteur reproduisent le bruit et les vibrations du lecteur CD au démarrage.
BrickStation ne dispose bien sûr pas d’un lecteur CD fonctionnel. Pour jouer à ses anciens jeux PS1, il faudra donc passer par un lecteur CD externe, afin de copier les données des disques originaux sous forme de fichiers à transférer sur la carte microSD de la console Lego, pour les lancer via l’émulateur intégré.
Vous voilà avec une PS1 en briques qui fonctionne, sans rien modifier au set. Il suffit de remettre le module Ape Escape d’origine pour retrouver le Lego tel qu’il a été conçu. Petit détail amusant, le kit BrickStation ajoute exactement 83 pièces Lego, dont une carte mémoire d’exposition. Le total passe ainsi à 1 994 pièces, soit l’année de lancement de la première PlayStation au Japon.
BrickStation est encore au stade du prototype et sa campagne Kickstarter est en préparation. Substance Labs n’a annoncé ni le prix ni la date de lancement. Vous pouvez vous inscrire sur la page de prélancement du projet pour être averti de son ouverture.

articles.title: Too much code, too little shipped: Why AI needs a software factory
articles.text:
Too much code, too little shipped: Why AI needs a software factory
Can AI run the entire software show? At TechSparks 2026, ForgeCode CEO Tushar Mathur explained how AI agents can automate software development while engineers focus on quality and results.
AI can generate code faster than ever, but getting it tested and reviewed and into production is a different challenge.
Engineering teams are increasingly using AI agents to write code, fix bugs, and build features. But faster coding does not necessarily mean faster software delivery.
As code generation accelerates, reviews pile up, testing slows down, and teams struggle to coordinate the growing volume of changes.
At TechSparks 2026, Tushar Mathur, CEO of Forge Code, explored this problem in his session, Anatomy of a software factory. He explained how AI-native engineering organisations can move beyond automating individual coding tasks to building systems that manage the entire software development lifecycle.
“Just because code is becoming easy and faster to generate doesn't mean your overall SDLC becomes faster,” Mathur said.
From coding assistants to software factories
The traditional software development process focused heavily on writing code efficiently. Teams spent time defining requirements, preparing specifications and designing architecture to reduce the effort needed during implementation, he said.
With AI taking over more coding work, the bottlenecks are moving elsewhere.
Mathur described how organisations can end up with large volumes of pull requests awaiting review, longer testing cycles and more bugs than existing regression suites can catch.
Hiring more engineers or running more AI agents is not necessarily the answer. More people can increase coordination costs, while adding agents without effective feedback loops can generate code that overwhelms the systems responsible for reviewing and testing it.
“The reason why this happens is because there's no signal,” Mathur said, explaining why simply connecting automated steps does not create an effective software factory.
An assembly line that learns
Mathur presented Forge Code as a software factory that coordinates AI agents across the development lifecycle. The process begins with triaging requests, creating specifications and implementing features.
Agents then verify changes before they move towards deployment, with human engineers stepping in when decisions or feedback are needed.
The system also monitors production, using the resulting insights to inform future tasks. This creates a feedback loop in which the factory can identify problems, improve its workflows and generate new work from what it learns.
Mathur said Forge Code was running around 100 agents in the background during his presentation, working on features, compatibility and bug detection.
He outlined six principles for an effective software factory: autonomous operation, scalability, cost efficiency, measurability, self-improvement and alignment with business goals.
The last principle is particularly important.
Instead of treating every request as a coding task, the factory should work towards outcomes such as improving customer retention or meeting compliance requirements. Teams can then prioritise features based on the value they deliver.
Engineers become supervisors
In this model, engineers spend less time directing every task and more time monitoring outcomes, reviewing signals and improving the system. Business leaders can also contribute requests and priorities directly, allowing the factory to translate organisational goals into a development backlog.
Writing code faster is great. Shipping better software is the real win.
For engineering teams, the trick is turning AI-powered speed into reliable products, measurable gains and business results.

articles.title: Excuses, démentis, IA et open source : Proton change de ton face à la polémique — Frandroid
articles.text:
Après Andy Yen, son CEO, c’est au tour de l’entreprise de s’exprimer. Dans un message publié ce vendredi 30 octobre sur X par son compte officiel @ProtonPrivacy, l’entreprise suisse reconnaît ne pas avoir été à la hauteur de ce qu’on attend d’elle et présente ses excuses. La veille, Andy Yen s’était contenté d’expliquer sur Reddit que ses propos avaient été sortis de leur contexte, sans démentir avoir parlé de « mentalité de loser ». Proton reprend la main sur la communication et passe donc d’une défense improvisée, signée par son patron, à une réponse d’entreprise aux accusations.
Pour rappel, ces accusations viennent de l’enquête de 404 Media publiée ce jeudi 29 octobre. Le média américain s’appuie sur huit salariés et un ancien employé, des conversations Slack, des enregistrements de réunions et un manifeste sur l’IA rédigé par le directeur technique, Bart Butler. Il affirmait notamment que Proton avait installé sur les ordinateurs de ses équipes un logiciel qui mesure la quantité de code écrite par l’IA. Le même Bart Butler aurait annoncé en réunion que l’IA avait écrit 90 % du code de Proton en octobre. Entre-temps, de nombreux utilisateurs ont annoncé sur les réseaux sociaux qu’ils résiliaient leur abonnement payant.
Pour Proton, tout part d’un malentendu
Concernant le logiciel de suivi, Proton dément et parle d’une incompréhension du fonctionnement de ses outils de MDM (Mobile Device Management). Les logiciels de gestion des appareils permettent au service informatique de piloter à distance les ordinateurs des salariés, par exemple pour installer des mises à jour, imposer le chiffrement du disque ou effacer une machine volée. Ils ont donc un accès large au poste de travail, ce qui peut inquiéter un salarié qui les voit tourner. L’entreprise affirme aussi avoir ajouté des étapes de revue de sécurité au cours de l’année écoulée. Elle cherche ainsi à se protéger des IA hostiles qui passent au crible son code, public puisque ses applications sont open source.
Proton indique qu’il ne procédera pas à de nouveaux entretiens avec le personne sur l’utilisation de l’IA et nie toute suppression de poste liée à ces entretiens. Lors de la réunion où l’entreprise a annoncé l’annulation de ces entretien, le CEO y aurait reconnu « un échec de communication » de sa part. Pourtant, des salariés interrogés par 404 Media affirment que ce que ces entretiens devaient mesurer sera intégré aux évaluations de performance.
Lumo en open source, une promesse déjà entendue
Proton s’engage enfin à publier en open source plusieurs outils internes, dont des versions plus avancées de Lumo, son assistant IA, jamais rendues publiques. L’entreprise promet aussi de publier ses méthodes de revue de code et de sécurité, ainsi que ses règles internes d’usage de l’IA.
Nous publierons également la manière dont les revues de code et les revues de sécurité sont réalisées chez Proton, et détaillerons nos politiques sur l’IA, y compris les endroits où l’IA est autorisée, et là où elle ne l’est pas, ainsi que nos justifications. Au lieu de pouvoir seulement voir le code open source final que nous produisons pour vérifier la sécurité, vous pourrez également évaluer comment ce code a été produit.
Sur Lumo, pourtant, le précédent appelle à la prudence. Au lancement de l’assistant, en juillet 2025, Proton le présentait déjà comme entièrement open source. Le European Open Source AI Index, un projet qui évalue l’ouverture réelle des IA, l’avait alors qualifié d’assistant « ouvert » le moins ouvert de sa base. Seul le code des applications mobile et web était public. Proton n’avait publié ni le prompt système de Lumo, ni le mécanisme qui choisit quel modèle répond à chaque question.

articles.title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
articles.text:
While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens.
Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI.
Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on.
The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies.
“As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.”
Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight
Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold.
At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI, a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther, a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS.
Nexus, a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument.
Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours.
Science Fact, Not Fiction
The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula.
Next, the team is evaluating open models including NVIDIA Nemotron for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon.
Learn more about NVIDIA AI for science.

articles.title: Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available
articles.text:
Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available
Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection. Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (WAF), caching, bot management, and Workers work just as they do for public origins.
In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin.
Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.
What is generally available today
During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group.
Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins:
- WAF and managed rules
- Bot management
- Rate limiting
- Caching
- Transform and rewrite rules
- Workers
Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Dedicated CDN Egress IPs aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing. See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations.
Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN, no connector software on the origin is required. With Cloudflare Mesh, a connector runs within your private network and can serve multiple origins.
How it works
Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually.
The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network.
The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error.
What the API looks like
For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record.
POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records
{
 "type": "A",
 "name": "app.example.com",
 "content": "10.0.0.50",
 "ttl": 300,
 "proxied": true,
 "private_routing": true
}
Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path:
{
 "zone_name": "example.com",
 "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"],
 "private_routing": true
}
The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec, GRE, Cloudflare Tunnel, CNI, or Cloudflare Mesh.
The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail.
Get started
Before you begin, you’ll need:
- The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on.
- Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh.
- Unified Routing enabled on your account, unless you connect over Cloudflare Tunnel (Tunnel doesn't need it). New and existing accounts can upgrade through their account team.
- If you connect over Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, configure a return route for Cloudflare’s source ranges: 100.64.0.0/12 for IPv4 and 2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64 for IPv6. Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.
Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.
One note from the beta: if requests time out and nothing arrives at the origin, check the return route first. A missing route for Cloudflare’s source range was the most common setup failure we saw.
Once enabled, follow our developer documentation, which walks through the full setup.
What comes next
Today’s release covers public traffic reaching private origins. Next, we’re working on private-to-private traffic: users, services, and AI agents on private networks reaching applications on other private networks through Cloudflare’s application services.
Engineering work is underway, and we’re targeting a closed beta in early 2027. If you’d like to participate, talk to your account team.
The goal is to give private applications the same protections and controls as public applications. An employee opening wiki.company.internal, for example, could benefit from WAF, rate limiting, and bot management. Service-to-service traffic between clouds and data centers could use those controls too, even when neither side touches the public Internet.
For now, today’s release brings the WAF, caching, bot management, and Workers you use for public applications to private origins over connectivity you already operate.
Questions or feedback? Join the conversation in our community forums or reach out to your account team.

articles.title: Hinter Pluto entdeckt: Algorithmus findet neuen Zwergplaneten
articles.text:
Hinter Pluto entdeckt: Algorithmus findet neuen Zwergplaneten
Im Juni 2025 lieferte das Vera-C.-Rubin-Observatorium in Chile erste Aufnahmen des Weltalls. In den kommenden zehn Jahren soll das riesige Spiegelteleskop den südlichen Himmel systematisch erfassen und dabei erdnahe Asteroiden, Zwergplaneten oder andere Himmelsobjekte sowie -ereignisse wie Supernovae kartieren. Außerdem erhoffen sich die Astronom:innen Hinweise auf Dunkle Energie und Dunkle Materie.
2026 ED138 kreist jenseits von Pluto
Jetzt haben der Astrophysiker Matthew Holman vom Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics und der Astronom Mario Jurić von der University of Washington einen vielversprechenden Zwergplaneten-Kandidaten aufgespürt. Der jenseits von Pluto kreisende eisige Himmelskörper firmiert derzeit unter dem Namen 2026 ED138.
Wie es in einer entsprechenden Mitteilung heißt, handelt es sich bei 2026 ED138 um einen der größten Zwergplaneten-Kandidaten im transneptunischen Bereich. Er soll einen Durchmesser von 600 bis 1.500 Kilometern haben. Zur Einordnung: Pluto ist knapp 2.400 Kilometer groß. Sollte 2026 ED138 als Zwergplanet bestätigt werden, wäre er neben Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea und Makemake erst der sechste seiner Art.
Dabei war es gar nicht so einfach, den möglichen Zwergplaneten ausfindig zu machen. Holman ließ dabei einen eigens entwickelten Algorithmus über Aufnahmen des Rubin-Observatoriums schauen. Der Algorithmus sichtet dabei unterschiedliche Aufnahmen von Milliarden von Objekten, vergleicht diese und ihre möglichen Bewegungen und identifiziert dann jene, die sich tatsächlich bewegt haben.
Zwergplaneten-Kandidat schon 2016 zu sehen
Mit dieser Methode stieß Holman schließlich auf 2026 ED138, da das Objekt trotz seiner großen Entfernung eine große Helligkeit aufwies. Daher war klar, dass es sich um einen ungewöhnlich großen Himmelskörper handeln musste. Um einen Fehler auszuschließen, überprüfte Holmans Kollege Jurić weitere Aufnahmen. Dabei entdeckte er den Zwergplaneten-Kandidaten in weiteren Daten, darunter Aufnahmen aus dem Jahr 2016.
Aktuell befindet sich 2026 ED138 rund 46 astronomische Einheiten von der Sonne entfernt. Zum Vergleich: Pluto kreist im Abstand von 40 astronomischen Einheiten um die Sonne. Ein Objekt von der Größe des möglichen neuen Zwergplaneten zu finden, sei etwas, das „wahrscheinlich nur einmal in einer Generation“ vorkommt, so Jurić.

articles.title: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
articles.text:
During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company’s still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions.
Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
RJ Scaringe spent nearly half of Rivian’s earnings call hyping self-driving tech. But taking on Tesla’s FSD with custom chips and pricey lidar is an enormous gamble while the mass-market R2 is still scaling up.
But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027. Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028. In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player.
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator,” Derek Mulvey, VP for finance, said during the call.
Success is not guaranteed. Tesla has a huge head start with its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in over 1.7 million active customer cars. But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.)
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.”
— Derek Mulvey
But it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider. That leaves the company in the middle of a difficult balancing act: launching an ambitious, mass-market electric vehicle while simultaneously reinventing itself as a full-stack autonomous driving powerhouse.
Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed. During the call, Scaringe revealed that he has been using the new point-to-point driving system in his own commute to the office every day, calling it “a wonderful” experience. He continued:
So, our view is that that is going to become a big driver of demand. And I think it’s unclear how quickly the whole — you know, the whole US market and the whole automotive market — starts to shift to really wanting this, and this being a major purchase criterion. But certainly, we’re at the front end of an inflection point where it’s more and more people exposed to what this could do… We do think it’s a really big driver, in the long term, for market share for us.
But Scaringe was cagey about other details. When asked about Rivian’s take rate for its Autonomy Plus package — in other words, what percentage of Rivian buyers who purchase or subscribe to the software out of the total customer base — the chief executive declined to share the exact number. “The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.”
Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported. Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year. And Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin.
Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems. On the call, the company pointed out that computer chips, memory, and electronics are getting pricier. It also warned that adding two processors and costly lidar sensors to some R2 models could eat into the profits it hoped to make by building the vehicle in large numbers.
The point-to-point system will face its own hurdles, including edge cases and the complexities of urban driving. A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD. And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong.
To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo. Self-driving tech could help Rivian post big, software-company-style profits, but paying for expensive AI development while also trying to build the R2 at scale makes the next year or two its riskiest period ever.
